docs.title: Hybernate
docs.text:
Intelligent Kubernetes workload lifecycle management.

Hybernate is a Kubernetes operator that predicts your workload demand using Holt-Winters forecasting and pauses and resumes workloads to cut infrastructure costs. It never deletes a workload or its data: the most it does is scale one to zero, and a request wakes it. It pauses a workload once nothing has used it for a configurable time, and supports dry run mode so you can observe its recommendations and build confidence before letting it drive actions.

docs.title: Why Hybernate?
docs.text:
Most Kubernetes clusters run workloads 24/7, even when no one is using them. Dev environments sit idle overnight. Staging clusters burn resources on weekends.

Hybernate fixes this by learning your workload patterns and acting on them:

  • Idle workloads get paused. They are scaled to zero when no one is using them and resumed automatically when demand returns.

docs.title: Demand Forecasting
docs.text: A Holt-Winters double seasonal model learns daily and weekly traffic patterns for each workload, starting from up to four weeks of its history in Prometheus. Its first week sets what it expects of each hour of the week; from the second it scores its predictions, and acts on them only when they're accurate enough: eager, balanced or cautious says how accurate. If traffic patterns shift, a built-in anomaly detector notices the drift, demotes the model's confidence, and re-learns from the new baseline, while a one-off day, such as a holiday, isn't learned as a pattern.

docs.title: Activity Clock
docs.text: Hybernate records the last time each workload was in use: CPU above a threshold, a deploy, an activity annotation from your own tooling, or a Prometheus query such as request rate. Once nothing has been active for idleAfter, it pauses the workload. There's no learning period.

docs.title: Safe by Default
docs.text: Hybernate never pauses a workload it can't measure, and a confident forecast can hold off a pause. Enable dryRun mode to see what Hybernate would do without it ever pausing anything. A paused workload scaled up by anyone else is treated as woken, and a GitOps tool undoing a pause is reported with the fix, not fought.

docs.title: Cost Tracking
docs.text: Track what each workload costs, what pausing it frees, and how much of that came off the bill as nodes scaled down, measured from the spare capacity left on each node pool. Freed capacity becomes money only once a node autoscaler removes nodes; kubectl hybernate nodes shows what keeps them, and Node Pools for Real Savings how to let them go.

docs.title: Label Opt-In
docs.text: Label a workload or namespace hybernate.io/managed: "true" and Hybernate manages it, with its settings as annotations. Both live in the manifests or Helm values you already keep in Git, so Argo CD and Flux work as they do today.

docs.title: Scan Before You Install
docs.text: kubectl hybernate scan shows which workloads in a cluster are idle right now and what they cost while running, with nothing installed in the cluster.

docs.title: Full Observability
docs.text: Prometheus metrics for operator health, lifecycle transitions, wakes on request, and prediction confidence, with alerting rules included.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    label["Deployment, StatefulSet, or namespace<br/>labelled hybernate.io/managed: "true""] --> mw["ManagedWorkload<br/>settings from annotations"]
    mw --> running["Running<br/>activity clock: CPU, deploys,<br/>activity annotations, Prometheus"]
    running -- "no activity for idleAfter,<br/>and no forecast of demand" --> paused["Paused<br/>scaled to zero; Services<br/>routed to the doorman"]
    paused -- "a request, an activity annotation,<br/>or autoResume ahead of demand" --> resuming["Resuming<br/>replicas restored,<br/>dependencies woken"]
    resuming -- "pods Ready;<br/>held requests passed through" --> running

docs.title: Quick Example
docs.text:
deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-api
  namespace: dev
  labels:
    hybernate.io/managed: "true"
  annotations:
    hybernate.io/dry-run: "true"
    hybernate.io/idle-after: "1h"

Hybernate watches my-api and records each time it's active: CPU above 10% of its requests, a deploy, or an activity annotation, and, with a Prometheus query, its request rate. In dry-run it only measures; once you run kubectl hybernate enable my-api -n dev, it pauses the Deployment after an hour with no activity, and wakes it when a request reaches its Service.

For every setting, see Opting In. For settings annotations don't cover, write a ManagedWorkload yourself.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: Ready to try it? Head to the Installation guide, then follow the Quickstart to manage your first workload in under 5 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Go 1.26+ (go.mod pins the toolchain)
  • Docker (make test-alerts runs promtool in a container, so you don't need it installed)
  • kubectl
  • Kind (for the end-to-end and Helm tests)
  • Helm, only for make check-chart and make test-alerts

make downloads controller-gen, kustomize, setup-envtest and golangci-lint into bin/ as it needs them.

docs.title: Clone and Build
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/okedeji/hybernate.git
cd hybernate
make build

docs.title: Run Tests
docs.text:
# Unit and integration tests (uses envtest for the K8s API)
make test

# Lint
make lint

# E2E tests: creates a Kind cluster, runs, and deletes it (KIND_NODE_IMAGE picks the Kubernetes version)
make test-e2e

# Install the Helm chart into Kind, and pause and wake a workload through the doorman
make test-helm-smoke

docs.title: Run Locally
docs.text:
# Install CRDs into your current cluster
make install

# Run the operator locally (outside the cluster)
make run

docs.title: Build the kubectl Plugin
docs.text:
make build-plugin
# Binary at bin/kubectl-hybernate

docs.title: Code Standards
docs.text:
Key coding standards:

  • No comments that restate what the code does. Comments are for why, not what.
  • Wrap errors with context: fmt.Errorf("doing X: %w", err)
  • Return early on errors. Happy path flows straight down.
  • Accept interfaces, return structs. Define interfaces at the point of consumption.
  • Test behavior, not implementation. Table-driven tests with testify.

docs.title: Commit Conventions
docs.text:
Use Conventional Commits:

feat(idle): add idle detection with detector and webhook signal
fix(idle): reset idle timer on active signal
refactor(forecast): extract confidence scoring into separate type
chore(crd): regenerate CRD manifests
docs(guides): add Prometheus signals guide
test(policy): add table tests for scale constraints

One logical change per commit. Generated code gets its own commit.

docs.title: Pull Requests
docs.text:
1. Fork the repository
  2. Create a feature branch from main
  3. Make your changes with tests
  4. Run make lint test and ensure everything passes
  5. Open a PR with a clear description of what and why

docs.title: PR Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Tests pass (make test)
  • [ ] Lint passes (make lint)
  • [ ] CRD manifests regenerated if types changed (make manifests), and generated code is current (make verify-generated)
  • [ ] DeepCopy regenerated if types changed (make generate)
  • [ ] The chart still lints and renders, with RBAC matching config/rbac (make check-chart), if you changed it or RBAC
  • [ ] Alert rules still pass their tests (make test-alerts), if you changed them
  • [ ] Documentation updated if user-facing behavior changed

CI also runs the end-to-end tests on Kubernetes 1.30 and 1.37, the Helm smoke test, and make vulncheck.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text: The docs are built with mkdocs: pip install --require-hashes -r docs/requirements.txt, then mkdocs serve. make test creates every ManagedWorkload shown in a yaml block in README.md and docs/, and in config/samples/, against the real CRD, so a doc example that doesn't validate fails the build. A partial one, a spec: block or spec fields such as dependsOn on their own, is wrapped into a whole ManagedWorkload first; title it managedworkload.yaml or leave it untitled, since a block titled as another file, such as application.yaml, isn't read as one. Helm values blocks, titled hybernate-values.yaml, values.yaml or values-<name>.yaml, or untitled with only the chart's keys, are checked against charts/hybernate/values.schema.json, and every value they set must be one the chart has. Put <!-- snippet --> on the line before a block that's deliberately partial and shouldn't be checked. Links to https://okedeji.io/hybernate in the code must point at a page in docs/.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text:
A release is a tag on main, vX.Y.Z. make release VERSION=X.Y.Z bumps the chart's version and appVersion, the kustomize image, and the install and verify commands and download links in the docs (the pages in the Makefile's VERSIONED_DOCS), dates the version's section of CHANGELOG.md, commits that, and tags it. Pushing the tag starts the release workflow:

  1. Checks the chart, the kustomize image, the docs and the dated changelog name the tag's version, and that no page's install link is to releases/latest or another release (make verify-version), then runs every check a pull request does, including Trivy on the image.
  2. Builds the plugin archives, the krew manifest, install.yaml and the chart; pushes the image by digest, untagged, and signs it and attaches its SBOMs and provenance; and drafts the GitHub release with every file, its signed checksums, and the changelog section, with a link to the release's docs, as its notes.
  3. Tags the image, pushes and signs the chart, tags the image latest, and publishes the GitHub release, which moves releases/latest.
  4. Writes the Homebrew formula from the published archives and pushes it to the tap: for a release, and for a release candidate until the first stable release.

Once the workflow succeeds, the docs workflow publishes the tag's docs, as the docs site describes.

Until step 3 nothing users install has changed, so a run that fails earlier can be run again: it replaces its draft. One that fails in step 3 can be too.

Rehearse a release with a release candidate first. A tag with a hyphen, such as v0.2.0-rc.1, runs the whole workflow as a pre-release: everything is published but latest, so the image, the chart and the GitHub release exist only for those who ask for that version, and its docs are published under next, with a banner saying it's a release candidate. Its notes are its version's changelog section, which needn't be dated yet. From a throwaway branch, so main keeps the release's version:

git switch -c rehearse-v0.2.0-rc.1 main
make release VERSION=0.2.0-rc.1
git push origin v0.2.0-rc.1

Once it succeeds, install the release candidate as the docs describe, with --version 0.2.0-rc.1, and check its signatures with the commands in Security. Then release from main:

git switch main
make release VERSION=0.2.0
git push origin main v0.2.0

docs.title: The Homebrew tap
docs.text:
brew install okedeji/tap/kubectl-hybernate installs the plugin from okedeji/homebrew-tap. For each release, the release workflow's last job writes the tap's Formula/kubectl-hybernate.rb with hack/brewformula, from the published macOS and Linux archives, and commits it as kubectl-hybernate X.Y.Z. A release candidate is brewed only while the tap has no stable release, so people trying it before 0.2.0 can install it with Homebrew; once a stable release is there, a release candidate never replaces it, since brew install and brew upgrade take whatever the formula is.

It pushes with the HOMEBREW_TAP_TOKEN secret: a fine-grained personal access token whose only permission is Contents read and write on okedeji/homebrew-tap. Without the secret, or if the push fails, the job warns and the tap stays on the last release, while the release, and its docs, go ahead; once the token is fixed, re-run the job. Fine-grained tokens expire, so renew it before its expiry date.

To check a change to the formula, render it from a release's archives and audit and install it from a local tap:

gh release download v0.2.0 -R okedeji/hybernate -D /tmp/release \
  -p 'kubectl-hybernate-darwin-*.tar.gz' -p 'kubectl-hybernate-linux-*.tar.gz'
go run ./hack/brewformula -tag v0.2.0 -dir /tmp/release > kubectl-hybernate.rb
brew tap-new hybernate/local --no-git
cp kubectl-hybernate.rb "$(brew --repository hybernate/local)/Formula/"
brew audit --strict --online --formula hybernate/local/kubectl-hybernate
brew install hybernate/local/kubectl-hybernate
brew test hybernate/local/kubectl-hybernate
brew uninstall hybernate/local/kubectl-hybernate
brew untap hybernate/local

docs.title: Krew
docs.text:
Each release carries a krew manifest, krew-hybernate.yaml, which the release workflow writes with hack/krew-manifest.sh and checks with krew's validate-krew-manifest. Until the plugin is in krew-index, the docs install it from that manifest's URL.

Once 0.2.0 is released, submit the plugin to krew-index, a pull request to that repository:

  1. Check the release's manifest installs on every platform. This needs krew installed:

    gh release download v0.2.0 -R okedeji/hybernate -p krew-hybernate.yaml
go install sigs.k8s.io/krew/cmd/validate-krew-manifest@v0.5.0
validate-krew-manifest -manifest krew-hybernate.yaml

  2. Fork kubernetes-sigs/krew-index, add the manifest as plugins/hybernate.yaml, and open a pull request. Krew's maintainers review a new plugin by hand, against their naming guide and best practices.

  3. Once it's merged, change the README's and the plugin page's Krew instructions to kubectl krew install hybernate, without a manifest URL.

For each later release, open a pull request to krew-index that sets plugins/hybernate.yaml's version, uris and sha256s to those in the release's krew-hybernate.yaml. One that changes only those is tested and merged automatically. krew-release-bot can open it from the release workflow.

docs.title: The docs site
docs.text:
The site keeps a version of the docs for each minor release, 0.2, 0.3 and so on, each built from its newest patch's tag, so the install commands on every page name the release that page documents. The docs workflow publishes them once the release workflow succeeds, with mike, to the gh-pages branch, which GitHub Pages serves:

  • A release's docs go to its minor version, and to latest when it's the newest release. The site's root sends readers to latest, or to next until there's a release.
  • A release candidate's docs go to next, with a banner saying they're for a release candidate. The release it rehearses removes next.
  • A link without a version, such as https://okedeji.io/hybernate/guides/gitops/, which the operator and the plugin print, goes to the same page in the version the root sends readers to, through the 404.html at the branch's root.

hack/docsite decides what a tag publishes, and never replaces a version's docs with an older release's. To republish a release's docs, run the docs workflow by hand with its tag. To see what a tag would publish, run it with -dry-run from a checkout with the docs requirements installed and the gh-pages branch fetched from origin:

go run ./hack/docsite -tag v0.2.0 -dry-run

mkdocs serve previews the docs you're editing, without versions; mike serve serves the versions on your local gh-pages.

The site has no domain of its own: okedeji.io belongs to the owner's user site, okedeji/okedeji.github.io, and GitHub serves this repository's Pages under it, at /hybernate/. So gh-pages has no CNAME file, and mustn't get one: it would claim okedeji.io for this repository.

Moving the site from the old Actions deployment to gh-pages takes two settings, once the docs workflow has published the first release or release candidate since versioning, which creates the branch:

  1. Settings, Environments, github-pages: add gh-pages to the deployment branches. Only main is allowed today, and GitHub's own Pages workflow deploys from the branch it serves.
  2. Settings, Pages, Build and deployment: set the source to Deploy from a branch, branch gh-pages, folder / (root).

Until then the old site stays as it is. Tags from before versioning can't be published this way: their docs have no mike configuration.

docs.title: Regenerating Generated Code
docs.text:
After changing CRD types in api/v1alpha1/:

make generate   # DeepCopy methods
make manifests  # CRD YAML, RBAC

Commit generated code separately: chore(crd): regenerate CRD manifests

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Hybernate is a Kubernetes operator built on controller-runtime. It runs as one binary inside your cluster, in two Deployments: the operator, which manages workloads through two kinds of reconciliation loop, and the doorman, which holds requests to paused workloads and wakes them.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph operator["Operator Deployment"]
        optin["Opt-in reconcilers<br/>Deployments, StatefulSets"]
        mwr["ManagedWorkload reconciler<br/>activity clock, pause and resume,<br/>dependencies, cost"]
        forecast["Forecast engine<br/>one per workload"]
        optin --> mwr
        mwr --- forecast
    end
    subgraph doorman["Doorman Deployment"]
        door["Holds requests to paused workloads,<br/>wakes them, passes requests through"]
    end
    clients["Clients, ingress controllers,<br/>load balancers"] -- "Service of a paused workload" --> door
    door -- "hybernate.io/last-request" --> api
    mwr --> api["Kubernetes API server"]
    mwr --> ms["metrics-server"]
    mwr -.-> prom["Prometheus<br/>optional"]

docs.title: ManagedWorkload Reconciler
docs.text:
The primary reconciler. Watches ManagedWorkload CRs and drives each workload through its lifecycle. On every reconcile it:

  1. Checks for another ManagedWorkload managing the same target
  2. Checks that the target Deployment or StatefulSet exists and isn't labelled hybernate.io/ignore; an ignored one is let go of, scaled back up first if it's paused
  3. Lets go of a workload whose namespace is protected, that is Hybernate's own operator or doorman, or that is a StatefulSet deleting its PVCs on scale-down, scaled back up first if it's paused
  4. Wakes a paused workload scaled up outside Hybernate
  5. Reports the HPA or KEDA ScaledObject that scales the workload
  6. Learns the workload's dependencies from its environment, and from the requests that woke it
  7. Routes a paused workload's Services to the doorman, or stops routing them
  8. Finishes a pause or resume an earlier reconcile started, taking a pause up again from the target's hybernate.io/paused-from if status lost it, and wakes a paused workload put in dry-run
  9. Leaves alone a target scaled to zero outside Hybernate
  10. Acts on a pause someone asked for with kubectl hybernate pause
  11. Runs the activity clock and the forecast: records activity, and pauses once there has been none for idleAfter and no demand is forecast, or sooner with pauseEarly when the forecast expects quiet hours; for a paused workload, checks whether anything, or autoResume, asks it to wake
  12. Adds up what dry-run held back, accumulates cost, and writes status

Each ManagedWorkload gets its own forecast engine, kept in memory and saved to the ManagedWorkload's status.prediction.state as it learns each hour, so it survives operator restarts and leader changes. Every reconcile is bounded by a 2-minute timeout, and --max-concurrent-reconciles (8 by default) workloads are reconciled at once, so one slow metrics or Prometheus query doesn't hold up another workload's wake. Reconciles wait in one queue ordered by priority: what wakes a workload (a request the doorman holds, an activity or pause annotation, a scale-up from zero) and a resume under way come first, then other changes, and the periodic checks of awake and paused workloads last, so a wake isn't queued behind every workload's metrics and Prometheus checks.

docs.title: Opt-In Reconcilers
docs.text: One for Deployments and one for StatefulSets. Each watches its workloads, their namespaces, and the ManagedWorkloads created from them. When a workload or its namespace is labelled hybernate.io/managed: "true", it creates a ManagedWorkload named after the workload (or <name>-<kind> when that name is taken) and owned by it, with a spec built from the workload's annotations, then its namespace's, then the cluster-wide defaults. It keeps the fields the annotations set in step with them, leaves the rest as you set them, and deletes the ManagedWorkload when the label goes. A ManagedWorkload someone wrote for the same workload always wins.

docs.title: Internal Packages
docs.text: Package Responsibility internal/controller The ManagedWorkload and opt-in reconcilers internal/forecast Holt-Winters model, phase lifecycle, confidence scoring, anomaly detection internal/signal Prometheus PromQL activity queries internal/autoscaler Finds a workload's HPA or KEDA ScaledObject, and holds a KEDA one at zero while it's paused internal/gitops Tells from field managers whether a GitOps tool (Argo CD, Flux, Fleet, kapp or Kluctl) sets a workload's replicas, and how to tell it to leave them internal/lifecycle Pause and resume, through the scale subresource internal/discovery The cluster scan behind kubectl hybernate scan internal/doorman Holds requests to a paused workload's Service and wakes it internal/cost Cost rates, node list prices, and monthly projection internal/metrics Prometheus metric definitions and K8s Metrics API reader

docs.title: External Dependencies
docs.text:
Hybernate reads from three external systems:

  • Kubernetes API Server: for scaling Deployments and StatefulSets, routing Services' EndpointSlices to the doorman, and reading what pricing and dependencies need: pods, PVCs, nodes' labels, ConfigMaps, HPAs and KEDA ScaledObjects
  • Metrics Server: for pod CPU usage (required)
  • Prometheus: for PromQL activity queries (optional)

docs.title: Freed and Saved
docs.text:
Hybernate operates at the workload layer. It does not manage nodes directly. When Hybernate pauses or scales down a workload, it frees CPU and memory on the node. A cluster autoscaler (Cluster Autoscaler, Karpenter, or a managed equivalent) is responsible for detecting underutilized nodes and removing them, and only then does what pausing freed come off the bill. Hybernate measures how much of what it freed has, as saved: every 5 minutes, the leader sets what it holds paused in each node pool against the spare capacity of the pool's nodes, read from cached nodes and pods. Every 10 minutes it also looks for which node autoscaler runs, and exports it as hybernate_node_autoscaler.

See the Cluster Autoscaler Guide for recommended configurations, and Node Pools for Real Savings for putting non-prod workloads on nodes that pausing empties.

docs.title: Leader Election
docs.text: When running multiple operator replicas for high availability, Hybernate uses controller-runtime's leader election (--leader-elect). Only the leader runs reconciliation loops; standby replicas take over if the leader fails. The doorman doesn't elect a leader: every replica serves traffic.

docs.title: Security Model
docs.text:
• The operator runs as a non-root user in a distroless container
  • RBAC is scoped to the minimum required permissions; see Data and Access
  • Metrics are served over HTTPS by default with authentication
  • HTTP/2 is disabled by default to mitigate known vulnerabilities

docs.title: Cost Tracking
docs.text: Hybernate tracks what each workload costs, what pausing it frees, and what that has saved, in its ManagedWorkload's status.cost. The figures cover the current calendar month in UTC.

docs.title: Freed and Saved
docs.text:
Hybernate reports two numbers for a pause, because they answer different questions:

  • Freed (freedThisMonth) is what the paused replicas requested, priced at their nodes' list price, for as long as they were paused: what pausing released on its nodes.
  • Saved (savedThisMonth) is the part of that which provably came off your bill.

Hybernate works at the workload layer: pausing removes pods, which frees the CPU and memory they requested on their nodes. Your cloud bill is for nodes. Freed capacity becomes money only once nodes go, which takes a cluster autoscaler (Cluster Autoscaler, Karpenter, or a managed equivalent) able to remove them. With no autoscaler, or with scale-down blocked, a pause frees capacity and saves nothing, and savedThisMonth says so. See the Cluster Autoscaler Guide for settings that let freed capacity go, and Node Pools for Real Savings for giving non-prod workloads nodes that pausing empties.

docs.title: How saved is measured
docs.text:
Every 5 minutes, the operator's leader looks at each node pool, and asks how much of what Hybernate holds paused there its nodes could hold if it came back now:

  • Paused is what the replicas Hybernate holds paused in the pool requested, in CPU and memory. A pause records which pools its pods ran in, and how many in each, in status.pause.resources.nodePools.
  • Spare is what the pool's schedulable, Ready nodes have left: their allocatable CPU and memory, less what the pods bound to them request, finished pods aside.
  • Shortfall is how much of the paused requests the spare capacity can't hold, in each of CPU and memory: max(0, paused − spare).

The shortfall is capacity that would have to be added to bring the paused replicas back, so it costs at least what that much CPU and memory costs. Over each 5 minutes it's credited to the paused workloads in the pool, shared in proportion to what each holds paused there, in CPU and in memory, as savedCPUHours and savedMemoryHours. savedThisMonth is those hours priced at the workload's rates, like the rest of its cost, so costTracking.rates applies to saved as it does to freed.

Each dimension is compared on its own, and a pool's spare capacity is summed across its nodes, as if paused pods could be split between nodes. Real scheduling only ever needs more, so saved is a lower bound: it never credits capacity that's still there, and can undercount, never overcount.

Why this needs no attribution. It never asks why a node went away. If other workloads scale down, they leave more spare capacity, and Hybernate's credit falls, since the paused replicas would fit in what they left. If nodes are removed for any reason, by an autoscaler after a pause, by consolidation, or by hand, and the paused replicas would need them back, that counts, because it's the capacity those replicas would need that's missing. What's credited is what Hybernate's pauses are actually holding off the bill right now, whoever made the nodes go.

Node pools. A node's pool is the first of its karpenter.sh/nodepool, cloud.google.com/gke-nodepool, eks.amazonaws.com/nodegroup and kubernetes.azure.com/agentpool labels. Nodes with none of them are one pool. A pool's spare capacity isn't lent to another: pods that ran on GPU nodes can't come back on general-purpose ones. The instance type isn't a pool: one pool can run several. A pause whose pools weren't recorded, because none of its pods was on a node as it paused, is compared with what every pool has left once its own paused replicas are held.

Worked example. A pool of three m6i.xlarge nodes in us-east-1, 4 vCPU and 16 GiB each, holds pods requesting 11 vCPU and 34 GiB, leaving 1 vCPU and 14 GiB spare. Hybernate holds paused api, 4 replicas of 500m and 1 GiB, and worker, 2 replicas of 1 vCPU and 4 GiB: 4 vCPU and 12 GiB in all.

CPU Memory Paused 4 vCPU 12 GiB Spare 1 vCPU 14 GiB Shortfall 3 vCPU 0

The memory would fit, so it saves nothing; 3 vCPU wouldn't, so that much came off the bill. api and worker hold 2 vCPU each, so each is credited 1.5 vCPU, 0.125 vCPU-hours every 5 minutes. At an m6i.xlarge's $0.0317 per vCPU-hour, api frees $0.080 an hour (2 vCPU and 4 GiB) and saves $0.048 an hour. If the autoscaler then removes a node, spare capacity falls and saved rises towards freed; if another team scales up into the spare vCPU, saved rises too, since the paused replicas now couldn't come back without a node.

What isn't credited. Time the operator wasn't sampling, such as across a restart or a change of leader, and an interval in which a sample failed: each sample credits at most the 5 minutes before it. What's credited is held in memory until the workload's cost is next brought up to date, at most 5 minutes later; a restart in between loses it. Each is a few minutes of a lower bound.

Where it can't be measured. An operator limited to some namespaces with watchNamespaces can't see what other namespaces' pods request of the nodes, so it can't know their spare capacity. There, savedThisMonth and projectedMonthlySavings read unknown, and savingsUnknown says why; freed is still measured.

To see pools' figures over time, the operator exports them as metrics.

To measure spare capacity, the operator caches nodes, without their image lists, and the pods bound to them, keeping of each only its node, its phase, and what it requests: about 2.6 KB a pod, so 26 MB for 10,000 pods.

docs.title: How Costs Are Calculated
docs.text: Cost tracking is always on. Everything is priced on what the workload's pods request, not on what they use: requests are what a pod reserves on a node, so they're what the workload costs in capacity, and what a pause frees. That includes sidecars injected when the pods were created, such as a service mesh proxy, which the Deployment's own template doesn't list but which pausing frees too.

docs.title: Resource Hours
docs.text:
Hybernate keeps the month's totals as resource-hours, brought up to date at every phase change, so time counts in the phase it was spent in, and at least every 5 minutes in between:

Field What it counts awakeCPUHours, awakeMemoryHours vCPU-hours and GiB-hours the workload's replicas requested while it was awake: in any phase but Paused storageHours GiB-hours of the PersistentVolumeClaims its pods mount, in every phase: a pause doesn't free storage pausedCPUHours, pausedMemoryHours vCPU-hours and GiB-hours the replicas Hybernate paused had requested, for as long as they were paused: what pausing freed savedCPUHours, savedMemoryHours The workload's share of the vCPU-hours and GiB-hours its node pools were short of holding the paused replicas: what pausing saved, at most the paused hours. See How saved is measured

While the workload is awake, its replicas are read from the target each time, or, if they can't be read, taken as last read, so the time before a phase change is still counted in the phase it was spent in; what one replica requests is read from its pods hourly and whenever its pod template changes. While it's paused, the paused hours are priced on what it ran when the pause began (status.pause.resources), and the saved hours are added as they're measured. If its pods can't be read as it pauses, that snapshot keeps what was last read of it awake, as it does the replicas of a pause finished after an interruption, which finds the target at zero already.

A gap between updates longer than 2 hours, such as while the operator wasn't running, counts as 2 hours, since what the workload did meanwhile isn't known. tracked is how much of the month the totals cover: less than the time since the month began when the workload was created during the month, or after such a gap.

The hours are kept to a billionth of an hour, as Kubernetes quantities, so the short pauses of small workloads still add up: 83333333n is 0.083 vCPU-hours. When a new month begins, the totals start again from zero; last month's aren't kept.

docs.title: Prices
docs.text:
Resource-hours are turned into dollars at a rate per vCPU-hour, per GiB-hour of memory, and per GiB-month of storage. For each of the three, the first of these that sets it applies:

  1. Your own rates, in spec.costTracking.rates.
  2. The list price of its nodes, in status.cost.listRates. Hybernate reads each pod's node's instance type and region from its labels (node.kubernetes.io/instance-type, topology.kubernetes.io/region), looks up its list price, on-demand or, for a spot node, spot, and averages over the workload's pods. status.cost.listPrice says which: OnDemand, Spot, or SpotAndOnDemand for pods on both. These are read again hourly while the workload is awake, and kept while it's paused, so what a pause frees and saves is priced at the nodes it last ran on. They set CPU and memory only.
  3. The defaults, for nodes Hybernate has no list price for, such as on-premises, custom, or kind nodes:
Resource Default Rate Source CPU $0.031/vCPU-hour AWS on-demand (m6i.large, us-east-1, 2026) Memory $0.004/GiB-hour AWS on-demand (m6i.large, us-east-1, 2026) Storage $0.08/GiB-month (priced at 730 hours a month) AWS EBS gp3, us-east-1

The rates are applied to the whole month's hours each time the dollar figures are worked out, so changing costTracking.rates reprices the month so far, not only what comes after.

How a node's price becomes rates. A cloud provider prices an instance as a whole, so Hybernate splits its hourly price between its vCPUs and its memory in the defaults' proportion: a vCPU costs as much as 7.75 GiB of memory. An m6i.large (2 vCPU, 8 GiB, $0.096 an hour) comes out at $0.0317 per vCPU-hour and $0.0041 per GiB-hour. A memory-optimized instance's memory and a compute-optimized one's CPU come out at what they cost there, and a pod pays for the share of the node it requests.

Where the prices come from. Hybernate ships with the on-demand Linux list price of every AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure instance type, in every region it's sold, and its spot price wherever it's sold as spot, taken from the providers' public price lists through instances.vantage.sh and refreshed each release. Nothing is looked up at runtime, so it works offline and air-gapped. An Azure constrained vCPU size, such as Standard_E4-2s_v5, is billed as its base size, Standard_E4s_v5, so it's priced at the base size's price spread over the vCPUs it has. Instances on GPU nodes are priced the same way, so a pod on a GPU node pays its share of the GPU too.

What list prices leave out. Savings plans, reserved instances, committed-use discounts, and negotiated rates aren't known to Hybernate, nor is the hour-by-hour price of AWS spot; set costTracking.rates for those.

Hybernate reads Nodes' labels to do this.

docs.title: Spot nodes
docs.text: A node labelled as spot or preemptible capacity is priced at its type's spot price in its region: karpenter.sh/capacity-type: spot (Karpenter, on any cloud), eks.amazonaws.com/capacityType: SPOT (EKS managed node groups), cloud.google.com/gke-spot: "true" or cloud.google.com/gke-preemptible: "true" (GKE), and kubernetes.azure.com/scalesetpriority: spot (AKS). Google Cloud and Azure publish one spot price per region; AWS's moves with demand, so Hybernate uses the average across the region's zones when its price table was generated, which is close but not what any one hour cost. A spot node of a type with no spot price, one its provider doesn't sell as spot, is priced at on-demand, and kubectl hybernate scan says which workloads that leaves costing less than shown.

docs.title: Custom Rates
docs.text:
Set your own rates to match what you pay:

managedworkload.yaml
spec:
  costTracking:
    rates:
      cpuPerHour: "0.045"      # GKE Autopilot pricing
      memoryPerHour: "0.005"    # GKE Autopilot pricing
      storagePerMonth: "0.10"   # Premium SSD

docs.title: Status Fields
docs.text:
status.cost
status:
  cost:
    tracked: 412h30m0s
    lastAccumulatedAt: "2026-10-18T14:30:00Z"
    awakeCPUHours: "160500m"
    awakeMemoryHours: "321"
    storageHours: "4125"
    pausedCPUHours: "664500m"
    pausedMemoryHours: "1329"
    savedCPUHours: "398700m"
    savedMemoryHours: "0"
    costThisMonth: "$6.84"
    freedThisMonth: "$26.47"
    savedThisMonth: "$12.62"
    costWithoutHybernateThisMonth: "$33.31"
    projectedMonthlyCost: "$12.35"
    projectedMonthlyFreed: "$47.74"
    projectedMonthlySavings: "$22.76"
    running:
      replicas: 2
      cpuMillis: 1000
      memoryBytes: 2147483648
      storageBytes: 10737418240
    pricedAt: "2026-10-18T14:00:00Z"
    pricedTemplateHash: 3f9c2a71d0e4b815
    listRates:
      cpuPerHour: 31660u      # $0.031660 per vCPU-hour
      memoryPerHour: 4085u    # $0.004085 per GiB-hour
    listPrice: OnDemand
Field Description tracked How much of the month the totals cover lastAccumulatedAt When the totals were last brought up to date awakeCPUHours, awakeMemoryHours, storageHours, pausedCPUHours, pausedMemoryHours, savedCPUHours, savedMemoryHours The resource-hours above: the record the dollar figures are worked out from costThisMonth The awake hours and the storage hours, priced freedThisMonth The paused hours, priced: what pausing freed. Money only once nodes go. Also the Freed column of kubectl get managedworkloads savedThisMonth The saved hours, priced: what pausing took off the bill, at least. Also the Saved column of kubectl get managedworkloads. unknown while savingsUnknown is set savingsUnknown Why saved can't be measured, such as an operator limited by watchNamespaces; unset when it's measured costWithoutHybernateThisMonth What the workload would have cost this month had it never been paused: costThisMonth plus freedThisMonth, to within a cent projectedMonthlyCost, projectedMonthlyFreed, projectedMonthlySavings costThisMonth, freedThisMonth and savedThisMonth carried to the whole month at the same rate: the amount ÷ tracked × the hours in the month. pending until a day has been tracked, including on the first day of each month, since a workload's pattern is daily running What the workload ran when the totals were last brought up to date while it was awake pricedAt, pricedTemplateHash When what a replica requests, and listRates, were last read, and the pod template's hash then listRates The list rates of the nodes the workload's pods last ran on, spot nodes at spot. Unset when its nodes aren't in Hybernate's price table, and the defaults apply listPrice Which list prices listRates are: OnDemand, Spot, or SpotAndOnDemand for pods on both. Unset with listRates resourceReduction What the current pause freed; only while the workload is paused

The dollar figures are rounded to the cent for display; the hours are the record.

docs.title: Resource Reduction
docs.text:
While a workload is paused, resourceReduction says what the pause freed on its nodes:

status.cost.resourceReduction
resourceReduction:
  cpuMillis: 3000            # 3 vCPUs freed
  memoryBytes: 6442450944    # 6 GiB freed
  replicas: 3                # 3 pod replicas removed

How much of that has come off the bill is what savedCPUHours and savedMemoryHours measure.

docs.title: In Dry-Run
docs.text: A workload in dry-run is never paused, so all its time is awake time. What pausing would have freed is kept apart, in status.dryRun: freedCPUHours, freedMemoryHours, and estimatedFreed, those hours priced at the same rates. Dry-run measures what pausing would free, never what it would save: that depends on whether the cluster's nodes would have gone, which they can't while the workload runs.

docs.title: Viewing Costs Across Workloads
docs.text:
kubectl get managedworkloads -A shows what pausing each workload has Freed this month, what of that it Saved, and, for one in dry-run, what it Would Free. For more:

kubectl get managedworkloads -A -o custom-columns=\
NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,PHASE:.status.phase,\
COST:.status.cost.costThisMonth,FREED:.status.cost.freedThisMonth,\
SAVED:.status.cost.savedThisMonth,PROJECTED:.status.cost.projectedMonthlyCost

kubectl hybernate status sums what pausing freed, and what of it was saved, across the cluster, and kubectl hybernate nodes shows what keeps nodes from going.

Per-workload cost isn't exported as Prometheus metrics; each node pool's paused and spare capacity, and what its shortfall saves an hour, are. See the Metrics Reference.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
Some workloads never see outside traffic: databases, message brokers, caches, workers. Their own activity clock can run out while the workloads that use them are still busy. Hybernate learns who needs what from each workload's environment, and dependsOn declares it by hand.

managedworkload.yaml
apiVersion: hybernate.io/v1alpha1
kind: ManagedWorkload
metadata:
  name: api
  namespace: preview-42
spec:
  target: {kind: Deployment, name: api}
  dependsOn:
    - {kind: StatefulSet, name: postgres}                         # same namespace
    - {namespace: messaging, kind: StatefulSet, name: nats}       # another namespace
  idlePolicy:
    idleAfter: 1h
  prediction: {}                                                  # the default, balanced

With the label instead, set hybernate.io/depends-on: "statefulset/postgres, messaging/statefulset/nats" on the workload; see Opting In.

Declare dependsOn on the workload that needs the other one. Each entry names the dependency's Deployment or StatefulSet, not its ManagedWorkload. namespace defaults to the ManagedWorkload's own.

docs.title: The rules
docs.text:
A dependency doesn't pause while anything that depends on it is awake. When its own clock runs out, it stays up and says why:

HeldByDependents=True   kept awake for preview-42/api, preview-43/api

Its clock keeps running. Once the last dependent has paused, the dependency pauses on its next check, provided its own clock has run out too.

Waking a workload wakes its dependencies. Before the workload starts resuming, Hybernate sets hybernate.io/last-activity on each dependency's ManagedWorkload, which wakes it through the usual activity annotation path. This chains: if Postgres itself depends on something, that wakes too. You can see it happen with kubectl describe.

By default, everything wakes at once, so a chain of dependencies doesn't add up to sequential cold starts.

Waking a dependency never holds up its dependent. One that can't be woken, such as one whose ManagedWorkload a policy engine won't let Hybernate annotate, gets a DependencyWakeFailed Warning event on the dependent, which wakes, or is handed back or deleted, all the same.

docs.title: Waiting for a dependency to be ready
docs.text:
Some workloads fail if they start before a dependency can serve: an API that gives up after a few connection retries while its database replays its write-ahead log. Set waitForReady on that dependency:

dependsOn:
  - {kind: StatefulSet, name: postgres, waitForReady: true}
  - {kind: Deployment, name: cache}          # wakes at the same time

The dependent then stays in Resuming, without scaling up, until every replica of that dependency is Ready, or until it serves with as many as it will have for now:

WaitingForDependencies=True   waiting for preview-42/statefulset/postgres (0 ready)

A dependency that has some replicas Ready but not all, such as one with a pod crash-looping, serves with those that are, so the dependent doesn't wait for the rest for good. A managed dependency counts once its own resume has finished, even short of every replica (its ResumeIncomplete=True); one Hybernate doesn't manage counts once the dependent has waited 2 minutes, the time a resume gives the rest of its replicas. A dependency with no replica Ready is always waited for.

The wait is long, because a slow start is exactly why you'd set it, but bounded: a dependency that's up but never Ready, such as one crash-looping or whose image can't be pulled, would otherwise leave the dependent at zero for good. The dependent waits, from when it began resuming, as long as the dependency's Deployment progressDeadlineSeconds (600 by default), past which Kubernetes itself reports the rollout failed, or 10 minutes for a StatefulSet, which has none. Then it starts anyway, with WaitingForDependencies=False, reason DependencyWontStart, and a Warning event naming the dependency:

WaitingForDependencies=False   not waiting for preview-42/statefulset/postgres (it isn't Ready after 10 minutes)

It doesn't wait at all for a dependency that can't start by waiting: one Hybernate doesn't manage that's scaled to zero, reported the same way. Nor for one that in turn waits, through waitForReady, for the dependent, directly or through others: each would wait for the other to start first. That's reason DependencyCycle, and both start together. A managed dependency that's still paused is woken again every few seconds while the dependent waits.

docs.title: Edge cases
docs.text: Situation What happens The dependency has no ManagedWorkload Hybernate never pauses it, so there's nothing to hold or wake The dependency doesn't exist DependencyNotFound=True on the dependent. Nothing is blocked, including a waitForReady resume The dependency is in a namespace outside watchNamespaces, or Hybernate isn't allowed to read it DependencyNotFound=True with reason DependencyNotVisible, naming why. It isn't held or woken, and nothing is blocked A cycle in dependsOn (A depends on B, B depends on A) Each would hold the other awake forever, so neither pauses and both report DependencyCycle=True until it's removed A workload listed as its own dependency Ignored: it's neither a cycle nor something to wait for A namespace's hybernate.io/depends-on names several workloads, such as statefulset/postgres, statefulset/redis The workloads it names don't take it: they're the dependencies, not dependents, so postgres and redis don't depend on each other. Neither does a workload one of them depends on by its own annotation: with the namespace naming deployment/auth and auth's own annotation naming statefulset/postgres, postgres doesn't depend on auth. The namespace's other workloads take the list A cycle through learned dependencies, such as two services that call each other Not a cycle: a learned dependent doesn't hold a workload it's itself a dependency of. Each pauses when idle, and waking either wakes the other kubectl hybernate pause on a dependency that's in use It isn't paused: the request is answered with PauseRequest=False, reason HeldByDependents, and a HeldByDependents event naming the dependents, as for an idle pause. Pause the dependents first dryRun: true The hold still applies and is reported; nothing is changed. A dependency in dry-run is measured as it would be live: a dependent in dry-run that would have paused (Idle) no longer holds it, so the whole chain's would-be pauses are counted. A dependency that pauses for real stays held by a dry-run dependent, whose pods are still up A dependent that manages nothing: one being deleted, a duplicate (DuplicateTarget=True), or one whose target is gone (TargetAvailable=False, reason TargetNotFound) It doesn't hold its dependencies: it has no running workload to keep them up for Many dependents awake at once HeldByDependents names the first 10, by namespace and name, and counts the rest

docs.title: Across namespaces
docs.text:
Dependencies can point into other namespaces, so preview environments can share a database or broker that lives elsewhere. The namespace the dependency is in has to agree, with the hybernate.io/dependents-from annotation listing the namespaces whose workloads may depend on its own, or "*" for any:

kubectl annotate namespace shared hybernate.io/dependents-from="preview-42, preview-43"

Without it, anyone who can write a ManagedWorkload, or a workload's environment, in one namespace could keep another namespace's workloads awake. A dependency in a namespace that doesn't list the dependent's, declared or learned, isn't held, woken or waited for, and the dependent reports it, without saying whether it exists:

DependencyNotAllowed=True   not in a namespace that allows dependents from preview-42 with hybernate.io/dependents-from, so not held or woken: shared/statefulset/postgres

A dependency can only be kept awake or woken by its dependents, never paused, scaled down, or deleted, so the most a dependent in another namespace can do is keep it running. HeldByDependents always names the holders by namespace.

docs.title: Learned dependencies
docs.text:
Hybernate reads the environment of every workload it manages, the way kubectl hybernate scan does: each variable, literal or from a ConfigMap, holding an address that names a Service, in any form cluster DNS gives it (postgres, postgres.preview-42.svc.cluster.local, or a headless Service's pod, postgres-0.postgres-hl), followed to the workload the Service selects. Each one it finds is held awake and woken exactly like a dependsOn, with no YAML to write:

status.learnedDependencies
learnedDependencies:
  from: 3f9c2a71d0e4b815
  at: "2026-10-04T09:12:00Z"
  dependencies:
    - {namespace: preview-42, kind: StatefulSet, name: postgres, source: environment, via: PGHOST, address: postgres-0.postgres-hl}
    - {namespace: preview-42, kind: StatefulSet, name: redis, source: wake}

with a DependenciesLearned event when the set changes. The event says of each whether it's woken with the workload, which only a dependency Hybernate manages is, in a namespace that allows it. Opt the dependency in too to have them paused and woken together:

api: depends on preview-42/postgres (PGHOST), which isn't managed by Hybernate, so it isn't woken with api: opt it in to have them paused and woken together

They're learned again when the pod template changes, and hourly for ConfigMaps changed since. Secrets are never read, so an address set only in a Secret isn't learned from the environment.

From wakes, too. When a request wakes a paused workload, the doorman records where it came from, and the operator finds the pod that sent it. If that pod belongs to a workload Hybernate manages, that workload depends on the one it woke, and the link is learned with source: wake. That covers addresses in Secrets, built in code, or read from files, the first time they're used. A request from a workload Hybernate doesn't manage, such as an ingress controller, or from a pod on the node's network, teaches nothing. Only an address the doorman wrote counts: the operator checks, from the field managers the API server records, that hybernate.io/last-request-from was set under Hybernate's own, so one set by hand teaches nothing, and the chart's admission policy refuses anyone but the doorman setting it at all. The sender is only looked for in the woken workload's namespace and those its hybernate.io/dependents-from allows. Links learned from wakes are kept when the environment is read again, for 14 days after the last request that woke the dependency: lastSeen records it, at most once a day. While a link is kept, the dependency is held awake with the workload and woken with it, so the workload's requests no longer reach the doorman and don't renew the link. A link in steady use is dropped too, 14 days after it was learned or last renewed, and learned again from the next request that wakes the dependency, at the cost of that request's cold start, about once a fortnight. A one-off call, such as someone's curl from a pod, is forgotten the same way, so it doesn't tie two workloads together for good.

A learned link is safe to apply on its own: a wrong one can only keep a workload awake longer, or wake it, never pause it. To drop one, name it in hybernate.io/ignore-dependencies on the workload or its ManagedWorkload, comma-separated, as namespace/name or a name in its own namespace:

metadata:
  annotations:
    hybernate.io/ignore-dependencies: "redis, messaging/nats"

dependsOn still applies alongside, and is the only way to set waitForReady. kubectl hybernate deps shows a workload's links in both directions, and where each came from.

docs.title: When you need dependsOn
docs.text:
A request through a normal Service wakes a paused workload by itself, through wake on request, and learned dependencies cover what's in the environment, headless addresses included. dependsOn is what you need for the rest:

  • waitForReady, so the first request doesn't wait for the database too, or the app doesn't fail starting before it.
  • Addresses Hybernate hasn't seen used yet: set in Secrets, built in code, or read from files, before a request to a paused dependency teaches it.
  • A dependency on a workload behind no Service, which no address names.

kubectl hybernate scan lists the dependencies it finds in each workload's environment, and what Hybernate does with each: woken and held with the workload that needs it, declared or learned, once Hybernate manages both; never paused, for a dependency it doesn't manage.

docs.title: Forecasting
docs.text:
• It always learns, for every managed workload, whatever autoResume says: from every hour it's awake, and every hour it's paused that the doorman or an activity query watches, the doorman's even while the queries can't be evaluated. Once it's confident, it holds off pauses before hours it expects to be busy, on its own.
  • With autoResume, it also wakes a paused workload 15 minutes ahead of the demand it expects. Turning autoResume on later loses nothing: the forecast has been learning all along, and wakes the workload ahead from then, once it acts.
  • With pauseEarly, off by default, it also pauses an idle workload before idleAfter runs out, when it's confident the coming hours are quiet and a request would wake it; see Pausing Early.

Hybernate uses a Holt-Winters double seasonal model to learn your workload's demand patterns and predict future resource needs. This page covers the mathematical model, how it builds confidence over time, how soon it acts and how to choose that, how it can bring a pause forward, how it starts from your Prometheus history, and how it handles pattern shifts. Every figure on it is measured by the simulator, which runs the operator's own engine and rules.

docs.title: The Idea
docs.text:
Most workloads follow predictable patterns:

  • Daily: Traffic peaks during business hours, drops overnight
  • Weekly: Weekdays are busier than weekends

Hybernate learns these two patterns independently by feeding hourly CPU utilization into a Holt-Winters model. Once it has enough data and confidence, it uses the learned patterns to:

  • Hold off a pause when it's confident demand is coming in the hour under way or the next
  • Wake paused workloads ahead of predicted demand, starting 15 minutes before an hour it expects to be busy
  • With pauseEarly, which is off unless you turn it on, pause an idle workload before idleAfter runs out when it's confident the hours ahead are quiet. Otherwise it never causes a pause: the activity clock decides that

docs.title: What an Hour Records
docs.text:
The forecast learns CPU utilization: usage as a percentage of what the workload's own containers request in the pods reporting it, the same measure cpuThreshold is set in (see Idle Detection). Holding back a pause and waking ahead of demand compare its forecast with cpuThreshold directly, so a forecast that keeps an idle workload awake would also wake it once paused.

It's fed each hour once it's over, as the busiest moment seen in it:

  • While the workload is awake, its CPU is read every minute, and the hour records the highest utilization. The peak, rather than the mean, is what the forecast's decisions need: the activity clock counts any minute above cpuThreshold as activity, so an hour busy only for its last ten minutes is an hour the workload has to be awake for. Usage in the first 15 minutes after a wake, including one by something else scaling it up such as kubectl scale, isn't counted: starting up isn't demand, and counted, a wake ahead of a busy hour would teach the forecast that the hour before it is busy too, so that it woke the workload earlier every week. Once it's warmed up, an hour the activity clock sees it in use in, from CPU above cpuThreshold, an activity annotation or a Prometheus query, counts as at least twice cpuThreshold, as an hour a request wakes it in does. A light-use workload's use may show only in an annotation or a query: taught its own light utilization on mornings autoResume had it ready, and a request's twice cpuThreshold on mornings people woke it, the forecast would have it ready only every other morning. A workload whose use stays under cpuThreshold with no other source is idle to Hybernate while it's awake, so autoResume can't learn its mornings; lower cpuThreshold below its use or add a source that sees it
  • While the workload is paused behind the doorman (WakeOnRequest=True), a request would wake it, so a check that finds it still paused finds no demand. A request that wakes it counts as at least twice cpuThreshold, however little it then uses, so the hour people arrive in is learned as busy. That stands while its Prometheus activity queries, if it has any, can't be evaluated: a request would still wake it, so the hour is learned, busy if a request woke it or a query found activity, and quiet otherwise
  • While the workload is paused with a Prometheus activity query, the query is evaluated every minute, as while it's awake, and wakes it when it finds activity. So a check that finds the query quiet finds no demand, and one that finds activity counts as at least twice cpuThreshold, as a request does. That's how a workload no Service routes requests to, such as a queue worker, learns its nights: from a query of its queue's length. Without the doorman, a check where a query can't be evaluated can't see demand, so the hour isn't recorded; behind the doorman, the hour is learned as above. A query that can't be evaluated never wakes the workload
  • While the workload is paused with neither watching it, demand can't be seen, and the hour isn't recorded: demand it can't see isn't zero
  • An hour is recorded only if it was checked from its start to its end. The hour under way is kept in memory, so after an operator restart or a leader change, the hour it happened in is skipped, unless it was only minutes old, rather than recorded from the part seen after it

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
The model tracks four components:

Component What it represents Smoothing parameter Level The mean demand \( \alpha = 0.01 \) Trend Whether demand is growing or shrinking \( \beta = 0.001 \) Daily components 24 offsets, one per hour of day: the shape of an average day \( \gamma_1 = 0.1 \) Weekly components 168 offsets, one per hour of week: how each weekday departs from that shape \( \gamma_2 = 0.5 \)

Each hour, the model takes the hour's utilization \( Y(t) \), compares it to what it predicted (for confidence scoring), and updates all four components using exponential smoothing. The model is additive: idle workloads spend much of their time at zero demand, where a multiplicative model, which divides by the level and the seasonal factors, diverges.

\[ \begin{aligned} L(t) &= \max\Bigl(0,\; \alpha \cdot \bigl(Y(t) - D(t) - W(t)\bigr) + (1 - \alpha) \cdot \bigl(L(t{-}k) + k \cdot T(t{-}k)\bigr)\Bigr) \\[6pt] T(t) &= \beta \cdot \frac{L(t) - L(t{-}k)}{k} + (1 - \beta) \cdot T(t{-}k) \\[6pt] D(t) &= \gamma_1 \cdot \bigl(Y(t) - L(t) - W(t)\bigr) + (1 - \gamma_1) \cdot D(t - s_1) \\[6pt] W(t) &= \gamma_2 \cdot \bigl(Y(t) - L(t) - D(t)\bigr) + (1 - \gamma_2) \cdot W(t - s_2) \end{aligned} \]

Where \( s_1 = 24 \) (daily season length), \( s_2 = 168 \) (weekly season length), and \( k \) is the number of hours since the previous observation (1, unless observations were missed).

After each update the components are renormalised: the daily components sum to zero, and for each hour of the day the weekly components across the seven days sum to zero. The shift is moved into the component above, which leaves every forecast unchanged and keeps the level the mean demand, so it is never negative.

The forecast for \( h \) hours ahead is never negative either:

\[ F(t+h) = \max\Bigl(0,\; L(t) + h \cdot T(t) + D(t+h) + W(t+h)\Bigr) \]

A gap in the observations, from the operator being down or a workload paused with neither the doorman nor an activity query watching it, is skipped rather than filled in: there is no honest value to fill it with, and since slots are wall-clock hours (below), skipping an hour doesn't shift what was learned. The trend is carried across a gap of at most a day.

The first week initialises the model, as the first season does in classical Holt-Winters. The first time an hour of the week is seen, its weekly component is set so the forecast for that hour is what was seen, and the level, trend and daily components learn only from hours seen again. So after one week of office hours, the forecast for the next week is the week it saw, weekends quiet. The forecast isn't scored on an hour of the week it's seeing for the first time, since it had nothing to forecast it from, and doesn't act on one it hasn't seen.

docs.title: Phase Lifecycle
docs.text:
The engine doesn't start making decisions immediately. It progresses through phases as it collects data and builds confidence:

Observing → DailySuggesting → DailyActive → WeeklySuggesting → FullyActive

Phase Requires Behavior Observing No day of forecasts scored yet Collecting data, its first week: an hour of the week is scored from the second time it's seen. No predictions yet. DailySuggesting Every hour of the day observed, and a day of forecasts scored Daily confidence is being scored; predictions aren't acted on yet. DailyActive Daily confidence >= threshold Predictions drive decisions. Weekly patterns still learning. WeeklySuggesting Every hour of the week observed at least once Weekly confidence still being earned. FullyActive Weekly confidence >= threshold Both daily and weekly patterns drive decisions.

The gates count hours of the calendar, not data points: a workload that is only ever observed from 9 to 5 hasn't shown what happens at night, however many hours it has been watched.

That has a consequence for workloads paused with nothing to watch them: an hour paused without the doorman or a Prometheus activity query isn't observed (see What an Hour Records), so a workload paused every night that way never has its nights observed, and its forecast never reaches DailySuggesting. Keep wake on request on if you want autoResume and the forecast's veto, and for a workload no Service routes requests to, such as a queue worker, give it an activity query that sees its demand, such as its queue's length.

The ManagedWorkload shows the phase per season, in status.prediction: dailyPhase and weeklyPhase are each Observing, Suggesting or Active, next to dailyConfidence and weeklyConfidence. DailyActive, for example, is dailyPhase: Active with weeklyPhase: Observing. The phase shown, there and in hybernate_prediction_phase, is the one the forecast is acting in: after a regime change leaves it at WeeklySuggesting with nothing scored, it's shown as DailySuggesting until a day of its forecasts has been scored and it drives decisions again.

The confidence threshold is the forecast setting's, and a change applies at the next reconcile. A phase is earned at the threshold and lost 5 points below it, so confidence hovering at the threshold doesn't switch the forecast on and off every hour.

docs.title: Forecast Setting
docs.text:
How soon the forecast acts on what it has learned is one setting, in plain words: eager, balanced (the default) or cautious. Set it with the hybernate.io/forecast annotation on an opted-in workload or its namespace, the Helm value defaults.forecast for every opted-in workload, or spec.prediction.mode on a ManagedWorkload you write:

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: preview-api
  annotations:
    hybernate.io/forecast: eager
Setting Acts at a confidence of What it trades eager 60% Acts on less regular patterns balanced waits out; wakes a workload for nothing more often balanced 75% The default: acts on a weekday pattern after 8 days, and wakes a steadily used one for nothing almost never cautious 85% Acts only on patterns it forecasts well; for workloads that are costly to keep awake for nothing, such as one on GPUs

A wrong forecast costs a little money, never availability: it only wakes a workload early or keeps it up a while longer, and a request still wakes a paused workload through the doorman whatever the forecast says. So the choice is between mornings ready and hours awake for nothing. Over eight weeks of office hours kept loosely, people arriving up to an hour either side of 09:10 and away one weekday in four, twenty simulated workloads averaged:

Setting Mornings ready, of 30 Hours woken for nothing eager 10 14 balanced 8 8 cautious 4 5

On office hours kept steadily, every setting acts after 8 days and has every morning after ready, and none wakes the workload on a weekend: the settings differ only on patterns the forecast can't get right every day. Below 60, a threshold gains a morning or so on the most irregular patterns for two more hours woken for nothing; above 85, it loses mornings about as fast as it saves hours.

spec.prediction.confidence on the ManagedWorkload, from 50 to 100, overrides the setting's threshold with your own; a label-created ManagedWorkload keeps it when its annotations are applied again.

docs.title: How Long It Takes
docs.text:
Learning live from a fresh start, with autoResume on, behind the doorman or, for the last row, woken by a Prometheus activity query, the simulator measures how many days the forecast takes to act (DailyActive) and to be fully active (FullyActive), for a workload at 40% of its CPU request while in use and 1% otherwise, over ten weeks (never: not within them):

Workload eager (60) balanced (75) cautious (85) Busy on weekdays from 09:10 to 17:30, quiet nights and weekends 8 / 14 8 / 14 8 / 14 The same, with people arriving and leaving up to 20 minutes either side and away one weekday in ten (the median of 20) 8 / 14 8 / 14 8 / 14 The same, with people arriving and leaving up to an hour either side and away one weekday in four (the median of 20) 8 / 29 9 / never 10 / never The same hours every day, weekends included 8 / 14 8 / 14 8 / 14 Always busy 8 / 14 8 / 14 8 / 14 Always idle 8 / 14 8 / 14 8 / 14 A queue worker with no Service, which a query of its queue's length wakes, busy every day from 07:00 to 19:00, paused every night 8 / 14 8 / 14 8 / 14

A test in the repo runs these and fails if they drift from this table.

Every pattern the forecast can get right takes the same time, at every setting: its first week is learned, not scored, since the first time it sees an hour of the week it has nothing to forecast it from, and once it has scored a day of the second week, it acts. On office hours that's the Tuesday of the second week, so the Monday before it is the only morning after the first week that the first request wakes the workload: every morning after is ready, Mondays included, and weekends are left asleep, since the first weekend taught the forecast they're quiet. A setting's threshold matters on patterns the forecast can't get right every day, such as the third row's, where a higher threshold waits for more evidence. An always-busy workload is never paused, and an always-idle one never woken or held awake by its forecast of no demand, so for them, acting changes nothing.

None of this delays idle detection or wake on request, which work from the first hour: until the forecast acts, the first request of the morning wakes the workload, instead of autoResume having it ready. And with a Prometheus, a new workload doesn't wait at all: it learns from its history first, and a workload with a few weeks of a steady pattern acts from the first day.

docs.title: When It Acts
docs.text:
status.prediction says whether the forecast is acting, and if it isn't, what it waits for and when it's expected to start:

Field What it says acting Whether the forecast drives decisions: it holds off pauses before hours it expects to be busy and, with autoResume, wakes the workload 15 minutes ahead of them, and with pauseEarly, brings pauses forward before hours it expects quiet threshold The confidence it acts at: the setting's, or spec.prediction.confidence reason Acting; Observing, it hasn't scored a day of its forecasts yet, as in its first week, or hasn't seen every hour of the day; EarningConfidence, its forecasts of the last day aren't yet right enough; Relearning, demand broke from what it had learned, after a regime change; NotLearning, the workload is paused with nothing to see its demand: neither the doorman, its message saying why requests don't wake it and how to fix that, nor a Prometheus activity query that can be evaluated. Behind the doorman it learns whatever its queries do, its message ending its Prometheus activity queries failing while they can't be evaluated message The same in a sentence, with its confidence and threshold once it has them, such as learning: it has seen 100 of the 168 hours of the week, and scores its forecast of an hour from the second time it sees it; expected to start acting around Tue 24 Mar 00:00 UTC, if the coming days repeat the last week. While the workload is paused, it ends with what it learns from then: requests through the doorman, its Prometheus activity queries, or both. Not learning, it says why and how to fix it, with a link, such as not learning while paused: no Service routes requests to it; a request can't wake it, so its demand can't be seen, and it learns only the hours it's awake. To learn the hours it's paused too, give it a Service, or, for a workload no request reaches, such as a queue worker, a Prometheus activity query that sees its demand: https://okedeji.io/hybernate/concepts/wake-on-request/#when-a-workload-isnt-routed startsActing When it's expected to start acting history What it learned from Prometheus when Hybernate began managing the workload; see Learning from History

startsActing is projected by running a copy of the forecast on through the demand it last saw in each hour of the week, until it would act: the same phase gates and confidence, on the assumption that the coming week looks like the last one. For an hour of the week it hasn't seen yet, it assumes the same hour on the nearest day it has; an hour of the day it has never seen, as a workload paused every night with nothing watching it leaves them, is never assumed, so such a workload is never projected to act. On office hours the projection is within a day of when the forecast does act from its second day, and within an hour once it has seen a weekend. It's unset while the forecast is acting, and, with the message saying so, when the forecast isn't expected to act within four weeks, as for a pattern too irregular for its setting. It's projected again once an hour, as the forecast learns.

kubectl get managedworkloads -o wide shows the reason in a Forecast column.

docs.title: Pausing Early
docs.text:
The forecast can bring a pause forward. With pauseEarly on, a workload that has been idle for 20 minutes is paused without waiting out idleAfter when all of these hold:

  • The forecast is acting, and sure the hours ahead are quiet: every hour until idleAfter would run out, and at least the hour under way and the next, is forecast below cpuThreshold, judged as the veto and autoResume judge them, at the same confidence threshold. An hour of the week it hasn't seen, and the hours after one far quieter than it forecast, as on a holiday, are hours it can't say are quiet, and nothing is brought forward
  • A request would wake it: wake on request is on, the doorman has a Ready pod, and the workload's last pause found nothing wrong with its routing (WakeOnRequest). Every Service that selects the workload's pods is one the doorman would route while it's paused, on every port but those its hybernate.io/doorman-ignore-ports annotation lists: it isn't headless, has no UDP or SCTP port, doesn't keep traffic on the caller's node (internalTrafficPolicy: Local), has no other workload's Ready pods behind it, and, behind GKE container-native load balancing, has the doorman's forwarder to reach it. At least one of them routes TCP, and their ports fit within the doorman ports the workload, and its namespace, may hold. A wrong forecast then costs a request a wake, a cold start, never its answer. If anything here doesn't hold, or can't be read, the workload waits out idleAfter as usual, and the operator logs why. Services without a selector, whose endpoints are written by hand, and ExternalName Services aren't checked, since nothing says which pods they reach
  • Nothing else holds it: an active-until hold, awake dependents and the hour Hybernate waits after a GitOps tool undid its last pause hold an early pause as they hold any. In dry-run, an early pause is a would-be pause, measured like any other

It's off unless you turn it on, with hybernate.io/pause-early: "true" on an opted-in workload or its namespace, the Helm value defaults.pauseEarly for every opted-in workload, or spec.idlePolicy.pauseEarly: true on a ManagedWorkload you write:

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: preview-api
  annotations:
    hybernate.io/auto-resume: "true"
    hybernate.io/pause-early: "true"

It's a setting of its own, apart from the forecast setting: that one says how sure the forecast must be before it acts at all, and this one whether, once it is, it brings pauses forward, so a cautious forecast can pause early too.

A pause the forecast brings forward has a PausedEarly event in place of IdleDetected, naming the hours it expects to be quiet: idle for 20 minutes, since its CPU use was last above the activity threshold, and the forecast expects the hours from 18:00 to 20:00 UTC to be quiet; pausing before idleAfter (1 hour) runs out. Until the workload wakes, status.activity.forecastQuietUntil holds when those hours end, and kubectl hybernate status says so in NEXT: paused early: the forecast expected quiet until Fri 20:00 UTC; wakes on a request or activity.

Behind the doorman, the hours an early pause sleeps through are learned as any paused hour is (see What an Hour Records): a request would have woken the workload, so a check that finds it still paused finds no demand, and the forecast keeps learning.

docs.title: What It Saves and Costs
docs.text:
The hour people leave in is learned as busy, so the forecast can't bring a pause forward before that hour is over: on office hours ending at 17:30, the pause comes at 18:00, where the clock would have paused the workload at 18:29, an idleAfter after the last busy minute. The longer idleAfter, the more that saves. What it costs is a cold start for anyone who uses the workload in an hour the forecast expected quiet, before idleAfter would have run out: their request waits for it to wake, where it would have been up. The simulator measures both at balanced, for a workload at 40% of its CPU request while in use, over the weeks after the forecast acts: for a holiday, the week it's in, and for a change of hours, the two weeks after it.

Workload Hours awake a week, without → with Extra cold starts a week Busy on weekdays from 09:10 to 17:30, quiet nights and weekends 48.7 → 46.3 0 The same, with idleAfter: 2h 53.7 → 46.3 0 The same hours every day, weekends included 68.1 → 64.8 0 Office hours, people arriving and leaving up to 20 minutes either side and away one weekday in ten (the average of 20) 45.2 → 43.3 0 Office hours, people arriving and leaving up to an hour either side and away one weekday in four (the average of 20) 38.2 → 37.8 0 Office hours, the week of a holiday on a Wednesday 39.8 → 37.8 0 Office hours moving to 13:00 to 21:00, the two weeks after 56.0 → 54.7 0 Office hours, someone coming back for ten minutes 15 to 50 minutes after people left, one weekday in three (the average of 20) 50.6 → 48.6 0.6 Office hours, someone working in the evening too, one weekday in three, in three bursts with up to 25 minutes between them (the average of 20) 55.4 → 52.2 0.5 Always busy 168.0 → 168.0 0 Always idle 0.0 → 0.0 0

A test in the repo runs these and fails if they drift from this table.

At the default idleAfter of an hour, that's half an hour a weekday, about 5% of the hours awake; at two hours, the same early pause saves an hour and a half a weekday. On every pattern the forecast has learned, holidays and changes of hours included, it costs no cold starts: it brings nothing forward on a holiday, since the forecast doubts what it expects from the holiday's first quiet hour, nor on the first two days of new hours, while it relearns, and nobody comes back in the hours it does pause through. Loosely kept hours save less: there are fewer days people leave to bring a pause forward from, and fewer evenings the forecast is sure of.

The cold starts come from use it can't foresee within idleAfter of the last: someone coming back after the others have left, or working in the evening in bursts, where each gap longer than 20 minutes, in an hour the forecast learned as quiet, finds the workload paused. That's what the 20 minutes are for: at 10, evening work like the row above's costs three times the cold starts for a quarter more of the hours saved, while on office hours any wait up to half an hour saves the same. So turn it on for workloads used to a pattern, where an hour after the last use is an hour paid for nothing every day; leave it off for one people come back to at odd hours, or set active-until while they do.

docs.title: Learning from History
docs.text:
With a Prometheus URL (prometheus.url, --prometheus-url), a new ManagedWorkload's forecast starts from the workload's history rather than from nothing: the operator reads up to the last four weeks of its CPU and learns them in one go, as it would have learned them live, then carries on live. A workload with a steady pattern acts from the first day, and one whose history is irregular or short goes on learning, as it would have, through the same phase gates and confidence.

Each hour of history is measured as a live hour is: the workload's own containers' usage, sidecars injected into its pods left out, against what they request, at its busiest moment in the hour, as at least twice cpuThreshold once above it. Its pods are found by the names a Deployment or StatefulSet gives them, so old revisions' pods are part of its history too. With a Prometheus that holds more than one cluster's series, such as Thanos, Mimir or a shared Prometheus, set prometheus.selector (--prometheus-selector), such as cluster="staging": its matchers are added to the query, so a same-named workload in another cluster isn't read as this one. It's one range query per workload, a point an hour, of the busiest five-minute rate of container_cpu_usage_seconds_total in each hour, so Prometheus works it out and answers with at most 672 points; the operator asks for one workload at a time, waits up to 30 seconds for an answer, and tries a query that fails twice more, two minutes apart, before the forecast learns live only. Reading history never holds up a reconcile: the forecast learns live meanwhile, and takes up what was learned once it's ready.

What history can't tell, it assumes:

  • Hours none of its pods ran in are learned as quiet, as an hour scaled to zero by something else is live. That includes hours Hybernate itself had it paused, if it managed the workload before: an hour paused behind the doorman or watched by an activity query is quiet anyway, but one paused with neither, whose demand live learning skips, can't be told from an hour nobody used
  • Requests are today's. If the workload's CPU requests changed over the four weeks, its earlier hours are measured against the new ones
  • Use that shows only in requests or activity annotations isn't in Prometheus: a light-use workload's history looks quieter than its live hours will
