  • Five-minute rates are smoother than the minute-by-minute readings live learning takes, so a burst of a minute or two counts for less

status.prediction.history says what came of it, with an event once:

history.reason Event Meaning Learned ForecastLearnedHistory Learned hours of history, from and to; the message says how much, such as the forecast learned from 4 weeks of the workload's CPU history in Prometheus NoHistory ForecastLearningLive Prometheus has no CPU for its pods, as for a workload deployed with it; the forecast learns from now NoCPURequests ForecastHistoryUnavailable (warning) Its containers request no CPU, so there's nothing to measure its use against QueryFailed ForecastHistoryUnavailable (warning) Prometheus didn't answer three times; the message has its error NoPrometheusURL none The operator has no Prometheus URL, so the forecast learns live from the start

History is read once per ManagedWorkload, when it's new: one that has learned live keeps what it learned. Deleting and creating a ManagedWorkload again starts it afresh, from history again.

To see what the forecast would make of your workloads' history before opting them in, run kubectl hybernate forecast.

docs.title: Confidence Scoring
docs.text:
Confidence is \( 1 - \text{WAPE} \), the weighted absolute percentage error: the total absolute error of the hourly forecasts over a window, divided by the total demand in it.

\[ C = 1 - \frac{\sum_{i} |F(i) - Y(i)|}{\max\bigl(\sum_{i} Y(i),\; n \cdot f\bigr)} \]

A confidence of 75% means the forecast's total error over the window is 25% of the demand in it. Unlike an average of per-hour percentage errors, it is defined when demand is zero, and an hour of zero demand forecast as zero isn't counted as a perfect hour. The denominator is never less than \( n \cdot f \), where \( f \) is the workload's mean hourly demand over about a week, and at least 1% of the CPU requested: a quiet weekend day is judged against the demand of a typical day, and a workload that idles at a sliver of its request isn't judged on its noise.

  • Daily confidence is scored over the last 24 scored hours
  • Weekly confidence is scored over the last 168 scored hours: a whole week of weekdays and weekend must be forecast well, not just the day just gone
  • Each needs its full window before it reports a score
  • An hour of the week seen for the first time isn't scored, or judged an anomaly: there was nothing to forecast it from

docs.title: Anomaly Detection
docs.text:
Traffic patterns change. A marketing campaign, a new feature launch, or a seasonal shift can invalidate what the model has learned.

Hybernate detects these regime changes using z-score anomaly detection:

  1. Each hour, the signed prediction error \( e(t) = Y(t) - F(t) \) is converted to a two-sided z-score using an exponentially weighted mean \( \mu \) and standard deviation \( \sigma \) of recent errors, which remember about a week:

    \[ z(t) = \frac{|e(t) - \mu|}{\max(\sigma, f)} \]

    A sudden surge and a sudden disappearance of demand both count.

  2. If \( z(t) > 3.0 \), the observation is flagged as an anomaly. The model learns from it only up to 3 standard deviations, so a single spike isn't learned as a pattern. An error that large in the same direction as the last one in the same hour of the week isn't an anomaly, though: it's a weekly pattern, such as a Tuesday night batch job, and the model learns it in full

  3. If 3 or more anomalies occur within 24 observed hours, the engine declares a regime change

What breaks from the learned pattern, an anomaly or any hour in the day after a regime change, isn't learned into the weekly components at once: the change it would make to its hour of the week is held until the same hour the next day. If that hour breaks from its forecast the same way, the change lasted and is made; if it goes as forecast, the day was a one-off, such as a holiday, and the change is dropped. The level and daily components learn it as usual. Learned at once, a weekday holiday had the same weekday a week later forecast quieter than it is.

The hour after one far quieter than forecast, an anomaly, the forecast doubts what it expects: it neither holds off a pause nor wakes the workload until an hour goes as forecast, or a regime change has it relearn. One far busier than forecast casts no doubt, since the workload is in use then anyway.

On a regime change, the engine ends up at least one level below the phase it held before the anomalies began:

  • FullyActive → WeeklySuggesting
  • WeeklySuggesting or DailyActive → DailySuggesting
  • DailySuggesting → Observing

If the anomalies have already cost it that level or more, by lowering its confidence, it stays where they left it: one regime change is never a second demotion, and never a promotion.

It then discards the evidence its confidence rested on: the scored errors, the anomaly statistics, and which hours of the week have been observed. Confidence has to be earned again on the new pattern before the forecast drives decisions again: whatever its phase, it neither holds back a pause nor wakes a workload until a full day of its forecasts has been scored again. A RegimeChange warning event is emitted once.

A weekday holiday looks like this: autoResume wakes the workload for the hours the forecast expects, and its first quiet office hour is an anomaly, so the forecast doubts the rest and the activity clock pauses the workload, an hour and a quarter awake for nothing. A regime change follows once three hours have been quiet. The forecast is off from then until a day has been scored, about 30 hours, so the first request of the next morning wakes the workload, and it's back on during that day. That day is busy again, so the holiday isn't learned into the week: the same weekday a week later, and every morning from the second after the holiday, is ready. Idle detection and wake on request carry on throughout. A single deviant day can't be told from the start of a new pattern until the next day shows which it was, so the forecast doesn't guess; it costs the next morning, and nothing after. A Saturday people come in on is the same: the Saturday after isn't woken, and the Monday after is the morning it costs.

A lasting change, such as a team moving its hours from 09:00 to 13:00, is noticed within the day as a regime change, and learned into the week from its second day. For about a week people wake the workload themselves; at balanced, from the second Tuesday every afternoon is ready, and within two weeks the forecast stops waking it for nothing, which until then it does a few times, for the old hours and, on weekends, for the new ones. A workload nobody uses any more is woken for its old hours twice, on its first quiet morning and the same weekday a week later, and then left asleep.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
The engine's learned state (the model's components, the scored errors, the anomaly statistics, the weekly changes held for the next day and whether it doubts the hour under way, the last hour observed, and the demand last seen in each hour of the week, which startsActing is projected from) is stored in the ManagedWorkload's status, in status.prediction.state: gzipped JSON, base64-encoded, about 2.5 KB. It is written with each hourly observation. This means:

  • The engine survives operator restarts and leader changes, and an hour observed before a restart isn't observed twice. The hour under way when the operator restarts is skipped. Restarted every day, at a different hour each day, the operator loses those hours and nothing else: the forecast starts acting within hours of when it would have without the restarts
  • A last observed hour more than an hour ahead of the operator's clock, recorded by a clock that was wrong, isn't trusted: the next hour is observed as usual rather than refused until real time catches up
  • No external database, persistent volume, or ConfigMap is needed
  • Each workload has its own independent engine

State that can't be read, from an older version or a hand edit, is discarded with a ForecastReset warning event, and the engine starts learning again.

docs.title: Wall-Clock Alignment
docs.text:
Seasonal slots are keyed to wall-clock time, not to a running counter. The hour of day and day of week are counted in the operator's timezone (--timezone, the Helm value timezone, UTC by default), so business hours stay in their slots when the clocks change for daylight saving. Each workload records it in status.prediction.timeZone, and kubectl hybernate status shows it. This means:

  • If a workload is paused for 6 hours without the doorman, the model doesn't lose alignment. The next observation goes into the correct hour-of-day slot
  • An hour paused behind the doorman, or watched by an activity query, is recorded as no demand: that's how the model learns that nights and weekends are quiet
  • Monday 9am always maps to the same slot, regardless of gaps. In a timezone whose hours start at half or quarter past the hour in UTC, such as India's, hours, and the 15 minutes autoResume wakes ahead of one, are counted on the local clock

With --timezone set to its users' zone, a workload in New York or London is up at 08:45 local time every weekday through the clock change. Left at UTC, the operator's clock is an hour off its users' after the change, and the forecast has to learn their mornings again: in the simulator, four mornings the week of the change find the workload paused, and the forecast holds it awake for nothing on others, until about two weeks on.

docs.title: Tuning
docs.text:
The forecast setting, or spec.prediction.confidence in its place, is the only thing to tune. The smoothing parameters are fixed, the same for every workload, and can't be configured:

Parameter Value What a higher value would do \( \alpha \) 0.01 Level reacts faster to demand changes \( \beta \) 0.001 Trend detection is more aggressive \( \gamma_1 \) 0.1 Daily pattern adapts faster \( \gamma_2 \) 0.5 Weekly pattern adapts faster

Lower values give more stable, smoother forecasts; higher ones a more reactive but noisier model. A weekly component is updated once a week, so \( \gamma_2 \) is high enough for a lasting change in a weekday's hours to be half learned the week after it; the first week sets each one outright (see How It Works). The values were chosen by simulating office-hours, always-on, idle, and noisy workloads.

docs.title: Proving It
docs.text:
A forecasting mistake, such as a wrong slot, a late wake or a weekend false wake, would otherwise show only after weeks in a real cluster. The repo's simulator, internal/forecast/sim, runs the operator's own forecast engine and decision rules through simulated time a minute at a time, as the operator looks at a ManagedWorkload: the activity clock pausing an idle workload, the forecast holding off a pause, autoResume waking it 15 minutes ahead of an hour expected busy, the doorman or an activity query waking it, the warm-up after a wake, each hour's peak fed to the forecast, and operator restarts through the state saved in status. Months of traffic take milliseconds, and a test runs six weeks of office hours through both the reconciler and the simulator and finds the same wakes and pauses at the same minutes.

The tests run in CI on every change, and check, besides How Long It Takes:

  • Office hours: once learned, the workload is up at 08:45 every weekday, 25 minutes before people arrive at 09:10, paused an hour after they leave, and left asleep at weekends; at every setting, every morning from the day the forecast acts is ready, Mondays included, and it never sleeps through a morning it acts on
  • Every day, always busy, always idle, light use seen only through an activity annotation: each acts as above, and the light-use workload is ready every morning
  • Loosely kept hours: ready on most mornings once learned, woken for nothing about twice a month, for an hour or two each time; and the settings trade ready mornings for hours woken for nothing as Forecast Setting says
  • A holiday, a Saturday at work, a permanent change of hours, a workload nobody uses any more, daylight saving in New York and London, with and without --timezone, daily operator restarts, and pauses with neither the doorman nor an activity query, which never let the forecast act: as described above
  • Pausing early: on office hours, every weekday's pause comes at 18:00, with mornings as ready and the same hours learned as without it; nothing is brought forward on a holiday or the first two days of new hours, and nobody finds the workload paused who wouldn't have; someone coming back after 18:00 finds the workload paused; and without the doorman nothing is brought forward. The six weeks run through the reconciler bring the same pauses forward at the same minutes. What It Saves and Costs is measured there too
  • A queue worker with no Service, woken by a query of its queue's length and paused every night: it acts after 8 days, as behind the doorman, and from then autoResume has it up before the morning's messages
  • Learning from history: a forecast that learned four weeks of office hours has the workload ready from the first morning, and the projection made in the first week is within a day of when the forecast starts acting

go run ./hack/forecastsim runs every scenario at every setting and prints what it measured; -scenario holiday -setting eager -days shows one day by day, and -pause-early has the forecast bring pauses forward, counting the hours that saved and the uses that then found the workload paused, and -wake-on-request=false -wake-on-query runs a scenario as a queue worker its activity query wakes. -history replays a workload's recorded CPU instead, as a percentage of its requests: a Prometheus range query's JSON, or CSV of time,percent rows, a step of at most seven minutes apart.

On your own cluster, kubectl hybernate forecast replays the forecast over each workload's own Prometheus history: whether it would act opted in today, and over the last two weeks, how many mornings it would have had each workload ready and how often it would have woken one for nothing. Named, as kubectl hybernate forecast api -n orders, it shows one workload's forecast: for one Hybernate manages, what its own forecast is doing, from its status and saved state, whatever history Prometheus has: its phase, the hours of the day and week it has seen, how many hours it has learned from history and live, whether it's acting or when it's expected to, why, and the hours of the next day it expects busy; then the replay of its history, day by day, when there's enough of it.

docs.title: Idle Detection
docs.text:
Hybernate keeps an activity clock for every ManagedWorkload: the last time anything showed the workload was in use. When the clock is older than idlePolicy.idleAfter, the workload is paused: scaled to zero, keeping its replica count and a resource snapshot. Any single sign of activity resets it. With idlePolicy.pauseEarly, a confident forecast can bring the pause forward (see Pausing Early).

There's no learning period. A new workload can be paused as soon as it has gone idleAfter without activity.

managedworkload.yaml
spec:
  idlePolicy:
    idleAfter: 1h        # default
    activity:
      cpuThreshold: 10   # percent of CPU requests; default

docs.title: What counts as activity
docs.text:
Every source is checked, and the most recent one wins. None has priority over another.

Source Counts as activity when Setup CPU Usage is above activity.cpuThreshold% of the CPU requested by the pods reporting it Requires metrics-server Deploy The target's pod template changes: a new image, environment variable, or other template edit None hybernate.io/last-activity The annotation holds a time newer than the last recorded activity Set by your own tooling hybernate.io/active-until The annotation holds a time in the future (a hold, not an activity time) Set by your own tooling hybernate.io/last-request The annotation holds a time newer than the last recorded activity Set by the doorman when it holds a request for the paused workload Prometheus Any query in activity.prometheus returns a value above zero --prometheus-url; see the Prometheus Activity Guide

Changes to the replica count don't count as a deploy, so Hybernate's own pause and resume never look like activity.

Memory isn't a source: it stays allocated whether or not anyone uses the workload.

CPU is measured for the containers in the target's pod template, including native sidecars (init containers with restartPolicy: Always). Sidecars injected when the pod is created, such as an Istio or Linkerd proxy, aren't counted: their own background work isn't use of the workload, and they aren't in the template's requests. Cost does count them, since they cost the same as any container and pausing frees them too.

Usage is measured over the pods metrics-server reports and compared with what those pods request, so one pod serving while the others are Pending or crash-looping, or before new pods from a scale-up report, reads at its own utilization rather than a fraction of it. Usage is compared with what those containers request in a running pod, not in the template, so a request set when the pod was created counts: a LimitRange default, or a Vertical Pod Autoscaler's recommendation. The pod read is a running one of the target's current revision: a failed pod, such as one evicted, keeps the requests of whatever revision it ran until it's cleaned up, and isn't read. The request is read again every 5 minutes, at once when the target's spec changes, and on every check while it's unclear which revision a replica will have, as during a Deployment's rollout. With no pod running, the newest that's starting is read, such as a Pending one in a Recreate rollout, and only with none at all are the template's requests used, a container that sets only a CPU limit taken to request its limit, as Kubernetes does.

docs.title: Activity annotations
docs.text:
Set either annotation on the ManagedWorkload or on its target Deployment or StatefulSet. Values are RFC 3339 times.

# Record activity now, e.g. from a developer portal when someone opens an environment
kubectl annotate deployment my-api -n staging --overwrite \
  hybernate.io/last-activity="$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)"

# Keep the workload awake until a time, e.g. during a demo
kubectl annotate deployment my-api -n staging --overwrite \
  hybernate.io/active-until="2026-10-03T18:00:00Z"

From a terminal, kubectl hybernate wake sets them for you and waits until the workload is Running.

  • A last-activity time in the future is treated as now. Use active-until for a deliberate hold, since it says when the hold ends.
  • Annotations can only keep a workload awake or wake it. They never cause a pause.
  • A value that isn't an RFC 3339 time, such as epoch seconds or a space in place of the T, is ignored everywhere: it neither keeps an awake workload awake nor wakes a paused one. Each such value gets one InvalidActivityAnnotation warning event on the ManagedWorkload, naming the annotation and where it is.

docs.title: The decision
docs.text:
A workload at zero replicas that Hybernate didn't pause isn't checked at all: it's already off, and left that way. For any other, each check runs in this order:

  1. CPU, or a configured Prometheus query, can't be read: stay awake (see below).
  2. active-until is in the future: stay awake.
  3. The last activity is less than idleAfter ago: stay awake, unless pauseEarly is on and the forecast brings the pause forward: the last activity was at least 20 minutes ago, the forecast is confident every hour until idleAfter would run out, and at least the hour under way and the next, is quiet, and a request would wake the workload through the doorman once it's paused. Then the pause goes on through the steps below, as if the clock had run out.
  4. The forecast is confident (shown as DailyActive or later, dailyPhase: Active) and predicts utilization above cpuThreshold in the hour under way or the next: stay awake. The IdleVetoed condition is True, with reason ForecastExpectsDemand and a message naming the hour, while this holds the pause back, and an IdleVetoed event marks the start of each veto. The hour after one far quieter than it forecast, as on a holiday, the forecast doubts what it expects and holds nothing back (see Anomaly Detection).
  5. Another workload that depends on this one is awake, or dependsOn forms a cycle: stay awake (HeldByDependents or DependencyCycle).
  6. Otherwise the clock has run out, or the forecast brought the pause forward. The phase becomes Idle, with an IdleDetected event, or a PausedEarly event naming the hours the forecast expects to be quiet, and the workload is paused.

Without an idlePolicy, none of this runs, and the workload is only paused when someone asks.

A pause request, from kubectl hybernate pause, runs the clock out at once. Steps 1 and 3 don't apply, and nor does the hour Hybernate waits after a GitOps tool undid its last pause, since someone asked; an active-until hold, awake dependents and a dependsOn cycle still keep the workload up, and so does the forecast (step 4) unless the request comes with hybernate.io/pause-overrides-forecast: "true", which kubectl hybernate pause --yes sets. A request held back is answered with the reason.

With dryRun: true, the phase still becomes Idle and the IdleDetected or PausedEarly event carries a [dry-run] prefix, but nothing is changed. If activity resumes, the phase goes back to Running. See Dry Run.

The forecast never blocks a pause until it's confident, so a workload with no history is handled by the clock alone.

docs.title: When a source can't be read
docs.text:
Hybernate never pauses a workload while one of its activity sources can't be read: without that data a busy workload looks idle. Nor does it count that time as idle: a check where a source can't be read doesn't count as watching, so a source out for longer than the gap allowed below restarts the clock (lastActivitySource: unobserved), and once the source is back, the workload pauses only after a full idleAfter in which every source saw nothing. A shorter blind spot, such as the minute before a woken workload's new pods have metrics, leaves its last activity as it was. A Prometheus query that answers "no requests in the last 5 minutes" as it comes back doesn't make the hour before it look idle. For CPU, the MetricsAvailable condition says why:

Reason Meaning NoPodMetrics The target's Ready pods have had no metrics for over 3 minutes. Check that metrics-server is installed and reports them (kubectl top pods). A warning event says so once NoCPURequests The target's running pods request no CPU for its containers, or, with none running, its pod template requests none, so utilization can't be measured. Set CPU requests, or a default in the namespace's LimitRange. MetricsUnavailable The Metrics API itself failed, or didn't answer within 2 seconds. The condition message has the error. Once it fails, it isn't read again for a minute, so every workload's check fails at once rather than waiting out a timeout.

A target scaled to zero isn't an error: it has no usage, which is real data. Nor are new pods: a pod has no metrics until it runs, and for a scrape or two of metrics-server's after, so after a wake or a rollout MetricsAvailable is Unknown, with no warning, until they arrive: reason NoReadyPods while none of the target's pods is Ready, then AwaitingPodMetrics for up to 3 minutes. Only Ready pods that go on without metrics after that are NoPodMetrics.

For Prometheus queries, the PrometheusAvailable condition reports EndpointNotConfigured or QueryFailed. A query that answers but has never matched a series, as one naming a metric or label that doesn't exist does, is reported by PrometheusQueryEmpty=True and a warning event, since it can never keep the workload awake; see the Prometheus Activity Guide.

docs.title: Restarts and outages
docs.text:
The clock is stored in status.activity, so it survives operator restarts. While a workload is awake it's checked about once a minute; the clock's timestamps are written to status at most every 5 minutes, along with cost, and immediately whenever the phase or a condition changes, or when new activity is more than a tenth of idleAfter (at most 5 minutes) ahead of what's written. Activity seen between writes is held in memory, so it still counts, and what's written is never far enough behind for a restart to pause a workload early.

If the operator stops watching a workload for a while, it can't know whether there was activity in the meantime, so the clock restarts from the time it resumes watching (lastActivitySource: unobserved). How long a gap it allows depends on idleAfter: half of it, but at least 2 minutes (two missed checks) and at most 7. After a restart or a change of leader, the operator only has what was written, which can be up to 5 minutes behind its last check, so any gap over 2 minutes restarts the clock: a restart can delay pauses by up to idleAfter. An outage can delay a pause, but never cause one.

status:
  activity:
    lastActivityTime: "2026-10-02T09:14:00Z"
    lastActivitySource: cpu    # created, woke, request, cpu, rollout, annotation, prometheus, unobserved, or scaled-up
    pauseAt: "2026-10-02T10:14:00Z"
    lastEvaluatedTime: "2026-10-02T09:41:00Z"

docs.title: Waking up
docs.text:
A paused workload wakes when:

  • A request reaches one of its Services. The request is held while the workload starts, then answered; see Wake on Request.
  • A hybernate.io/last-activity, last-request or active-until annotation on the ManagedWorkload or its target changes after the pause began to an RFC 3339 time, whatever time it states, so a clock that's behind the operator's can't lose a wake. Only a change counts: the pause records the annotations as they stood, so a value set before it, even one stating a later time, doesn't wake it. kubectl hybernate wake sets one, and this is how a "start environment" button in a developer portal works.
  • A Prometheus activity query shows activity: the queries are run about once a minute while it's paused, as while it's awake. One that already showed activity as a requested pause began wakes it only once it has been quiet, so it doesn't undo the request, and one that can't be evaluated never wakes it.
  • autoResume: true is set and a confident forecast (dailyPhase: Active) predicts utilization above cpuThreshold for the current hour, or for the next hour once it's 15 minutes away, so the workload is ready before people arrive; not the hour after one far quieter than it forecast.
  • Something other than Hybernate scales it up, such as kubectl scale.
  • Dry-run is turned on: dry-run never leaves a workload paused.

Each wake restarts the clock, so a woken workload gets a full idleAfter before it can pause again, unless pauseEarly is on and the forecast expects the coming hours quiet: then the pause can come 20 minutes after the wake. The clock records lastActivitySource: request when a held request woke it, prometheus when an activity query did, scaled-up when something else scaled it up, and woke for any other wake.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text: Every ManagedWorkload moves through a defined set of phases. The operator drives transitions based on workload activity, forecasts, and pauses asked for with kubectl hybernate pause. Its one action is to pause: it never deletes a workload or its storage.

docs.title: Phases
docs.text:
(new) ──► Running ──► Idle ──► Pausing ──► Paused
             ▲                                │
             │                                ▼
             └──────────────────────────── Resuming
Phase Description (none) A ManagedWorkload that has just been created has no phase until its first reconcile, which sets Running. kubectl hybernate status shows it as creating. (Creating is accepted by the API but never set.) Running Workload is active. Its activity clock is evaluated on each reconcile. Idle No activity for idleAfter, or a pause was requested. The operator pauses it, or in dry-run reports the pause it would make. Pausing What the pause will change is recorded, and the workload is being scaled to zero and its pods stopped. Paused Workload is at zero replicas. Resuming Previous replica count is being restored. Transitions to Running when the pods are Ready, or when Hybernate stops waiting for those that aren't.

A workload already at zero replicas, scaled there by a person, a pipeline or KEDA, stays Running with the ScaledToZero condition: Hybernate only pauses what's running, and only wakes what it paused. See Workloads Already at Zero.

docs.title: Automatic
docs.text:
• Running → Idle: No activity for idleAfter, or with pauseEarly, for 20 minutes before hours a confident forecast expects quiet (see Pausing Early); no active-until hold, no confident forecast of demand, no awake dependents, CPU (and any Prometheus query) readable, and at least one replica; see Idle Detection
  • Idle → Pausing: Right away, unless the workload is in dry-run, or a GitOps tool undid its last pause within the hour
  • Idle → Running: Activity resumes (in dry-run, or while a GitOps tool's undoing holds the pause off; otherwise the pause has already started), or the workload is scaled to zero outside Hybernate
  • Paused → Resuming: A request to its Service, a change to an activity annotation since the pause, a Prometheus activity query showing activity, autoResume ahead of forecast demand, or dry-run being turned on
  • Paused → Running: Something other than Hybernate scales it up, see GitOps tools; or Hybernate lets go of it, see When Hybernate Lets Go. The same goes for a workload still Pausing once Hybernate has scaled it to zero (status.pause.pausedAt is set), while its pods stop: it isn't scaled back down
  • Resuming → Running: Something other than Hybernate scales it back to zero after the resume has scaled it up (status.pause.resumedAt): it's left off, with ScaledToZero, rather than scaled up again. Otherwise, every replica it was restored to is Ready. Short of that, Hybernate stops waiting 2 minutes after the first replica is Ready, or, while none is, once the Deployment's progressDeadlineSeconds has passed since the scale-up (10 minutes by default, and for a StatefulSet). Stopping short sets ResumeIncomplete until every replica is Ready, and with none Ready, requests fail until one is, since the doorman no longer holds them. A StatefulSet with the default OrderedReady pod management starts its pods one at a time, so a slow-starting one may have only its first pods Ready when the 2 minutes are up: it runs with those, and the rest follow. The wait starts once its waitForReady dependencies serve; see Dependencies

docs.title: On request
docs.text:
• Running or Idle → Pausing → Paused: kubectl hybernate pause, which sets a new hybernate.io/pause-requested value. The idle clock runs out at once, and the workload is paused by the rules of an idle pause, except that the hour after a GitOps conflict doesn't hold it back. A forecast expecting demand within the hour declines it, saying when, unless the request overrides the forecast. In dry-run it goes Running → Idle instead, as a would-be pause. See Pause Now
  • Paused → Resuming → Running: kubectl hybernate wake, which changes an activity annotation, or any of the automatic wakes above: a requested pause wakes like any other

docs.title: Idempotency
docs.text:
Every lifecycle operation is idempotent. What a pause changes is recorded in status.pause (previousReplicas, the KEDA ScaledObject and its own paused-replicas value) in the same status write that enters Pausing, before anything is scaled, so that:

  • A pause interrupted at any point, by a restart or a conflicting write, is finished or undone from the record
  • Resuming restores the recorded replica count, not a hardcoded value
  • Re-pausing an already-paused workload is a no-op
  • Before the workload is scaled, the record is also copied to its hybernate.io/paused-from annotation, until it's handed back. A ManagedWorkload that loses its status while paused, to a restore without status or by being created again, takes the pause up from that copy (PauseRecovered): back to Paused if the workload is still at zero, or released if it has been scaled up since. One left Pausing, Paused or Resuming with neither had nothing scaled, and is Running again (PauseRecordLost)

This means the operator can crash and restart at any point without leaving workloads in an inconsistent state. spec.target can't be changed once set, so a paused target is never left behind at zero: create another ManagedWorkload to manage another workload.

docs.title: Status Conditions
docs.text:
The operator sets standard Kubernetes conditions on the CR, each with Reason, Message, and LastTransitionTime. A condition appears once it first applies. After that, one that no longer applies is shown as False, with the reason listed after False below, rather than removed; only GitOpsConflict and Autoscaled are removed instead.

Type True means Reasons TargetAvailable The Deployment or StatefulSet exists and Hybernate manages it TargetExists; False: TargetNotFound, TargetIgnored (labelled hybernate.io/ignore) MetricsAvailable CPU can be measured, so the activity clock and the forecast can run MetricsReported; Unknown, while new pods have no metrics yet: NoReadyPods, AwaitingPodMetrics; False: NoPodMetrics, NoCPURequests, MetricsUnavailable PrometheusAvailable The Prometheus activity queries answer; only set when there are some QueriesEvaluated; False: QueryFailed, EndpointNotConfigured PrometheusQueryEmpty A Prometheus activity query has matched no series since it was first evaluated, which usually means a misspelt metric or label; informational, it doesn't stop a pause NoSeries; False: QueriesMatchSeries IdleVetoed It's idle, but a confident forecast expects demand in the coming hour, so the pause waits; the message names the hour ForecastExpectsDemand; False: NotVetoed WakeOnRequest Requests to the paused workload's Services wake it DoormanRouted; False: see When a workload isn't routed (NoServices, ServedByOtherPods, UnsupportedIPFamily, UnsupportedLoadBalancer, ForwarderNotReady, DoormanUnavailable, NoFreePort, TooManyPorts, RoutingFailed, DoormanDisabled, NodeLocalTraffic), TurnedOff while its wake.onRequest is false, or NotPaused, TargetNotFound, DuplicateTarget once routing is removed. A problem with its Services stays once it's awake, its message starting at its last pause: HeldByDependents It's kept awake for the workloads that depend on it DependentsAwake; False: NoAwakeDependents, or NotIdle once its own activity restarts its clock WaitingForDependencies Its resume waits for a waitForReady dependency to be Ready DependencyNotReady; False: DependenciesReady; DependencyWontStart, naming a dependency it doesn't wait for because it can't start or wasn't Ready in time; or DependencyCycle, naming one that waits for it in turn DependencyCycle dependsOn forms a cycle through it, so it won't pause DependencyCycle; False: NoCycle DependencyNotFound A dependsOn workload doesn't exist, or can't be seen DependencyNotFound, or DependencyNotVisible when it's only outside watchNamespaces or not readable; False: DependenciesFound, NoDependencies DependencyNotAllowed A dependency, declared or learned, is in another namespace whose hybernate.io/dependents-from doesn't list this one, so it isn't held, woken or waited for DependencyNotAllowed; False: DependenciesAllowed, NoDependencies DuplicateTarget Another, older ManagedWorkload manages the same target, so this one does nothing, after handing back a pause it had made DuplicateTarget; False: Resolved Protected Its namespace is protected, it's Hybernate's own operator or doorman, or it's a StatefulSet that deletes its PVCs when scaled down, so it's never paused ProtectedNamespace, HybernateComponent, PVCsDeletedOnScaleDown; False: NotProtected PauseRequest The last pause request paused the workload, or found it paused; False says why it didn't. It stays until the next request, saying what happened and when, such as paused as requested at 2026-10-21 03:32 UTC Paused, AlreadyPaused; False: DryRun, ForecastExpectsDemand, ActiveUntil, HeldByDependents, DependencyCycle, Protected, ScaledToZero, TargetNotFound, TargetIgnored, DuplicateTarget GitOpsConflict A GitOps tool undid its last pause; removed once a pause holds for an hour. See GitOps tools PauseUndone ResumeIncomplete The last resume stopped waiting with some replicas not Ready, and the workload runs with those that are, until they all are; see Workload resumed with replicas not Ready ReplicasNotReady; False: AllReplicasReady PauseIncomplete The last pause stopped waiting for its pods with some still running, after their termination grace period and a minute more, and the workload is Paused regardless; see Workload paused with pods still running PodsStillRunning; False: PodsStopped, NotPaused Autoscaled An HPA or KEDA ScaledObject scales it, and its range; removed when neither does. See HPA and KEDA HPA, KEDA ScaledToZero It was scaled to zero outside Hybernate, so Hybernate leaves it off: it doesn't pause it, wake it, or route requests for it until its replicas are set above zero ScaledToZero; False: HasReplicas

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
User-visible state changes emit Kubernetes events that show up in kubectl describe, each once, when the change happens:

  • Lifecycle: IdleDetected, PausedEarly (the forecast brought the pause forward, with pauseEarly), PauseRequested, Paused, Resumed, ActivityResumed (in dry-run, with what the would-be pause would have freed)
  • A pause record lost from status: PauseRecovered (taken up again from the target's hybernate.io/paused-from), PauseRecordLost (a warning: nothing to finish it from)
  • A pause request Hybernate didn't act on: an event whose reason says why, the same as the PauseRequest condition's
  • What woke it: WokeByActivity, WokenByRequest (from the doorman), AutoResume, ScaledUp, DryRunWake
  • Scaled to zero outside Hybernate, and left off: ScaledToZero
  • What holds it awake: IdleVetoed, HeldByDependents, DependencyCycle
  • A GitOps tool undoing a pause, and the conflict ending: GitOpsConflict, GitOpsConflictResolved
  • Dependencies: DependencyWontStart and DependencyCycle (warnings: a resume that starts without waiting for a waitForReady dependency), DependencyWakeFailed (a warning: a dependency couldn't be woken)
  • Problems: TargetNotFound, DuplicateTarget, NoPodMetrics, NoCPURequests, MetricsUnavailable, QueryFailed, EndpointNotConfigured, PrometheusQueryEmpty, InvalidActivityAnnotation, RoutingFailed, UnsupportedLoadBalancer, NoReadinessProbe (a routed workload whose pods have no readiness probe, which requests that wake it may reach before its app can answer; see Readiness probes), RequestNotServed, Protected, ResumeIncomplete (a resume that stopped waiting for replicas not Ready, in place of Resumed; AllReplicasReady once they are), PauseIncomplete (a pause that stopped waiting for pods that didn't stop, in place of Paused), HandBackAbandoned (a ManagedWorkload in a namespace being deleted letting go of its workload), ManagedByAnotherInstall (a ManagedWorkload this install leaves to the one that took it on)
  • The forecast: PredictionFed each hour it learns, RegimeChange when it's demoted, ForecastReset when its saved state can't be read, and, when Hybernate begins managing a workload, ForecastLearnedHistory once it has learned the workload's CPU history from Prometheus, ForecastLearningLive when there's none to learn from, and the warning ForecastHistoryUnavailable when it couldn't be read
  • Learned dependencies: DependenciesLearned
  • With the optional forwarder for GKE NEGs: ForwarderStarted when it starts beside a paused workload, ForwarderStopped when it's removed after the workload wakes

Events about the workload's own Deployment or StatefulSet, from the opt-in controller, are on that workload: Managed, NoLongerManaged, InvalidSetting, LabelIgnored, Protected.

In dry-run, the events for decisions it holds back carry a [dry-run] prefix; see Dry Run.

docs.title: Wake on Request
docs.text:
A paused workload has no pods, so nothing answers its Service. With wake on request, the first request wakes it instead: the connection is held while the workload starts, then passed to one of its Ready pods. The caller usually sees one slow response, not an error; What the caller sees lists when it doesn't.

It's on by default for every workload Hybernate pauses on its own. There's nothing to configure.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Hybernate runs a small proxy, the doorman, as its own Deployment (two replicas, with a PodDisruptionBudget) next to the operator.

  1. When a workload pauses, the operator finds every Service that selects its pods and adds an extra EndpointSlice to each, one per IP family, pointing at the doorman's pods on a port of their own (20000-29999). The Service, its ClusterIP, and its DNS name don't change, so callers and Ingresses need no changes. IPv4, IPv6 and dual-stack Services are all supported.
  2. A connection to the Service reaches the doorman. If one of the Service's pods is already Ready, because the workload is waking or another workload's pods serve the Service, the connection goes straight to it. Otherwise, once the caller has sent something, the doorman holds the connection and sets hybernate.io/last-request on the ManagedWorkload, which wakes it the same way as an activity annotation. A WokenByRequest event names the Service, and once the workload is Running, its clock shows lastActivitySource: request.
  3. The doorman watches the Service's own EndpointSlices. As soon as a pod is Ready, it connects to one of the Ready pods and passes the held connection through, including any bytes the caller already sent. Ready is what the pod's readiness probe says, so the app needs one that passes only once it can serve; see Readiness probes.
  4. Once the workload is Running, the operator removes the doorman's EndpointSlices and traffic goes straight to the pods again. For 30 seconds after that, the doorman still passes connections that reach it to the Ready pods, without waking anything, while kube-proxy and load balancers catch up.

The doorman works on TCP connections, not HTTP requests, so it handles any TCP protocol: HTTP, gRPC, Postgres, Redis. Waking a workload also wakes its dependencies.

Ingress controllers, Gateway API implementations, and cloud load balancers that read EndpointSlices reach the doorman the same way. See Compatibility for which have been checked.

WakeOnRequest=True   DoormanRouted   requests are held and wake the workload

docs.title: Readiness probes
docs.text:
The doorman passes a held request on as soon as one of the workload's pods is Ready, and Kubernetes decides Ready from the pod's readiness probe. A pod without one is Ready as soon as its containers start, which is often before the app inside can answer: while it loads its configuration or schema, connects to its database, or warms a cache. The request that woke it then gets whatever the app answers while it starts, such as a 503, instead of waiting for it. An app that isn't listening yet is fine: the doorman tries again every second until maxWait. Wake on request relies on a readiness probe that passes only once the app can serve:

deployment.yaml
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready   # answers 200 only once the app can serve requests
              port: 8080
            periodSeconds: 2

A short periodSeconds passes held requests on sooner once the app is ready. A startupProbe gates readiness too, and a tcpSocket probe on the app's port is enough for an app that only listens once it's ready. Hybernate reads the workload's pod template when it routes a paused workload: when none of its containers has a readiness or startup probe, and the pod has no readiness gates, the WakeOnRequest condition says so, and a NoReadinessProbe warning event points here, once each pause.

docs.title: What wakes a workload, and what doesn't
docs.text:
The caller What happens Sends bytes: an HTTP request, a TLS handshake, a database protocol's first message Held, and the workload wakes Connects and sends nothing for 3 seconds Held, and the workload wakes: it's taken for a protocol where the server speaks first, such as MySQL Connects and closes without sending anything, like a TCP health check Closed; nothing wakes An HTTP GET or HEAD from a known probe, scraper or uptime monitor: one whose User-Agent starts with kube-probe/, Prometheus/, Blackbox Exporter/, vm_promscrape, GrafanaAgent/, Alloy/, OpenTelemetry Collector, otelcol, Datadog Agent/, Datadog/Synthetics, ELB-HealthChecker/, Amazon-Route53-Health-Check-Service, GoogleStackdriverMonitoring-UptimeChecks, Envoy/HC, Mozilla/5.0+(compatible; UptimeRobot/, Pingdom.com_bot, NewRelicPinger/, Uptime-Kuma/ or Gatus/ Answered 503 Service Unavailable with Connection: close while no pod is Ready; nothing wakes. Probes, scrapers and monitors would otherwise keep a workload awake forever. Once a pod is Ready they're passed through like any other request An HTTP GET or HEAD from Google Cloud's load balancer health check, User-Agent: GoogleHC/ Answered 200 OK while no pod is Ready; nothing wakes. Google's load balancers send nothing to a backend that fails its health check, so told the workload is down, they'd drop the request that should wake it. Once a pod is Ready it's passed through like any other request An HTTP GET or HEAD whose User-Agent starts with one you added with the Helm value doorman.healthCheckUserAgents, such as an in-house uptime monitor's. Any of these, built in or added, also matches when it follows (compatible;, as in Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; MyCorpMonitor/3.1) from a monitor that presents itself as a browser Answered 503 as above; nothing wakes Any other method from those agents, such as a Prometheus remote write or an Alertmanager notification POST Held, and the workload wakes: it's data for the workload, not a check on it An HTTP request for a hidden file: a path with a part that starts with a dot, such as /.env, /.git/config or /.aws/credentials, except under /.well-known/ Answered 404 Not Found; nothing wakes. Scanners probe every address on the internet for these, hunting for leaked secrets, and no app serves them to its users

Your own health checkers and scrapers are recognised once you add their User-Agent prefixes, cluster-wide:

doorman:
  healthCheckUserAgents: ["MyCorpMonitor/", "status-checker"]

To keep the doorman off a port altogether, such as a metrics port something else scrapes, list it on the Service. Ports are named in the Service's ports, and the annotation takes either the name or the number:

kind: Service
metadata:
  annotations:
    hybernate.io/doorman-ignore-ports: "metrics"   # or "9090", or both: "metrics,9090"
spec:
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
    - name: metrics
      port: 9090

Listed ports are never routed, so connections to them fail while the workload is paused, as they would without Hybernate.

docs.title: Health checks the doorman can't recognise
docs.text:
The doorman can only tell a health check from a real caller by reading it. Two kinds reach a paused workload on its traffic port and wake it every time they run, so it never stays paused for longer than their interval:

  • HTTPS and other TLS health checks. The request is encrypted, so the doorman can't see its User-Agent. AWS target groups that use HTTPS check over HTTPS by default, as do Google Cloud backend services that use HTTPS or HTTP/2.
  • HTTP checks and scrapers whose User-Agent isn't recognised, such as an uptime monitor you haven't added to doorman.healthCheckUserAgents.

hybernate.io/doorman-ignore-ports can't help when the checked port is the traffic port, since ignoring it would stop requests waking the workload too. Instead, either:

  • Check over plain HTTP. The AWS and Google Cloud health checkers send a User-Agent the doorman recognises, so it answers them without waking anything: AWS's 503, Google's 200, as below.
  • Check a port of its own, one the workload serves only for health checks, and list it in hybernate.io/doorman-ignore-ports. Not behind a GKE Ingress or Gateway: nothing answers an ignored port while the workload is paused, so Google's load balancer sees no healthy backend and sends nothing on; keep its check on the traffic port, over plain HTTP.

Either way, most load balancers see the workload as unhealthy while it's paused, as they would without Hybernate, and still send requests when every target is unhealthy: AWS's Application and Network Load Balancers fail open, so the first request reaches the doorman and wakes the workload. Google Cloud's Application Load Balancers, behind a GKE Ingress or Gateway, don't: until a backend passes its health check they answer 502 and send nothing on. So the doorman answers Google's health check, GoogleHC/, with 200 OK while the workload is paused, without waking it, and holds the request that follows. Check any other load balancer before relying on wake on request behind it.

docs.title: Environments on the public internet
docs.text:
Wake on request wakes a paused workload for any request it can't recognise as a health check, and on the public internet most requests are robots: search engine crawlers, and scanners that try every address for known weaknesses. Many of them present an ordinary browser's User-Agent on purpose, so no list of agents can keep up with them. A paused workload anyone on the internet can reach is woken by them every few minutes, and frees little.

The doorman turns away the scanners hunting for leaked secrets in hidden files, as above, but not the rest. Put non-production environments behind a VPN, single sign-on at the ingress, or an allowlist of your offices' and VPN's addresses. That keeps the robots away from them, which pausing needs, and keeps unfinished work away from the internet, which a staging or preview environment needs anyway.

docs.title: Services shared with other workloads
docs.text:
A Service is routed to the doorman only while none of its pods is Ready. When several workloads sit behind one Service, such as a canary and a stable Deployment, traffic goes to whichever has Ready pods, and a paused one behind it reports WakeOnRequest=False with reason ServedByOtherPods. Once every workload behind the Service is paused, the Service is routed and a request wakes them.

The operator reads the Service's own EndpointSlices from the API server when it decides, since it doesn't cache other workloads' endpoints, and decides again every 30 seconds while another workload's pods serve the Service. So a Service whose other pods all go is routed within 30 seconds; until then, requests to it fail as they would without Hybernate.

docs.title: Browsers
docs.text:
A browser opening a paused workload doesn't sit on a blank tab. The doorman answers straight away with a page that says the environment is starting, and reloads itself every 3 seconds. It shows the address the person opened, so it reads as part of their environment, and, once the workload is Resuming, how long it has been starting. It names no namespace, workload or Service. As soon as any of the workload's pods is Ready, the next reload is passed through to the app.

The page is only for a browser loading a page: a GET or HEAD with Sec-Fetch-Mode: navigate, which browsers send when you open a URL, or, from older browsers, one that asks for HTML. Scripts' requests, API clients, form posts, WebSockets, TLS, and other protocols are held as usual. The doorman tells them apart from the first bytes the caller sends, then passes those bytes on unchanged when it holds the connection. It reads up to 16 KiB of a request's headers; longer ones, as large single sign-on cookies can make them, are judged by the headers in those first 16 KiB, which browsers send before their cookies.

The page is sent as 503 Service Unavailable with Cache-Control: no-store, Retry-After: 3 and X-Robots-Tag: noindex, so caches, crawlers, and monitors don't mistake it for the app. Because it answers at once, a proxy's timeout doesn't matter for browsers, however long the workload takes to start.

A browser only reaches the doorman if it asks the server. Pages an app serves without a Cache-Control header, as static file servers often do, can be shown from the browser's cache instead, so a reload of a page opened a moment ago may show the cached copy rather than the waking-up page. Apps that send Cache-Control: no-cache for their HTML, as most do so that new releases take effect, always reach the doorman.

To hold browsers too, set:

spec:
  wake:
    page: false

For a workload opted in with the label, set the annotation hybernate.io/wake-page: "false" on it instead.

docs.title: How long a connection is held
docs.text:
The doorman holds each connection for up to wake.maxWait, 2 minutes by default and at most 1 hour, which is the most the ManagedWorkload accepts. If no pod is Ready by then, it closes the connection. The wake carries on, so a retry a little later succeeds.

spec:
  wake:
    maxWait: 5m     # a slow starter, such as a database replaying its log

For a workload opted in with the label, set the annotation hybernate.io/wake-max-wait: "5m" on it instead.

Callers have their own timeouts. Most HTTP clients wait at least 30 seconds, and browsers wait minutes. A proxy in front of the Service can give up sooner: ingress-nginx closes an upstream request after 60 seconds by default. For a workload that takes longer than that to start, raise the Ingress timeout to match maxWait:

metadata:
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "120"

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
So that a flood of connections can't exhaust the doorman, or wake workloads faster than the cluster can start them:

  • Each doorman pod holds at most 2048 connections: at most 256 for one workload, at most 1024 from one source IP, and at most 128 from one source IP for one workload. A connection over these caps is closed at once, with nothing sent.
  • Each doorman pod passes through at most 1024 connections at once, at most 512 from one source IP. A connection over these caps is held, as if the workload weren't Ready yet, until a place frees or maxWait runs out. A passed-through connection that carries nothing either way for 10 minutes is closed, so a caller that vanished without closing doesn't keep its place; one whose client or server pings, as WebSockets and database pools do, stays open. Once the workload is awake and its route starts draining, connections still passing through the doorman are closed after 5 minutes, so long-lived callers reconnect to the pods directly.
  • Wakes are rate-limited per source IP (a burst of 30, then one every 2 seconds) and overall (a burst of 200, then 10 a second). Only a request that would actually wake a paused workload counts, and one refused overall doesn't use up its source's allowance. A caller whose wake is over the limit isn't turned away: a browser gets the waking-up page, anything else is held, and the wake is retried every 2 seconds until the allowance lets it through or maxWait runs out.
  • While a connection is held, the doorman reads what the caller sends, so that a caller who gives up is let go at once: up to 1MiB per connection, and 32MiB across all of them. The first 8KiB of each doesn't count towards the 32MiB, so a caller who sent an ordinary request and left is let go at once even while large uploads have used it up. A larger request body waits in the network until the workload is up, or until other held connections free some of the 32MiB, and a caller who leaves partway through one is let go only then. A caller that closes its connection has left, whatever its protocol, and is never passed to the workload: over TCP, closing and shutting down only the sending side look the same, and nearly every caller that does either has given up. So a client that sends its request and then shuts down its side to wait for the answer, as nc -N does, is dropped while the workload is asleep; leave the connection open instead.

The source IP is the address the doorman sees, which for traffic through an ingress controller is the controller's pod. That's why the caps are per workload as well as per source: every user behind one ingress pod shares its address, and a burst to one environment mustn't crowd out the others. The cap on one workload, whatever the source, keeps one that never becomes Ready from taking every place.

When a doorman pod shuts down, it reports itself not Ready at once, so the operator moves paused workloads' EndpointSlices to the other doorman pods: it rewrites only their endpoints, many at once, so a thousand paused Services move in about ten seconds. A rollout of the doorman starts each new pod, and waits 5 seconds after it's Ready, before stopping an old one. Only the operator can move them, and when it's being upgraded or restarted at the same time it takes a few seconds to take over, so the stopping pod goes on holding and passing through new connections for 15 seconds. Then it stops accepting them, and gives those it holds or passes through the rest of 25 seconds to finish. The chart gives the pod 40 seconds in all, after a 5-second sleep that lets kube-proxy and load balancers stop sending it new connections.

When a workload stops being routed, the doorman goes on serving its port for 30 seconds, so a browser's last refresh of the waking-up page doesn't land on a closed port, and the operator gives that port to no other workload for a minute. The operator records the minute in the ManagedWorkload's status, so a newly elected leader honours it too, and a deleted ManagedWorkload stays until it's over, up to a minute after its routing is removed.

docs.title: Turning it off
docs.text:
spec:
  wake:
    onRequest: false

Requests to the paused workload then fail, as they would without Hybernate, and it reports WakeOnRequest=False with reason TurnedOff. With the label, set hybernate.io/wake-on-request: "false". To turn it off for the whole cluster, set the Helm value doorman.enabled: false, or run the operator with --doorman-service=""; workloads then report WakeOnRequest=False with reason DoormanDisabled.

docs.title: When a workload isn't routed
docs.text:
Situation What happens No Service selects the workload, or none has a TCP port that isn't in hybernate.io/doorman-ignore-ports WakeOnRequest=False, reason NoServices. A workload no request reaches, such as a queue worker, wakes on a Prometheus activity query that sees its demand instead, such as its queue's length, and its forecast learns the hours it's paused from it A headless Service (clusterIP: None) Not routed. Callers resolve pod IPs from DNS and never reach the doorman; wake the workload with an activity annotation instead A Service without a selector, or an ExternalName Service Not routed, since its endpoints aren't the workload's pods UDP or SCTP ports Not routed; only TCP ports are A Service another workload's Ready pods serve Not routed; reason ServedByOtherPods if no Service is. See Services shared with other workloads A Service with internalTrafficPolicy: Local Not routed: kube-proxy sends each caller only to endpoints on its own node, and the doorman's pods are on one or two nodes, so most callers would reach nothing. Reason NodeLocalTraffic if no Service is routed; otherwise the condition's message names it. Wake the workload with an activity annotation, or give it a Service with the default policy (Cluster) A Service in an IP family no doorman pod has an address in Not routed; reason UnsupportedIPFamily if no Service is A Service behind GKE container-native load balancing: one a GKE Ingress uses, one with standalone NEGs, or one cloud.google.com/neg-status lists NEGs for Not routed, with a warning event, unless the optional forwarder is on. Reason UnsupportedLoadBalancer if no Service is routed; otherwise the condition stays True and its message names the Services left out. GKE's own cloud.google.com/neg: '{"ingress": true}' on every Service doesn't count by itself; see On GKE A Service behind GKE container-native load balancing, with the forwarder on, before a forwarder pod is Ready Not routed until one is, usually a few seconds after the pause. Reason ForwarderNotReady if no Service is routed, saying why, such as an image that can't be pulled or a quota that refuses the forwarder's pods; otherwise the condition's message names the Service. See GKE container-native load balancing The Deployment or StatefulSet is deleted Routing is removed, since nothing would start the pods a held request waits for. TargetAvailable=False, reason TargetNotFound; requests fail as they would without Hybernate No doorman pod is Ready WakeOnRequest=False, reason DoormanUnavailable, and routing is removed. Requests fail until a doorman pod is back All doorman ports are in use WakeOnRequest=False, reason NoFreePort. The doorman has 10,000 ports, one per paused Service port in the cluster The workload would hold more than 32 doorman ports, or its namespace more than 256 WakeOnRequest=False, reason TooManyPorts, so one tenant can't use up the ports every namespace shares. Set the caps with the Helm values doorman.portsPerWorkload and doorman.portsPerNamespace Routing failed, such as an EndpointSlice write being refused, or an EndpointSlice that isn't the doorman's already having the name the doorman's would take (<service>-o<hash>), which it never overwrites WakeOnRequest=False, reason RoutingFailed, with a warning event. It's retried with backoff, from 5 seconds up to 5 minutes. Routing problems never hold up a pause or a wake

Once the workload is awake, WakeOnRequest goes to False, reason NotPaused, unless the last pause found a problem with its Services: ServedByOtherPods, NodeLocalTraffic, UnsupportedIPFamily, UnsupportedLoadBalancer or TooManyPorts. That stays, its message starting at its last pause:, since the next pause meets it again unless it's fixed, and kubectl hybernate status lists it under Needs attention while the workload runs. Every pause works routing out afresh.

docs.title: On GKE
docs.text:
GKE adds cloud.google.com/neg: '{"ingress": true}' to every new Service of a VPC-native cluster, which is the default. It asks GKE to use container-native load balancing, network endpoint groups (NEGs) of the Service's pods, only should a GKE Ingress use the Service, so Hybernate routes a Service with it like any other: callers in the cluster, and ingress controllers that read EndpointSlices, such as ingress-nginx, wake the workload.

A Service that really is in NEGs isn't routed, unless the optional forwarder is on, with reason UnsupportedLoadBalancer: GKE's NEG controller refuses endpoints whose pods are in another namespace, as the doorman's are, and can stop syncing the load balancer altogether. That's a Service:

  • that a GKE Ingress uses, one with kubernetes.io/ingress.class gce, gce-internal, gce-regional-external or gce-multi-cluster, or with no class at all, while the Service has {"ingress": true}. GKE reads only the annotation: an Ingress that sets ingressClassName isn't GKE's
  • with standalone NEGs, exposed_ports in its cloud.google.com/neg, as GKE Gateway sets on the Services its routes use
  • that GKE's NEG controller lists NEGs of pods for in cloud.google.com/neg-status

Hybernate looks again whenever an Ingress or a Service in the namespace changes, so a Service is taken off the doorman as soon as a GKE Ingress starts using it, and routed again once none does. To see what GKE has set on a Service:

kubectl get service api -n preview-42 -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations}'

Requests through a GKE Ingress on instance groups, whose Service has cloud.google.com/neg: '{"ingress": false}', reach the doorman through the Service's node port and wake a paused workload, since the doorman tells Google's health check it's up. Without the forwarder, requests through a GKE Ingress whose Service is in NEGs, or through a GKE Gateway, which always uses NEGs, don't: the Service isn't routed, and the load balancer answers 502 while the workload is paused. Wake it another way, such as kubectl hybernate wake, an activity annotation from your developer portal, or the forecast's autoResume. Or reach it through an ingress controller that reads EndpointSlices, such as ingress-nginx, in place of the GKE Ingress or behind it: the GKE Ingress then uses the ingress controller's Service, which never pauses, and the controller sends requests on to the workload's Service, which is routed.

With the forwarder on, callers in the cluster wake the workload through the Ingress's own Service too. Without it, for callers in the cluster to wake a workload whose Service a GKE Ingress uses, give them a Service of their own, which no GKE Ingress uses, so it's routed:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: api-internal
  namespace: preview-42
spec:
  selector:
    app: api
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: 8080

Turning NEGs off on the Ingress's own Service, with cloud.google.com/neg: '{"ingress": false}', gets it routed too, so requests through the Ingress wake the workload, but moves a gce Ingress onto instance groups, which needs the Service to be type: NodePort, and a gce-internal Ingress can't do without NEGs. GKE warns against changing the annotation on a Service a load balancer uses, since the change replaces the load balancer's backends.

docs.title: GKE container-native load balancing (NEGs)
docs.text:
GKE's NEG controller only accepts endpoints whose pods are in the Service's own namespace, so a Service in NEGs can't be pointed at the doorman's pods, and by default isn't routed (see On GKE). So a request through a GKE Ingress whose Service is in NEGs, or through a GKE Gateway, wakes a paused workload only with the forwarder on, an optional mode, off by default, for teams whose paused environments are reached that way. GKE uses NEGs for an Ingress's Services by default on VPC-native clusters, and always for a Gateway's. Requests to Services no GKE Ingress or Gateway uses, from inside the cluster or through other ingress controllers and load balancers, wake workloads without it.

doorman:
  negForwarder:
    enabled: true

docs.title: What it runs
docs.text:
While a workload with a Service behind NEGs is paused, the operator runs a Deployment beside it, hybernate-forwarder-<workload>, in the workload's namespace, and points that Service at the forwarder's pods instead of the doorman's. GKE's NEG controller accepts them, since they're in the Service's namespace. The forwarder passes every connection to the doorman, bytes untouched, and the doorman holds it and wakes the workload as it does any other. Once the workload is Running and its route has drained, a minute later, the operator deletes the forwarder. The ManagedWorkload owns it, so deleting the ManagedWorkload deletes it too. The workload's other Services, those no NEG uses, are routed to the doorman directly, as usual.

  • Size and cost: two pods by default (doorman.negForwarder.replicas), spread across nodes, so a node drain doesn't leave the workload unreachable while GKE registers a new pod. Each requests 10m of CPU and 32Mi of memory, limited to 64Mi (doorman.negForwarder.resources), and runs only while the workload is paused.
  • Access: it runs the operator's image as the namespace's default ServiceAccount, without its token, and needs no access to the API server. Its pods meet the Pod Security Standards' restricted level, and keep Istio's and Linkerd's sidecars out. It carries hybernate.io/ignore, so a namespace opted in with its label doesn't have Hybernate manage it.
  • Ports: it listens on the ports the workload's own pods serve, the Services' target ports, since those are the ports GKE's firewall rules let Google's load balancers reach. For a port below 1024 it sets the net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start sysctl, which the restricted level allows, rather than run as root.
  • Readiness: a forwarder pod is Ready only while it reaches the doorman on every port it passes connections to. It finds the doorman's pods through a headless Service the chart adds, hybernate-doorman-pods for a release named hybernate. Until a forwarder pod is Ready, the Service isn't routed, and the workload reports WakeOnRequest=False, reason ForwarderNotReady, with why.

To see it:

kubectl get deployments -n preview-42 -l app.kubernetes.io/name=hybernate-forwarder
kubectl get endpointslices -n preview-42 -l hybernate.io/forwarded=true

The route of a Service sent through the forwarder shows forwarded: true in the ManagedWorkload's status.doorman.

docs.title: Health checks behind NEGs
docs.text: The endpoint Google's load balancer checks is now the forwarder, which passes the check to the doorman, and the doorman answers Google's health check (User-Agent: GoogleHC/) with 200 OK, as on every route, without waking anything; every other checker still gets 503. As anywhere, an HTTPS or HTTP/2 health check can't be read, and wakes the workload every time it runs: keep the backend service's health check on the traffic port, over plain HTTP, as a GKE Ingress sets up for an HTTP backend. A port of its own doesn't work here: the forwarder listens only on the ports it routes, so a check on another fails, and Google's load balancer then sends nothing on (see Health checks the doorman can't recognise).

docs.title: Timeouts behind NEGs
docs.text:
Google's load balancer waits 30 seconds for a backend's answer by default. A browser gets the waking-up page at once, but anything else waits for the workload, so for a workload that takes longer to start, raise the backend service's timeout to match wake.maxWait. For a GKE Ingress, with a BackendConfig, which the Service names in its cloud.google.com/backend-config annotation, '{"default": "slow-start"}':

apiVersion: cloud.google.com/v1
kind: BackendConfig
metadata:
  name: slow-start
  namespace: preview-42
spec:
  timeoutSec: 120

For a GKE Gateway, set spec.default.timeoutSec in a GCPBackendPolicy.

docs.title: Network policies behind NEGs
docs.text:
The chart's doorman NetworkPolicy (networkPolicy.enabled) admits forwarders besides doorman.networkPolicy.ingressFrom, by their labels, app.kubernetes.io/name: hybernate-forwarder and hybernate.io/operator naming Hybernate's namespace, from any namespace. Anyone who can create pods can give them those labels, and so reach the doorman's routing ports, as any caller in ingressFrom can.

In the workload's namespace, a default-deny policy must let the forwarder's pods be reached by whatever reaches the workload, Google's load balancers and health checks from 130.211.0.0/22 and 35.191.0.0/16 among them, and let them reach the doorman and DNS:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-hybernate-forwarder
  namespace: preview-42
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: {app.kubernetes.io/name: hybernate-forwarder}
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - ipBlock: {cidr: 130.211.0.0/22}
        - ipBlock: {cidr: 35.191.0.0/16}
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: hybernate-system}
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: {control-plane: doorman}
      ports:
        - {port: 20000, endPort: 29999, protocol: TCP}
    - ports:
        - {port: 53, protocol: UDP}
        - {port: 53, protocol: TCP}

Add your in-cluster callers to ingress.from if apps in the cluster call the Service too.

docs.title: Limits behind NEGs
docs.text:
• Right after a pause: GKE takes a while, typically under a minute, to register the forwarder's pods in the NEG and see them pass health checks. Until it has, requests through the load balancer can get a 502, as after any scale-down, and the Service can show a SyncNetworkEndpointGroupFailed warning event from GKE, endpoint count from endpointPodMap cannot be zero, for the moment between the workload's pods going and the forwarder's arriving; GKE retries it within seconds. After a wake, the Service goes back to the workload's own pods as soon as one is Ready; the forwarder goes on passing what still reaches it to the doorman, which passes it to the workload for the 30 seconds its route drains, and is deleted a minute after the wake.
  • The caller's address: the doorman sees the forwarder's, not the caller's, so dependencies aren't learned from requests that come through it, and the doorman's per-source limits count each forwarder pod as one source. Through a load balancer, the caller is one of Google's proxies anyway.
  • Images from a private registry: the forwarder pulls the operator's image in the workload's namespace, as its default ServiceAccount, so a mirror that needs a pull secret needs it there too. GKE nodes pull from Artifact Registry in their own project without one.
  • Turning it off leaves running forwarders in place, since the operator no longer may delete them: kubectl delete deployments -A -l app.kubernetes.io/name=hybernate-forwarder.
  • With the Kustomize manifests, set it up by hand: run the operator with --neg-forwarder, --neg-forwarder-image naming its own image, and --neg-forwarder-doorman-service, grant it create and delete on Deployments, and add a headless Service selecting the doorman's pods. See Configuration.

docs.title: Network policies
docs.text:
The doorman connects to woken pods directly, from the Hybernate namespace. If a workload's namespace has a default-deny NetworkPolicy, allow ingress from the doorman:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-hybernate-doorman
  namespace: preview-42
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: hybernate-system}
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: {control-plane: doorman}

Callers reach the doorman on ports 20000-29999, so a default-deny policy on the Hybernate namespace needs to allow those too.

docs.title: Restricting who can reach the doorman
docs.text:
The doorman is a way in to every paused workload

Any client that can reach a doorman pod can reach every routed, paused workload, in any namespace, on its Service ports. The workload's own NetworkPolicy sees the doorman as the source, not the client, so a policy that admits the doorman admits everyone who can reach it. The rate limits slow a port scan through the doorman; they don't stop one.

The chart's NetworkPolicy (networkPolicy.enabled, off by default) leaves the routing ports open to every source unless you say who may use them. List the callers your paused workloads really have, such as your ingress controller's namespace and the namespaces whose apps call paused services, in doorman.networkPolicy.ingressFrom:

networkPolicy:
  enabled: true
doorman:
  networkPolicy:
    ingressFrom:
      - namespaceSelector:
          matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: ingress-nginx}
      - namespaceSelector:
          matchLabels: {team: checkout}

Each entry is a NetworkPolicy peer, so podSelector and ipBlock work too. Everyone else is refused before reaching the doorman. The chart's policy also keeps the doorman's metrics port open to namespaces labelled metrics: enabled. Setting ingressFrom without networkPolicy.enabled is refused at install, since it would create no policy and leave the doorman open. Don't add a policy of your own beside the chart's: NetworkPolicies add up, so the chart's open routing ports would still admit everyone.

Traffic from outside the cluster through a NodePort or LoadBalancer Service usually arrives with a node's address, since kube-proxy rewrites the source of connections it forwards to another node. A namespace or pod selector doesn't match a node, so with ingressFrom set those callers are refused: add your nodes' CIDRs as an ipBlock entry, or the load balancer's addresses if it preserves the client's. A routed Service with externalTrafficPolicy: Local keeps the client's address, but kube-proxy then sends it only to endpoints on the node it arrived at, so external callers reach the doorman only through nodes that run a doorman pod.

With install.yaml or the Kustomize manifests, write the policy yourself:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: hybernate-doorman-callers
  namespace: hybernate-system
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      control-plane: doorman
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: ingress-nginx}
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: {team: checkout}
      ports:
        - {port: 20000, endPort: 29999, protocol: TCP}
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring}
      ports:
        - {port: 8443, protocol: TCP}

The second rule keeps the doorman's metrics port reachable for Prometheus; leave it out if you don't scrape it.

Limit the doorman's egress too. It only ever dials Pod-backed IP endpoints of EndpointSlices the EndpointSlice controller manages, never loopback, link-local, or cloud metadata addresses (AWS's fd00:ec2::254 and Alibaba Cloud's 100.100.100.200 included), and only an address that the pod the endpoint names, in the Service's namespace, really has. Anyone who can write EndpointSlices in a namespace can forge the controller's label, but that sends the doorman only to the namespace's own pods. An egress policy enforces the same bounds in the network. The chart can create one, allowing only your pod CIDRs and the API server:

doorman:
  networkPolicy:
    egress:
      enabled: true
      podCIDRs: [10.244.0.0/16]
      apiServer: [172.18.0.2/32]   # kubectl get endpointslices -n default -l kubernetes.io/service-name=kubernetes
      apiServerPorts: [443, 6443]

List every IP family your cluster uses, and the node CIDRs too if a routed workload uses hostNetwork. apiServer is the API server's endpoint addresses, not the kubernetes Service's ClusterIP, since policies apply after the Service is resolved.

The doorman's ServiceAccount can patch ManagedWorkloads, to set hybernate.io/last-request. The chart's ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (doorman.admissionPolicy.enabled, on by default, and in the Kustomize manifests too) narrows that: it lets the ServiceAccount change only the hybernate.io/last-request and hybernate.io/last-request-from annotations. A second policy lets no one else set those two, so only the doorman can say a request woke a workload, or where it came from. See Security.

docs.title: What the caller sees
docs.text:
• A browser: the waking-up page at once, then the app on the first reload after one of its pods is Ready.
  • Anything else, from a pod in the cluster or through an Ingress: usually one slow response while the workload starts, then a normal one. Not when something between the caller and the workload gives up first: behind ingress-nginx, a workload that takes longer than its 60-second default proxy-read-timeout gets the caller a 504 (see How long a connection is held); with Istio's STRICT mTLS, the woken pod's sidecar refuses the doorman and the caller gets a 503 (see Compatibility). The cases below are the others.
