  • The client's source IP: the woken pod sees the doorman's IP for held connections, not the caller's. Only the connections that arrive while the workload is paused or waking go through the doorman. The doorman records the caller's address on the ManagedWorkload as hybernate.io/last-request-from, so Hybernate can learn which workload sent it.
  • Right after a wake, an error from the app itself, such as a 503: the workload's pods were Ready before the app could answer, because they have no readiness probe, or one that passes too soon. See Readiness probes.
  • Right after the pause: for a few seconds, until kube-proxy, ingress controllers and the doorman itself pick up the new route, a request can be refused or get a 502 from an ingress, as after any scale-down. A retry is held.
  • A connection held past maxWait, or one whose woken pods can't be reached: it's closed with no response, which most clients report as an empty reply or a connection reset. A RequestNotServed warning event on the ManagedWorkload names the Service, how long the request waited and why; each doorman pod emits it at most once a minute per workload.
  • A connection over a limit: over the held-connection caps, closed at once with nothing sent; over the wake rate limits, held, or shown the waking-up page, while the wake is retried.

Track wakes with hybernate_doorman_wakes_total and hybernate_doorman_wait_seconds; see Metrics. The HybernateDoormanWakesFailing alert fires when held connections keep timing out or failing for a workload.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Kubernetes v1.30+ (tested in CI on 1.30 and 1.37)
  • kubectl v1.30+
  • metrics-server installed (Hybernate reads pod CPU via the Kubernetes Metrics API)
  • Helm v3.8+ (if using Helm install), for OCI charts

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Hybernate is packaged two ways: a Helm chart, and the Kustomize manifests, the repository's config/default, which install.yaml is built from. Both install the same operator and doorman. Use Helm unless your cluster's config is kept as Kustomize.

HelmkubectlKustomizeSource

Put your settings in a values file, starting with your users' time zone, such as America/New_York:

hybernate-values.yaml
timezone: Europe/London

Then install directly from the OCI registry; there's no helm repo to add:

helm install hybernate oci://ghcr.io/okedeji/charts/hybernate \
  --version 0.2.0-rc.5 \
  --namespace hybernate-system \
  --create-namespace \
  -f hybernate-values.yaml

Keep the file, and upgrade with it too: Helm reuses a release's values only on an upgrade given none, so one given --set alone drops the rest; see Keeping your settings. The chart's version has no v; the image it runs is tagged with one, such as v0.2.0-rc.5. The chart installs the ManagedWorkload CRD too, and upgrades it with each helm upgrade.

Helm Values Value Default Description replicaCount 1 Number of operator replicas image.repository ghcr.io/okedeji/hybernate Container image image.tag the chart's appVersion Image tag leaderElection.enabled true Enable HA leader election metrics.secure true Serve metrics over HTTPS metrics.readerSubjects [] Who may scrape the metrics, such as your Prometheus's ServiceAccount timezone UTC Time zone the forecast learns hours and weekdays in watchNamespaces [] Namespaces to work in; empty means all defaults.idleAfter 1h Idle time before pausing, for opted-in workloads that don't set their own defaults.cpuThreshold 10 CPU percentage of requests that counts as active defaults.dryRun false Measure every opted-in workload without pausing, unless it sets its own defaults.pauseEarly false Let a confident forecast pause workloads before idleAfter runs out defaults.forecast balanced How soon the forecast acts: eager, balanced or cautious resources.limits.cpu 500m CPU limit resources.limits.memory 512Mi Memory limit

Every value is in the Helm Values Reference.

Apply install.yaml, the Kustomize manifests built into one file:

kubectl apply -f https://github.com/okedeji/hybernate/releases/download/v0.2.0-rc.5/install.yaml

This installs the CRD, RBAC, the operator Deployment, and the doorman Deployment, Service and PodDisruptionBudget into the hybernate-system namespace. The operator is deployment/hybernate-controller-manager.

Then set your users' time zone, such as America/New_York, on the operator:

kubectl patch deployment hybernate-controller-manager -n hybernate-system --type=json \
  -p '[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/args/-","value":"--timezone=Europe/London"}]'

An install.yaml that changes the operator's arguments replaces them, so after upgrading, check --timezone is still there, or install with Kustomize, which keeps it in your kustomization. For Prometheus and NetworkPolicies, see below.

Use the Kustomize manifests as a remote base, pinned to the release, in a kustomization of your own, here with your users' time zone set on the operator:

kustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
resources:
  - https://github.com/okedeji/hybernate//config/default?ref=v0.2.0-rc.5
patches:
  - target:
      kind: Deployment
      name: hybernate-controller-manager
    patch: |-
      - op: add
        path: /spec/template/spec/containers/0/args/-
        value: --timezone=Europe/London

kubectl apply -k .

It installs what install.yaml does, into hybernate-system, and the operator's other flags are set the same way. To upgrade, change ref to the new release. Kustomize fetches each base with git, so whatever runs it, kubectl or a GitOps tool, needs to reach github.com. For Prometheus and NetworkPolicies, see below.

Clone the repo and build the image:

git clone https://github.com/okedeji/hybernate.git
cd hybernate
make docker-build IMG=hybernate:dev

The image is only in your local Docker, so make it available to the cluster's nodes before deploying. For a Kind cluster, load it into the nodes:

kind load docker-image hybernate:dev --name <cluster>
make deploy IMG=hybernate:dev

For any other cluster, push it to a registry the nodes can pull from:

make docker-build docker-push IMG=<registry>/hybernate:dev
make deploy IMG=<registry>/hybernate:dev

make deploy installs the Kustomize manifests, config/default, with the operator and the doorman running IMG. It writes IMG into config/manager/kustomization.yaml; git checkout config/manager puts it back. From the clone, kubectl apply -k config/prometheus and kubectl apply -k config/network-policy add the bases below.

docs.title: Prometheus and NetworkPolicies without Helm
docs.text:
With install.yaml or the Kustomize manifests, two more bases, pinned to the same release, add what these chart values turn on in a Helm install. Add them to your kustomization's resources, or apply one on its own, such as kubectl apply -k "https://github.com/okedeji/hybernate//config/prometheus?ref=v0.2.0-rc.5".

Base Adds Chart values https://github.com/okedeji/hybernate//config/prometheus?ref=v0.2.0-rc.5 ServiceMonitors for the operator and the doorman, and the alerting rules. Needs the Prometheus Operator's CRDs, and your Prometheus allowed to read the metrics metrics.serviceMonitor.enabled, metrics.prometheusRule.enabled https://github.com/okedeji/hybernate//config/network-policy?ref=v0.2.0-rc.5 NetworkPolicies: only namespaces labelled metrics: enabled may scrape the operator and the doorman, and the doorman's routing ports (TCP 20000-29999) stay open to every caller of a paused workload's Services networkPolicy.enabled

docs.title: With Argo CD or Flux
docs.text:
The chart is published only to an OCI registry, which Argo CD and Flux each name their own way. Commit one of these to the repository your GitOps tool syncs from, with your users' time zone:

Argo CDFlux application.yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: hybernate
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: ghcr.io/okedeji/charts
    chart: hybernate
    targetRevision: 0.2.0-rc.5
    helm:
      valuesObject:
        timezone: Europe/London
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: hybernate-system
  syncPolicy:
    automated: {}
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true

repoURL is the registry and path without oci://, which is how Argo CD knows the chart is in an OCI registry, and chart is the chart's name. The registry is public, so Argo CD needs no credentials for it. Argo CD 3.3 and later runs the chart's uninstall guard when the Application is deleted; see Uninstall. To install the Kustomize manifests instead, point an Application's path at your kustomization.

hybernate.yaml
apiVersion: source.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1
kind: OCIRepository
metadata:
  name: hybernate
  namespace: flux-system
spec:
  interval: 1h
  url: oci://ghcr.io/okedeji/charts/hybernate
  ref:
    tag: 0.2.0-rc.5
  layerSelector:
    mediaType: application/vnd.cncf.helm.chart.content.v1.tar+gzip
    operation: copy
---
apiVersion: helm.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v2
kind: HelmRelease
metadata:
  name: hybernate
  namespace: flux-system
spec:
  interval: 1h
  chartRef:
    kind: OCIRepository
    name: hybernate
  releaseName: hybernate
  targetNamespace: hybernate-system
  storageNamespace: hybernate-system
  install:
    createNamespace: true
  values:
    timezone: Europe/London

This takes Flux 2.6 or later, where OCIRepository is v1. releaseName keeps the release hybernate, as these docs call it, rather than Flux's default of hybernate-system-hybernate, and storageNamespace keeps its Helm history beside it, where helm list -n hybernate-system shows it. To install the Kustomize manifests instead, point a Flux Kustomization at your kustomization.

To upgrade, change the version, targetRevision or tag, to the new release's.

docs.title: Moving a Helm install to Argo CD or Flux
docs.text:
An install made with helm install, as in the Helm tab, can be handed to Argo CD or Flux where it runs, given the same values: nothing is reinstalled, the operator isn't restarted, and paused workloads stay paused. Don't uninstall it first. helm uninstall refuses while ManagedWorkloads are left, as in Uninstall, and doing what it asks, stopping managing every workload, wakes every paused one and throws away what Hybernate has learned of each, its forecast and its tally of what pausing freed.

Give Argo CD or Flux the values the release has now, which this prints, and the version it runs, which helm list -n hybernate-system shows in its CHART column:

helm get values hybernate -n hybernate-system
Argo CDFlux
  1. Commit the Application above, with those values under valuesObject and that version as targetRevision. Argo CD renders the chart, finds every resource already there as it would make it, and shows the Application Synced and Healthy without applying anything, so an automated sync doesn't start.

  2. Sync it once by hand, which applies the resources and marks them as the Application's own, with Argo CD's argocd.argoproj.io/tracking-id annotation: Sync in Argo CD's UI, or with kubectl, giving the Application's sync options:

    kubectl patch application hybernate -n argocd --type merge -p '{"operation":{"sync":{"syncOptions":["CreateNamespace=true"]}}}'

    The sync's result warns, for each resource, that it's missing the kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration annotation, which Helm doesn't set and the sync adds.

  3. Check it's Synced and Healthy:

    kubectl get application hybernate -n argocd

  4. Delete Helm's record of the release, its sh.helm.release.v1.hybernate.v<revision> Secrets, so helm no longer acts on it:

    kubectl delete secrets -n hybernate-system -l owner=helm,name=hybernate

helm list -n hybernate-system no longer shows the release. From then on, change it in Git: Argo CD applies a change to the values or targetRevision, and, from 3.3, runs the uninstall guard when the Application is deleted.

Commit the OCIRepository and HelmRelease above, with those values under values and that version as tag. Their releaseName and storageNamespace are the release's own, so Flux's helm-controller finds it in Helm's storage and takes it over in place: it upgrades the release to a new revision, with the same values, and nothing is deleted. helm list -n hybernate-system goes on showing it, its chart version now followed by + and the start of the chart's digest, as Flux names it. From then on, change it in Git: a helm upgrade by hand is undone at Flux's next reconcile.

docs.title: Time zone
docs.text:
The forecast learns when each workload is busy by hour of day and day of week, counted in the operator's time zone, holds off pausing ahead of those hours and, with autoResume, wakes workloads before them. Set it to your users' IANA time zone, such as Europe/London, America/New_York or Asia/Kolkata: Helm's timezone value, or the operator's --timezone flag. Left at the default, UTC, a team whose clocks change for daylight saving finds its workloads woken an hour early or late for half the year. For teams in different zones, pick the zone most of them work in, or give each team an install of its own, as below. The chart's install notes say which zone the forecast uses, and Wall-Clock Alignment has the details.

To change it on a Helm install, change it in your values file:

hybernate-values.yaml
timezone: America/New_York

and upgrade with the file, at the version you run, which helm list -n hybernate-system shows in its CHART column, so the change doesn't upgrade Hybernate too:

helm upgrade hybernate oci://ghcr.io/okedeji/charts/hybernate \
  --version 0.2.0-rc.5 \
  --namespace hybernate-system \
  -f hybernate-values.yaml

The operator restarts with it. Installed without a values file, write one from the release first, or change the one value without it; see Keeping your settings. With Argo CD or Flux, change it in Git, in the Application's valuesObject or the HelmRelease's values.

docs.title: More than one install
docs.text:
One install per cluster is the usual setup. Several can share a cluster, such as one per team, as long as each:

  • runs in a namespace of its own, with a release name of its own, since the chart names its ClusterRoles and admission policies after the release, and
  • sets watchNamespaces, with no namespace in two installs' lists.

All but one set crds.install: false: they share the ManagedWorkload CRD, which belongs to the release that installed it and is upgraded with it, so make that one the newest Hybernate.

Each operator stamps the ManagedWorkloads it takes on, and labels the doorman EndpointSlices it writes, with hybernate.io/operator, its namespace. Another install leaves a ManagedWorkload stamped by a different one alone, with a ManagedByAnotherInstall warning event, and doesn't move that one's EndpointSlices to its own doorman, so two installs watching the same namespace by mistake don't both pause and wake its workloads: the first to take each one on keeps it. The uninstall and upgrade guards don't count the ManagedWorkloads another install took on. The Kustomize manifests, and so install.yaml, are a single install, in hybernate-system, watching every namespace.

docs.title: Verify Installation
docs.text:
# Check the operator and the doorman are running
kubectl get pods -n hybernate-system

# Verify the CRD is installed
kubectl get crd managedworkloads.hybernate.io

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
Stop managing workloads while the operator is still running, so it can scale any paused ones back up:

  1. Remove the hybernate.io/managed label from your workloads and namespaces, in Git if that's where they live. Hybernate deletes the ManagedWorkloads it created from them.

  2. Delete the ManagedWorkloads you wrote yourself:

    kubectl delete managedworkloads --all --all-namespaces

    Deleting a ManagedWorkload scales its workload back to the replicas it had before it was paused.

  3. Remove the operator:

    helm uninstall hybernate -n hybernate-system

    helm uninstall keeps the CRD, since deleting it deletes every ManagedWorkload. Once none is left, delete it yourself:

    kubectl delete crd managedworkloads.hybernate.io

    Installed from install.yaml or the Kustomize manifests, delete what you applied, the same way: kubectl delete -f with the install.yaml URL, kubectl delete -k . in your kustomization, or make undeploy from a clone. These delete the CRD along with the operator, with no guard like helm uninstall's below, so first check kubectl get managedworkloads -A lists none.

helm uninstall refuses to go ahead while any ManagedWorkload is left. A pre-delete hook, the <fullname>-uninstall-guard Job, first waits up to two and a half minutes for ManagedWorkloads being deleted, so the operator can restore them and drain their doorman ports, which takes up to a minute; then, if any are left, it lists them and fails, so the uninstall stops before removing anything, with job hybernate-uninstall-guard failed from Helm 3 and resource Job/hybernate-system/hybernate-uninstall-guard not ready from Helm 4. A ManagedWorkload deleted just before you uninstall doesn't hold it up. Above that error, Helm 3.18 and later print the hook's output, which starts with a sentence naming the ManagedWorkloads left, as they are after the wait, what to do, and a link here. Helm 4 prints it as one log message, its line breaks escaped:

level=INFO msg="Hybernate refuses to uninstall: these ManagedWorkloads' workloads would stay paused with no operator: staging/web. Remove the hybernate.io/managed label from them and their namespaces, and delete ManagedWorkloads you created, then uninstall again; see https://okedeji.io/hybernate/getting-started/installation/#uninstall\n\n..."

The rest, after the first \n, lists each one and the steps above. Helm before 3.18, such as 3.16, doesn't print a hook's output. Nor does any Helm for a release revision such a Helm wrote, as with a helm rollback after a refused uninstall: it drops the hook's helm.sh/hook-output-log-policy from the revision, until a newer Helm upgrades the release. Whenever Helm prints only the error, kubectl logs job/hybernate-uninstall-guard -n hybernate-system shows the output, with its line breaks, for an hour.

With watchNamespaces, the hook counts those in the watched namespaces, and any elsewhere that the operator took on, with its hybernate.io/cleanup finalizer. It never counts those another install took on. The hook runs the operator's own image. Pass --no-hooks to skip it, or set guard.uninstall: false to drop it.

A refused uninstall leaves the release marked uninstalling, which helm list shows only with -a, though everything still runs. Uninstalling again, once the ManagedWorkloads are gone, finishes it. Until then helm upgrade fails with has no deployed releases; helm rollback hybernate <revision>, with the last revision helm history hybernate lists, marks it deployed again. Argo CD 3.3 and later runs the guard as a PreDelete hook: deleting the Application while ManagedWorkloads are left is blocked, with a DeletionError condition, and Argo CD retries the hook until they're gone. To delete it anyway, set guard.uninstall: false in Git and sync first. Earlier versions of Argo CD don't run Helm's pre-delete hooks, so deleting the Application isn't guarded: stop managing the workloads before deleting it.

Warning

Removing the operator or the CRD first skips step 2's restore: workloads that were paused stay at zero replicas, and their Services still send traffic to the doorman's deleted pods. Restore them by hand, as below.

docs.title: Restoring workloads after the operator is gone
docs.text:
If the operator was removed while ManagedWorkloads were left, with helm uninstall --no-hooks, kubectl delete -f install.yaml, or by deleting an Argo CD Application before Argo CD 3.3, nothing restores their workloads. Each ManagedWorkload also keeps its hybernate.io/cleanup finalizer, which only the operator removes, so deleting it, or the CRD, hangs in Terminating. Reinstalling the operator, then following the steps above, is the simplest fix. Without it:

  1. Scale each paused workload back to the replicas it had, which its ManagedWorkload records:

    kubectl get managedworkloads -A -o jsonpath='{range .items[?(@.status.pause)]}{.metadata.namespace} {.spec.target.kind} {.spec.target.name} {.status.pause.previousReplicas}{"\n"}{end}' |
  while read -r ns kind name replicas; do
    kubectl scale "$kind/$name" -n "$ns" --replicas="$replicas"
  done

    A workload scaled by KEDA was held at zero through its ScaledObject, named in the ManagedWorkload's status.pause.scaledObject. Remove that ScaledObject's autoscaling.keda.sh/paused-replicas annotation, or set it back to status.pause.scaledObjectPausedReplicas if that's set.

    Each paused workload also carries the same record in its hybernate.io/paused-from annotation, which you can read when its ManagedWorkload is gone. Remove the annotation once the workload is restored:

    kubectl annotate deployments,statefulsets --all -A hybernate.io/paused-from-

  2. Delete the EndpointSlices that route paused workloads' Services to the doorman, so the Services use their own pods again:

    kubectl delete endpointslices -A -l endpointslice.kubernetes.io/managed-by=doorman.hybernate.io

  3. Remove the finalizers, so the ManagedWorkloads, and the CRD, can be deleted:

    kubectl get managedworkloads -A -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.namespace} {.metadata.name}{"\n"}{end}' |
  while read -r ns name; do
    kubectl patch managedworkload "$name" -n "$ns" --type=merge -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":null}}'
  done
kubectl delete managedworkloads --all --all-namespaces
kubectl delete crd managedworkloads.hybernate.io

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: Follow the Quickstart to manage your first workload.

docs.title: kubectl Plugin
docs.text: The kubectl hybernate plugin scans a cluster for idle workloads, replays Hybernate's forecast over their history, shows what Hybernate is doing in it and why its nodes aren't scaling down, ends dry-run for workloads you've opted in, pauses workloads on demand, and wakes paused ones.

docs.title: Which Command
docs.text:
scan and status both show idle workloads and money, from opposite ends: scan is the survey of a whole cluster, managed or not, of what could be paused and what that could free; status is what Hybernate is doing with the workloads it manages. The rest answer narrower questions.

Command Use it to Needs the operator scan Find what's idle in a cluster, what it costs, and what pausing it could free, replaying the last week from Prometheus. Before you install Hybernate, or after, to see what's left to opt in No. Once it's installed, the scan also shows what it has paused and freed status See what Hybernate is doing with what it manages: each workload's state, when it pauses next or what holds it awake, what needs attention, what pausing has freed and saved, and the latest pauses and wakes Yes forecast Check, before you turn on autoResume, how the forecast would do on your workloads' own history; name a workload to see its forecast, and for one Hybernate manages, what its own forecast is doing now No, but it needs Prometheus history. A workload's own forecast needs the operator, and no history nodes Find out why what pausing frees isn't coming off the bill: the node autoscaler, and what keeps each node from being removed No. Once it's installed, it also shows what paused workloads would request if they woke enable End dry-run for a workload, or a namespace, once you trust what Hybernate measured Yes pause Pause a workload now rather than when its idle clock runs out, such as a preview at the end of the day Yes wake Wake a paused workload now, or keep one awake for a while with --for, such as for a demo Yes deps See what Hybernate wakes and holds awake with a workload, and what depends on it Yes version Print the plugin's version No

docs.title: Namespaces and Connections
docs.text:
scan, forecast and status read every namespace you can, and fall back to your kubeconfig context's namespace, with a note, when your access doesn't allow listing them all; -n names namespaces instead, and -A (--all-namespaces) insists on every one, failing rather than falling back. pause, wake, deps and enable work in one namespace: -n, or your context's, as kubectl does.

Every command takes kubectl's connection flags: --kubeconfig, --context, --cluster, --user, --as, --as-group, --as-uid, --token, --server, --certificate-authority, --client-certificate, --client-key, --insecure-skip-tls-verify, --tls-server-name, --proxy-url, --username, --password, --disable-compression and --request-timeout. Each request to the API server gives up after 30 seconds unless --request-timeout sets otherwise (0 keeps the 30 seconds, unlike kubectl, where it means no limit), so a cluster that stops answering ends a command with an error, not a hang. kubectl hybernate version prints the plugin's version.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
HomebrewKrewDownloadSource

On macOS and Linux:

brew install okedeji/tap/kubectl-hybernate
kubectl hybernate version

Homebrew installs the newest release, or, until the first stable release, the newest release candidate, and brew upgrade keeps it current. For this version of the docs exactly, use Krew or a download.

With krew, kubectl's plugin manager, installed:

kubectl krew install --manifest-url \
  https://github.com/okedeji/hybernate/releases/download/v0.2.0-rc.5/krew-hybernate.yaml
kubectl hybernate version

Krew installs the plugin on Linux and macOS (amd64 and arm64) and on Windows (amd64). kubectl krew upgrade doesn't upgrade a plugin installed from a manifest URL: to move to a later release, run kubectl krew uninstall hybernate, then install that release's manifest.

Note

Once the plugin is accepted into the krew-index, you'll be able to install it with just kubectl krew install hybernate, and upgrade it with kubectl krew upgrade.

Download the archive for your platform from the release, and put the binary on your PATH as kubectl-hybernate. On macOS and Linux:

os=$(uname -s | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')
arch=$(uname -m | sed -e 's/x86_64/amd64/' -e 's/aarch64/arm64/')
curl -fLO "https://github.com/okedeji/hybernate/releases/download/v0.2.0-rc.5/kubectl-hybernate-${os}-${arch}.tar.gz"
tar xzf "kubectl-hybernate-${os}-${arch}.tar.gz"
sudo install "kubectl-hybernate-${os}-${arch}" /usr/local/bin/kubectl-hybernate
kubectl hybernate version

On Windows, download kubectl-hybernate-windows-amd64.tar.gz from the release, extract it with tar xzf, and rename kubectl-hybernate-windows-amd64.exe to kubectl-hybernate.exe in a folder on your PATH. To check that an archive came from the release workflow, see Verifying a release.

git clone https://github.com/okedeji/hybernate.git
cd hybernate
make build-plugin
# Binary is at bin/kubectl-hybernate

docs.title: Scan a Cluster
docs.text:
kubectl hybernate scan

staging (EKS us-east-1): 214 workloads in 38 namespaces
Node autoscaler: Karpenter (consolidates when underutilized after 1m)
What pausing frees comes off the bill only as nodes scale down.
History: the last 7 days, from monitoring/prometheus-operated

  Hybernate has 12 workloads paused right now, freeing $1.84 an hour.
  Hybernate has freed $96 this month pausing 14 live workloads, and saved $71 of it.
  3 workloads are in dry-run: measured by Hybernate since starting, they would have slept 312 hours, freeing $41,
  about $140 a month.
  4 workloads are scaled to zero by hand; Hybernate can pause them while idle and wake them on the
  next request instead.
  61 workloads are idle right now, reserving 48.0 vCPU and 190.0 GiB of memory.
  They cost $3,180/month while running, $4.36 an hour: each hour asleep frees that.
  Replaying the last 7 days, Hybernate would have paused 58 of 190 unmanaged workloads for 6,120 hours in all,
  and freed $1,240: about $5,380/month.
  Not counted: 4 scaled to zero by hand and 1 without CPU history to replay.

  NAMESPACE    WORKLOAD               STATE                BECAUSE                                                  COST/MO   FREED THIS MONTH   SAVED   COULD SLEEP   WAKES   COULD FREE/MO
  preview-42   statefulset/postgres   idle (unmanaged)     CPU under 1% of its request; last deployed 23 days ago   $140      -                  -       167h          0       $139
  preview-7    deployment/api         idle (dry-run)       no activity for 5h; measuring since Oct 1                $96       -                  -       41h           4       $40
  preview-3    deployment/web         paused (live)        paused 3h ago                                            $48       $12                $9      -             -       -
  preview-9    deployment/demo        paused (unmanaged)   scaled to zero, not by Hybernate                         $0        -                  -       -             -       -
  payments     deployment/ledger      active (unmanaged)   CPU 64% of its request                                   $210      -                  -       0h            0       $0
  ...

Notes:
  - 2 workloads set no CPU requests, so their use can't be measured: kube-tools/agent, ops/exporter
  - 23 infrastructure workloads are left out of the totals and next steps: monitoring (9), argocd (7), ingress-nginx (3) and 2 more. Hybernate never pauses Kubernetes' own workloads or itself; anything else, infrastructure included, pauses only if you opt it in
  - the history replay sees CPU and rollouts only; requests and activity annotations aren't in Prometheus, so a workload used with little CPU can look like it would sleep more than it would

Costs use the on-demand and spot list prices of the cluster's 4 node types (m6i.xlarge, m6i.2xlarge, r6i.xlarge and 1 more, AWS us-east-1). 6 workloads run on spot nodes, priced at spot.
Pass --cpu-price and --memory-price for yours.

scan only reads, with your own kubeconfig, and needs nothing installed in the cluster. It works before you install Hybernate, and after: once Hybernate manages a workload, the scan shows what it has paused and reads its activity clock.

How it decides a workload is idle, using the same signals Hybernate uses to pause:

  • Workloads Hybernate manages: the activity clock it keeps for them, which already combines every source configured, including Prometheus queries. Idle means no activity for idleAfter; the scan says when Hybernate is holding one awake, for example for its dependents.
  • Other workloads: what the scan can see without Hybernate. Any of these makes a workload active: CPU above --cpu-threshold (10% by default) of what it requests, a rollout within --idle-after (1h by default), a hybernate.io/last-activity annotation within it, or a hybernate.io/active-until in the future. Otherwise, with CPU measured, it's idle.
  • Workloads it can't judge, because they set no CPU requests or have no metrics yet, are listed in the notes rather than the table, and left out of the headline's totals. Without metrics-server, as on EKS by default, an unmanaged workload with CPU history is judged from it instead: its state is where replaying its history left the activity clock, and BECAUSE says so.
  • Replicas set from Git: a workload whose replicas a GitOps tool (Argo CD, Flux, Fleet, kapp or Kluctl) last set, from the field managers the API server records, is listed in the notes by tool: its tool would undo every pause until it's told to leave the replicas to Hybernate, a one-time setting given in GitOps tools. Once it's told, the workload isn't listed: for Argo CD, the scan reads that from the workload's Application and argocd-cm, as enable does, and when your access doesn't allow reading them, the note says so and lists the workload as one to check. JSON gives the tool in each workload's replicasFromGit, with gitOpsLeavesReplicas once it's told, and gitOpsUnchecked saying why that couldn't be read. The next steps never suggest one, since its tool would revert a label put on by hand too.

  • The cluster's own infrastructure is left out of the table, the totals and the next steps, and a note says how many workloads in which namespaces. The first line counts only the namespaces the listed workloads are in, so a cluster with 15 namespaces, 12 of them infrastructure, reads 14 workloads in 3 namespaces; JSON's namespaces is every namespace read. JSON and YAML list the infrastructure in platform, each with what it is. Two kinds are left out, for different reasons:

    • What Hybernate never pauses: Kubernetes' namespaces (kube-*, and openshift-*, cattle-*, gke-* and gmp-*), the namespace Hybernate runs in, found by its Deployment's app.kubernetes.io/name: hybernate label, and, in any namespace, the operator's and the doorman's own Deployments, found by their control-plane: controller-manager or control-plane: doorman label with app.kubernetes.io/name: hybernate or a hybernate helm.sh/chart label. Apps' dependencies on these aren't listed, as Hybernate never needs to wake them.
    • What the scan guesses nobody means to pause: well-known infrastructure such as ingress controllers, cert-manager, Vault, Argo CD, Flux, service meshes, policy engines and monitoring, by their usual namespaces (ingress-nginx, cert-manager, vault, argocd, flux-system, istio-system, linkerd, gatekeeper-system, kyverno, monitoring and others) or their app.kubernetes.io/name, app.kubernetes.io/part-of, app, k8s-app or helm.sh/chart labels. This is only the estimate's exclusion, not an operator rule: opted in, Hybernate pauses these like any app, so apps' dependencies on them are still listed, and none is guessed at in a namespace labelled hybernate.io/managed=true, such as a preview environment with its own Vault, or for a workload Hybernate already manages.

    A namespace labelled hybernate.io/allow-protected=true is scanned like any other, apart from Hybernate's own Deployments.

History from Prometheus: when the cluster has a Prometheus, the scan replays Hybernate's activity clock over the last week of each workload's CPU and rollouts, as if Hybernate had managed it with --idle-after and --cpu-threshold:

  • It finds Prometheus by the Services the Prometheus Operator (and so kube-prometheus-stack) and the community Helm chart create, and queries it through the API server's service proxy, so there's no port-forward or URL to give. The History: line under the node autoscaler, and the report's subtitle, name the one it read and how much history it replayed (JSON history.prometheus and history.hours).
  • With several Prometheus, it reads the one with the most of the window's CPU history: one with cAdvisor's container CPU from the start of the window, then one with any, then any that answers. Among equals, it prefers one in a monitoring namespace (monitoring, prometheus, observability, kube-prometheus-stack, cattle-monitoring-system, openshift-monitoring, in that order), then one with a usual name (prometheus-operated, kube-prometheus-stack-prometheus, prometheus-server, prometheus, prometheus-k8s), then the Prometheus Operator's Service over the community chart's, then the first by namespace and name, and it tries five at most. The History: line lists the others it found (JSON history.others).
  • To choose another, --prometheus-service namespace/name reads that Service through the API server the same way, whether the scan found it or not, on its API port or the one you add, as in monitoring/thanos-query:http. --prometheus-url reads one outside the cluster, such as Thanos or Mimir; see A Prometheus elsewhere. Either fails the scan if it can't be read, rather than carrying on without history.
  • It reads CPU per container from cAdvisor's container_cpu_usage_seconds_total, which every common setup scrapes, at five-minute steps (coarser for windows over about 34 days), and matches pods to their workload by name. Sidecars added at pod creation are left out of activity, as for the activity clock.
  • A step counts as active when the workload's own CPU is above the threshold of what its running pods request, as the operator counts it, or it rolled out. After --idle-after with none, it would be asleep until the next, which is one wake.
  • STATE is right now: idle means no activity for --idle-after, so Hybernate would pause it now. Money is in whole dollars, as status shows it: <$1 for an amount above zero that rounds to nothing, and $0 only for none. Each money and history cell has one source:
    • COULD SLEEP and WAKES are what Hybernate measured for a workload in dry-run, since dry-run started (BECAUSE says when), and for an unmanaged workload come from the replay: had Hybernate been managing it, the running hours it would have been paused, after waiting --idle-after from each activity, and how many times activity would have arrived while it was asleep, each starting it again and making whoever caused it wait.
    • FREED THIS MONTH, for live workloads, is what Hybernate has freed pausing it since the 1st, from the ManagedWorkload's status.cost.freedThisMonth, priced at the rates Hybernate uses for the workload, and SAVED the part of it that came off the bill as nodes scaled down (savedThisMonth). A workload put back in dry-run keeps what it freed and saved while live; dry-run's would-be pauses never add to them. The headline's pausing 14 live workloads counts only the live workloads Hybernate pauses, and what they and any put back in dry-run freed; with none live, it says the money came from workloads since put back in dry-run only when there are some. Those it never pauses, in a protected namespace, part of Hybernate, or a StatefulSet that deletes its PVCs when scaled down (Protected=True on its ManagedWorkload), are counted on a line of their own, with what they freed this month before they were protected, if anything: 1 more live workload is protected, so Hybernate never pauses it; it freed $12 this month before it was, and saved $5 of that. (JSON totals.live, totals.liveProtected, and totals.protectedFreedThisMonth and protectedSavedThisMonth, which are part of freedThisMonth and savedThisMonth).
    • COULD FREE/MO, for workloads Hybernate doesn't pause yet, is what pausing would free a month: what Hybernate measured for one in dry-run, the same figure its BECAUSE line gives, or what the replay estimates for an unmanaged one. The scan can't know what of it would be saved before Hybernate runs, so it never calls it a saving.
  • A live workload isn't replayed: while it's paused, there are no pods for Prometheus to record. Its pauses are what FREED THIS MONTH counts.
  • The headline's replay count, such as 0 of 13 unmanaged workloads would have slept, is of the unmanaged workloads replayed. When the table lists others it doesn't count, a Not counted: line says which and why, as the report's summary does: ones that won't pause (1 that won't pause (PVCs deleted on scale-down)), in protected namespaces, scaled to zero by hand, or without CPU history to replay.
  • Node autoscaler, under the first line, is what would turn what pausing frees into savings by removing nodes, found as nodes finds it (JSON nodeAutoscaler): Karpenter, Cluster Autoscaler, EKS Auto Mode or GKE Autopilot; none found, when nothing in the cluster will remove nodes, so nothing pausing frees comes off the bill; or unknown, when your access doesn't allow reading what would tell.
  • A Deployment's history is its pods' CPU, including pods of ReplicaSets since deleted, which are known by the names Kubernetes gives them, <deployment>-<hash>-<suffix>. A Deployment whose name is long enough for Kubernetes to cut its pods' names short has only its current ReplicaSets' pods replayed.
  • Requests and activity annotations aren't recorded in Prometheus, so the replay only knows CPU and rollouts, and a workload used with little CPU can look like it would sleep more than it would. Requests and prices are today's.
  • History gets the first 60% of --timeout, so a Prometheus or Thanos too slow for the window can't use up the whole scan. Each namespace's reads from the API server come before its history query and share that time, and a namespace reached once it's spent isn't queried at all. A namespace's query may take whatever is left of that time, however long, and isn't cut short by --request-timeout. Namespaces whose history isn't read in that time are judged from CPU right now, and the notes name them and say a longer --timeout gives history more time, or --window 0 skips it. When Prometheus, or the API server's proxy in front of it, gives up on a query by itself with time left, a longer --timeout wouldn't help: the notes name those namespaces and suggest a shorter --window.
  • If Prometheus has less history than the window, the replay covers what it has, and says how much wherever it names the window, such as "Replaying the last 30 minutes", with a note that it's shorter than asked. Under a day of it can't show a day's pattern, so the headline says so and to run the scan again after a few days, in the terminal and the report. Without Prometheus, or without permission to reach it, the scan judges from CPU right now, and says why.

Dependencies: the scan reads each workload's environment variables, from literal values and ConfigMaps, and lists the workloads they point at:

  3 dependencies found, and what Hybernate does with each:
  preview-42   deployment/checkout-api   ->   statefulset/postgres         DATABASE_URL   declared; woken and held with it
  preview-42   deployment/checkout-api   ->   messaging/statefulset/nats   NATS_URL       not managed, so never paused
  preview-42   deployment/worker         ->   statefulset/postgres         PGHOST         woken with it once both are managed
  • An address counts when it names a Service in a scanned namespace, in any form cluster DNS gives it (postgres, postgres.preview-42, postgres.preview-42.svc.cluster.local, or a headless Service's pod, postgres-0.postgres-hl), inside a URL, a host:port, or a list of either. The workload is the one the Service's selector picks. A bare word on its own, such as MODE=postgres, isn't taken for an address.
  • Variable names don't matter, and Service names come from the cluster, not a list the scan keeps.
  • An address is shown as its scheme, host and port alone, such as postgres://postgres:5432: a user, a password, a path and a query string can each hold a credential, so none of them is. The terminal shows the variable each dependency was found in; only JSON and YAML carry the address itself.
  • Hybernate wakes a dependency with the workload that needs it, so the first request doesn't wait for it too, and keeps it up while that workload is, when it manages both; see Dependencies. The last column says what it does with each: woken with it once both are managed, for a workload it doesn't manage yet; not managed, so never paused, for a dependency it doesn't manage, which stays up anyway; woken and held with it, learned from the workload's environment or a wake; declared; woken and held with it, with hybernate.io/depends-on; or not learned yet, for one Hybernate manages but hasn't learned. Before Hybernate manages any of the workloads that need them, every dependency would say the first, so the scan and the report say it once above the list and leave the column out.
  • Secrets are never read, so addresses set there, and ones built in code or read from files, aren't found. The notes say which workloads take variables from Secrets.

What the numbers mean:

  • Costs are what the workloads' requests cost while running, sidecars included, at the list price of the nodes each one's pods run on, from their instance type and region, spot nodes at their spot price; see Prices. A workload with no pod on a node is priced where Hybernate last saw it run, or at the cluster's most common node type. Nodes Hybernate has no list price for, and every workload when your access doesn't allow listing nodes, use assumed prices from AWS on-demand in us-east-1, and the report says which.
  • --cpu-price and --memory-price set your own prices, which price every workload in place of list prices: use them for discounts, savings plans, or negotiated rates.
  • Spot and preemptible nodes are priced at their type's spot price, and the report says how many workloads run on them. A spot node of a type its provider doesn't sell as spot is priced at on-demand, and the report names those workloads' node types and says they cost less than shown. JSON gives each workload's onSpot and spotAtOnDemand, and each node type in nodePrices its spot and atSpot; see Spot nodes.
  • Without history, the scan shows what idle workloads cost and what each hour asleep frees, not what pausing would free a month: from one moment it can't tell how often a workload would be woken. To measure it once Hybernate is installed, label workloads hybernate.io/managed=true and annotate them hybernate.io/dry-run=true: Hybernate measures how often it would have paused them, for how long, and what that would have freed, without ever pausing them. The scan then shows it in each one's COULD SLEEP, WAKES, and COULD FREE/MO, with BECAUSE saying since when, a total in the headline, and the kubectl hybernate enable command to start pausing. It's from Hybernate's own activity clock, which sees more than the history replay, so it's what to judge going live by.
  • An hour asleep frees capacity; it becomes money only when a node autoscaler removes it. kubectl hybernate nodes shows what keeps nodes from scaling down.
  • BECAUSE gives the evidence for the state, then facts such as when a workload was last deployed, if a week or more ago.
  • A StatefulSet whose persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy.whenScaled is Delete would lose its data to a pause, so Hybernate refuses to pause it: BECAUSE says won't pause: PVCs deleted on scale-down (JSON wontPause), and it's left out of what pausing could free and of next steps.

The HTML report: run in a terminal, the scan also writes the same report as a web page and opens it in your browser. It's one self-contained file, with no scripts, fonts, or images loaded from anywhere (its sorting and filtering are built in), so it can be emailed or attached, and it prints cleanly to PDF. It's written for whoever you send it to:

  • the node autoscaler, under the prices
  • two headline figures. Until Hybernate has paused anything, they're the opportunity: what pausing could free a month (measured for dry-run workloads, estimated from history for unmanaged ones), as a share of what those workloads cost, "over the same time" when history was replayed, since a replayed workload is measured against what it cost over the history, with the pods it ran then, or, without either, what's idle right now costs while running, the most pausing it could free; and beside it, what the workloads cost a month. A zero says why: with under a day of history, short of the window, that it's too little history yet, so run the scan again after a few days. Once Hybernate has paused workloads, the first is what it has freed this month, with what of it was saved, and the second what pausing could free, while there's something to
  • four facts: how many workloads in how many namespaces (what they cost, once that's left the headline), what's idle right now, how many unmanaged workloads would have slept and which listed ones the replay doesn't count (with history) or what idle workloads cost an hour (without), and how many Hybernate manages
  • a table by namespace (with a filter), every workload scanned that the scan could judge, with the same columns as the terminal (sortable, with a filter), and the dependencies found
  • what the numbers mean, in plain words, and the next steps

Dependency addresses are left out of the page, since it's meant to be passed around; JSON and YAML keep them. The report file is created readable only by you. A scan covers one cluster, the current kubeconfig context or the one you name with --context.

The file goes to your temporary directory unless you pass --html FILE. It opens only when the table is shown in a terminal on a machine with a desktop; piped output, -o json, CI, and SSH sessions (unless X forwarding gives a Linux one a display) get no report unless you ask for one with --html. --open=false keeps it from opening.

Cluster names: EKS and GKE contexts are shortened to the cluster with its provider and region, such as staging (EKS us-east-1) for arn:aws:eks:us-east-1:123456789012:cluster/staging. Any other context is shown as named. JSON and YAML keep the full context name.

STATE is what the workload is doing right now, and the bracket how Hybernate is involved: unmanaged, not at all; dry-run, it measures but never pauses; live, it pauses the workload while idle; protected, its namespace is labelled hybernate.io/protected, so Hybernate won't manage it, and it's left out of what pausing could free and of the next steps. The operator's protectedNamespaces patterns aren't visible to the scan, which only sees the label. A workload someone scaled to zero shows as paused (unmanaged): it costs nothing now, but nothing will wake it on a request, and the headline counts it apart from what Hybernate has paused. Workloads labelled hybernate.io/ignore=true aren't listed.

# Another cluster in your kubeconfig
kubectl hybernate scan --context staging

# Some namespaces, as JSON or YAML, at your own prices
kubectl hybernate scan -n preview-42 -n preview-918 -o json --cpu-price 0.045 --memory-price 0.006

# A month of history from a Thanos that holds many clusters, with a 2h idleAfter
kubectl hybernate scan --window 30d --idle-after 2h --prometheus-url https://thanos.example.com \
  --prometheus-selector 'cluster="staging"'

# CPU right now only
kubectl hybernate scan --window 0

# Save the report to send around
kubectl hybernate scan --html workload-scan.html

# The terminal only
kubectl hybernate scan --open=false
Flag Short Default Description --namespace -n all you can read Namespace to scan; repeat for several --all-namespaces -A Read every namespace, and fail rather than fall back when your access doesn't allow that. Can't be combined with -n --exclude-namespaces kube-system, kube-public, kube-node-lease Namespaces to skip --output -o table table, json, or yaml --limit 25 Workloads listed in the table, idle first, then paused, then active, each by what pausing could free; 0 for all. Also caps the dependency list. JSON and YAML list everything --cpu-threshold 10 CPU use, as a percentage of requests from 1 to 100, above which a workload counts as active, now and in the replay. Workloads Hybernate manages use their own setting --cpu-price 0.031 Your price per vCPU-hour, in dollars, zero or more --memory-price 0.004 Your price per GiB-hour of memory, in dollars, zero or more --window 7d How much Prometheus history to replay, such as 7d or 36h, up to 366d; 0 judges from CPU right now only --idle-after 1h How long without activity makes a workload idle, now and in the replay, as Hybernate's idleAfter. Workloads Hybernate manages use their own setting --prometheus-service the one found in the cluster with the most history Prometheus Service in the cluster to read history from, as namespace/name or namespace/name:port, through the API server --prometheus-url the one found in the cluster with the most history Prometheus API to read history from, such as Thanos, Mimir, or Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus --prometheus-selector Label matchers added to every history query, such as 'cluster="prod"', for a Prometheus that holds more than one cluster. Values are double-quoted, as in PromQL --prometheus-header Header to send to --prometheus-url, as "Name: value", such as "X-Scope-OrgID: tenant" for Mimir; repeat for several --prometheus-bearer-token-file File holding a bearer token to send to --prometheus-url --prometheus-ca-file PEM file of CA certificates to trust for --prometheus-url, besides the system's --prometheus-insecure-skip-verify false Don't verify --prometheus-url's certificate --timeout 5m How long the scan may take before it gives up --html a temporary file Save the HTML report to this file, to share --open true Open the HTML report in your browser, when the table is shown in a terminal

docs.title: A Prometheus elsewhere
docs.text:
--prometheus-url reads history from a Prometheus API your machine can reach, rather than one found in the cluster, and needs no cluster permission at all. If it doesn't answer like a Prometheus API, the scan fails rather than carrying on without history.

  • Several clusters in one store, such as Thanos or Mimir: pass --prometheus-selector with the label that tells them apart, so the scan reads only this cluster's series. When it finds series from more than one source, the notes suggest it.
  • Authentication: --prometheus-header (for example X-Scope-OrgID for a Mimir tenant, or an Authorization header), or --prometheus-bearer-token-file, but not both for the same header. --prometheus-ca-file and --prometheus-insecure-skip-verify are for its certificate. These flags only apply with --prometheus-url: a Prometheus found in the cluster is reached through the API server with your kubeconfig.

  • Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus, GKE's managed Prometheus, keeps its data in Cloud Monitoring rather than in the cluster: gmp-system runs its collectors, which have nothing to query, so the scan doesn't find it there and reads another Prometheus if the cluster has one. To read it instead, give it an access token and name your project and cluster, as the store holds every cluster in the project:

    kubectl hybernate scan \
  --prometheus-url https://monitoring.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/location/global/prometheus \
  --prometheus-bearer-token-file <(gcloud auth print-access-token) \
  --prometheus-selector 'cluster="CLUSTER_NAME"'

    If you've deployed its frontend in the cluster, --prometheus-service NAMESPACE/frontend reads it through that instead, with the frontend's own credentials. Either way, its history has the CPU the replay reads only if it collects cAdvisor's metrics, which kubeletScraping in its OperatorConfig turns on. - Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus needs requests signed with SigV4, which the scan doesn't do: point --prometheus-url at a signing proxy in front of it.

The source is shown in the report with any password in its URL hidden.

docs.title: Exit status
docs.text:
The scan exits 0 when it read everything your access allows. Namespaces or resources your access doesn't allow (a 403) are explained in the notes, and don't change the exit status, unless you named the namespace with -n.

It exits 1, after writing the report, when it couldn't read something it should have: a timeout, throttling, a server error, a failed Prometheus query, or a 403 or missing namespace among those you named with -n. The notes say what was missed, the error says what to do about it (check a namespace's name, ask for access, or try again with a longer --timeout), and JSON and YAML list the namespaces in incomplete, by why: missing, denied, failed, or unscanned. JSON and YAML also give the number of namespaces read in namespaces, and "workloads": [] for a cluster with none.

A scan that runs out of --timeout still reports the namespaces it scanned in time, and lists the rest as unscanned; only one that scanned none fails without a report. Scanning every namespace, the scan lists each kind of object across the cluster at once, a page at a time, rather than in each namespace, so a cluster of thousands of namespaces takes a few dozen requests. A kind your access only lets you list namespace by namespace is read that way.

Workloads someone else already scaled to zero count toward nothing the scan says could be freed: they cost nothing now, and the headline counts them apart.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
Your user needs to list Deployments, StatefulSets, ReplicaSets, ControllerRevisions, Pods, pod metrics, Services and ManagedWorkloads in the namespaces scanned, and to read the namespaces and the ConfigMaps workloads take variables from; to list namespaces unless you name them with -n; and to list nodes, to price workloads at their nodes. forecast also lists Deployments, across the cluster or else in the operator's namespace (hybernate-system by default), to read the doorman's settings from the operator's own flags; without either it assumes the doorman's defaults, on and without the NEG forwarder, and its notes say so. Naming the node autoscaler reads what nodes does for that. The standard view role covers the namespaced reads, ManagedWorkloads too, which Hybernate's chart and manifests add to view; it doesn't cover nodes, which are cluster-wide. Without one of these the scan carries on, and the notes say what it couldn't see. Reading history through the service proxy also needs get on services/proxy for the Prometheus Service, which view doesn't include. Without it, the scan judges from CPU right now and prints what an admin can run to let you, for that one Service and nothing else:

To replay history, an admin can let you read Prometheus, and nothing else, with:
  kubectl create role hybernate-scan -n monitoring --verb=get --resource=services/proxy --resource-name=prometheus-operated:web
  kubectl create rolebinding hybernate-scan -n monitoring --role=hybernate-scan --user=jane@example.com
Or pass --prometheus-url if Prometheus is reachable from your machine.

A Prometheus you name with --prometheus-service fails the scan instead, with the same commands in its error; reading it also needs get on that Service, to find its port, which view covers.

That's only when the API server refuses you the proxy. A 403 from behind it, such as from a kube-rbac-proxy in front of Prometheus, is shown as Prometheus's own answer, since a Role for services/proxy wouldn't change it.

docs.title: Replay the Forecast
docs.text:
kubectl hybernate forecast -n preview-42

staging: the forecast replayed over 28 days of CPU history from monitoring/prometheus-operated, times in UTC

NAMESPACE   NAME              FORECAST             READY  COLD  WOKEN FOR NOTHING  WOKEN             WAKES ON
preview-42  api               acts from day one    9/10   1     0                  08:45, 25m ahead  request
preview-42  worker (managed)  acts from Mon 2 Nov  3/10   7     2 (3.5h)           09:45, 20m ahead  query
preview-42  reports           not within 4 weeks   0/6    6     0                  -                 nothing

forecast shows what Hybernate's forecast would make of your workloads, from their own CPU history, before you trust autoResume with them. It runs the operator's own forecast and decision rules, through the simulator, over the history scan reads:

  • FORECAST is when the forecast would act if the workload were opted in today, having learned all its history as the operator does for a new workload: acts from day one, from a date it projects, or not within 4 weeks for a pattern too irregular for the setting. For a workload Hybernate already manages, marked (managed) beside its name, it's that forecast's own, from status.prediction: acting, learning, from a date it projects, not within 4 weeks when it's earning its confidence, or relearning, and isn't expected to act within four weeks, or, while it's paused with nothing to see its demand, not learning while paused: and why, such as no Service routes requests to it. Name the workload to see what its forecast is doing in full, and the fix, from its status.prediction.message.
  • READY, COLD, WOKEN FOR NOTHING and WOKEN replay the last half of the history as Hybernate with autoResume would have managed it, from a forecast that learned only the first half: the mornings it had the workload up before its first use, those whose first use found it paused and woke it, the wakes ahead of demand that didn't come and how long they kept it up, and when it usually woke it. Having learned less, the replay is a little less ready than opting in now would be.
  • WAKES ON is what wakes the workload once it's paused, in the replay, as it would under Hybernate: request, through the doorman, when a Service with a cluster IP selects its pods on a TCP port, keeps traffic cluster-wide, and isn't in GKE NEGs, unless the doorman's forwarder is on; query, when its ManagedWorkload has a Prometheus activity query, so only for a workload Hybernate manages; request, query for both; or nothing, so people wake it by hand, and the forecast doesn't learn the hours it's paused. For a workload Hybernate manages, what its operator found of its routing stands, as at its last pause, such as Services served by other workloads' pods. A workload not yet managed is judged by the ManagedWorkload opting it in would make, with hybernate.io/wake-on-request from its own annotations, then its namespace's, as opting in reads it. Whether the doorman is on (doorman.enabled), and its NEG forwarder, are read from the flags of the operator that manages the namespace, whose Deployment forecast finds by its labels across the cluster, or, without access to list Deployments there, in the operator's namespace, hybernate-system or the one a ManagedWorkload's hybernate.io/operator annotation names; when it can't read one, it assumes Hybernate's defaults, the doorman on and the forwarder off, and says so in its notes, with why and the access that reads it. The JSON has it in forecast.wakes: request, query, and noRequest, why a request wouldn't wake it.

A workload counts as used whenever its CPU is above --cpu-threshold, as the activity clock counts it; use that shows only in requests or activity annotations isn't in Prometheus.

It reads Prometheus as scan does, found in the cluster or at --prometheus-url, with the same flags and permissions, and fails when there's no history to read. With less than two days of it, a day to learn from and a day to replay, it says so and when there will be enough, and, when Hybernate manages a workload, how to see its own forecast, which needs no history. It leaves out scan's notes on dependencies, GitOps tools and the cluster's infrastructure, which are about what pausing could free. It only reads.

docs.title: One Workload's Forecast
docs.text:
Name a workload, as api or statefulset/postgres, to see its forecast:

kubectl hybernate forecast api -n preview-42

staging (EKS us-east-1): the forecast of preview-42/api, times in Europe/London

Hybernate's forecast, from ManagedWorkload api: acting
  acting, on 4 weeks of CPU history and what it has seen since: its forecasts of the last day were 91% right, and it acts from 75%, so it holds off pauses before hours it expects to be busy and wakes the workload 15 minutes ahead of them
  Phase:       daily Active, weekly Active
  Hours seen:  24 of the 24 hours of the day, 168 of the 168 hours of the week
  Learned:     790 hours: 672 from its CPU history in Prometheus, and 118 live in the 5 days Hybernate has managed it
  Confidence:  91% right over the last day, 88% over the last week; it acts from 75%
  Acts from:   now
  Busy hours:  Thu 22 Oct 09:00–18:00, up to 64% of its CPU requests
  autoResume:  on: it holds off pauses before the hours it expects busy, and wakes the workload 15 minutes ahead of them

Replayed over its last 28 days of CPU history, from monitoring/prometheus-operated:
  Opted in today: acts from day one, at a confidence of 75%.

From Thu 8 Oct to Thu 22 Oct, with autoResume, from a forecast that learned only the history before; while it's paused, a request through the doorman wakes it:
DAY         FIRST USE  FOUND IT  WOKEN AT  FORECAST  WOKEN FOR NOTHING
Thu 8 Oct   09:12      ready     08:45     acting    -
Fri 9 Oct   09:20      ready     08:45     acting    -
Sat 10 Oct  -          -         -         acting    -
...

Ready on 9 of 10 mornings, woken 25m ahead; it never woke it for nothing.

For a workload Hybernate manages, it first shows what Hybernate's own forecast of it is doing, from its ManagedWorkload's status.prediction and the state the forecast saves there, as the operator restores it:

  • The first line says whether it's acting, as status shows it in FORECAST: acting, learning, relearning or not learning. Under it is the operator's own message, as it wrote it in status.prediction.message: what it's waiting for and why.
  • Phase is the phase of each season, daily and weekly: Observing, Suggesting or Active. See Phase Lifecycle.
  • Hours seen are the hours of the day it has seen since it started or last relearned, all 24 of which it needs before it can act, and the hours of the week it has seen.
  • Learned is how many hours of demand it has learned, how many of them came from the workload's CPU history in Prometheus when Hybernate began managing it (status.prediction.history), and how many it has learned live since, out of how long Hybernate has managed it. When it learned no history, the History line gives the operator's reason.
  • Confidence is how right its forecasts of the last day and the last week were, and the confidence it acts from.
  • Acts from is now, when it's acting; the time it's expected to start (status.prediction.startsActing), if the coming days repeat the last week; not known until it has seen every hour of the day, or not known until it has scored a day of its forecasts while it's otherwise still observing; or not expected within 4 weeks, for a pattern too irregular for its setting.
  • Busy hours are the hours of the next 24 it expects demand at or above the workload's cpuThreshold in, with the most it expects as a share of the CPU it requests. It holds off a pause before each, and with autoResume wakes the workload 15 minutes ahead of it. It forecasts none until it's acting.
  • autoResume says whether it's on, what that changes, and when it's off, how to turn it on: the workload's hybernate.io/auto-resume: "true" annotation for a workload opted in with the label, or spec.idlePolicy.autoResume: true for a ManagedWorkload written by hand, which annotations don't change.
  • Its state says why the plugin couldn't read the saved state, such as a plugin of another version than the operator; the lines read from it are left out. A workload the operator hasn't recorded a forecast for yet says so, and what to check. One its ManagedWorkload says Hybernate leaves alone (TargetAvailable=False), labelled hybernate.io/ignore=true or gone, says that instead of what the forecast last recorded (JSON operator.stopped), as status does in NEXT.

Then, for any workload, managed or not, comes the replay of its history: when the forecast would act were the workload opted in today, and the last half of the history day by day, with each day's first use, how it found the workload, when the forecast woke it, and whether the forecast was acting. When it can't be replayed, the line that takes its place says why and what to do: too little history, a day to learn from and a day to replay, with when there will be enough; no Prometheus to read, or one it couldn't; no CPU requests to measure use against; no CPU history of its pods; or a workload scaled to zero outside Hybernate. A workload Hybernate manages shows its own forecast whatever its history, and exits 0. One it doesn't manage, with nothing else to show, exits 1 when there's no Prometheus it can read; with too little history, it says so and exits 0.

NAME is looked for in every namespace forecast reads, or those given with -n. It matches a Deployment or StatefulSet, and a ManagedWorkload's own name, for one written under another name. When it matches more than one, such as api in two namespaces, forecast names them and asks for -n or kind/name. A name that matches nothing says so; in a namespace named with -n, a workload labelled hybernate.io/ignore=true, which the forecast leaves out as Hybernate does, is named as such. Times are in the operator's time zone, as the workload's ManagedWorkload records it, unless --timezone says otherwise. -o json and -o yaml give the same in each workload's operator (with learned: hours, fromHistory, hoursOfDay, hoursOfWeek, and busy, each span's from, to and peak), forecast and noReplay. Reading the ManagedWorkload takes list on managedworkloads, which view has; without it, the workload is shown as one Hybernate doesn't manage.

Flag Short Default Description --namespace -n all you can read Namespace to replay; repeat for several --all-namespaces -A false Every namespace, failing rather than falling back when your access doesn't allow it --exclude-namespaces system namespaces Namespaces to skip --window 28d How much history to read, from 2d to 34d; the operator learns up to four weeks --forecast balanced How soon the forecast acts, eager, balanced or cautious, for workloads Hybernate doesn't manage; see Forecast setting --timezone the operator's The time zone whose hours and weekdays the forecast learns, and that times are shown in: by default the operator's timezone, as its ManagedWorkloads record it in status.prediction.timeZone, or UTC when you can read none --cpu-threshold 10 CPU use, as a percentage of requests, above which a workload is in use; managed workloads use their own --idle-after 1h How long without use before a pause; managed workloads use their own --output -o table table, json, or yaml; JSON and YAML give every workload's days --timeout 5m How long the replay may take before it gives up --prometheus-url and the other --prometheus-* flags As for scan

docs.title: See What Hybernate Is Doing
docs.text:
kubectl hybernate status

staging (EKS us-east-1): Hybernate manages 4 workloads.
  1 paused, 2 running, 1 resuming; 1 in dry-run, never paused: pausing it would have freed $7 since Oct 1
  Node autoscaler: Karpenter (consolidates when underutilized after 1m)
  Forecast time zone: Europe/London
  Freed $42 this month, and saved $9 of it.

Needs attention:
  Pausing freed $42 this month, but only $9 of it came off the bill: nodes aren't scaling down.
  kubectl hybernate nodes shows why.
  preview-7/worker   GitOpsConflict   Argo CD set the replicas from Git, undoing the pause; ...
  preview-7/worker   Stuck            resuming for 25m: waiting for preview-42/statefulset/postgres

  NAMESPACE    WORKLOAD               STATE               FOR   LAST ACTIVITY      NEXT                                        FORECAST                    FREED THIS MONTH   SAVED   WOULD FREE
  preview-42   deployment/api         paused              3h    request, 4h ago    wakes on a request or activity              acting                      $12                $9      -
  preview-42   statefulset/postgres   running             5h    cpu, 2h ago        held awake while preview-7/worker uses it   -                           $30                $0      -
  preview-7    deployment/web         running (dry-run)   2h    rollout, 15m ago   would pause in 45m                          learning, acts from Oct 8   -                  -       $7
  preview-7    deployment/worker      resuming            25m   -                  -                                           -                           <$1                $0      -

Recent pauses and wakes:
  30m ago   preview-7/worker   scaled up to 2 replicas by argocd-controller outside Hybernate; counted as activity
  3h ago    preview-42/api     paused
  5h ago    preview-42/api     request on Service api, waking

status is one screen of every workload Hybernate manages, read from their ManagedWorkloads and events:

  • The summary: how many workloads are in each phase, and how many are in dry-run, with what pausing them would have freed since the first started measuring, by what dry-run measured (status.dryRun.estimatedFreed, the would-be pause under way included); the node autoscaler, found as nodes finds it, or none found, or unknown when your access doesn't allow reading what would tell; and what pausing live workloads has freed this month, its requests at list price, and how much of that has been saved, come off the bill as nodes scaled down, in whole dollars, as scan shows them: <$1 for an amount above zero that rounds to nothing, and $0 only for none. Freed capacity is only money once a node autoscaler removes the nodes it was on. When the operator can't measure what's saved for some workloads, the summary says why, once for each reason. It also says which time zone the forecast counts hours in, the operator's timezone as each workload's status.prediction.timeZone records it, and, when that's UTC, the default, how to set it to your users' zone, so autoResume follows their clock through daylight saving.
  • Needs attention: when pausing freed at least a dollar this month and less than half of it was saved, counting only workloads whose savings are measured, a line saying nodes aren't scaling down, pointing at kubectl hybernate nodes. Then what keeps Hybernate from doing its job, from each workload's conditions: a GitOps tool undoing pauses (GitOpsConflict), a dependency that's missing, in a cycle, or in a namespace that doesn't allow it (DependencyNotAllowed), two ManagedWorkloads for one target, a protected namespace, a target that's gone, metrics or Prometheus that can't be read, a Prometheus query that has never matched a series (PrometheusQueryEmpty), a workload whose requests can't wake it while it's paused (WakeOnRequest), which for one that's awake now is what its last pause found with its Services, to fix before the next, but not its being awake (NotPaused) or the doorman being turned off, a resume that stopped with replicas not Ready (ResumeIncomplete), a pause that stopped waiting with pods still running (PauseIncomplete), and a pause or wake taking over 10 minutes (Stuck), with what it waits for. kubectl describe managedworkload has the rest.
  • The table: each workload as kind/name, with its ManagedWorkload's name in brackets when you wrote one under another name; its state and for how long; its last activity and where it came from; what pausing it has freed this month and what of that it has saved, in whole dollars or <$1, as scan shows them, - for a workload only ever in dry-run, or unknown when what's saved can't be measured, where totals last brought up to date in an earlier month count as none, and one in dry-run now keeps what its pauses freed and saved before dry-run was turned on; when any workload is in dry-run, WOULD FREE, what pausing it would have freed since dry-run started measuring it, $0 until a would-be pause has, and - for one that isn't in dry-run; and NEXT:
    • when it pauses: pauses in 45m, pauses now once it's Idle, with or without an idlePolicy, as after a pause request, and would pause … in dry-run; pauses now, early: the forecast expects quiet until Fri 20:00 UTC once the forecast has brought the pause forward, or expected once that time has passed, as for a would-be pause in dry-run, which stays Idle until activity. After a GitOps tool undid its last pause, Hybernate waits an hour before pausing it again, which reads pauses at 14:20 UTC (after GitOps conflict); see GitOps tools. Status is written every few minutes, so for up to 7 minutes after the time it showed, a workload still running reads pauses soon; after that, overdue to pause, which means something the table can't see holds it, and kubectl describe managedworkload says what
    • why it won't pause yet, and until when: held awake while preview-7/worker uses it (its dependents, until they pause), held awake for 2h (active-until) (hybernate.io/active-until on the ManagedWorkload or the workload, as wake --for sets), or held awake by the forecast: busy from 13:00 UTC (the hour the forecast expects demand in)
    • why it won't pause at all: never pauses: no idlePolicy, never pauses: namespace protected, never pauses: part of Hybernate (the operator's or the doorman's own Deployment), never pauses: PVCs deleted on scale-down (a StatefulSet whose persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy.whenScaled is Delete), nothing: labelled hybernate.io/ignore, nothing: workload not found, nothing: another ManagedWorkload has it, won't pause: dependsOn cycle, won't pause: no CPU metrics, or won't pause: Prometheus failing
    • for a paused one, what wakes it: wakes on a request or activity, or wakes on activity without the doorman. When the forecast brought the pause forward, before idleAfter ran out, it says so first, and until when the forecast expected quiet: paused early: the forecast expected quiet until Fri 20:00 UTC; wakes on a request or activity
  • FORECAST: whether the workload's forecast acts: acting; learning, with acts from Oct 8 when the operator expects it to start, if the coming days repeat the last week it saw; relearning, after demand broke from what it had learned; or not learning while paused: and why, such as no Service routes requests to it, while it's paused with neither the doorman nor a Prometheus activity query to see its demand; its status.prediction.message says how to fix it. - until the operator has recorded one. JSON gives the reason from status.prediction.reason in forecast, and forecastStartsActing.
  • Recent pauses and wakes, newest first, as far back as the cluster keeps events, or --since: each pause, and each wake with its cause, a request on a Service, an activity annotation (including kubectl hybernate wake and a dependent waking), the forecast, or a scale-up from outside Hybernate. Requests the doorman closed without reaching the workload are listed too, and a wake whose cause wasn't recorded, such as a hand-back when a namespace becomes protected, is listed by its resumed event alone. The table shows the latest 10; -o json has every one. The API server keeps events for an hour unless its --event-ttl says otherwise, so on most clusters that's what status can show.
kubectl hybernate status --context staging -n preview-42
kubectl hybernate status --since 1h -o json

docs.title: Share it as a web page
docs.text:
kubectl hybernate status --html              # opens it in your browser
kubectl hybernate status --html status.html  # saves it, to send around

--html writes the same status as a web page, for a team or a manager: the summary, with the node autoscaler and the forecast's time zone; what pausing freed this month, what of that was saved, and what dry-run measured pausing would have freed; what needs attention; every workload, with its state and for how long, its last activity, what happens to it next, and what it freed or would free, in a table you can sort and filter; and every pause and wake since --since, with what caused it, at its time in UTC. Given a file, it writes it there; given none, to a new temporary file. Either is readable only by you, since it names the cluster's workloads. In a terminal, it opens the page in your browser, as scan does with its report, unless --open=false; otherwise it prints where the page is. The terminal table, or -o json, is printed as well. The page loads nothing from elsewhere, so it works offline and attached to an email.

Flag Short Default Description --namespace -n all you can read Namespace to show; repeat for several --all-namespaces -A Read every namespace, and fail rather than fall back when your access doesn't allow that. Can't be combined with -n --output -o table table, json, or yaml --since 24h How far back to list pauses and wakes --html Also write the status as a web page to this file; given without one, to a temporary file --open true Open the --html page in your browser, when run in a terminal --timeout 1m How long to wait for the cluster before giving up

Your user needs list on managedworkloads and events, in every namespace or the ones passed with -n. Without access to events, it shows the rest and says so.
