To name the node autoscaler, it reads what nodes does for that: Karpenter's NodePools, nodes' metadata, the cluster-autoscaler-status ConfigMap and Deployments' metadata in kube-system; without enough of them to tell, it says the autoscaler is unknown. It also lists deployments and statefulsets, reading only their metadata, for a hybernate.io/active-until annotation on the workload itself, and goes without it when it can't. A namespace named with -n that doesn't exist is an error, which takes get on namespaces to tell; without it, the namespace shows as one Hybernate manages nothing in.

docs.title: See Why Nodes Don't Scale Down
docs.text:
Pausing a workload frees what its pods requested, but that comes off the bill only once a node autoscaler removes the node they ran on. nodes shows what's in the way:

kubectl hybernate nodes

staging (EKS us-east-1): 3 nodes
Node autoscaler: Karpenter (NodePool batch consolidates only empty nodes after 1m; NodePool default consolidates when underutilized after 1m)
Hybernate's 2 paused workloads would request 2.0 vCPU and 4.0 GiB of memory if awake.
  in pool batch: 0.5 vCPU and 1.0 GiB
  in pool default: 1.5 vCPU and 3.0 GiB

  NODE      POOL      INSTANCE TYPE   CPU REQUESTED     MEMORY REQUESTED   UTILISATION   BLOCKED BY
  batch-1   batch     c5.large        0.1 of 1.9 vCPU   0.3 of 3.0 GiB     10%           NodePool consolidates only empty nodes
  quiet-1   default   m5.large        0.2 of 1.9 vCPU   1.0 of 7.0 GiB     14%           PDB allows no disruption (shop/db)
  busy-1    default   m5.xlarge       3.0 of 3.9 vCPU   8.0 of 14.0 GiB    77%           -

Next steps:
  1. A NodePool consolidates only empty nodes, which a node running anything never is. Set spec.disruption.consolidationPolicy: WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized.
     For example: NodePool batch consolidates only empty nodes, and this one runs 1 pod
  2. A PodDisruptionBudget allows no disruptions, so its pods can't be moved. Raise maxUnavailable, lower minAvailable, or run more replicas than it requires.
     For example: shop/db: PodDisruptionBudget db allows no disruptions
  See https://okedeji.io/hybernate/guides/cluster-autoscaler/
  To have pausing empty whole nodes, put non-production workloads on a node pool of their own: https://okedeji.io/hybernate/guides/node-pools/
  • Node autoscaler: what scales the cluster's nodes, which status and scan show too:
    • Karpenter, from the nodepools.karpenter.sh CRD or nodes labelled karpenter.sh/nodepool, with each NodePool's spec.disruption.consolidationPolicy and consolidateAfter
    • EKS Auto Mode, from nodes labelled eks.amazonaws.com/compute-type: auto; its NodePools are Karpenter's, and read the same way
    • Cluster Autoscaler, self-managed or the one GKE Standard and AKS run for you, from the cluster-autoscaler-status ConfigMap it writes in kube-system, with the cloud its nodes are on. Without the ConfigMap, a Deployment in kube-system whose name ends in cluster-autoscaler is named as a hint that it may not be running
    • GKE Autopilot, from that ConfigMap and nodes all named gk3-, as Autopilot names them; it scales nodes itself
    • none found, when every place was read and none of them showed one: freed capacity won't come off the bill until something removes nodes
    • unknown, when your access didn't allow reading what would tell, which it names. It never says none when it couldn't look
  • The table: each node, least used first, with its pool (Karpenter NodePool, EKS node group, GKE node pool or AKS agent pool), its instance type, what its running pods request of what it can allocate, and its utilisation: the larger of the two, as Cluster Autoscaler measures it against its scale-down threshold. DaemonSet pods count towards what's requested, as they do for the autoscaler.
  • BLOCKED BY: why the autoscaler won't remove the node, however little of it is used, the first two in the table and every one in -o json. On a node a Karpenter NodePool owns, Karpenter's reasons: the node or a pod annotated karpenter.sh/do-not-disrupt: "true", a pod whose PodDisruptionBudget allows no disruptions (status.disruptionsAllowed is 0), a NodePool with consolidationPolicy: WhenEmpty and anything but DaemonSet pods on the node, or consolidateAfter: Never. On any other node, Cluster Autoscaler's: the node annotated cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/scale-down-disabled: "true", a pod annotated cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/safe-to-evict: "false", a pod with an emptyDir not in memory or a hostPath volume it doesn't name in cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/safe-to-evict-local-volumes, a pod no controller owns, a kube-system pod without a PodDisruptionBudget, and the PodDisruptionBudget rule. DaemonSet and static pods never block, and a pod annotated safe-to-evict: "true" blocks only by its PodDisruptionBudget, as with Cluster Autoscaler. Local storage and kube-system pods block only while Cluster Autoscaler's --skip-nodes-with-local-storage and --skip-nodes-with-system-pods are on, as they are by default upstream; AKS turns the first off. While the autoscaler is unknown, nodes Karpenter doesn't own are judged by Cluster Autoscaler's rules. A node no autoscaler found scales is not autoscaled.
  • Next steps: how to clear each kind of reason the table shows, with one example of it, the node autoscaler guide, and the node pools guide.

A node with nothing in BLOCKED BY that stays is still in use: paused workloads share it with busy ones. Node Pools for Real Savings shows how to give non-prod workloads nodes that pausing them empties.

What paused workloads would request is what Hybernate recorded their pause freed, in all and by the node pool their pods ran in, as each pause recorded it: the pools that would need room for them if they woke. A workload whose pods ran in several pools is shared between them by how many ran in each. Pauses that recorded no pool are counted in all but not by pool.

kubectl hybernate nodes --context staging -o json
Flag Short Default Description --output -o table table, json, or yaml --timeout 1m How long to wait for the cluster before giving up

Your user needs list on nodes, and on pods and poddisruptionbudgets in every namespace; list on nodepools.karpenter.sh; get on the cluster-autoscaler-status ConfigMap and list on deployments in kube-system; and list on managedworkloads. It reads what it can, and the notes say what it couldn't: without pods, what each node runs and the reasons that come from its pods are left out; without nodes, there's no table.

docs.title: Pause a Workload
docs.text:
kubectl hybernate pause my-api -n staging

pausing staging/my-api...
staging/my-api is Paused after 4s; a request to it, or kubectl hybernate wake, wakes it

pause asks Hybernate to pause a workload now, instead of when its idle clock runs out: a preview environment at the end of the day, say. It's an ordinary pause, the same as an idle one: a request to the workload through the doorman, activity, autoResume or wake wakes it. It works whether or not the workload has an idlePolicy. See Pause and Resume for exactly what Hybernate does with the request.

# Pause it even if the forecast expects it to be busy soon, without asking
kubectl hybernate pause my-api -n staging --yes

# Request the pause and return straight away
kubectl hybernate pause my-api -n staging --wait=false

NAME is found as for wake.

What it says depends on the phase:

Phase What happens Running It pauses, and pause waits until it's Paused Idle It pauses now Resuming It pauses once it's up Pausing Already pausing; pause waits until it's Paused Paused Already paused; pause returns at once dry-run Never paused: Hybernate counts a would-be pause, and pause says so

Hybernate pauses it by the same rules as an idle pause, so pause exits 1 with Hybernate's reason when it won't: workloads that are awake depend on it, a dependsOn cycle runs through it, its namespace is protected, or the workload doesn't exist, is labelled hybernate.io/ignore or is managed by another ManagedWorkload. A workload scaled to zero outside Hybernate is off already, which pause says, exiting 0. Asking does override the hour Hybernate waits after a GitOps tool undid its last pause.

When a confident forecast expects the workload to be busy within the hour, Hybernate declines the pause and says when, since it would likely be woken straight back, and pause asks:

preview-42/api wasn't paused: the forecast expects demand at 80% of requests in the hour from 09:00 UTC
Pause it anyway? [y/N]

Answering y asks again overriding the forecast, and it pauses; anything else leaves it running, exiting 0. The question waits for you as long as you take: --timeout counts only the time spent on the cluster, and starts again after your answer. --yes overrides the forecast from the start, without asking. With no terminal to ask on, such as in a script, pause exits 1 with the reason and says to pass --yes.

When a hybernate.io/active-until annotation holds it awake, on the ManagedWorkload, as wake --for sets, or on the workload itself, Hybernate would refuse the pause, so pause asks first, naming which holds it:

preview-42/api wasn't paused: the hybernate.io/active-until annotation on its ManagedWorkload keeps it awake until 2026-10-17T20:00:00Z
Clear it and pause now? [y/N]

Answering y removes the annotation, from both when both hold it, and pauses it; anything else leaves it running, exiting 0. --clear-hold clears it without asking; with no terminal to ask on and without --clear-hold, pause exits 1 and says to pass it. --yes doesn't clear a hold, so a nightly script that pauses with --yes doesn't end one someone set for a demo.

When a GitOps tool sets the workload's replicas from Git and isn't told to leave them to Hybernate, pause warns before asking, with the one-time fix: the tool sets them again on its next sync, which undoes the pause. See GitOps tools for how it tells:

Warning: Argo CD application argocd/shop sets preview-42/api's replicas from Git, as argocd-controller, so its next sync will likely scale it back up, undoing this pause. To have Argo CD leave replicas to Hybernate, once:
  Add RespectIgnoreDifferences=true to the syncPolicy.syncOptions of Argo CD application argocd/shop, so syncs leave the replicas it ignores.
See https://okedeji.io/hybernate/guides/gitops/#argo-cd

When it can't tell, such as without access to Argo CD's namespace, the warning says why, and to make the fix if you haven't already.

If the workload isn't Paused, and Hybernate hasn't said why, within --timeout, pause exits 1 with its phase and the kubectl describe command that says why.

Flag Short Default Description --namespace -n kubeconfig context's Namespace of the workload --wait true Wait until the workload is Paused, or Hybernate says why it isn't --yes -y false Pause it even if the forecast expects it to be busy within the hour, without asking --clear-hold false Clear a hybernate.io/active-until hold on its ManagedWorkload, as wake --for sets, or on the workload, without asking --timeout 5m How long to wait, cluster calls included; it starts again after you answer a question

Your user needs get, list and patch on managedworkloads in the namespace, and get on the workload for the GitOps warning and its own hold, which are left out without it. Clearing a hold on the workload takes patch on it. For a workload Argo CD applies, telling whether Argo CD leaves its replicas takes list on applications.argoproj.io in every namespace, or get in argocd, and get on the argocd-cm ConfigMap; without them, the warning says it couldn't check.

docs.title: Wake a Workload
docs.text:
kubectl hybernate wake my-api -n staging

waking staging/my-api...
staging/my-api is Running after 23s

wake marks the ManagedWorkload as active now by setting its hybernate.io/last-activity annotation, the same activity annotation a developer portal would set. A paused workload wakes, along with the workloads it depends on; a running one has its idle clock restarted. It then waits until the workload is Running.

# Keep it awake for the next two hours, e.g. for a demo
kubectl hybernate wake my-api -n staging --for 2h

# Request the wake and return straight away
kubectl hybernate wake my-api -n staging --wait=false

NAME is the workload, as status shows it, such as api or statefulset/postgres, or its ManagedWorkload's name. When a bare name answers to more than one ManagedWorkload, such as when a Deployment and a StatefulSet share it, or one ManagedWorkload is named after a workload another one manages, it lists them and asks for the workload as kind/name, which only matches workloads.

What it says depends on the phase:

Phase What happens Paused It wakes, and wake waits until it's Running Pausing It wakes once the pause finishes Resuming It's already waking Idle Marked active, so it stays up Running Already running; its idle clock restarts, and wake returns at once dry-run, not paused Never paused; its idle clock restarts, and wake returns at once

It refuses, and says why, when activity can't wake the workload: the workload doesn't exist or is labelled hybernate.io/ignore, or another ManagedWorkload manages it.

If the workload isn't Running within --timeout, wake exits 1 with its phase and the kubectl describe command that says why.

Flag Short Default Description --namespace -n kubeconfig context's Namespace of the workload --for Also keep the workload awake for this long, by setting hybernate.io/active-until on its ManagedWorkload. A hold there that ends later stays, and wake says so --wait true Wait until the workload is Running --timeout 5m How long to wait, cluster calls included

Your user needs get, list and patch on managedworkloads in the namespace.

docs.title: Show a Workload's Dependencies
docs.text:
kubectl hybernate deps postgres -n preview-42

preview-42/postgres (StatefulSet, Paused)
Depends on:
  nothing
Depended on by:
  preview-42/api      learned from PGHOST                   Running
  preview-42/worker   declared in dependsOn, waitForReady   Paused
Learned links come from the dependent's environment or its requests; hybernate.io/ignore-dependencies drops one.

deps shows what Hybernate holds awake and wakes with a ManagedWorkload, in both directions: what it depends on, and what depends on it, in any namespace. Each link says where it comes from, a dependsOn or what Hybernate learned from the dependent's environment or from a wake, and what the other workload is doing now; one Hybernate doesn't manage shows as not managed. It only reads ManagedWorkloads. Without access to them in every namespace, it reads the workload's own and says that dependents elsewhere aren't shown; a dependency in another namespace then shows as unknown (can't read <namespace>). NAME is found as for wake.

Flag Short Default Description --namespace -n kubeconfig context's Namespace of the workload --timeout 1m How long to wait for the cluster before giving up

docs.title: Enable a Workload
docs.text:
A workload in dry-run, whether from its own hybernate.io/dry-run: "true", its namespace's, the cluster default, or spec.dryRun on a ManagedWorkload you wrote, is measured but never paused. enable ends that, so Hybernate starts pausing it while idle:

kubectl hybernate enable checkout-api -n preview-42
kubectl hybernate enable statefulset/postgres -n preview-42
kubectl hybernate enable --all -n preview-42

deployment/checkout-api: dry-run ended, Hybernate will pause it while idle

For a workload opted in with the hybernate.io/managed label, it sets the workload's own hybernate.io/dry-run annotation to "false", which wins over its namespace's annotation and the cluster's default. It reads the workload's ManagedWorkload to tell whether it's in dry-run, so a dry-run from the cluster default counts too. For a ManagedWorkload you wrote, it sets spec.dryRun: false. It doesn't wait: Hybernate pauses the workload once its clock runs out.

enable only ends dry-run for a workload Hybernate manages. Otherwise it changes nothing and exits non-zero with the reason: the namespace is protected (labelled hybernate.io/protected=true, or a kube-* namespace, unless labelled hybernate.io/allow-protected=true); the workload is labelled hybernate.io/ignore=true, or its own hybernate.io/managed is anything but "true", which opts it out of a managed namespace; no ManagedWorkload manages it, because the operator isn't running, doesn't watch the namespace, or protects it by its own settings; or its ManagedWorkload says Hybernate never pauses it: Protected=True (such as by a protectedNamespaces pattern, or for Hybernate's own operator and doorman), a target labelled hybernate.io/ignore, or DuplicateTarget=True. Right after you label a workload, the operator may not have made its ManagedWorkload yet; run enable again a few seconds later. Without the ManagedWorkload CRD, it says Hybernate isn't installed.

--all ends dry-run for every workload in the namespace. When the namespace's own hybernate.io/dry-run annotation, or the cluster default, keeps any of them in dry-run, it sets the namespace's annotation to "false" and drops the workloads' own annotations, so the namespace decides for all of them. When each is in dry-run by its own annotation, it leaves the namespace alone and sets each workload's annotation to "false". Either way, it sets spec.dryRun: false on ManagedWorkloads written by hand in the namespace. When Git owns the namespace, its annotation is left for you to change there, which also ends dry-run for the workloads that take it, and workloads with their own annotation get "false". When your access doesn't allow changing the namespace, as with edit or admin bound in it, enable leaves its annotation alone, says so, and sets every workload's own annotation to "false", which wins over it; with nothing but the namespace's annotation to change, it exits non-zero. Labelled workloads no ManagedWorkload manages are left alone. When enable just set the namespace's annotation to "false", that ends their dry-run too once Hybernate picks them up, unless they have an annotation of their own, so they're covered. The rest are listed, and enable exits non-zero. When none of the namespace's workloads has been picked up yet, enable changes nothing, the namespace's annotation included, and exits non-zero, since the operator may not be running. Workloads Hybernate never pauses, by their ManagedWorkload, are left alone and listed too.

When a GitOps tool (Argo CD, Flux, Fleet, kapp or Kluctl) applies the setting enable would change, the hybernate.io/dry-run annotation on the workload or its namespace, or a ManagedWorkload's spec.dryRun, enable changes nothing there, because the tool would put the old value straight back. It tells by the field managers the API server records as owning that setting, as pause does for replicas, so it doesn't matter how the tool tracks what it applies; for an object with no managed fields recorded, it goes by the tracking label or annotation Argo CD or Flux adds. A tool that applies the workload but not the annotation, such as when Git doesn't have it, leaves a change to it alone. It names the tool, prints the change to make in Git, and exits non-zero:

deployment/checkout-api is managed by Argo CD application shop, which would undo a change made here. In its manifest:
  set the annotation  hybernate.io/dry-run: "false"
Or pass --force to change the cluster anyway.

When Helm set it, enable changes it, since Helm only applies a chart when you run it, and warns that the next helm upgrade puts the chart's value back, so set it in the chart too. See GitOps tools.

Ending dry-run lets Hybernate pause the workload, and a GitOps tool that sets its replicas from Git scales it back up on its next sync after each pause. So whatever enable does, ends dry-run, finds it ended already, or leaves the change to Git, it warns as pause does, with the one-time fix, unless the tool is told to leave the replicas to Hybernate. With --all, workloads a tool treats alike, such as those of one Argo CD application, get one warning between them.

A bare name is looked up as a Deployment and as a StatefulSet. When both have it, enable lists them and asks for the kind; prefix the name with deployment/ or statefulset/ to be exact.

Flag Short Default Description --namespace -n kubeconfig context's Namespace of the workload --all false Enable every workload in the namespace --force false Change the cluster even when a GitOps tool applies the setting from Git --timeout 1m How long to wait for the cluster before giving up

Your user needs get and patch on the workload, get on its namespace, and list on managedworkloads in it. Without list on ManagedWorkloads, enable goes by the annotations alone, so it can't check that Hybernate manages the workload or see a dry-run from the cluster default, and it says so. With --all, it also needs list on Deployments and StatefulSets, and patch on the namespace to end its dry-run there; without it, each workload gets its own annotation instead. The GitOps warning reads Argo CD as pause's does. See Opting In for the label and every setting.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
This guide takes one workload from "idle and costing money" to "paused while idle, woken when used", measuring it first so nothing is paused until you say so.

It assumes Hybernate is installed and you have the kubectl plugin.

Hybernate reads CPU from metrics-server, and while it can't read a workload's CPU it doesn't pause it, since a busy workload would look idle. GKE and AKS run it by default; EKS, kind and a new minikube don't. Check that the Metrics API is there:

kubectl get apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io

If it's missing or not Available, install it. On minikube, run minikube addons enable metrics-server; on EKS, add the metrics-server add-on, or apply the manifest below. Elsewhere:

kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server/releases/latest/download/components.yaml

On kind, the kubelets' certificates aren't signed for their addresses, so also tell metrics-server not to verify them. Do this only on a local test cluster:

kubectl patch deployment metrics-server -n kube-system --type=json \
  -p '[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/args/-","value":"--kubelet-insecure-tls"}]'

kubectl top pods -A shows numbers within a minute or so once it's working. If a workload still doesn't pause, see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: 1. A sample workload
docs.text:
If you don't have one to try, create a Deployment:

kubectl create namespace dev
kubectl create deployment my-api --image=nginx:1.27-alpine --replicas=2 -n dev
kubectl set resources deployment my-api -n dev --requests=cpu=100m,memory=64Mi
kubectl expose deployment my-api -n dev --port=80
kubectl rollout status deployment/my-api -n dev

docs.title: 2. See what's idle
docs.text:
kubectl hybernate scan -n dev

The scan shows each workload, whether it's idle right now and why, and what it costs while running. A workload deployed in the last hour counts as active, as Hybernate would treat it, so a brand-new one shows as active until then.

On your own cluster, leave out -n to scan every namespace. When Argo CD or Flux applies your workloads, the scan's notes list those whose replicas it sets from Git; see step 5 before letting Hybernate pause them.

docs.title: 3. Opt it in, measuring first
docs.text:
kubectl annotate deployment my-api -n dev hybernate.io/dry-run=true hybernate.io/idle-after=5m
kubectl label deployment my-api -n dev hybernate.io/managed=true

The annotations are the workload's settings, set first so it starts in dry-run; the label opts it in. Here, dry-run means it's measured and never paused, and idle-after: 5m makes the example quick (the default is an hour). In real use, these usually go in the workload's manifest or Helm values, or on its namespace to cover everything in it; see Opting In. With Kustomize, don't use commonLabels, which changes the workload's selector: With Kustomize gives the ways that work.

Hybernate creates a ManagedWorkload for it:

kubectl get managedworkloads -n dev

NAME     PHASE     FREED   SAVED   WOULD FREE   AGE
my-api   Running   $0.00   $0.00   $0.00        10s

docs.title: 4. Watch it measure
docs.text:
kubectl hybernate status -n dev

status is one screen of what Hybernate is doing with every workload it manages. For my-api, STATE reads running (dry-run), LAST ACTIVITY says when it was last active and from what (created, until something else is seen), and NEXT when it would pause. Once there's been no activity for idle-after, STATE becomes idle (dry-run) and an event says it would have paused. Nothing is scaled down in dry-run:

kubectl describe managedworkload my-api -n dev

Each would-be pause is added up: how many times it would have paused, how long it would have slept, and what that would have freed. Mark it active to end one, as a developer portal or your own tooling would, then look again:

kubectl annotate deployment my-api -n dev --overwrite hybernate.io/last-activity=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
kubectl hybernate status -n dev
kubectl get managedworkloads -n dev

status leads with what dry-run has measured, and kubectl get managedworkloads shows in WOULD FREE what the would-be pauses would have freed. A few minutes of a sample this small free less than a cent, so expect $0.00 here; left in dry-run for a few days, across a weekend if it's used on weekdays, a real workload's figure is what to judge going live by. kubectl hybernate scan -n dev shows the same, with how long it would have slept and how often it would have been woken. For scripts, kubectl get managedworkload my-api -n dev -o jsonpath='{.status.dryRun}' gives the summary as data, its hours as Kubernetes quantities; see Dry Run.

Requests to a running workload don't count as activity by themselves: Hybernate sees its CPU, deploys and activity annotations, and requests only through a Prometheus query you give it, or once it's paused, through the doorman. An nginx serving the odd request uses almost no CPU, so it would pause. On a workload of your own that doesn't turn idle, LAST ACTIVITY in status says what keeps it active, such as cpu, and NEXT says why it won't pause when something holds it.

docs.title: 5. Applied by Argo CD or Flux? Leave the replicas to Hybernate
docs.text:
Skip this for the sample. Hybernate pauses a workload by setting its replicas to zero, and a GitOps tool that applies replicas from Git sets them straight back. Hybernate reports that as a GitOpsConflict and, rather than fight the tool, waits an hour before pausing again, so until the tool is told, pausing seems not to work. Tell it once, before step 6:

  • Argo CD: ignore /spec/replicas on Deployments and StatefulSets, in argocd-cm for every app or in an Application's ignoreDifferences, and add RespectIgnoreDifferences=true to the Application's sync options.
  • Flux: leave replicas out of the workload's manifest, or remove it with a post-renderer for a chart that always sets it.

An HPA needs the same, so a workload that already has one under Argo CD or Flux is set. GitOps tools has the YAML, and the settings for Fleet, kapp and Kluctl. The scan's notes from step 2 list the workloads whose replicas are set from Git, and kubectl hybernate enable and pause warn when it isn't in place.

docs.title: 6. Let it pause
docs.text:
When you're happy with what you see:

kubectl hybernate enable my-api -n dev

This sets the workload's hybernate.io/dry-run annotation to "false". Once the workload has had no activity for idle-after, which NEXT in kubectl hybernate status -n dev counts down, Hybernate scales it to zero, remembering it had 2 replicas:

kubectl get deployment my-api -n dev
# READY: 0/0

docs.title: 7. Use it again
docs.text:
Send it a request. The doorman holds the request, wakes the workload, and answers once it's Ready:

kubectl run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl:8.7.1 -n dev --restart=Never -- curl -s http://my-api

A browser that reaches it through an Ingress or a Gateway gets a waking-up page instead, which loads the app once it's up. kubectl port-forward doesn't go through the Service but straight to a pod, so it can't reach a paused workload; wake it first:

kubectl hybernate wake my-api -n dev

docs.title: 8. Stop managing it
docs.text:
kubectl label deployment my-api -n dev hybernate.io/managed-

Removing the label removes the ManagedWorkload. If the workload is paused, it's scaled back to its replicas first, so it's never left switched off.

docs.title: What's next?
docs.text:
• Opting In: every setting, namespaces, Kustomize, and GitOps
  • Idle Detection: how the activity clock decides
  • Wake on Request: how requests wake a paused workload
  • ManagedWorkload Guide: writing a ManagedWorkload yourself, for settings annotations don't cover

docs.title: HPA and KEDA
docs.text:
Hybernate works alongside a HorizontalPodAutoscaler or a KEDA ScaledObject, with nothing to set up. While a workload runs, its autoscaler decides how many replicas it needs, and Hybernate leaves the replica count alone. Once it's idle, Hybernate pauses it to zero, and on a wake brings it back within the autoscaler's range.

The ManagedWorkload says what scales it:

Autoscaled=True   HPA web scales it between 2 and 10 replicas; Hybernate pauses it at zero, where the HPA stops scaling, and resumes it within that range

docs.title: HPA
docs.text:
An HPA stops scaling a workload at zero replicas, so a pause holds: Hybernate scales the workload to zero, and the HPA leaves it there. On a wake, Hybernate restores the replicas it had, kept within the HPA's minReplicas and maxReplicas should those have changed while it was paused, and the HPA takes over again.

CPU from the workload's own pods counts as activity whatever the HPA does, so a workload busy enough for its HPA to scale it up isn't idle.

docs.title: KEDA
docs.text:
KEDA scales its workloads itself, and would scale a paused one straight back up to its minReplicaCount, or as soon as a trigger fired. So for a workload a ScaledObject scales, Hybernate pauses through KEDA: it sets autoscaling.keda.sh/paused-replicas: "0" on the ScaledObject, which has KEDA hold the workload at zero and stop scaling it, and records the ScaledObject in status.pause.scaledObject. If the ScaledObject already had a paused-replicas value of your own, it's recorded too, in status.pause.scaledObjectPausedReplicas.

On a wake, Hybernate has KEDA hold the workload at the replicas it's restored to until they're all Ready, or Hybernate stops waiting for those that aren't (see Resume), then puts back your own paused-replicas value, or removes the annotation if there was none, so KEDA carries on from there. Released any earlier, a ScaledObject with minReplicaCount: 0 and no active trigger could take a starting workload straight back to zero, and a request the doorman held would wait for nothing.

When Hybernate lets go of a paused workload, because its ManagedWorkload is deleted, it's labelled hybernate.io/ignore, or its namespace is protected, the ScaledObject is released the same way. If the ScaledObject, or KEDA itself, is removed while the workload is paused, there's nothing to release, and the workload is woken as usual.

The annotation isn't in your manifests, so Argo CD and Flux leave it alone.

docs.title: KEDA or Hybernate?
docs.text: KEDA already scales a workload to zero when its triggers say there's no work, such as an empty queue. Hybernate leaves a workload KEDA has taken to zero to KEDA: it doesn't pause it, which would stop KEDA's triggers from starting it, and doesn't route its Services to the doorman; see Workloads Already at Zero. Hybernate adds what KEDA doesn't do: waking on the first HTTP request, holding dependencies awake, the forecast, and pausing by activity it can see without a trigger. A workload KEDA already takes to zero gains little; a KEDA workload with a minReplicaCount above zero, such as one that should stay warm during working hours, is where pausing it frees capacity.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: The operator reads HPAs, and reads and annotates ScaledObjects. Without KEDA installed there are no ScaledObjects, and Hybernate looks for them again every 10 minutes in case it's installed later. The Autoscaled condition reflects a ScaledObject created or changed within 15 seconds; a pause or wake always reads them afresh.

docs.title: Cluster Autoscaler Configuration
docs.text:
Hybernate manages workloads at the pod layer: it pauses idle Deployments and StatefulSets, scaling them to zero. But pods run on nodes, and your bill is for nodes. What a pause frees, the CPU and memory its pods requested, comes off the bill only once a node autoscaler removes the nodes it freed it on:

Hybernate pauses pods → capacity freed on their nodes → autoscaler removes nodes → saved

Without a node autoscaler, or with scale-down blocked, pausing frees capacity and saves nothing. Hybernate reports the two apart: freedThisMonth is what pausing released, and savedThisMonth is what it measurably took off the bill, worked out every 5 minutes from the spare capacity left on each node pool. See Freed and Saved.

This guide covers the autoscaler settings that let freed capacity go. Freed becomes saved fastest when non-prod workloads have nodes of their own, so that pausing them empties whole nodes; Node Pools for Real Savings shows how.

docs.title: What Hybernate Detects
docs.text:
The operator looks every 10 minutes for what scales the cluster's nodes, logs what it finds when that changes, and exports it as hybernate_node_autoscaler:

  • Karpenter, from its nodepools.karpenter.sh NodePools (karpenter.sh/v1) or nodes labelled karpenter.sh/nodepool, which covers AKS node auto-provisioning
  • EKS Auto Mode, from nodes labelled eks.amazonaws.com/compute-type: auto
  • Cluster Autoscaler, self-managed or the one GKE Standard and AKS run for you, from the cluster-autoscaler-status ConfigMap it writes in kube-system
  • GKE Autopilot, from that ConfigMap and nodes named gk3-
  • none, when it looked everywhere and found nothing: the operator logs that what pausing frees won't come off the bill until something scales nodes down
  • unknown, when it found nothing and wasn't allowed to look everywhere, as in a watchNamespaces install, which can't read Cluster Autoscaler's ConfigMap in kube-system

kubectl hybernate status and kubectl hybernate scan name it at the top. kubectl hybernate nodes goes further: for each node, what keeps the autoscaler from removing it. See See Why Nodes Don't Scale Down.

docs.title: Cluster Autoscaler
docs.text: Cluster Autoscaler manages node groups across EKS, GKE, AKS, and self-managed clusters.

docs.title: Recommended Settings
docs.text:
cluster-autoscaler-values.yaml
autoDiscovery:
  clusterName: my-cluster

extraArgs:
  # How long a node must be unneeded before it's removed. The default is 10m.
  # A paused workload's node keeps costing money for this long, so keep it
  # short next to idleAfter.
  scale-down-unneeded-time: 5m

  # A node is unneeded when the CPU or memory its pods request, whichever is
  # higher, is below this fraction of what it can allocate. 0.5 is the default.
  # It counts requests, not usage: a node frees up once paused pods are gone,
  # not when they go quiet.
  scale-down-utilization-threshold: "0.5"

  # How long after a scale-up before scale-down is considered again. The
  # default is 10m. A wake can scale nodes up, so a shorter delay lets the
  # next pause free them sooner; much shorter, and nodes churn.
  scale-down-delay-after-add: 5m

  # How long after removing a node before scale-down is considered again.
  # The default, 0s, lets the nodes of several workloads paused together go
  # one after another, so leave it.
  scale-down-delay-after-delete: 0s

  # How often the autoscaler evaluates the cluster. 10s is the default and
  # needs no change for Hybernate.
  scan-interval: 10s

GKE doesn't let you set these flags: its optimize-utilization autoscaling profile scales down sooner than the default balanced. AKS sets them cluster-wide in its cluster autoscaler profile (az aks update --cluster-autoscaler-profile). See Node Pools for Real Savings.

docs.title: Key Interactions
docs.text: Hybernate Action Autoscaler Response Pause (scale to 0) Pods removed; a node whose remaining pods request less than the threshold is removed after scale-down-unneeded-time, if nothing on it blocks that Resume (scale back up) Autoscaler provisions new nodes if no capacity exists

docs.title: What Keeps a Node
docs.text:
Cluster Autoscaler won't remove a node, however little of it is used, when it runs:

  • a pod annotated cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/safe-to-evict: "false"
  • a pod whose PodDisruptionBudget allows no disruptions
  • a pod with an emptyDir not in memory or a hostPath volume, while --skip-nodes-with-local-storage is on, as it is by default upstream (AKS turns it off; GKE 1.22 and later ignores local storage)
  • a pod no controller would recreate elsewhere
  • a kube-system pod without a PodDisruptionBudget, while --skip-nodes-with-system-pods is on, its default

or when the node is annotated cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/scale-down-disabled: "true". DaemonSet and static pods never keep a node. Hybernate scales replica counts directly, so its own pauses never go through eviction or PodDisruptionBudgets; it's what's left on the node that can hold it. kubectl hybernate nodes lists each of these per node, with how to clear it.

docs.title: Karpenter
docs.text: Karpenter is an open-source node autoscaler, a Kubernetes SIG Autoscaling project, with providers for AWS, Azure (as AKS node auto-provisioning), and other clouds. Instead of managing node groups, it provisions individual nodes sized to fit pending pods and consolidates underutilized nodes proactively. Hybernate reads karpenter.sh/v1 NodePools.

docs.title: Recommended Settings
docs.text:
nodepool.yaml
apiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1
kind: NodePool
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      nodeClassRef:
        group: karpenter.k8s.aws
        kind: EC2NodeClass
        name: default
      requirements:
        - key: karpenter.sh/capacity-type
          operator: In
          values: ["on-demand", "spot"]
        - key: kubernetes.io/arch
          operator: In
          values: ["amd64"]
      # Maximum time a node can live, regardless of utilization, so nodes
      # pick up new images. In v1 it's here, not under disruption.
      expireAfter: 720h
  disruption:
    # Removes empty nodes, and moves pods off underutilized ones to remove
    # those too. WhenEmpty never touches a node that runs anything but
    # DaemonSets, so pausing one workload on a shared node saves nothing.
    consolidationPolicy: WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized

    # How long after a pod was last added to or removed from a node before
    # it's considered. A pause is deliberate, not transient, so there's no
    # need to wait long. Never turns consolidation off.
    consolidateAfter: 1m

nodeClassRef names your provider's node class: EC2NodeClass in karpenter.k8s.aws on AWS, or NodeClass in eks.amazonaws.com on EKS Auto Mode.

docs.title: Key Interactions
docs.text:
Hybernate Action Karpenter Response Pause (scale to 0) Node becomes empty or underutilized, consolidated after consolidateAfter Resume (scale back up) Karpenter provisions a right-sized node for the pending pods

Karpenter won't consolidate a node that's annotated karpenter.sh/do-not-disrupt: "true", or that runs a pod so annotated, or a pod whose PodDisruptionBudget allows no disruptions. Without budgets, it disrupts at most 10% of a NodePool's nodes at once. kubectl hybernate nodes shows each NodePool's consolidation settings and what holds each node.

docs.title: Why Karpenter Works Well With Hybernate
docs.text:
• Right-sizing on resume: When Hybernate resumes a workload, Karpenter provisions a node sized to fit the exact pod requirements rather than falling back to a fixed node group size. This avoids over-provisioning on resume.
  • Consolidation: Karpenter repacks underutilized nodes as well as removing empty ones, so more of what pausing frees on shared nodes becomes saved, and sooner.
  • Spot instances: Non-critical workloads that Hybernate manages are good candidates for spot capacity. Hybernate prices spot nodes at their spot list price; see Spot nodes.

docs.title: Autopilot and Serverless Modes
docs.text:
Some managed Kubernetes offerings handle node scaling for you, and bill for what pods request rather than for nodes:

Service How It Works With Hybernate GKE Autopilot Google manages nodes entirely. You pay per pod resource request. What pausing frees stops being billed with the pods. No autoscaler configuration needed. EKS with Fargate AWS runs each pod on a dedicated microVM. No shared nodes. Pausing a pod stops billing for that pod. No autoscaler configuration needed. AKS node auto-provisioning Azure manages nodes using Karpenter under the hood. Use the Karpenter settings above. EKS Auto Mode AWS runs Karpenter for you; you pay for the nodes it provisions. Use the Karpenter settings above in your own NodePools.

On GKE Autopilot and Fargate what pausing frees is what you stop paying for. Hybernate's saved still measures the spare capacity left on nodes, so there it can read lower than what's taken off your bill, never higher. Set costTracking.rates to the provider's per-pod prices to price freed at what you pay.

docs.title: Verifying It Works
docs.text:
After configuring your autoscaler, verify the end-to-end flow:

  1. Pause a workload now, rather than waiting for its idle clock:

    kubectl hybernate pause my-api -n staging

    It returns once the workload is Paused, or says why Hybernate won't pause it, such as workloads that depend on it being awake. See Pause Now.

  2. Watch node count:

    kubectl get nodes -w

  3. Confirm a node is removed after the autoscaler's configured delay. If none is, kubectl hybernate nodes shows what keeps each node.

  4. Watch SAVED grow with FREED: the node's going is measured within 5 minutes, and written to the workload's status within another 5:

    kubectl hybernate status -n staging

  5. Wake the workload, with a request to its Service or:

    kubectl hybernate wake my-api -n staging

    It returns once the workload is Running, all its replicas Ready. Its idle clock starts again, so it pauses on its own once it's idle.

  6. Confirm a node is provisioned and the workload pods become ready. A wake that has to wait for a node may need a longer wake.maxWait; see What waking costs.

If nodes are not being removed after pause, run kubectl hybernate nodes, and check:

  • Autoscaler logs for why scale-down was skipped
  • Whether non-managed pods on the same node prevent removal; a node pool of their own for non-prod workloads avoids this
  • Whether PodDisruptionBudgets allow no disruptions
  • Whether the utilization threshold is set too low

See Freed but not saved.

docs.title: Dry Run Guide
docs.text: Dry run mode lets you observe what Hybernate would do without it ever reducing a workload's availability. The activity clock, dependency holds and the forecast all run as they do live, and only the scale to zero is skipped, so what dry-run can't show is what happens once a workload is paused: how long a wake on request takes, and whether a GitOps tool scales it straight back up. Wakes are never held back.

docs.title: On a Labelled Workload
docs.text:
deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-api
  namespace: staging
  labels:
    hybernate.io/managed: "true"
  annotations:
    hybernate.io/dry-run: "true"

docs.title: On a Namespace
docs.text:
Every opted-in workload in the namespace is measured, unless it sets its own hybernate.io/dry-run: "false":

apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: staging
  labels:
    hybernate.io/managed: "true"
  annotations:
    hybernate.io/dry-run: "true"

docs.title: Across the Cluster
docs.text:
Set defaults.dryRun: true in the Helm values to measure every opted-in workload that doesn't say otherwise, on the workload or its namespace.

A hybernate.io/dry-run value that can't be read, such as "True" or "yes", turns dry-run on, with an InvalidSetting warning event on the workload: a typo in the setting meant to stop pauses must never start them.

docs.title: On a ManagedWorkload You Wrote
docs.text:
managedworkload.yaml
apiVersion: hybernate.io/v1alpha1
kind: ManagedWorkload
metadata:
  name: my-api
  namespace: staging
spec:
  target:
    kind: Deployment
    name: my-api
  idlePolicy:
    idleAfter: 1h
  prediction:
    mode: balanced
  dryRun: true

On a ManagedWorkload created from the label, spec.dryRun follows the annotations: setting it there by hand is overwritten.

docs.title: What Happens in Dry Run
docs.text:
The operator runs its full evaluation pipeline:

Action Dry Run Behavior Idle detection The activity clock runs and the phase becomes Idle when it runs out, but the workload is not paused Forecast veto and dependency holds Applied and reported as usual: IdleVetoed, HeldByDependents, DependencyCycle. A dependent in dry-run that would have paused no longer holds a dependency in dry-run, so a whole app measured in dry-run counts every pause it would make, and when the dependent's would-be pause ends, its dry-run dependencies are stamped with activity, as its wake would have woken them, so theirs end with it and their clocks restart; see Dependencies A pause request Counted as a would-be pause: the phase becomes Idle, with a [dry-run] PauseRequested event and PauseRequest=False, reason DryRun, and the workload keeps running. Activity after the request ends the would-be pause, as it would wake a paused workload, except a Prometheus activity query that already showed activity as it was asked for, which ends it only once it has been quiet, as for a real pause A workload Hybernate had already paused Woken as soon as dry-run is turned on, with a DryRunWake event: dry-run never leaves a workload paused Wakes Never held back: kubectl hybernate wake and activity work as usual Cost tracking Costs are accumulated normally, all as awake time, since the workload never pauses; see Cost Tracking Prediction engine Data points are observed and confidence builds normally Events The events for decisions dry-run holds back carry a [dry-run] prefix; see Events Status Phase and conditions reflect what would happen, and status.dryRun sums it up

docs.title: What Dry Run Measured
docs.text:
Hybernate keeps a running summary of the pauses it would have made. A would-be pause starts when the activity clock runs out, and ends at the next activity, which is when a paused workload would have been woken. Two wakes are the exception. A request reaching a paused workload wakes it, but a workload in dry-run is still running, so a request counts only through the activity it shows, its CPU use or a Prometheus activity query; and autoResume wakes a paused workload ahead of hours the forecast expects to be busy, which dry-run doesn't count. So for a workload that serves the odd light request, or has autoResume on, real pauses would be shorter than the would-be ones. A would-be pause also ends when Hybernate stops measuring it: the workload is scaled to zero outside Hybernate, labelled hybernate.io/ignore, or its namespace becomes protected; see When Hybernate Lets Go. It's counted up to that moment.

For a workload that serves the odd light request, add a Prometheus activity query on its request rate at its ingress, with the operator's prometheus.url set, so that dry-run sees requests as activity, as the doorman would see them and wake the workload. Use the ingress's metrics, not the app's own: a paused workload has no pods to export them, so a query on them shows nothing once it pauses for real. On a workload opted in with the label, add the query to the ManagedWorkload Hybernate created, which keeps it:

kubectl patch managedworkload my-api -n staging --type=json -p '[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/idlePolicy/activity/prometheus","value":[{"promQL":"sum(rate(nginx_ingress_controller_requests{exported_namespace=\"staging\",exported_service=\"my-api\"}[5m]))"}]}]'

The ingress keeps counting requests once the workload pauses for real, so the query wakes it then too, as in While the Workload Is Paused.

What it would have freed is in the list of ManagedWorkloads:

kubectl get managedworkloads -n staging

NAME     PHASE   FREED   SAVED   WOULD FREE   AGE
my-api   Idle    $0.00   $0.00   $7.50        4d

kubectl hybernate status leads with it too, in its summary and its WOULD FREE column. The whole summary is in status.dryRun:

kubectl get managedworkload my-api -n staging -o jsonpath='{.status.dryRun}'
status.dryRun
since: "2026-10-01T09:00:00Z"
pauses: 4
slept: 96h12m0s
freedCPUHours: "192400m"
freedMemoryHours: "384800m"
estimatedFreed: $7.50

freedCPUHours and freedMemoryHours are the vCPU-hours and GiB-hours the workload's replicas requested during slept: what the would-be pauses would have freed, kept to a billionth of an hour. estimatedFreed is those hours priced at the workload's cost rates, for display; the hours are the record. It's what pausing would free, not what it would save: freed capacity becomes money only once nodes go, which Hybernate measures for real pauses.

slept and the freed hours count finished would-be pauses. While the phase is Idle, the one under way, which began at status.lastTransitionTime, is added to them when it ends; resources is what the workload ran when it began. estimatedFreed counts it as it goes, up to the last status write, at most 5 minutes ago, so a workload idle all weekend shows what it would have freed before Monday's activity ends the pause.

The summary starts when dry-run does, and is removed when dry-run ends: once Hybernate is pausing, status.cost records what it actually frees.

kubectl hybernate scan shows the same summary in each dry-run workload's COULD SLEEP, WAKES, and COULD FREE/MO columns, with a total in the headline and the command to start pausing:

  2 workloads are in dry-run: measured by Hybernate since starting, they would have slept 140 hours, freeing $18.20,
  about $134 a month.

  NAMESPACE   WORKLOAD         STATE            BECAUSE                                     COST/MO   COULD SLEEP   WAKES   COULD FREE/MO
  preview-7   deployment/api   idle (dry-run)   no activity for 5h; measuring since Oct 1   $96       96h           4       $91

The scan prices the hours at its own prices, so --cpu-price and --memory-price apply.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
kubectl describe managedworkload my-api -n staging

When the clock runs out, and when activity ends the would-be pause:

[dry-run] my-api: idle for 1 hour, since its CPU use was last above the activity threshold; would have paused
[dry-run] my-api: activity resumed (cpu): would have slept 3 hours 12 minutes, freeing $0.25; since Oct 1: would have paused 4 times, slept 4 days, freeing $7.50

The [dry-run] prefix marks the decisions dry-run holds back: IdleDetected, PausedEarly, ActivityResumed, IdleVetoed, HeldByDependents, DependencyCycle, and the PauseRequested event for a pause request it doesn't act on. Events about what really happens, such as a wake, a forecast update, or a metrics problem, have no prefix.

docs.title: Phase
docs.text: In dry-run the phase goes Running → Idle when the clock runs out, or a pause is requested, and back to Running at the next activity. The workload is never scaled down.

docs.title: Recommended Workflow
docs.text:
1. Opt in with hybernate.io/dry-run: "true". Let it measure for a few days, across a weekend if the workload is used on weekdays.
  2. Review what it measured. kubectl hybernate status leads with what it would have freed, and kubectl hybernate scan adds how often it would have paused and for how long; the events say when.

  3. End dry run:

    kubectl hybernate enable my-api -n staging
kubectl hybernate enable --all -n staging   # every workload in the namespace

    For a labelled workload, enable sets its own hybernate.io/dry-run annotation to "false", which wins over its namespace's and the cluster default. With --all, when the namespace's annotation or the cluster default keeps any workload in dry-run, it sets the namespace's annotation to "false" instead and drops the workloads' own, or, when your access doesn't allow changing the namespace, sets each workload's own; when each is in dry-run by its own annotation, it sets each to "false". For a ManagedWorkload you wrote, it sets spec.dryRun: false. If a GitOps tool (Argo CD, Flux, Fleet, kapp or Kluctl) applies the setting, it changes nothing and prints the change to make in Git instead. See kubectl hybernate enable.

docs.title: When to Use Dry Run
docs.text:
• The first time you opt a workload or namespace in
  • After changing its settings
  • In environments where you want to validate before acting

docs.title: GitOps tools
docs.text:
Hybernate pauses a workload by setting its replicas to zero. If a GitOps tool such as Argo CD, Flux, Fleet, kapp or Kluctl applies that workload from Git with replicas in its manifest, it sees the cluster no longer matches Git and sets them back, undoing the pause. Each tool has a one-time setting that leaves the replicas to Hybernate; this page gives it.

Teams that already run an HPA or KEDA under Argo CD or Flux usually have it in place, since an autoscaler changes replicas too.

docs.title: What Hybernate does
docs.text:
Hybernate never fights Git. When a paused workload is scaled up by anything other than Hybernate, it counts as activity: the workload goes back to Running, and status.lastScaledUp records when, how many replicas, and what did it, by the field manager the API server recorded (argocd-controller, kustomize-controller, kubectl-client-side-apply, ...). A scale through the scale subresource, as kubectl scale, an HPA and KEDA do, records no field manager, so it shows as unknown.

When that was Argo CD, Flux, Rancher Fleet, kapp or Kluctl, the workload also reports it, with what to change and a link to the tool's section below:

GitOpsConflict=True   Argo CD set the replicas from Git, undoing the pause; Hybernate pauses it again from 14:20 UTC. To stop it, have Argo CD ignore replicas, as for an HPA: https://okedeji.io/hybernate/guides/gitops/#argo-cd

along with a GitOpsConflict warning event. Hybernate waits an hour before pausing again, so it doesn't restart the workload in a loop with the tool; kubectl hybernate status shows when, as pauses at 14:20 UTC (after GitOps conflict). Pausing again is also how it finds out the fix is in: once a pause holds for an hour, the condition clears with a GitOpsConflictResolved event. A pause Hybernate wakes sooner doesn't show the tool has stopped, so the condition stays until a later pause holds for the hour.

Before you opt anything in, kubectl hybernate scan lists the workloads whose replicas are set from Git, by tool.

docs.title: Checking the fix is in
docs.text:
kubectl hybernate enable and pause warn when a GitOps tool will undo pauses, and say nothing once it's told not to:

  • Argo CD keeps owning the replicas it applied even once it ignores them, so they read the workload's Application, found by its argocd.argoproj.io/tracking-id annotation, or the argocd.argoproj.io/instance or app.kubernetes.io/instance label it tracks by, in the namespace an <namespace>_<name> value gives, or in any namespace, or argocd. Argo CD leaves the replicas when the Application has RespectIgnoreDifferences=true in its sync options and ignores /spec/replicas (or .spec.replicas, or all of spec) for the workload's kind, in its own spec.ignoreDifferences or in argocd-cm, beside the Application or in argocd: a resource.customizations.ignoreDifferences.apps_Deployment (or apps_StatefulSet, or all) key, or the older resource.customizations block. The warning gives only the step that's missing. When the Application or argocd-cm can't be read, such as without access to Argo CD's namespace, or with Argo CD running in another cluster, it says why, and to make the fix if you haven't already.
  • Flux, Fleet and Kluctl set only the fields their manifests have, so they set the replicas exactly when the API server records them as owning spec.replicas.
  • kapp keeps the replicas a rebase rule tells it to as its own, and the rule isn't on the workload, so the warning says it can't tell.

docs.title: Argo CD
docs.text:
Have Argo CD ignore the replicas of Deployments and StatefulSets, once for every app, in the argocd-cm ConfigMap:

argocd-cm
data:
  resource.customizations.ignoreDifferences.apps_Deployment: |
    jsonPointers:
      - /spec/replicas
  resource.customizations.ignoreDifferences.apps_StatefulSet: |
    jsonPointers:
      - /spec/replicas

When Argo CD was installed with its Helm chart, the chart writes argocd-cm from its values, so set the same keys under configs.cm there, with the rest of Argo CD's settings:

argo-cd-values.yaml
configs:
  cm:
    resource.customizations.ignoreDifferences.apps_Deployment: |
      jsonPointers:
        - /spec/replicas
    resource.customizations.ignoreDifferences.apps_StatefulSet: |
      jsonPointers:
        - /spec/replicas

Then add RespectIgnoreDifferences=true to each app's sync options, so a sync leaves them too and not only the diff:

application.yaml
spec:
  syncPolicy:
    syncOptions:
      - RespectIgnoreDifferences=true

This is the setting Argo CD's own docs give for an HPA, so apps that already have it need nothing more. To keep it to some apps, put the same jsonPointers in their spec.ignoreDifferences instead.

Argo CD can also ignore fields by the field manager that set them, but not for this: when a server-side-applied object is scaled through its scale subresource, Kubernetes drops the field's owner without recording a new one, so the replicas Hybernate sets aren't attributed to any manager.

docs.title: Flux
docs.text:
Flux only sets the fields a manifest has. Leave replicas out of the workload's manifest in Git, and Flux leaves them to Hybernate; Kubernetes starts a new Deployment at one replica.

For a Helm chart that always renders replicas, remove it in the HelmRelease with a post-renderer:

helmrelease.yaml
spec:
  postRenderers:
    - kustomize:
        patches:
          - target: {kind: Deployment, name: my-api}
            patch: |
              - op: remove
                path: /spec/replicas

docs.title: Rancher Fleet
docs.text: Fleet applies what its bundle renders. Leave replicas out of the workload's manifest in Git and Fleet leaves them to Hybernate. For a Helm chart that always renders them, remove them with a kustomize patch in the bundle's fleet.yaml.

docs.title: kapp
docs.text:
Have kapp keep the replicas it finds in the cluster, as its docs give for an HPA, with a rebase rule in a kapp Config:

kapp-config.yaml
apiVersion: kapp.k14s.io/v1alpha1
kind: Config
rebaseRules:
  - path: [spec, replicas]
    type: copy
    sources: [existing, new]
    resourceMatchers:
      - apiVersionKindMatcher: {apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment}
      - apiVersionKindMatcher: {apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: StatefulSet}

docs.title: Kluctl
docs.text: Leave replicas out of the workload's manifest in Git. For a Helm chart that always sets them, remove them with a patch in the deployment item's kustomization.yaml. Kluctl's conflict settings, such as kluctl.io/ignore-conflicts-manager, can't help: a scale through the scale subresource leaves the replicas with no field manager, so Kluctl's next deploy sets them back without a conflict to ignore.

docs.title: Opting in a whole namespace
docs.text: A namespace is opted in by a label on the Namespace, which isn't in Git when the tool creates it: an Argo CD Application with CreateNamespace=true, or a Flux HelmRelease with install.createNamespace. For Argo CD, put the label in the Application's managedNamespaceMetadata; for Flux, add the Namespace to the kustomization. See A whole namespace.

docs.title: Ending dry-run
docs.text:
A workload's dry-run lives in its hybernate.io/dry-run annotation, its namespace's, or a ManagedWorkload's spec.dryRun. When Git has that setting, change it there: a change made in the cluster is put back on the tool's next sync. kubectl hybernate enable knows this. It reads who owns the setting from the field managers the API server records, so it finds Argo CD whether it tracks apps by label (app.kubernetes.io/instance, its default) or by annotation, Flux whether it applies a Kustomization or a HelmRelease, and Fleet, kapp and Kluctl. For those it changes nothing, prints the change to make in Git, and exits non-zero; --force changes the cluster anyway. When the tool applies the workload but Git doesn't have the annotation, nothing would put it back, so enable sets it.

A chart installed with plain helm is different: Helm only applies it when you run it, so enable sets the annotation and warns that the next helm upgrade restores the chart's value. Set it to "false" in the chart's values too.

docs.title: ManagedWorkload Guide
docs.text: The ManagedWorkload CR is the core resource in Hybernate. It declares a single Deployment or StatefulSet whose lifecycle Hybernate manages.

docs.title: Minimal Example
docs.text:
managedworkload.yaml
apiVersion: hybernate.io/v1alpha1
kind: ManagedWorkload
metadata:
  name: my-api
  namespace: staging
spec:
  target:
    kind: Deployment
    name: my-api

This is the absolute minimum: only target is required, and everything else takes its default. The operator will watch the Deployment, track its cost and learn its forecast, but won't pause it on its own until you add an idle policy; kubectl hybernate pause pauses it when you ask.

For most workloads you don't need to write one: the hybernate.io/managed label creates one from annotations; see Opting In. Settings annotations don't cover, such as Prometheus queries, waitForReady, or cost rates, can be set on the ManagedWorkload the label creates, which keeps them, or in one you write yourself. A ManagedWorkload you write for a workload wins over the label.

docs.title: Full Example
docs.text:
managedworkload.yaml
apiVersion: hybernate.io/v1alpha1
kind: ManagedWorkload
metadata:
  name: my-api
  namespace: staging
spec:
  target:
    kind: Deployment
    name: my-api

  idlePolicy:
    idleAfter: 1h
    activity:
      cpuThreshold: 10
      prometheus:
        - promQL: 'sum(rate(nginx_ingress_controller_requests{exported_namespace="staging", exported_service="my-api"}[5m]))'
    autoResume: true

  wake:
    onRequest: true
    maxWait: 2m
    page: true

  prediction:
    mode: balanced

  costTracking:
    rates:
      cpuPerHour: "0.031"
      memoryPerHour: "0.004"
      storagePerMonth: "0.08"

  dryRun: false

docs.title: target
docs.text:
Field Type Default Description kind Deployment or StatefulSet Deployment The kind of workload to manage name string (required) Name of the workload (must be in the same namespace)

target can't be changed once the ManagedWorkload exists, since a paused target would be left at zero; the API server refuses the edit. To manage another workload, create another ManagedWorkload.

docs.title: idlePolicy
docs.text:
See Idle Detection for how the activity clock works.

Field Type Default Description idleAfter duration, at least 1m 1h How long without any activity before pausing activity.cpuThreshold int (percent) 10 CPU utilization, as % of requests, above which the workload counts as active (1-100) activity.prometheus[].promQL string (none) PromQL query; a result above zero counts as activity. At most 10. See the Prometheus Activity Guide autoResume bool false Wake ahead of the demand a confident forecast predicts pauseEarly bool false Pause before idleAfter runs out, once idle for 20 minutes, when a confident forecast expects the hours until then to be quiet and a request would wake the workload through the doorman. See Pausing Early

Deploys and the hybernate.io/last-activity and hybernate.io/active-until annotations always count as activity; see Idle Detection.

docs.title: dependsOn
docs.text:
Workloads this one needs, at most 20. A dependency isn't paused while this workload is awake, and waking this workload wakes it. See Dependencies.

Field Type Default Description namespace string this namespace Namespace of the dependency kind Deployment, StatefulSet (required) Kind of the dependency name string (required) Name of the dependency's workload waitForReady bool false Don't scale this workload up on resume until the dependency's pods are Ready

docs.title: wake
docs.text:
While the workload is paused, a request to any of its Services wakes it and is answered once it's Ready. See Wake on Request.

Field Type Default Description onRequest bool true Hold requests to the paused workload and wake it. When false, requests fail while it's paused maxWait duration 2m How long a request is held while the workload wakes, at most 1h. After it, the connection is closed; the wake carries on page bool true Answer a browser loading a page with a waking-up page that reloads until the workload is Running. Other requests are held either way

docs.title: prediction
docs.text:
Field Type Default Description mode eager, balanced, cautious balanced How soon the forecast acts on what it has learned: eager sooner, waking the workload for nothing more often; cautious later, for workloads costly to keep awake. See Forecast setting confidence int (50-100) the mode's: 60, 75, 85 Accuracy, as 1 − WAPE, a season's forecasts must reach before they drive decisions, in place of the mode's. See Forecasting

Leave prediction out, or write prediction: {}, for the default.

docs.title: costTracking
docs.text:
Cost tracking is always on, priced at the list price of the nodes the workload runs on, or AWS on-demand defaults where there's none. Set costTracking.rates to override pricing with what you pay; each rate you set wins over the others. See Cost Tracking.

Field Type Default Description rates.cpuPerHour quantity 0.031 $/vCPU-hour rates.memoryPerHour quantity 0.004 $/GiB-hour rates.storagePerMonth quantity 0.08 $/GiB-month

None of the rates may be negative.

docs.title: Scaled up outside Hybernate
docs.text: A paused workload scaled up by anything else, such as kubectl scale or a deploy, wakes: whoever did it wants it running. status.lastScaledUp records when and what did it. When that was a GitOps tool setting replicas from Git, see GitOps tools. While a workload is running, Hybernate doesn't manage its replica count, so changes by its team or an HPA are left alone.

docs.title: dryRun
docs.text: When true, the operator evaluates all policies and emits events but never pauses the workload, and wakes it if it had. Use this to validate configuration before enabling. See Dry Run.

docs.title: One Workload Per Target
docs.text: Only one ManagedWorkload can manage a given Deployment or StatefulSet. If you create a second ManagedWorkload pointing at the same target, the newer one gets a DuplicateTarget condition naming the other, and does nothing until the older one is gone.

docs.title: Node Pools for Real Savings
docs.text: Pausing a workload frees what its pods requested on their nodes. Your cloud bill is for nodes, so what's freed becomes money only once a node goes. Hybernate reports the two apart: freed is what pausing released, and saved is what it measurably took off the bill (see Freed and Saved). This guide is about closing the gap between them, by giving non-prod workloads node pools of their own, so that pausing an environment empties whole nodes.

docs.title: Why a pool of their own
docs.text:
A paused app on a node shared with busy workloads frees space on that node, but no node. The node stays as long as anything else on it does, and the bill doesn't change. A node autoscaler that consolidates, such as Karpenter with WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized, moves pods around to empty nodes it can then remove, and Cluster Autoscaler removes nodes whose requests fall under its threshold, but packing is never perfect: a node a quarter full of busy pods costs as much as a full one, and some pods can't be moved at all (see what keeps a node).

Put staging, preview and dev environments on a node pool that nothing else runs on, and pausing them takes away everything that holds those nodes. The pool empties as its workloads pause, the autoscaler removes the empty nodes, and saved rises to meet freed. A pool scaled to no nodes at all saves everything its paused workloads freed.

What makes it work:

  • A taint on the pool's nodes, so nothing lands there that doesn't tolerate it: not your always-on workloads, not most kube-system pods, which would otherwise hold a node Cluster Autoscaler won't remove, and not Hybernate's own operator and doorman, which are never paused and must stay up to wake what is.
  • A label on the pool's nodes, and a nodeSelector (or node affinity) with a matching toleration on the workloads that belong there.
  • An autoscaler that removes empty nodes promptly, and a minimum size of zero where the provider allows it.

DaemonSet pods run on every node and don't keep a node from being removed, by either autoscaler.

docs.title: Steering workloads to the pool
docs.text:
The workloads need both the nodeSelector and the toleration: the taint keeps others off, the selector keeps these on. In the manifests you keep in Git:

deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-api
  namespace: staging
  labels:
    hybernate.io/managed: "true"
  annotations:
    hybernate.io/wake-max-wait: "5m"
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: my-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: my-api
    spec:
      nodeSelector:
        example.com/tier: non-prod
      tolerations:
        - key: example.com/tier
          operator: Equal
          value: non-prod
          effect: NoSchedule
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/example/my-api:1.4.2
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 512Mi

example.com/tier: non-prod stands for whatever label and taint you give the pool. wake-max-wait is there because a wake may have to wait for a node; see What waking costs.

To put a whole namespace on the pool without editing every workload, add the selector and toleration as pods are created. Any of these works, and Hybernate depends on none of them:

  • A mutating admission policy from a policy engine, such as a Kyverno mutate rule or a Gatekeeper Assign mutation, matching pods in the namespaces you choose.
  • The PodNodeSelector and PodTolerationRestriction admission plugins, where your control plane enables them, which managed providers mostly don't: they read a default node selector and tolerations from annotations on the namespace.
  • Your templating, such as a Helm chart's or a Kustomize component's nodeSelector and tolerations for every non-prod release.

Keep anything that never sleeps off the pool, such as a shared database no ManagedWorkload pauses: one always-on pod holds its node, and every pod that fits beside it. If it's a dependency of the paused workloads, consider managing it too: Hybernate won't pause it while anything that depends on it is awake, and wakes it first when they wake.

docs.title: Karpenter
docs.text:
A NodePool for non-prod, with its own taint and label, that consolidates empty and underutilized nodes, and prefers spot capacity. This uses Karpenter's karpenter.sh/v1 API and the AWS provider's EC2NodeClass; for another provider, or EKS Auto Mode, change nodeClassRef (on EKS Auto Mode it's group: eks.amazonaws.com, kind: NodeClass).

nodepool.yaml
apiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1
kind: NodePool
metadata:
  name: non-prod
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        example.com/tier: non-prod
    spec:
      nodeClassRef:
        group: karpenter.k8s.aws
        kind: EC2NodeClass
        name: default
      taints:
        - key: example.com/tier
          value: non-prod
          effect: NoSchedule
      requirements:
        - key: karpenter.sh/capacity-type
          operator: In
          values: ["spot", "on-demand"]
        - key: kubernetes.io/arch
          operator: In
          values: ["amd64"]
      expireAfter: 720h
  disruption:
    consolidationPolicy: WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized
    consolidateAfter: 5m
    budgets:
      - nodes: "100%"
        reasons: [Empty]
      - nodes: "10%"
  limits:
    cpu: "200"
    memory: 800Gi
  • consolidationPolicy: WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized removes empty nodes and repacks underutilized ones, which matters when only some of a pool's environments are paused. WhenEmpty removes only nodes with nothing but DaemonSet pods left, which a pool shared by several environments rarely has; Balanced repacks only when the saving outweighs the disruption.
  • consolidateAfter: 5m: Karpenter restarts this timer whenever a pod is added to or removed from the node, so a node becomes a candidate 5 minutes after its last pod changed. A pause is deliberate, after idleAfter with no activity, so there's no need to wait long; much shorter, and a workload woken soon after its pause finds its node already gone. Never turns consolidation off.
  • budgets: without any, Karpenter disrupts at most 10% of a pool's nodes at once. When a whole environment pauses at once, the first budget lets every empty node go together, while the second still limits repacking busy ones.
  • expireAfter is under spec.template.spec in v1, not under disruption.
  • limits caps what the pool can grow to, so a runaway preview environment can't.

Spot capacity suits non-prod: it's interrupted now and then, which a staging environment can live with, and Karpenter picks spot when the requirements allow it. Karpenter deletes spot nodes it can empty by default, but replacing one spot node with a cheaper spot node needs its SpotToSpotConsolidation feature gate. Hybernate prices spot nodes at their spot list price, so freed and saved are close to what you pay; AWS's spot price moves through the day, which Spot nodes explains.

Karpenter also won't consolidate a node whose pods are annotated karpenter.sh/do-not-disrupt: "true", or whose pods' PodDisruptionBudgets allow no disruption. kubectl hybernate nodes lists both.

docs.title: Cluster Autoscaler, GKE, AKS and EKS managed node groups
docs.text:
With Cluster Autoscaler, managed or your own, the pool is a separate node group with a taint and a label, and a minimum size of zero.

GKE StandardAKSEKS managed node groupSelf-managed Cluster Autoscaler 
gcloud container node-pools create non-prod \
  --cluster my-cluster --location us-central1 \
  --machine-type e2-standard-4 --spot \
  --enable-autoscaling --total-min-nodes 0 --total-max-nodes 20 \
  --node-labels example.com/tier=non-prod \
  --node-taints example.com/tier=non-prod:NoSchedule

gcloud container clusters update my-cluster --location us-central1 \
  --autoscaling-profile optimize-utilization

GKE never scales a Standard cluster to zero nodes, since its system pods need somewhere to run, so keep another pool for them; the non-prod pool itself can scale to zero. Its nodes are labelled cloud.google.com/gke-nodepool: non-prod too, which you can select instead. GKE doesn't let you set Cluster Autoscaler's flags; the optimize-utilization profile makes it scale down sooner and more often than the default balanced, and applies to the whole cluster. On GKE 1.22 and later, pods with local storage don't block scale-down.

az aks nodepool add \
  --resource-group my-rg --cluster-name my-cluster \
  --name nonprod --mode User \
  --node-vm-size Standard_D4s_v5 \
  --priority Spot --eviction-policy Delete --spot-max-price -1 \
  --enable-cluster-autoscaler --min-count 0 --max-count 20 \
  --labels example.com/tier=non-prod \
  --node-taints example.com/tier=non-prod:NoSchedule

az aks update --resource-group my-rg --name my-cluster \
  --cluster-autoscaler-profile scale-down-unneeded-time=5m,scale-down-delay-after-add=5m

User pools can autoscale to zero with --min-count 0; system pools can't. AKS adds its own taint, kubernetes.azure.com/scalesetpriority=spot:NoSchedule, to spot pools, so workloads there tolerate that too. The autoscaler profile applies to every autoscaled pool in the cluster, not one. AKS already defaults skip-nodes-with-local-storage to false. Its nodes are labelled kubernetes.azure.com/agentpool: nonprod.

nodegroup.yaml
apiVersion: eksctl.io/v1alpha5
kind: ClusterConfig
metadata:
  name: my-cluster
  region: us-east-1
managedNodeGroups:
  - name: non-prod
    instanceTypes: ["m6i.xlarge", "m5.xlarge", "m6a.xlarge"]
    spot: true
    minSize: 0
    desiredCapacity: 1
    maxSize: 20
    labels:
      example.com/tier: non-prod
    taints:
      - key: example.com/tier
        value: non-prod
        effect: NoSchedule
    iam:
      withAddonPolicies:
        autoScaler: true

EKS doesn't scale managed node groups itself, but tags their Auto Scaling groups for Cluster Autoscaler to find: run it with --node-group-auto-discovery=asg:tag=k8s.io/cluster-autoscaler/enabled,k8s.io/cluster-autoscaler/my-cluster. To scale a group up from zero, Cluster Autoscaler must know its nodes' labels and taints before any node exists: give its IAM role eks:DescribeNodegroup and it reads them from the EKS API, or tag the Auto Scaling group with k8s.io/cluster-autoscaler/node-template/label/example.com/tier: non-prod and k8s.io/cluster-autoscaler/node-template/taint/example.com/tier: non-prod:NoSchedule. Its nodes are labelled eks.amazonaws.com/nodegroup: non-prod.

cluster-autoscaler-values.yaml
autoDiscovery:
  clusterName: my-cluster
extraArgs:
  scale-down-unneeded-time: 5m
  scale-down-delay-after-add: 5m
  scale-down-utilization-threshold: "0.5"

Give the node group a minimum of zero in your cloud, and set the node group's labels and taints as your provider's Cluster Autoscaler docs say, so it can scale up from zero.

The settings that decide how soon a paused environment's nodes go:

Setting Default For a non-prod pool scale-down-unneeded-time 10m How long a node must be unneeded before it's removed. A paused environment's node costs money for this long; 5m is plenty for workloads paused after an hour idle scale-down-utilization-threshold 0.5 A node is unneeded when the larger of its pods' CPU and memory requests is under this share of what it can allocate. A pool that empties when its environments pause doesn't depend on it: an empty node is always under scale-down-delay-after-add 10m How long after a scale-up before scale-down is considered again. A wake scales up, so a shorter delay lets the next pause's nodes go sooner --skip-nodes-with-local-storage true upstream, false on AKS Whether pods with emptyDir or hostPath volumes keep a node. Annotate pods with cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/safe-to-evict-local-volumes rather than turning it off cluster-wide --skip-nodes-with-system-pods true Whether kube-system pods without a PodDisruptionBudget keep a node. The pool's taint keeps most of them off

These follow the Cluster Autoscaler FAQ, its AWS provider README, GKE's cluster autoscaler and node-pools create pages, and AKS's cluster autoscaler page. They live outside Hybernate and change with your provider's releases, so check them for your versions.

docs.title: What waking costs
docs.text:
A paused workload whose pool has scaled to nothing needs a node before it can start. The first request after a quiet night waits for the node to be provisioned and join, often 30 to 90 seconds, longer for a node group scaling up from zero, then for its images to be pulled onto a fresh node, then for the app to start.
