  • Raise wake.maxWait (hybernate.io/wake-max-wait on a workload opted in with the label) above the 2-minute default, such as to 5m, or the doorman gives up on held requests before the node is ready. The wake carries on regardless; see How long a connection is held.
  • Raise your ingress controller's timeout to match. ingress-nginx gives up on an upstream after 60 seconds by default. Browsers don't care: they get the waking-up page at once.
  • Use autoResume for traffic the forecast can learn, such as a team that starts at 9 every weekday. It wakes the workload 15 minutes before an hour the forecast expects to be busy, so the node has started before anyone arrives. See Resume.
  • Keep one node warm if every first request must be quick: a minimum of one node, or in Karpenter a small always-on workload in the pool. You pay for that node, and pausing saves the rest.

docs.title: Check it's working
docs.text:
kubectl hybernate status shows what pausing freed this month beside what it saved, per workload and in total. With the pool doing its job, SAVED follows FREED, a little behind, since a node takes consolidateAfter or scale-down-unneeded-time to go. When less than half of what was freed was saved, status says nodes aren't scaling down under Needs attention. See See What Hybernate Is Doing.

kubectl hybernate nodes names the node autoscaler it found and, for each node, what keeps the autoscaler from removing it, in BLOCKED BY: pods annotated karpenter.sh/do-not-disrupt or cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/safe-to-evict: "false", PodDisruptionBudgets that allow no disruption, local storage, pods without a controller, kube-system pods without a PodDisruptionBudget, nodes with scale-down disabled, NodePools that consolidate only empty nodes or never, and nodes no autoscaler scales. A node of the non-prod pool with a low utilisation and something in BLOCKED BY is the one to look at. See See Why Nodes Don't Scale Down.

The metrics, by node pool, with pool the pool's name, such as non-prod:

# What the pool's paused workloads requested, against its spare capacity
hybernate_capacity_paused_cpu_cores{pool="non-prod"}
hybernate_capacity_spare_cpu_cores{pool="non-prod"}

# What pausing takes off the bill an hour, in the pool
hybernate_savings_realised_dollars_per_hour{pool="non-prod"}

# Which node autoscaler the operator found
hybernate_node_autoscaler

Spare capacity should fall towards zero as the pool's nodes go, and what's saved an hour rise towards what the paused replicas would cost. Spare capacity that stays above what's paused means the pool's nodes are still there: check kubectl hybernate nodes. See the Metrics Reference, and Freed but not saved for the causes.

docs.title: Opting In
docs.text:
Install Hybernate once per cluster, then label what it should manage. The label says which workloads Hybernate manages; annotations say how.

deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: checkout-api
  namespace: preview-42
  labels:
    hybernate.io/managed: "true"
  annotations:
    hybernate.io/dry-run: "true"      # measure first; nothing is paused
    hybernate.io/idle-after: "2h"

The label is usually one line in your Helm values or manifests, in a file you already keep in Git. It goes on the Deployment or StatefulSet itself: a chart's podLabels and podAnnotations put it on the pods, where Hybernate doesn't look, and a LabelIgnored warning event on the workload says so. With Kustomize, don't use commonLabels, which changes the workload's selector; see With Kustomize. Hybernate then creates a ManagedWorkload for the workload and keeps it in step with the annotations.

docs.title: A whole namespace
docs.text:
Label the namespace to opt in every Deployment and StatefulSet in it. Annotations on the namespace set the defaults for its workloads:

NamespaceArgo CDFlux 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: preview-42
  labels:
    hybernate.io/managed: "true"
  annotations:
    hybernate.io/dry-run: "true"
    hybernate.io/idle-after: "2h"

An Application that creates its namespace, with CreateNamespace=true, has no Namespace in Git to label. Put the label and annotations in its managedNamespaceMetadata, which Argo CD sets on the namespace it creates:

application.yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: preview-42
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/your-org/environments.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: previews/preview-42
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: preview-42
  syncPolicy:
    automated: {}
    managedNamespaceMetadata:
      labels:
        hybernate.io/managed: "true"
      annotations:
        hybernate.io/dry-run: "true"
        hybernate.io/idle-after: "2h"
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true

Argo CD sets managedNamespaceMetadata only in a sync with CreateNamespace=true. A namespace the Application created before, without it, gets it at the next sync, but adding it doesn't start an automated sync unless the Application has both prune: true and selfHeal: true. Otherwise sync once by hand: Sync in Argo CD's UI, which takes the Application's sync options, or with kubectl, giving them:

kubectl patch application preview-42 -n argocd --type merge -p '{"operation":{"sync":{"syncOptions":["CreateNamespace=true"]}}}'

To stop managing the namespace, remove the label from managedNamespaceMetadata and sync. Removing managedNamespaceMetadata altogether leaves the label on the namespace, since Argo CD then leaves a namespace that exists alone. Have Argo CD leave the workloads' replicas to Hybernate too, as in With GitOps.

Flux doesn't create a Kustomization's namespace, so it's in Git already. Label and annotate the Namespace there, as in the first tab, saved as namespace.yaml beside the kustomization Flux applies:

kustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
namespace: preview-42
resources:
  - namespace.yaml
  - ../../base

A HelmRelease's install.createNamespace creates its namespace unlabelled, so add the Namespace to the Kustomization that applies the HelmRelease. To stop managing the namespace, remove the label, not the Namespace: with prune: true, Flux deletes a Namespace that leaves Git, and everything in it.

This covers dev and preview namespaces, and third-party charts that don't let you add labels to their workloads. To leave one workload out of a managed namespace, label it hybernate.io/ignore: "true", or hybernate.io/managed: "false".

docs.title: With Kustomize
docs.text:
Don't use commonLabels for the label. Kustomize puts it in each Deployment's and StatefulSet's spec.selector too, and in a StatefulSet's volumeClaimTemplates, neither of which Kubernetes lets change. Applied to a workload that already exists, it fails with field is immutable, while the workload's Service, applied with it, can take the new selector, which none of the running pods has, so it stops sending them traffic. A tool set to recreate what it can't change, such as Flux with force: true, deletes and recreates the workloads instead. On a new workload it applies, but the label is then part of the selector, so removing it to stop managing the workload fails the same way. labels with includeSelectors: true, which is what kustomize edit fix turns commonLabels into, does the same.

These leave the selectors alone:

  • A whole namespace: when the kustomization has the Namespace, label and annotate it there, as in A whole namespace. Nothing on the workloads changes.

  • Everything the kustomization applies: labels with includeSelectors: false, which labels each resource's own metadata and nothing else:

    kustomization.yaml
    resources:
  - ../../base
labels:
  - pairs:
      hybernate.io/managed: "true"
    includeSelectors: false

    Leave includeTemplates out: it labels the pods too, which restarts them for nothing, since Hybernate doesn't read pods' labels, and a StatefulSet's volumeClaimTemplates, which fails as the selector does. Services and ConfigMaps get the label as well, and Hybernate ignores it there, but a Namespace in the kustomization gets it too, which opts in the whole namespace.

  • Chosen workloads, with their settings: a patch, which changes only the workload's own labels and annotations:

    kustomization.yaml
    resources:
  - ../../base
patches:
  - target:
      kind: Deployment
      name: checkout-api
    patch: |
      apiVersion: apps/v1
      kind: Deployment
      metadata:
        name: checkout-api
        labels:
          hybernate.io/managed: "true"
        annotations:
          hybernate.io/dry-run: "true"
          hybernate.io/idle-after: "2h"

    Keep the target: without one, the patch has to give the workload's namespace too when its manifest has one, or the build fails with no resource matches strategic merge patch. To patch every Deployment and StatefulSet, target kind: Deployment|StatefulSet with no name; the patch still needs a name, which is then ignored.

commonAnnotations can carry the settings, but it puts them on the pod templates too, so adding or changing one, such as dry-run to "false" to start pausing, restarts the pods of every workload in the kustomization, and Hybernate counts each restart as a deploy, which is activity. Set them on the Namespace or in a patch instead.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Annotation Values Default Description hybernate.io/dry-run "true", "false" "false" Measure without pausing: the activity clock runs as normal, and what pausing would free is recorded, but the workload is never paused hybernate.io/idle-after duration of at least 1m, e.g. "90m", "2h" 1h How long without activity before pausing hybernate.io/cpu-threshold whole number, "1" to "100" 10 CPU use, as a percentage of requests, above which the workload counts as active hybernate.io/auto-resume "true", "false" "false" Wake ahead of the demand a confident forecast predicts hybernate.io/pause-early "true", "false" "false" Pause before idle-after runs out when a confident forecast expects the hours until then to be quiet and a request would wake the workload; see Pausing Early hybernate.io/forecast "eager", "balanced", "cautious" "balanced" How soon the forecast acts on what it has learned; see Forecast setting hybernate.io/depends-on comma-separated kind/name or namespace/kind/name none Workloads this one needs; see Dependencies hybernate.io/wake-on-request "true", "false" "true" Wake when a request reaches the workload's Service; see Wake on Request hybernate.io/wake-max-wait duration, at most 1h 2m How long a request is held while the workload wakes hybernate.io/wake-page "true", "false" "true" Show browsers a waking-up page

Leaving an annotation out means its default. A value that can't be read, such as idle-after: "soon" or dry-run: "True", is reported in an InvalidSetting warning event on the workload and skipped, as if it weren't there: the setting comes from the next place in Which setting wins, and the others still apply. Booleans are exactly "true" or "false"; idle-after is at least 1m, and wake-max-wait above zero and at most 1h. In depends-on, an entry that can't be read is skipped and the rest apply.

dry-run is the exception: a value that can't be read turns dry-run on, whatever comes after it, since a typo in the setting meant to stop pauses must never start them.

hybernate.io/depends-on: "statefulset/postgres, messaging/statefulset/nats"

On a namespace, depends-on reaches every workload in it except those it names, and those they depend on by their own depends-on: they're what the others depend on, and taking the list too would make them depend on each other, so none could pause.

Settings that need more than one value aren't annotations: Prometheus activity queries, waitForReady on a dependency, cost rates, and the forecast's prediction.confidence, a percentage that overrides hybernate.io/forecast. Set those on the ManagedWorkload Hybernate creates, such as with kubectl patch, which keeps them (see What Hybernate does with the label), or write a ManagedWorkload yourself.

docs.title: Which setting wins
docs.text:
1. The workload's own annotation.
  2. Its namespace's annotation.
  3. The cluster-wide defaults, set in the Helm values (defaults.idleAfter, defaults.cpuThreshold, defaults.dryRun, defaults.pauseEarly, defaults.forecast).
  4. The built-in default.

So a namespace can measure everything with dry-run: "true" while one workload in it goes live with dry-run: "false".

docs.title: From measuring to pausing
docs.text:
Start with hybernate.io/dry-run: "true". Hybernate runs each workload's activity clock without pausing anything, and keeps a summary of the pauses it would have made in its ManagedWorkload's status.dryRun: how many, how long it would have slept, and what that would have freed. kubectl hybernate scan lists the same for every workload in dry-run. See Dry Run. When you're ready:

kubectl hybernate enable checkout-api -n preview-42
kubectl hybernate enable --all -n preview-42     # every workload in the namespace

enable sets the workload's own hybernate.io/dry-run annotation to "false", which wins over its namespace's annotation and the cluster default, wherever the dry-run came from. enable --all ends dry-run for everything in the namespace that's in it. When the namespace has its own hybernate.io/dry-run, or a workload takes its dry-run from the namespace or the cluster default, it sets the namespace's annotation to "false" and drops the workloads' own; otherwise it sets each workload's own to "false" and leaves the namespace alone. A ManagedWorkload you wrote has its spec.dryRun set to false.

If a GitOps tool (Argo CD, Flux, Fleet, kapp or Kluctl) applies the hybernate.io/dry-run annotation on the workload or namespace from Git, enable doesn't change the cluster, since the tool would put the annotation back. It names the tool, prints the change to make in Git, and exits non-zero; --force changes the cluster anyway. One Helm set is changed, with a warning that the next helm upgrade puts the chart's value back.

docs.title: Protected namespaces
docs.text:
Label a namespace hybernate.io/protected: "true", such as production, and Hybernate never manages anything in it, whatever labels its workloads or the namespace carry. Nothing there is opted in, a ManagedWorkload written for one reports Protected=True and is never paused, and a workload Hybernate had paused before the namespace was protected is woken, so protecting a namespace never leaves anything off. A warning event says why on each.

kubectl label namespace payments hybernate.io/protected=true

To protect namespaces by name instead, such as every prod-*, set the Helm value protectedNamespaces. A protected namespace is managed again only when labelled hybernate.io/allow-protected: "true" on purpose; Hybernate never sets either label.

Some namespaces are always protected, with no label or Helm value:

  • Kubernetes' own, kube-system and every other kube-* namespace, so labelling every namespace managed can't pause CoreDNS or metrics-server.
  • Hybernate's own, the namespace it's installed in, and the doorman's if it runs elsewhere, so Hybernate can't pause itself.

Labelling one of them hybernate.io/allow-protected: "true" lets Hybernate manage it like any other, except that the operator's and the doorman's own Deployments are never managed: nothing would be left to wake them.

To keep Hybernate out of namespaces altogether, not by its own rule but by Kubernetes RBAC, install it with watchNamespaces; see Helm values.

docs.title: With GitOps
docs.text:
The decision to manage a workload lives in Git, as the label. The ManagedWorkload Hybernate creates from it is owned by the workload, like the ReplicaSets a Deployment creates, so Argo CD and Flux leave it alone and Argo CD shows it under the workload. Hybernate never copies the workload's labels onto it, so a GitOps tool's tracking label can't make the tool claim and prune it.

GitOps tools do notice the replica count of a paused workload changing, and would scale it back up. Tell them to leave spec.replicas alone; for Fleet, kapp and Kluctl, see GitOps tools:

  • Argo CD: ignore the field in the Application, and keep the ignored field out of syncs:

    spec:
  ignoreDifferences:
    - group: apps
      kind: Deployment
      jsonPointers:
        - /spec/replicas
    - group: apps
      kind: StatefulSet
      jsonPointers:
        - /spec/replicas
  syncPolicy:
    syncOptions:
      - RespectIgnoreDifferences=true

  • Flux: leave replicas out of the workload's manifest. Flux applies with server-side apply, so a field the manifest doesn't set stays with whoever set it last: Hybernate, while the workload is paused. Many charts let you leave it out, for example when their autoscaling value is on.

docs.title: What Hybernate does with the label
docs.text:
• Labelled: creates a ManagedWorkload named after the workload, owned by it, marked with hybernate.io/from-label: "true", and announces it with a Managed event on the workload. If that name is taken, for example by a StatefulSet's of the same name as a Deployment, it's named after the workload and its kind instead, such as api-statefulset.
  • Annotations changed: updates the ManagedWorkload within seconds. The annotations are the source of truth for what they set: dryRun, idlePolicy (idleAfter, activity.cpuThreshold, autoResume, pauseEarly), which workloads dependsOn lists, and wake. Direct edits to those are overwritten. Everything else is yours to set on the ManagedWorkload and is kept: prediction, costTracking, idlePolicy.activity.prometheus, and waitForReady on a dependency the annotation lists. The target never changes.
  • Label removed, or hybernate.io/ignore added: deletes the ManagedWorkload. If the workload is paused, it's first scaled back to the replicas it had.
  • Workload deleted: its ManagedWorkload goes with it.
  • A ManagedWorkload you wrote for the workload exists: yours wins, and the label does nothing.
  • A label value other than "true", such as hybernate.io/managed: "dry-run", doesn't opt the workload in, and is pointed out in an event. Settings like dry-run are annotations.

docs.title: Pause and Resume
docs.text: Hybernate's one action is to pause: scale a workload to zero replicas. The Deployment or StatefulSet stays, and so do its PVCs and their data; only the pods are removed. Hybernate never deletes a workload or its storage. A StatefulSet whose persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy.whenScaled is Delete has its own controller delete its PVCs as it scales down, so Hybernate never pauses one: it reports Protected=True, reason PVCsDeletedOnScaleDown, until whenScaled is Retain.

docs.title: What Happens When a Workload Is Paused
docs.text:
1. What the pause will change is recorded in status.pause, in the same status write that moves the phase to Pausing, before anything is scaled: the replica count (previousReplicas), the KEDA ScaledObject and its own autoscaling.keda.sh/paused-replicas value if it has one, what each replica requests (for cost tracking), and the activity annotations as they stand
  2. A copy of what undoing the pause needs, the replica count and the KEDA ScaledObject with its own paused-replicas value, is written to the workload's hybernate.io/paused-from annotation, where it stays until the workload is handed back. Should the ManagedWorkload lose its status while the workload is paused, such as to a Velero restore without status, or being deleted without its finalizer and created again, Hybernate takes the pause up again from it, with a PauseRecovered event, and the workload wakes as it would have
  3. A KEDA ScaledObject, if the workload has one, is held at zero with autoscaling.keda.sh/paused-replicas: "0"
  4. The workload is scaled to 0 through its scale subresource. The API server records no field manager for a write that way, so the replicas show as no one's rather than Hybernate's
  5. status.pause.pausedAt is set. Once its pods have stopped, the phase moves to Paused, with a Paused event. Pods that don't stop, such as a StatefulSet's under OrderedReady pod management waiting on one that isn't Ready, are waited for as long as their termination grace period and a minute more (one pod after another for a StatefulSet); then it's Paused anyway, with PauseIncomplete=True and a PauseIncomplete warning event in place of Paused, until they've gone

Because the record is written first, a pause interrupted at any point, by an operator restart or a conflicting write, is finished or undone from the record, and a resume always goes back to the replica count the workload had.

docs.title: Triggering a Pause
docs.text:
Automatically: once the workload has had no activity for idlePolicy.idleAfter; see Idle Detection.

Now: with kubectl hybernate pause, to wake when it's next used.

Either way it's the same pause, which wakes on a request, on activity, or by autoResume. To keep a workload off until someone starts it again, scale it to zero yourself: Hybernate leaves it alone; see Workloads Already at Zero.

docs.title: Pause Now
docs.text:
When you're done with a workload for the day, such as a preview environment, pause it now rather than waiting for idleAfter:

kubectl hybernate pause my-api -n staging

The result is an ordinary pause, the same as one the idle clock makes: a request to the workload through the doorman, a change to its activity annotations, a Prometheus activity query, autoResume, or kubectl hybernate wake wakes it. A query already showing activity as you pause it, such as a queue with messages still on it, wakes it only once it has been quiet, so it doesn't undo the pause. It doesn't need an idlePolicy, and it works on a ManagedWorkload created from the hybernate.io/managed label as on one you wrote: name the workload, as kubectl hybernate status shows it.

The plugin asks by setting the hybernate.io/pause-requested annotation on the ManagedWorkload to a token, the time of the request. Any tool can do the same; the value only has to differ from the last request's:

kubectl annotate managedworkload my-api -n staging --overwrite \
  hybernate.io/pause-requested="$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)"

To pause it even when the forecast expects demand within the hour, also set hybernate.io/pause-overrides-forecast: "true"; set it, or remove it, with every request, since it applies to the request it comes with.

It's an annotation rather than a spec field so that Argo CD and Flux, which own the spec of a ManagedWorkload kept in Git, leave it alone. Hybernate acts on each value once: it records the value it handled in status.lastPauseRequest, which survives an operator restart, and says what came of it in the PauseRequest condition.

The request runs the idle clock out now, and the workload is paused by the same rules as an idle pause:

The workload What Hybernate does PauseRequest condition Running or Idle Pauses it, with a PauseRequested event, then Paused True, Paused A confident forecast expects demand within the hour Leaves it running and says when the demand is expected, since a pause would likely be woken straight back. kubectl hybernate pause asks whether to pause it anyway; a request with hybernate.io/pause-overrides-forecast: "true", which --yes sets, pauses it False, ForecastExpectsDemand Within the hour Hybernate waits after a GitOps tool (Argo CD, Flux, Fleet, kapp or Kluctl) undid its last pause Pauses it: you asked. If the tool undoes it again, that's a new GitOpsConflict True, Paused Pausing Finishes the pause, then marks the request handled True, AlreadyPaused Paused Marks the request handled True, AlreadyPaused Resuming Lets the wake finish, then pauses it True, Paused In dry-run Never scales it: counts a would-be pause in status.dryRun, moves it to Idle, and emits a [dry-run] PauseRequested event. Activity after the request ends the would-be pause, as it would wake a paused workload False, DryRun Held awake by hybernate.io/active-until on it or its workload Leaves it running, with a Warning event False, ActiveUntil Depended on by awake workloads Leaves it running, with a HeldByDependents event, as for an idle pause False, HeldByDependents In a dependsOn cycle Leaves it running, with a Warning event False, DependencyCycle In a protected namespace, or Hybernate's own operator or doorman Leaves it running, with a Warning event False, Protected Scaled to zero outside Hybernate Nothing to do: it's off already False, ScaledToZero Its workload is missing, labelled hybernate.io/ignore, or managed by another ManagedWorkload Nothing, with a Warning event False, TargetNotFound, TargetIgnored or DuplicateTarget

The condition answers the last request until the next one, through any wakes and idle pauses since, so its message says what happened and when, in UTC: paused as requested at 2026-10-21 03:32 UTC, already paused at …, or not paused at 2026-10-21 03:32 UTC: and why. Hybernate keeps it rather than dropping it at the next wake, so kubectl hybernate pause, or a script that set the annotation, can always read the answer to its request, and kubectl describe shows why last night's pause didn't happen long after its events have expired. status.lastPauseRequest says which request it answers.

A request Hybernate won't act on is answered once, not retried: ask again once the reason is gone. Activity from before the request doesn't undo it: the pause records the activity annotations as they stood, and only a change made since wakes the workload.

docs.title: Resume
docs.text:
Resuming wakes the workload's dependencies, scales it back to status.pause.previousReplicas (kept within its HPA's or ScaledObject's range if that changed), and moves it to Running once all those replicas are Ready, by a status its Deployment or StatefulSet controller wrote after seeing the scale-up. A workload that wasn't wholly Ready before its pause, such as one with a pod crash-looping, would never get there, so Hybernate stops waiting 2 minutes after the first replica is Ready, or, while none is, once the Deployment's progressDeadlineSeconds has passed since the scale-up (10 minutes by default, and for a StatefulSet). It's then Running with the replicas that are Ready, and ResumeIncomplete=True until they all are. With none Ready, its doorman routes are removed all the same, so requests fail until a pod is Ready rather than wait at the doorman for a workload its own controller reports stuck. A StatefulSet with the default OrderedReady pod management starts its pods one at a time, so a slow-starting one may have only its first pods Ready when the 2 minutes are up: it runs with those, and the rest follow. Once it's scaled back up, its replicas are left to its autoscaler, so an HPA scaling it down as it starts isn't undone. A KEDA ScaledObject is held at the restored count until then, and afterwards gets back the paused-replicas value it had before the pause, or none.

Automatically:

  • A request to the workload's Service, through wake on request
  • A change to hybernate.io/last-activity, hybernate.io/last-request or hybernate.io/active-until on the ManagedWorkload or its target since the pause began, whatever time the new value states; kubectl hybernate wake sets one
  • A Prometheus activity query showing activity, such as messages waiting for a queue worker
  • With autoResume: true, 15 minutes ahead of the hour a confident forecast expects demand in
  • Something else scaling it up, such as kubectl scale: it's counted as activity and the workload goes straight to Running; see GitOps tools for when that's a GitOps tool
  • Turning on dry-run, which never leaves a workload paused (DryRunWake event)

A paused workload is looked at again at least every 5 minutes, or every minute when it has Prometheus activity queries, 15 minutes before each hour and on the hour, as well as whenever it or its target changes.

On demand:

kubectl hybernate wake my-api -n staging

wake marks the workload active, which wakes it and restarts its idle clock, so it pauses again once it's had no activity for idleAfter. --for 2h keeps it awake for at least that long, as for a demo. To keep a workload running for good, remove the idlePolicy of a ManagedWorkload you wrote. One created from the hybernate.io/managed label always has an idlePolicy, rewritten from its annotations, so label the workload hybernate.io/ignore: "true" instead: Hybernate stops managing it, and wakes it first if it's paused. See kubectl Plugin.

docs.title: When Hybernate Lets Go
docs.text:
Hybernate hands a paused workload back, scaled to the replicas it had and released from KEDA without waiting for it to be Ready, and stops routing its Services to the doorman, whenever it stops managing it:

  • The ManagedWorkload is deleted, or the hybernate.io/managed label that created it is removed
  • The workload is labelled hybernate.io/ignore: "true"
  • Its namespace becomes protected, or it's Hybernate's own operator or doorman Deployment (labelled control-plane: controller-manager or doorman in Hybernate's namespace), which is never paused whatever its namespace allows; or it's a StatefulSet that deletes its PVCs when scaled down
  • Another, older ManagedWorkload for the same workload takes it over, and this one becomes the DuplicateTarget

Each of these emits a Resumed event saying why and how many replicas it has. No longer managing a workload never leaves it switched off.

If the target itself is deleted while paused, its Services stop routing to the doorman, since nothing would start the pods a held request waits for; TargetAvailable turns False with reason TargetNotFound.

docs.title: Workloads Already at Zero
docs.text:
A workload scaled to zero outside Hybernate, by kubectl scale, a pipeline, or KEDA with no active trigger, is off on purpose, and Hybernate leaves it that way:

  • It isn't paused, whatever its idle clock says, and a pause request is answered with ScaledToZero: there's nothing running to pause, and a pause would record zero replicas to restore
  • It isn't woken: Hybernate only wakes what it paused, so neither a request, an activity annotation, autoResume nor kubectl hybernate wake scales it up
  • Its Services aren't routed to the doorman, so a request to it fails as it would without Hybernate, rather than being held for pods that nothing will start

The ManagedWorkload stays Running, with the ScaledToZero condition and one ScaledToZero event saying so. That makes scaling it to zero yourself the way to keep a workload off until someone starts it. Once its replicas are set above zero, by whoever scaled it down, Hybernate manages it again, and counts that as activity, so its idle clock starts afresh.

Hybernate never scales up a workload it didn't scale down. Handing back a pause recorded at zero replicas, Hybernate releases it at zero, with a Resumed event that says so.

docs.title: Cost While Paused
docs.text: Cost tracking is always on. While a workload is paused, what its paused replicas requested in CPU and memory accrues as freed, and the part of that its nodes' spare capacity couldn't hold accrues as saved; its PVCs still cost, since they stay. See Cost Tracking.

docs.title: Workloads Nobody Comes Back To
docs.text: A paused workload costs only its storage. To remove one for good, delete it the way it was created: from Git, by the pipeline that made the environment, or with a TTL tool such as kube-janitor. Those know when an environment is finished; Hybernate only knows it's idle.

docs.title: Finalizer
docs.text: The hybernate.io/cleanup finalizer is added to every ManagedWorkload, so that deleting one while its workload is paused scales the workload back to the replicas it had first. A hand-back that fails is retried, except when the namespace itself is being deleted: there the workload goes with it, so after 5 minutes of failures, such as a KEDA webhook that's down rejecting the release of its ScaledObject, the ManagedWorkload lets go with a HandBackAbandoned Warning event rather than hold the namespace's deletion forever.

docs.title: Prometheus Activity Guide
docs.text: CPU tells Hybernate whether a workload is doing work. A Prometheus query tells it whether anyone is using it: requests through an ingress, open connections, messages arriving on a queue. Add queries as activity sources, and any result above zero keeps the workload awake, and wakes it once it's paused.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
On every check, about once a minute whether the workload is awake or paused, Hybernate runs each query in turn as an instant query against the Prometheus API (/api/v1/query), stopping at the first that shows activity. Each query has 2 seconds to answer, and all of a workload's queries 5 seconds together.

  • Any series above zero: activity. The activity clock resets. With a series per pod, one busy pod is enough.
  • Zero, or an empty result: no activity from this source. The clock keeps running.
  • NaN or infinite values are ignored, as no evidence either way: NaN is what a ratio of two idle counters gives (0/0). A result with nothing else in it is treated like an empty one: it doesn't confirm activity, and the other sources decide.

The query must return an instant vector or a scalar; a range vector (metric[5m] on its own) fails as QueryFailed. A response larger than 4 MiB, from a query that returns a series per pod across the cluster, is refused too: aggregate with sum or max.

Write the query so that it measures activity, not idleness: "how many requests per second", not "are there no requests".

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
managedworkload.yaml
spec:
  idlePolicy:
    idleAfter: 1h
    activity:
      prometheus:
        - promQL: 'sum(rate(nginx_ingress_controller_requests{exported_namespace="staging", exported_service="my-api"}[5m]))'

Queries are combined with the other activity sources: CPU, deploys, and activity annotations. Any one of them is enough to keep the workload awake.

docs.title: While the Workload Is Paused
docs.text:
A paused workload's queries are run about once a minute too, and one that shows activity wakes it, with a WokeByActivity event, a Prometheus activity query shows activity, waking, and lastActivitySource: prometheus once it's awake. It wakes the workload's dependencies with it, as any wake does. That's how a workload no request reaches wakes on its own, such as a queue worker, which no Service routes requests to, with a query of its queue's length:

managedworkload.yaml
spec:
  idlePolicy:
    idleAfter: 30m
    activity:
      prometheus:
        - promQL: 'sum(rabbitmq_queue_messages{queue="tasks"})'
  • Query something that's there while the workload is paused, such as the queue's broker. A metric the workload exports itself has no series while it has no pods, so it can't wake it.
  • A pause you ask for isn't undone by a query already showing activity. If a query shows activity as a requested pause begins, such as a queue that still has messages on it, it wakes the workload only once a check has found it quiet and it shows activity again. An idle pause begins only once every query is quiet, so this is only ever a requested one.
  • A query that can't be evaluated never wakes the workload. PrometheusAvailable is False, as while it's awake, and its message says the queries can't wake it until Prometheus answers, and whether a request through the doorman still does.
  • The forecast learns the hours the queries watch: quiet while they find nothing, busy when they find activity. So a worker paused every night still learns whole days, and with autoResume is woken ahead of its first messages once the forecast acts. While the queries can't be evaluated, a workload behind the doorman goes on learning its paused hours through it, as without queries: busy if a request woke it, quiet otherwise. One without the doorman doesn't learn them until Prometheus answers.

A workload with queries is checked every minute while it's paused, rather than every 5 minutes, so a query wakes it within a minute of its activity showing in Prometheus.

Prometheus queries can't be set with an annotation. On a ManagedWorkload created from the hybernate.io/managed label, add them to its spec.idlePolicy.activity.prometheus: the opt-in controller keeps them when it updates the rest from the annotations.

docs.title: Prometheus Endpoint
docs.text:
Set the Prometheus URL with the prometheus.url Helm value, which passes --prometheus-url to the operator. Add it to your values file:

hybernate-values.yaml
timezone: Europe/London
prometheus:
  url: http://prometheus.monitoring.svc.cluster.local:9090

and upgrade with the file. Pass the chart version you have installed as --version, which helm list -n hybernate-system shows, or Helm upgrades to the newest chart too:

helm upgrade hybernate oci://ghcr.io/okedeji/charts/hybernate --version X.Y.Z \
  --namespace hybernate-system -f hybernate-values.yaml

Installed without a values file, see Keeping your settings.

The URL is the base of the Prometheus HTTP API, http or https; the operator refuses to start with any other. Hybernate appends /api/v1/query and keeps any path prefix, so endpoints like https://mimir.example.com/prometheus work as-is. It sends no credentials or headers, so a Prometheus that needs them must be reached through a proxy that adds them.

With a Prometheus URL, each new workload's forecast also starts from up to four weeks of its CPU history rather than from nothing, so autoResume can act from the first day; see Learning from history. For a Prometheus that holds more than one cluster's series, prometheus.selector (--prometheus-selector), such as cluster="staging", narrows that history query to this cluster. It isn't added to activity queries, which run as you write them: narrow those in the query itself.

docs.title: When a Query Can't Be Evaluated
docs.text:
If a query fails, Hybernate can't see that activity, so it doesn't pause the workload, and a paused one isn't woken by it. The PrometheusAvailable condition says why:

Reason Meaning EndpointNotConfigured Queries are configured but the operator has no --prometheus-url QueryFailed Prometheus returned an error, didn't answer a query within 2 seconds or all of the workload's within 5, or returned a range vector or an oversized result. The condition message has the details 
kubectl get managedworkload my-api -n staging \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="PrometheusAvailable")]}'

The condition only appears on workloads that configure Prometheus queries.

A query that answers but matches no series at all looks just like a quiet workload, and that's also what a misspelt metric or label name gives. Hybernate can't tell the two apart, so the workload pauses on its other sources as usual, but a query that has matched no series since it was first evaluated is pointed out: PrometheusQueryEmpty=True, reason NoSeries, with the queries in its message, and a PrometheusQueryEmpty warning event when it begins. It clears once the query matches a series, even one at zero. A counter that's only created on the first request, as many client libraries' labelled counters are, also matches nothing until then; once it exists the condition clears. What a query has matched is remembered in memory, so after an operator restart a query is checked again from its first evaluation.

When Prometheus itself fails, by not answering, answering with a server error or 429, or timing out on three queries in a row, the operator doesn't ask it again for a minute: every workload's queries fail at once, as QueryFailed with the error that failed, so none waits out a timeout and holds up the wakes queued behind it. The message is the same for the whole outage, whether or not a check asked Prometheus. A query Prometheus rejects, such as one that doesn't parse, fails only for the workloads that use it. Time that a query can't be evaluated isn't counted as idle: Prometheus out for longer than a couple of checks restarts the clock (lastActivitySource: unobserved), so a workload is never paused because Prometheus was down. A query that times out while other queries are answered fails only for the workloads that use it, so one tenant's slow query doesn't hold off everyone's. Still keep queries cheap: aggregate, and use recording rules for anything heavy.

docs.title: Example Queries
docs.text:
Use case PromQL Requests through ingress-nginx sum(rate(nginx_ingress_controller_requests{exported_namespace="staging", exported_service="api"}[5m])) Requests seen by the app sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="api"}[5m])) Open WebSocket connections sum(websocket_connections{service="api"}) Messages waiting on a queue sum(rabbitmq_queue_messages{queue="tasks"}) Kafka consumer lag sum(kafka_consumer_lag{group="worker"})

ingress-nginx labels each request with the namespace and Service it went to. Scraped by the Prometheus Operator, which keeps its own namespace and service labels for the scrape's target, they become exported_namespace and exported_service. Give the namespace as well as the Service: preview environments often share Service names, and another one's traffic would keep this workload awake.

A request-rate query is also how dry-run sees a workload's requests: while it runs, nothing goes through the doorman, so without one a request counts only through the CPU it uses.

docs.title: Use a rate window that matches how quiet "idle" is
docs.text: rate(...[5m]) stays above zero for about five minutes after the last request. That's usually what you want: a single request keeps the workload awake, and the clock starts once traffic has stopped.

docs.title: Exclude traffic that isn't people
docs.text:
Health checks, uptime monitors, and scrapers keep a workload awake if the query counts them, and wake it once it's paused. Filter them out by path or user agent where your metrics allow it:

sum(rate(nginx_ingress_controller_requests{exported_namespace="staging", exported_service="api", path!~"/healthz|/metrics"}[5m]))

docs.title: Test the query directly
docs.text:
curl -s 'http://prometheus:9090/api/v1/query' \
  --data-urlencode 'query=sum(rate(nginx_ingress_controller_requests{exported_namespace="staging", exported_service="api"}[5m]))'

Then check what kept the workload awake:

kubectl get managedworkload my-api -n staging -o jsonpath='{.status.activity.lastActivitySource}'

prometheus means a query was the most recent source of activity.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text: Hybernate ships with Prometheus metrics for the operator and the doorman, and a set of alerting rules. See the Metrics Reference for every metric.

docs.title: Scraping
docs.text:
Metrics are served over HTTPS, and only to a scraper whose token is allowed to get the /metrics URL.

With Helm, turn on the ServiceMonitors (one for the operator, one for the doorman) and bind your Prometheus's ServiceAccount to the chart's <fullname>-metrics-reader ClusterRole:

hybernate-values.yaml
metrics:
  serviceMonitor:
    enabled: true
  prometheusRule:
    enabled: true
  readerSubjects:
    - kind: ServiceAccount
      name: prometheus-k8s
      namespace: monitoring

With install.yaml or the Kustomize manifests, apply the ServiceMonitors and the alerting rules into hybernate-system, from the config/prometheus base pinned to your release, or add it to your kustomization's resources:

kubectl apply -k "https://github.com/okedeji/hybernate//config/prometheus?ref=v0.2.0-rc.5"

and bind your Prometheus's ServiceAccount to the hybernate-metrics-reader ClusterRole yourself:

kubectl create clusterrolebinding hybernate-metrics-reader \
  --clusterrole=hybernate-metrics-reader --serviceaccount=monitoring:prometheus-k8s

Without that binding, the targets show as down with 401 or 403, and the HybernateDown and HybernateDoormanDown alerts fire. With metrics.secure: false in the chart, metrics are plain HTTP and need no binding, but anyone who can reach the port can read them.

Prometheus must select the ServiceMonitors. A Prometheus picks up only the ServiceMonitors that match its serviceMonitorSelector (and serviceMonitorNamespaceSelector). The chart's carry no label a Prometheus selects by default, so targets that never appear usually mean the selector doesn't match. kube-prometheus-stack selects release: <its release name>, and its Prometheus runs as the <its release name>-kube-prometheus-prometheus ServiceAccount. For a stack installed as kube-prometheus-stack in monitoring:

hybernate-values.yaml
metrics:
  serviceMonitor:
    enabled: true
    additionalLabels:
      release: kube-prometheus-stack
  prometheusRule:
    enabled: true
    additionalLabels:
      release: kube-prometheus-stack
  readerSubjects:
    - kind: ServiceAccount
      name: kube-prometheus-stack-kube-prometheus-prometheus
      namespace: monitoring

Check what yours selects with kubectl get prometheus -A -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}: {.spec.serviceMonitorSelector}{"\n"}{end}'; the same goes for ruleSelector and the PrometheusRule. Find its ServiceAccount with kubectl get prometheus -A -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.serviceAccountName}'.

The ServiceMonitors set honorLabels: true. The metrics' namespace label is the workload's namespace, and without it Prometheus would overwrite it with the scraped pod's (hybernate-system), so alerts would name the wrong namespace and merge same-named workloads. With your own scrape config, set honor_labels: true for the same reason.

They authenticate with the Prometheus's own ServiceAccount token, through bearerTokenFile. The Prometheus Operator marks that field deprecated in favor of authorization, which only takes a token from a Secret, so a long-lived token would have to be created and kept for it. A Prometheus with arbitraryFSAccessThroughSMs.deny: true refuses bearerTokenFile; scrape it with metrics.secure: false behind a NetworkPolicy instead, or with a scrape config of your own.

docs.title: Key Metrics to Watch
docs.text:
Cluster health dashboard:

# Is the operator acting on workloads?
rate(hybernate_lifecycle_transitions_total[1h])

# Are there errors?
rate(hybernate_reconcile_errors_total[5m]) > 0

# Are requests to paused workloads waking them?
sum by (result) (rate(hybernate_doorman_wakes_total[1h]))

Per-workload health:

# Is the prediction engine learning?
hybernate_prediction_confidence_percent{season="daily"}

# Are workloads cycling too fast?
rate(hybernate_lifecycle_transitions_total[1h])

docs.title: Alerting Rules
docs.text:
The Helm chart creates these rules when metrics.prometheusRule.enabled is true; config/prometheus, above, creates the same rules for an install from install.yaml or the Kustomize manifests.

Alert Fires when Severity HybernateReconcileErrorsHigh Reconcile errors exceed 0.1/sec for 10 minutes critical HybernateDown No healthy operator target has been scraped for 5 minutes, so nothing is paused or woken critical HybernateDoormanDown No healthy doorman target has been scraped for 5 minutes, so requests to paused workloads fail instead of waking them. Only with the doorman enabled critical HybernateWorkloadStuck A workload stays in Pausing or Resuming for 15 minutes warning HybernateTargetUnavailable A ManagedWorkload's target goes missing more than 3 times in an hour warning HybernateDoormanWakesFailing More than 3 requests to one paused workload timed out or failed (result timeout or error) in 15 minutes, for 5 minutes warning

HybernateDown and HybernateDoormanDown match the scrape job of the operator's and the doorman's metrics Service that the ServiceMonitors above make, so the chart creates them only with metrics.serviceMonitor.enabled: with no such job, they'd fire forever. If you scrape Hybernate some other way, write them on your own job's up series.

docs.title: Health Checks
docs.text:
The operator and the doorman expose health endpoints on port 8081, which the chart and the Kustomize manifests already use as liveness and readiness probes. To check them yourself, forward the port first, here the operator's, from a Helm install named hybernate:

kubectl port-forward -n hybernate-system deployment/hybernate 8081:8081

# Liveness
curl http://localhost:8081/healthz

# Readiness
curl http://localhost:8081/readyz

docs.title: Operator Logs
docs.text:
Logs are JSON by default. For debugging, check the operator logs; the label selectors work for every install:

kubectl logs -n hybernate-system -l control-plane=controller-manager -f
kubectl logs -n hybernate-system -l control-plane=doorman -f

The Deployments themselves are hybernate and hybernate-doorman for a Helm release named hybernate, and hybernate-controller-manager and hybernate-doorman with install.yaml or the Kustomize manifests.

Log entries to look for:

  • "phase transition": lifecycle state changes, with from, to and reason
  • "paused workload scaled up outside Hybernate": someone scaled up a paused workload
  • "managing workload from its label": the opt-in controller created a ManagedWorkload
  • "routing requests through the doorman": an error routing a paused workload's Services to the doorman
  • "ignoring malformed activity annotation": an activity annotation that isn't an RFC 3339 time

Forecast regime changes, idle detection and wakes are recorded as events on the ManagedWorkload rather than logged.

docs.title: A labelled workload has no ManagedWorkload
docs.text:
kubectl get managedworkloads -n <namespace> doesn't list it. The opt-in controller says why in events on the Deployment or StatefulSet itself:

kubectl describe deployment <name> -n <namespace>
  • LabelIgnored, the label is on the pod template: it was put on the pods, as a chart's podLabels does, where Hybernate doesn't look. Put it on the Deployment or StatefulSet itself, or on its namespace; see Opting In.
  • LabelIgnored, a value that isn't "true": hybernate.io/managed opts in only with "true"; settings such as dry-run are annotations.
  • Protected: its namespace is protected, such as kube-system; see Protected namespaces.
  • LabelIgnored, Hybernate's own: the operator's and the doorman's Deployments are never managed.
  • No event: it's labelled hybernate.io/ignore: "true", or someone wrote a ManagedWorkload for it, which wins over the label. With Kustomize, check the label reached the workload at all: commonLabels fails to apply to an existing workload (see With Kustomize).

docs.title: Workload is idle but not being paused
docs.text:
Check 1: Is dry run enabled?

kubectl get managedworkload my-api -n staging -o jsonpath='{.spec.dryRun}'

If true, the operator evaluates but doesn't act. To end it, run kubectl hybernate enable my-api -n staging, which does the right thing however the workload was set up. On a ManagedWorkload created from the hybernate.io/managed label, spec.dryRun follows the hybernate.io/dry-run annotation on the workload, its namespace, or the cluster default (defaults.dryRun), so setting it on the ManagedWorkload is overwritten: set the annotation to "false" instead. A value that can't be read, such as "False", counts as dry-run, with an InvalidSetting event on the workload. Only on a ManagedWorkload you wrote yourself do you set spec.dryRun: false.

Check 2: When was it last active?

kubectl get managedworkload my-api -n staging -o jsonpath='{.status.activity}'

lastActivitySource says what last kept it awake, and pauseAt is when it will pause if nothing else happens. If pauseAt keeps moving forward, something is still counting as activity:

  • cpu: usage is above activity.cpuThreshold% of requests. Background work (polling, cron loops) can keep a workload busy; raise the threshold if that's expected.
  • annotation: a hybernate.io/last-activity annotation is being refreshed, or hybernate.io/active-until is in the future. Check both the ManagedWorkload and its target.
  • rollout: the pod template changed recently.
  • prometheus: one of activity.prometheus returns a value above zero.
  • unobserved: the operator wasn't watching for a while, such as during a restart, or CPU or a Prometheus query couldn't be read for longer than a couple of checks, so the clock restarted then. If it keeps moving, check the MetricsAvailable and PrometheusAvailable conditions.

Check 3: Can Hybernate read CPU?

kubectl get managedworkload my-api -n staging \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="MetricsAvailable")]}'

Without CPU data a busy workload looks idle, so Hybernate doesn't act. MetricsAvailable=False says why:

  • NoPodMetrics: the target's Ready pods have had no metrics for over 3 minutes. Check that metrics-server is installed and reports them: kubectl top pods -n staging.
  • NoCPURequests: the target's containers request no CPU, in its running pods or, with none running, in its pod template, so utilization can't be measured. Set CPU requests on its containers, or a default in the namespace's LimitRange; a LimitRange default applies to pods created after it, so restart the workload's pods once it's set.
  • MetricsUnavailable: the Metrics API itself failed. The condition message has the error; a missing metrics.k8s.io API means metrics-server isn't installed.

A target scaled to zero replicas is not an error: it's recorded as zero usage. Nor is MetricsAvailable=Unknown just after a wake or a rollout: new pods have no metrics until they're running and metrics-server has scraped them, so it's NoReadyPods while none is Ready, then AwaitingPodMetrics for up to 3 minutes, without a warning.

Check 4: Is the forecast holding it awake?

A confident forecast that expects demand in the hour under way or the next defers the pause. While it does, the IdleVetoed condition is True, and its message says when the forecast expects demand; an IdleVetoed event marks when the veto began.

kubectl get managedworkload my-api -n staging \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="IdleVetoed")]}'

Check 5: Is anything else holding it?

kubectl hybernate status gives the reason in its NEXT column. Otherwise:

  • Without an idlePolicy, nothing pauses it on its own; kubectl hybernate pause pauses it when you ask.
  • PrometheusAvailable=False: a Prometheus activity query fails, or the operator has no --prometheus-url.
  • Protected=True: its namespace is protected (ProtectedNamespace), it's Hybernate's own operator or doorman (HybernateComponent), which is never paused, or it's a StatefulSet whose persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy.whenScaled is Delete (PVCsDeletedOnScaleDown), which would lose its PVCs to a pause: set whenScaled: Retain to let Hybernate pause it.
  • GitOpsConflict=True: a GitOps tool undid its last pause, and Hybernate waits an hour before pausing again.

Check 6: Is something depending on it?

kubectl get managedworkload postgres -n staging \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="HeldByDependents")]}'

HeldByDependents=True names the awake workloads that depend on this one, declared in dependsOn or learned. It pauses once they have; kubectl hybernate deps postgres -n staging shows each link and where it came from. DependencyCycle=True means two workloads depend on each other; remove the cycle. See Dependencies.

docs.title: Workload stuck in Resuming
docs.text: WaitingForDependencies=True means a waitForReady dependency isn't Ready yet; the condition names it and how many replicas are ready. Check that dependency's pods. A dependency that serves with some of its replicas Ready counts once its own resume has finished, or, if Hybernate doesn't manage it, after 2 minutes; one with none Ready is waited for until the dependency's Deployment progressDeadlineSeconds, or 10 minutes for a StatefulSet, has passed since the resume began, and then the workload starts without it, with WaitingForDependencies=False, reason DependencyWontStart. Otherwise, the workload's own pods aren't becoming Ready. Resume completes once every replica it was restored to is Ready. Short of that, Hybernate stops waiting 2 minutes after the first replica is Ready, or, while none is, once the Deployment's progressDeadlineSeconds has passed since the scale-up (10 minutes by default, and for a StatefulSet), and the workload is Running with the replicas that are Ready, possibly none, and ResumeIncomplete=True. A StatefulSet with the default OrderedReady pod management starts its pods one at a time, so a slow-starting one may have only its first pods Ready when the 2 minutes are up: it runs with those, and the rest follow. The HybernateWorkloadStuck alert fires after 15 minutes, and kubectl hybernate status lists it under Stuck after 10.

docs.title: Workload paused with pods still running
docs.text: A pause is Paused once the workload's pods have stopped. PauseIncomplete=True, with a PauseIncomplete warning event in place of Paused, means some were still running after their termination grace period and a minute more (one pod after another for a StatefulSet), and Hybernate stopped waiting so the workload isn't stuck Pausing: it's Paused, and wakes as usual. A StatefulSet with the default OrderedReady pod management stops its pods one at a time and won't stop the rest while one isn't Ready; a pod stuck terminating, such as on a finalizer or an unreachable node, holds a Deployment's. kubectl describe the pods to see why. It's set False once they've gone, or when the workload wakes.

docs.title: Workload resumed with replicas not Ready
docs.text: ResumeIncomplete=True, with a ResumeIncomplete warning event, means the last resume stopped waiting with some replicas not Ready, as above: it's Running with those that are, its KEDA ScaledObject scales it again, and requests go to its Ready pods. With none Ready, the doorman no longer holds its requests either, so they fail until a pod is Ready. This is common for a workload that wasn't wholly Ready before it was paused, such as one with a pod crash-looping or unschedulable; kubectl describe its pods to see why. Once every replica is Ready, later or at the next resume, it's set False with an AllReplicasReady event.

docs.title: Waking a workload by hand
docs.text:
kubectl hybernate wake my-api -n staging

It waits until the workload is Running, or tells you why it can't wake it. See the kubectl plugin.

docs.title: Pausing a workload by hand
docs.text:
kubectl hybernate pause my-api -n staging

It waits until the workload is Paused, or prints why Hybernate didn't pause it. The answer to the last request stays in the PauseRequest condition until the next request, saying what happened and when, such as paused as requested at 2026-10-21 03:32 UTC; a pause since, or a wake, doesn't change it:

kubectl get managedworkload my-api -n staging \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="PauseRequest")]}'

True is Paused, or AlreadyPaused when it was paused already. False, with a message starting not paused at and the time, gives the reason: a confident forecast expects demand within the hour (ForecastExpectsDemand; kubectl hybernate pause --yes pauses it anyway), workloads that depend on it are awake (HeldByDependents) or it's in a dependsOn cycle (DependencyCycle), a hybernate.io/active-until annotation holds it (ActiveUntil), it's in dry-run (DryRun) or protected (Protected), it's scaled to zero already (ScaledToZero), or its target is missing, ignored or managed by another ManagedWorkload (TargetNotFound, TargetIgnored, DuplicateTarget). Each request is answered once: fix the reason, then run pause again. See Pause Now.

docs.title: Requests to a paused workload fail instead of waking it
docs.text:
kubectl get managedworkload my-api -n staging \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="WakeOnRequest")]}'
  • TurnedOff: its wake.onRequest is false, or hybernate.io/wake-on-request: "false" when it's opted in with the label, so it doesn't wake on request.
  • No condition, or NotPaused: the workload isn't paused, so nothing is routed yet.
  • A message starting at its last pause:: the workload is awake now, and what follows is what its last pause found with its Services. The next pause meets it again unless it's fixed, so fix it now, by the reason below.
  • NoServices: no Service with a selector and a ClusterIP selects the workload's pods on a TCP port, or every such port is in hybernate.io/doorman-ignore-ports. Headless Services aren't routed; see Wake on Request. A workload no request reaches, such as a queue worker, can wake on a Prometheus activity query instead.
  • ServedByOtherPods: another workload's Ready pods are behind the same Service, so requests go to them. See Services shared with other workloads.
  • UnsupportedLoadBalancer, or a Service named in the message as not routed: the Service is behind GKE container-native load balancing, which can't use the doorman: a GKE Ingress uses it, it has standalone NEGs, or cloud.google.com/neg-status lists NEGs for it. GKE's own cloud.google.com/neg: '{"ingress": true}', on every Service, doesn't count by itself. The optional forwarder routes it. See On GKE.
  • ForwarderNotReady: the Service is behind GKE container-native load balancing, and the forwarder that stands in for the workload's pods has no Ready pod yet; the message says why. For a few seconds after a pause that's expected. Otherwise, look at its pods with kubectl describe pods -n staging -l app.kubernetes.io/name=hybernate-forwarder: an image that can't be pulled needs the operator's image reachable from the workload's namespace, a quota or LimitRange there may refuse its pods (doorman.negForwarder.resources), and a pod that runs but isn't Ready can't reach the doorman, usually because of a NetworkPolicy; see Network policies behind NEGs.
  • NodeLocalTraffic: the workload's Services have internalTrafficPolicy: Local, which sends each caller only to endpoints on its own node, so they aren't routed. See Wake on Request.
  • UnsupportedIPFamily: no doorman pod has an address in the Service's IP family, such as an IPv6-only Service in a cluster whose doorman pods have only IPv4 addresses.
  • DoormanUnavailable: no doorman pod is Ready. Check kubectl get pods -A -l control-plane=doorman.
  • NoFreePort: every doorman port (20000-29999) is in use.
  • TooManyPorts: the workload would hold more than doorman.portsPerWorkload doorman ports (32 by default), one per Service port, or its namespace more than doorman.portsPerNamespace (256); the message says which. Raise the cap, or list ports that needn't wake it in hybernate.io/doorman-ignore-ports.
  • RoutingFailed: writing the doorman's EndpointSlices failed; the message has the error, and it's retried with backoff. Check the operator's RBAC and logs.
  • DoormanDisabled: the doorman isn't installed (doorman.enabled: false).
  • TargetNotFound: the Deployment or StatefulSet is gone, so there's nothing to wake.

If the condition is DoormanRouted but requests still fail:

  • The request is closed after a while with no response: the workload didn't become Ready within wake.maxWait, or its pods couldn't be reached. A RequestNotServed warning event says which, and hybernate_doorman_wakes_total{result=~"timeout|error"} counts these. Raise maxWait, or check why the pods are slow to become Ready.
  • The connection is closed at once, with nothing sent: a limit on held connections or wakes was hit; hybernate_doorman_wakes_total{result="limited"} counts these.
  • An error from the app itself, such as a 503 with the app's own body, on the first requests after a wake: its pods were Ready before it could answer, as a pod with no readiness probe is as soon as its containers start. A NoReadinessProbe warning event, and the WakeOnRequest message, say when that's so. Give the app a readiness probe that passes only once it can serve; see Readiness probes.
  • A 503 with no body: the caller's User-Agent looks like a health check or scraper, such as kube-probe/ or Prometheus/, which the doorman never lets wake a workload. It answers them this way only while none of the workload's pods is Ready.
  • A 502 from ingress-nginx right after the workload paused: nginx hadn't picked up the change yet and sent the request to the removed pod. A retry a second later is held and wakes the workload.
  • A 502 from a GKE Ingress or GKE Gateway while the workload is paused: its Service is in NEGs and the optional forwarder isn't on, so the Service isn't routed and Google's load balancer has no healthy backend; see On GKE. Right after a pause, GKE also takes up to a minute to see the doorman, or the forwarder, pass its health checks.
  • A 504 from an Ingress after 60 seconds: the ingress controller gave up first. Raise its upstream timeout, for ingress-nginx nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout.
  • The request is refused right after the workload paused: the Service's backends hadn't switched to the doorman yet, which takes a second or two. A retry is held and wakes the workload.
  • The request is refused or times out right away, every time: a NetworkPolicy may block traffic to the doorman (ports 20000-29999) or from it to the workload's pods. See Network policies.

The doorman's logs name the workload and Service for each held connection: kubectl logs -n hybernate-system -l control-plane=doorman (use the namespace you installed into).

docs.title: Workload keeps cycling between paused and running
docs.text:
Something keeps waking it. Check the events for WokeByActivity (an activity annotation changed since the pause, or a held request: WokenByRequest names the Service) or AutoResume (the forecast expected demand). A health check or monitor that calls the Service on a timer and sends a request wakes the workload each time. The doorman already ignores connections that close without sending anything, and HTTP requests from common probes and scrapers (see Wake on Request); for anything else, point it elsewhere, list its port in hybernate.io/doorman-ignore-ports on the Service, or opt the workload out with wake.onRequest: false (hybernate.io/wake-on-request: "false"). A tool that refreshes hybernate.io/last-activity on a timer, rather than on real use, will keep waking the workload.

ScaledUp means something scaled it up outside Hybernate, named in the event and status.lastScaledUp. If it's a GitOps tool, the workload also reports GitOpsConflict=True: it sets the replicas from Git and will undo every pause until it's told to leave them; see GitOps tools.

docs.title: A dependency isn't held awake, woken or waited for
docs.text:
kubectl hybernate deps my-api -n preview-42

deps lists the workload's dependencies and where each came from. The ManagedWorkload's conditions say why one is left out:

  • DependencyNotAllowed=True: the dependency is in another namespace, and that namespace's hybernate.io/dependents-from annotation doesn't list this one, so it isn't held, woken or waited for. Annotate the dependency's namespace; see Across namespaces.
  • DependencyNotFound=True: a dependsOn workload doesn't exist (reason DependencyNotFound), or is outside watchNamespaces or can't be read by the operator (reason DependencyNotVisible). Neither blocks the workload.
  • A DependencyWakeFailed warning event: Hybernate couldn't set the activity annotation that wakes a dependency, such as when a policy engine refuses the write; the message has the error. The workload wakes anyway, and the dependency may still be paused.

docs.title: A Prometheus query never matches
docs.text: PrometheusQueryEmpty=True, reason NoSeries, with a warning event, means one of the workload's Prometheus activity queries has matched no series since Hybernate first evaluated it, which usually means a misspelt metric or label. Such a query can never keep the workload awake. It doesn't stop a pause either: the other sources decide. Run the query in Prometheus to check it; see Test the query directly.

docs.title: An activity annotation is ignored
docs.text: An InvalidActivityAnnotation warning event means a hybernate.io/last-activity, last-request or active-until value isn't an RFC 3339 time, such as epoch seconds or a date without a time. It neither keeps the workload awake nor wakes it. Write the time as date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ gives it; see Activity annotations.

docs.title: A paused workload's ManagedWorkload lost its status
docs.text:
A ManagedWorkload restored from a backup without its status, or deleted without its finalizer and created again, no longer has the record of its pause. Hybernate takes the pause up again from the copy on the workload's hybernate.io/paused-from annotation, with a PauseRecovered event: the workload is Paused again if it's still at zero, and wakes as usual. Leave the annotation alone; Hybernate removes it when it hands the workload back.

A PauseRecordLost warning event means there was no record to finish from, or the annotation couldn't be read; the message says which. A workload left Pausing, Paused or Resuming with no record anywhere was never scaled, since the copy is written first, and is Running again. If its replicas are at zero all the same, Hybernate takes it for a workload scaled to zero outside it and leaves it off: scale it back up yourself.

docs.title: A ManagedWorkload let go of its workload without handing it back
docs.text: A HandBackAbandoned warning event means the ManagedWorkload's namespace is being deleted, and handing its paused workload back failed for 5 minutes, such as when a KEDA webhook that's down refuses the release of its ScaledObject. The ManagedWorkload lets go rather than hold up the namespace's deletion; the workload is deleted with the namespace. The message has the error.

docs.title: Prediction confidence stays at 0
docs.text:
The confidence scorer needs a full 24-hour window of observed hours before reporting daily confidence, and 168 for weekly. An hour isn't observed while the operator is down, while CPU can't be read, or while the workload is paused with neither the doorman nor a Prometheus activity query to see its demand, so a workload paused every night that way never gets a full day; its status.prediction.message says why requests don't wake it and how to fix it. status.prediction.reason and message say what the forecast waits for, and startsActing when it's expected to act; see When It Acts. With a Prometheus URL, a new workload starts from its history instead: status.prediction.history says what came of reading it.

Also check that metrics-server is running and returning data:

kubectl top pods -n staging

docs.title: Target not found
docs.text:
kubectl get managedworkload my-api -n staging -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions}'

If TargetAvailable is False with reason TargetNotFound (a TargetNotFound warning event says so too):

  • Verify the target exists: kubectl get deployment my-api -n staging
  • Check that target.kind matches (Deployment vs StatefulSet)
  • Ensure the ManagedWorkload is in the same namespace as the target

spec.target can't be changed. To manage another workload, create another ManagedWorkload. Reason TargetIgnored means the target is labelled hybernate.io/ignore.

docs.title: Duplicate target error
docs.text:
Only one ManagedWorkload can manage a given workload: the oldest wins, and the others report DuplicateTarget=True naming it, and do nothing. Check for duplicates:

kubectl get managedworkloads -n staging -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}: {.spec.target.name}{"\n"}{end}'

docs.title: A ManagedByAnotherInstall warning
docs.text: Another Hybernate install, in the namespace the event names, took this ManagedWorkload on first, and this one leaves it alone: two installs watch its namespace. Give each install its own watchNamespaces, as in More than one install. If the install it names is gone, kubectl annotate managedworkload <name> -n <namespace> hybernate.io/operator- hands it over.

docs.title: Cost data shows $0.00
docs.text:
• Cost is priced on what the workload's pods request, read from its pods. A workload whose containers set no requests costs nothing.
  • projectedMonthlyCost, projectedMonthlyFreed and projectedMonthlySavings show pending until 24 hours of the month have been tracked, including on the first day of every month.
  • freedThisMonth stays $0.00 until Hybernate has paused the workload this month: dry-run workloads record what they would have freed in status.dryRun instead.
  • savedThisMonth stays $0.00 while the cluster's nodes have room for everything Hybernate holds paused: nothing has come off the bill until nodes go. See Freed but not saved. It reads unknown, with why in savingsUnknown, for an operator limited by watchNamespaces; see Saved reads unknown.
  • Totals start again from zero each calendar month, in UTC. See Cost Tracking.

docs.title: Freed but not saved
docs.text:
kubectl hybernate status shows FREED THIS MONTH well above SAVED, and may say under Needs attention that nodes aren't scaling down. Pausing freed capacity on the nodes, but the nodes are still there, so little of it came off the bill. Saved is measured from the spare capacity left on each node pool: while a pool's nodes could hold everything Hybernate holds paused there, nothing is credited (see How saved is measured).

Is anything scaling the nodes? The first lines of kubectl hybernate status and kubectl hybernate nodes name the node autoscaler, as does the operator's hybernate_node_autoscaler metric. With none found, nothing removes nodes, and what pausing frees never comes off the bill: enable Cluster Autoscaler on the node groups, or install Karpenter. See the Cluster Autoscaler Guide.

What's keeping the nodes? kubectl hybernate nodes lists, for each node, what keeps the autoscaler from removing it, in BLOCKED BY, with how to clear each below the table:

  • not autoscaled: no autoscaler found scales the node, such as a node group Cluster Autoscaler doesn't manage
  • NodePool never consolidates and NodePool consolidates only empty nodes: a Karpenter NodePool with consolidateAfter: Never, or with consolidationPolicy: WhenEmpty on a node that runs anything but DaemonSets
  • scale-down disabled and do-not-disrupt on the node: the node is annotated cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/scale-down-disabled: "true" or karpenter.sh/do-not-disrupt: "true"
  • PDB allows no disruption: a pod's PodDisruptionBudget allows no disruptions, so it can't be moved
  • safe-to-evict=false and do-not-disrupt: a pod annotated cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/safe-to-evict: "false" or karpenter.sh/do-not-disrupt: "true"
  • local storage: a pod with an emptyDir or hostPath volume, which Cluster Autoscaler won't move while --skip-nodes-with-local-storage is on
  • bare pod: a pod no controller would recreate elsewhere
  • kube-system pod without PDB: which Cluster Autoscaler won't move while --skip-nodes-with-system-pods is on

Are paused workloads sharing nodes with busy ones? A node is removed only once everything on it can go. A paused workload on a node that also runs busy pods frees room on it, but the node stays, and a cluster where every node is a little busy can keep all of them. The UTILISATION column of kubectl hybernate nodes shows it: low, with nothing in BLOCKED BY, and the node is waiting for the autoscaler's threshold or delay; middling, and it's still in use. Putting non-prod workloads on a node pool of their own lets pausing them empty whole nodes.

Is the autoscaler keeping spare capacity? Some settings keep nodes around on purpose: a node group's minimum size above what's in use, a long scale-down-unneeded-time or scale-down-delay-after-add, a scale-down-utilization-threshold lower than the nodes' use, a long consolidateAfter, Karpenter disruption budgets that allow few nodes at once, or over-provisioning placeholder pods kept for fast scale-up. Saved catches up only as those nodes go. See Node Pools for Real Savings for settings that let a non-prod pool empty.

hybernate_capacity_spare_cpu_cores and hybernate_capacity_paused_cpu_cores, by pool, show which pools still have room for what's paused there; see the Metrics Reference.

docs.title: Saved reads unknown
docs.text:
savedThisMonth and projectedMonthlySavings read unknown, and kubectl hybernate status shows unknown in SAVED and says why above the table. status.cost.savingsUnknown has the reason:

kubectl get managedworkload my-api -n staging -o jsonpath='{.status.cost.savingsUnknown}'

An operator limited to some namespaces with watchNamespaces can't see the pods in other namespaces, so it can't tell how much of each node they request, nor what's left over for the paused replicas. Saved can't be measured there, and the operator exports no hybernate_capacity_* or hybernate_savings_realised_dollars_per_hour series. Freed is still measured. To measure saved, install the operator without watchNamespaces; it then watches pods cluster-wide, caching only what each pod bound to a node requests (see Data and Access).

docs.title: helm uninstall fails with job hybernate-uninstall-guard failed
docs.text:
Helm 4 reports it as resource Job/hybernate-system/hybernate-uninstall-guard not ready. ManagedWorkloads are left, and uninstalling now would leave their workloads paused. Helm 3.18 and later print them above the error, in a message that starts Hybernate refuses to uninstall: and names them; when Helm prints only the error, as Helm before 3.18 does, and any Helm after a helm rollback with one, kubectl logs job/hybernate-uninstall-guard -n hybernate-system shows them. Remove the hybernate.io/managed label from those workloads and their namespaces, delete the ManagedWorkloads you wrote yourself, and uninstall again, as in Uninstall.

The refused uninstall leaves the release marked uninstalling, which helm list hides without -a, though the operator and the doorman keep running. If you decide to keep Hybernate instead, helm upgrade fails with has no deployed releases until helm rollback hybernate -n hybernate-system marks the release deployed again.

The hook waits two and a half minutes for ManagedWorkloads being deleted before it lists what's left, so one it still lists as being deleted is one the operator didn't finish in that time, usually because it isn't running: uninstall with --no-hooks and restore the workloads by hand. Without the CRD, as can happen with crds.install: false, nothing is left to guard, and the hook lets the uninstall go ahead. With Argo CD 3.3 and later the same refusal blocks deleting the Application, with a DeletionError condition; set guard.uninstall: false in Git to delete it anyway.

docs.title: helm upgrade fails with job hybernate-upgrade-guard failed
docs.text:
The upgrade sets watchNamespaces to leave out namespaces where the operator manages workloads, which would leave them paused with no operator; Helm 4 reports it as resource Job/hybernate-system/hybernate-upgrade-guard not ready. Helm 3.18 and later print them above the error, in a message that starts Hybernate refuses this upgrade: and names them, or kubectl logs job/hybernate-upgrade-guard -n hybernate-system shows them. Keep those namespaces in watchNamespaces, or stop managing the workloads there first, then upgrade again; see Narrowing watchNamespaces. Under Argo CD the same refusal fails the sync, in its PreSync hook.

helm rollback to a revision with a narrower watchNamespaces is refused the same way, by the pre-rollback hook, but Helm still records the attempt as a new revision and leaves it pending-rollback in helm history hybernate, while the operator keeps running as it was. Until another revision replaces it, helm upgrade fails with another operation (install/upgrade/rollback) is in progress. helm rollback hybernate -n hybernate-system, with no revision, rolls back to the one before it, the release as it runs, and marks that deployed again.

docs.title: Workloads stay at zero after the operator was removed
