docs.text: The operator was removed, or its CRD deleted, while ManagedWorkloads were left, so nothing scales their workloads back up, their Services still send traffic to the doorman's deleted pods, and deleting the ManagedWorkloads or the CRD hangs in Terminating on the hybernate.io/cleanup finalizer. Reinstall the operator and stop managing the workloads, or restore them by hand: see Restoring workloads after the operator is gone.

docs.title: Debug Checklist
docs.text:
1. Operator running? kubectl get pods -n hybernate-system (or the namespace you installed into)
  2. CRDs installed? kubectl get crd managedworkloads.hybernate.io
  3. Metrics server running? kubectl top nodes
  4. RBAC correct? kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:hybernate-system:hybernate (the ServiceAccount is hybernate for a Helm release named hybernate, and hybernate-controller-manager with install.yaml or the Kustomize manifests)
  5. Events? kubectl describe managedworkload <name> -n <ns>
  6. Logs? kubectl logs -n hybernate-system -l control-plane=controller-manager
  7. Status? kubectl get managedworkload <name> -n <ns> -o yaml

docs.title: Getting Help
docs.text:
If you've gone through this checklist and still have issues:

  1. Check the GitHub Issues for known problems
  2. Open a new issue with:
  3. Operator version (kubectl get deploy -n hybernate-system -o wide shows the image), plugin version (kubectl hybernate version), and Kubernetes version
  4. ManagedWorkload YAML (sanitized)
  5. Relevant operator logs
  6. Output of kubectl describe managedworkload

docs.title: General Upgrade Process
docs.text:
1. Read the release notes in the changelog for the target version. Check for breaking changes, CRD schema changes, or required steps.

  2. Upgrade. The CRD is upgraded with the operator:

    HelmkubectlKustomizeArgo CD or Flux

    With the values file you install with:

    helm upgrade hybernate oci://ghcr.io/okedeji/charts/hybernate \
  --version X.Y.Z \
  --namespace hybernate-system \
  -f hybernate-values.yaml

    Give it the file every time, or no values at all: given --set alone, Helm drops the values set before; see Keeping your settings. The chart is only published as an OCI artifact: there's no helm repo to update. Its version has no v. The CRD is a template in the chart, so helm upgrade upgrades it too, unless you installed with crds.install: false and manage it yourself.

    kubectl apply -f https://github.com/okedeji/hybernate/releases/download/vX.Y.Z/install.yaml

    Change each Hybernate base's ref in your kustomization to vX.Y.Z, then:

    kubectl apply -k .

    Change the Application's targetRevision, or the OCIRepository's tag, to X.Y.Z in Git, and let it sync. To hand an install made with helm install to Argo CD or Flux, see Moving a Helm install to Argo CD or Flux.

  3. Verify the upgrade:

    kubectl get pods -n hybernate-system
kubectl logs -n hybernate-system -l control-plane=controller-manager --tail=20

  4. Check workloads: Verify ManagedWorkloads are reconciling correctly:

    kubectl get managedworkloads --all-namespaces

docs.title: Keeping your settings
docs.text:
Helm reuses a release's values only on an upgrade given none. Given any, with --set or -f, it starts again from the chart's defaults and adds only those. On a release installed with timezone and prometheus.url, an upgrade with --set timezone=America/New_York sets the time zone and drops prometheus.url, and the next upgrade with --set drops whatever that one didn't name. Helm 3 and Helm 4 do the same.

So keep every value you set in one file, give it to helm install and every helm upgrade, and change a setting by changing the file. The file is the whole of your settings, in one place you can review, the same in every Helm, and it's what you'd commit to Git: Argo CD and Flux take the same values, so moving to one is a copy. Installed with --set, write the values the release has now to a file first:

helm get values hybernate -n hybernate-system -o yaml > hybernate-values.yaml

A release installed with no values writes null; replace it with your settings.

To change a setting, such as the time zone, change it in the file and upgrade with it, at the version you run, which helm list -n hybernate-system shows in its CHART column, so the change doesn't upgrade Hybernate too:

helm upgrade hybernate oci://ghcr.io/okedeji/charts/hybernate \
  --version X.Y.Z \
  --namespace hybernate-system \
  -f hybernate-values.yaml

Without a file, --reuse-values keeps the release's values and adds yours:

helm upgrade hybernate oci://ghcr.io/okedeji/charts/hybernate \
  --version X.Y.Z \
  --namespace hybernate-system \
  --reuse-values \
  --set timezone=America/New_York

Upgrading to a newer version with it, Helm renders with the installed version's defaults rather than the new one's, and those lack every value added since. From 0.2.0 on, the chart fills those in from its own defaults, so upgrading with --reuse-values from any 0.2.0 release candidate works, in Helm 3 and Helm 4 alike. From 0.1.x it doesn't: 0.1.x's values have settings 0.2.0 no longer takes, such as grafana, so install 0.2.0 new, as 0.2.0's changelog says. What --reuse-values still keeps is the installed version's default for each value both versions have, so a default the new version changes isn't picked up. Helm keeps those older defaults with the release, too, and goes on reusing them, which has one more catch: after such an upgrade, a default you remove by setting it to null doesn't stay removed. Helm 4 renders the default for the upgrade that sets it to null, and removes it from the next; Helm 3 brings it back at every other --reuse-values upgrade. To remove a default after such an upgrade, upgrade once with the values file, or with --reset-then-reuse-values (Helm 3.14 and later), which renders with the new version's defaults and keeps your values over them. From then on, --reuse-values keeps a removed default removed.

docs.title: Narrowing watchNamespaces
docs.text:
Upgrading to a watchNamespaces that leaves out a namespace, or setting it where it was empty, removes the operator's and the doorman's Roles in the namespaces left out, and stops them watching there. Workloads paused in those namespaces would stay at zero replicas, their Services still routed to doorman ports nothing serves, and their ManagedWorkloads' finalizers would never run.

So the chart refuses it. A pre-upgrade hook, the <fullname>-upgrade-guard Job, lists the ManagedWorkloads the running operator took on, with its hybernate.io/cleanup finalizer, in namespaces the new watchNamespaces leaves out, and fails if there are any, before anything changes: helm upgrade stops with job hybernate-upgrade-guard failed, or with Helm 4 resource Job/hybernate-system/hybernate-upgrade-guard not ready, and Helm 3.18 and later print them in a message whose first sentence, Hybernate refuses this upgrade: ..., names them and what to do, followed by the steps below; kubectl logs job/hybernate-upgrade-guard -n hybernate-system shows the same. It waits two and a half minutes for any being deleted first. helm rollback to a revision with a narrower watchNamespaces is guarded the same way.

To narrow it, stop managing the workloads in the namespaces you're dropping first, while the operator still watches them, so it scales each one back up:

  1. Remove the hybernate.io/managed label from the workloads and namespaces there.

  2. Delete the ManagedWorkloads you wrote yourself there:

    kubectl delete managedworkloads --all -n preview-1

  3. Upgrade.

The hook reads ManagedWorkloads' metadata cluster-wide, through a ClusterRole that, like its ServiceAccount, exists only while it runs. It runs only when watchNamespaces is set: widening to every namespace strands nothing. Argo CD runs it as a PreSync hook, before every sync. helm upgrade --no-hooks skips it, and guard.upgrade: false drops it; then restore the workloads left behind by hand, as in Restoring workloads after the operator is gone, for those namespaces.

A refused upgrade is recorded as a failed revision, and the release keeps running the previous one. helm uninstall is still guarded after it, though it runs with the failed revision's values: it also counts ManagedWorkloads the operator took on outside them.

docs.title: CRD Compatibility
docs.text:
Hybernate follows these CRD versioning rules:

  • v1alpha1: Breaking changes may occur between minor versions. Always read release notes.
  • Field additions are non-breaking (new optional fields with defaults).
  • Field removals or type changes are breaking and will be called out in release notes.

The CRD is kept when the chart is uninstalled, so uninstalling and reinstalling never deletes your ManagedWorkloads.

docs.title: Forecast Engine State
docs.text:
The forecast engine state is serialized in each ManagedWorkload's status, in status.prediction.state. On upgrade:

  • Compatible state versions are imported automatically
  • State an older version saved is discarded, with a ForecastReset event, and the engine learns again: from the workload's CPU history, read again, when prometheus.url is set, otherwise from scratch
  • State that can't be read otherwise, such as after a hand edit, is discarded the same way, with a ForecastReset warning

docs.title: The forecast setting, from before 0.2.0
docs.text:
Before 0.2.0, spec.prediction.confidence defaulted to 75, so every ManagedWorkload created then has it stored, and a confidence overrides the forecast setting. On one created from the label, Hybernate drops a stored 75, balanced's own threshold, so hybernate.io/forecast and defaults.forecast apply. On one you wrote, remove it for spec.prediction.mode to apply:

kubectl patch managedworkload my-api -n staging --type=json \
  -p '[{"op":"remove","path":"/spec/prediction/confidence"}]'

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
If something goes wrong:

HelmkubectlKustomize, Argo CD or Flux 
helm rollback hybernate -n hybernate-system

kubectl apply -f https://github.com/okedeji/hybernate/releases/download/vPREVIOUS/install.yaml

Put the previous release's ref, targetRevision or tag back, and apply or sync it.

Paused workloads remain paused during rollback. The previous operator version resumes managing them. Rolling back across a breaking API change isn't supported.

docs.title: Version History
docs.text: Check the GitHub Releases page and the changelog for every change.

docs.title: ManagedWorkload
docs.text:
Group: hybernate.io | Version: v1alpha1 | Kind: ManagedWorkload | Scope: Namespaced

kubectl get managedworkloads shows each one's Phase, what pausing it has Freed this month and what of that it Saved, what dry-run measured it Would Free, blank for one that isn't in dry-run, and its Age.

docs.title: Spec (ManagedWorkloadSpec)
docs.text:
Field Type Required Default Description target WorkloadRef Yes The workload to manage. Can't be changed once set target.kind Deployment | StatefulSet No Deployment Target kind target.name string Yes Target name (same namespace) idlePolicy IdlePolicySpec No Idle detection configuration. Without it, the workload is never paused automatically idlePolicy.idleAfter duration (at least 1m) No 1h Time without activity before pausing idlePolicy.activity.cpuThreshold int No 10 CPU utilization % of requests above which the workload is active (1-100) idlePolicy.activity.prometheus[].promQL string Yes (per entry) PromQL instant query; a result above zero is activity. At most 10 queries idlePolicy.autoResume bool No false Wake ahead of confident forecast demand idlePolicy.pauseEarly bool No false Pause before idleAfter runs out, once idle for 20 minutes, when a confident forecast expects the hours until then to be quiet and a request would wake the workload through the doorman. See Pausing Early dependsOn[] DependencyRef No Workloads this one needs, at most 20 dependsOn[].namespace string No this namespace Namespace of the dependency dependsOn[].kind Deployment | StatefulSet Yes Kind of the dependency dependsOn[].name string Yes Name of the dependency's workload dependsOn[].waitForReady bool No false Hold this workload's resume until the dependency is Ready wake WakeSpec No Waking on request while paused wake.onRequest bool No true Route the workload's Services to the doorman while paused wake.maxWait duration (at most 1h) No 2m How long a request is held while the workload wakes wake.page bool No true Answer a browser loading a page with a waking-up page instead of holding it prediction PredictionSpec No {} Forecast engine config; left out or {}, it takes the defaults prediction.mode eager | balanced | cautious No balanced How soon the forecast acts on what it has learned: at a confidence of 60, 75 or 85. See Forecast setting prediction.confidence int (50-100) No the mode's Accuracy (1 − WAPE, %) a season's forecasts must reach before they drive decisions, in place of the mode's costTracking CostTrackingSpec No Custom cost rate overrides costTracking.rates CostRates No node list prices, then AWS defaults Custom cost rates, none of them negative dryRun bool No false Measure without pausing; see Dry Run. A workload already paused when it's turned on is woken

A duration is a Go duration above zero, such as 45s, 90m or 1h30m. Days and weeks (1d, 2w) and spaces aren't durations: write 24h or 168h. The API server rejects any other value.

docs.title: CostRates
docs.text: Field Type Default Description cpuPerHour quantity 0.031 USD per vCPU-hour memoryPerHour quantity 0.004 USD per GiB-hour storagePerMonth quantity 0.08 USD per GiB-month

docs.title: Status (ManagedWorkloadStatus)
docs.text: Field Type Description phase WorkloadPhase Current lifecycle phase conditions[] Condition Standard Kubernetes conditions; see Lifecycle lastActedAt time When the target was last paused or woken: by Hybernate, or scaled up from zero outside it, such as with kubectl scale or by a GitOps tool lastPauseRequest string The last hybernate.io/pause-requested value acted on, so each request is acted on once; the PauseRequest condition says what came of it. See Pause Now lastTransitionTime time Last phase change activity.lastActivityTime time Most recent activity from any source activity.lastActivitySource string created, woke, request, cpu, rollout, annotation, prometheus, unobserved, or scaled-up activity.pauseAt time When the workload pauses if no further activity is seen activity.lastEvaluatedTime time When activity was last checked activity.templateHash string Fingerprint of the target's pod template, used to detect deploys activity.heldByDependents []string The awake workloads that use this one, as namespace/name, while they keep it from pausing (HeldByDependents): at most 10, the first by name activity.forecastBusyFrom time The start of the hour the forecast expects demand in, while it keeps the workload from pausing (IdleVetoed) activity.forecastQuietUntil time The end of the hours the forecast expected to be quiet when it brought the workload's pause forward (PausedEarly), until the pause, or the would-be pause in dry-run, ends pause PauseStatus What a pause changed, from before the workload is scaled to zero until it's running again pause.previousReplicas int32 Replicas before the pause, restored on resume pause.pausedAt time When it was scaled to zero; unset until then. The pause is Paused once its pods have stopped pause.resumedAt time When the resume under way scaled it back up; scaled to zero after that by something other than Hybernate, it's left off pause.firstReadyAt time When the resume under way first saw one of its replicas Ready; the rest get 2 minutes from then pause.scaledObject string The KEDA ScaledObject held at zero while paused; see HPA and KEDA pause.scaledObjectPausedReplicas string The ScaledObject's own autoscaling.keda.sh/paused-replicas from before the pause, put back after it pause.resources ResourceSnapshot What the workload ran when the pause began: replicas, and per replica cpuMillis, memoryBytes, and its claims' storageBytes; and nodePools, the node pools its pods ran in (name, "" for nodes without a pool label) and how many pods in each, which what it saves is measured against pause.wakeAnnotations object The activity annotations on the ManagedWorkload (workload) and its target (target) as the pause began; one that changes since wakes it pause.queryActiveSincePause bool A Prometheus activity query has shown activity at every check since the pause began, as one can when it was requested; until a check finds every query quiet, they don't wake it learnedDependencies LearnedDependencies Dependencies Hybernate found, held and woken like dependsOn: from, at, and dependencies (namespace, kind, name, source: environment or wake, via and address for one found in the environment, and lastSeen for one learned from a wake). See Learned dependencies lastScaledUp ScaledUp The last time the workload was scaled up outside Hybernate while paused, which wakes it: at, replicas, by (the field manager, such as argocd-controller, or unknown for a scale through the scale subresource, as kubectl scale makes, which records none), and gitOps (Argo CD, Flux, Fleet, kapp or Kluctl, when it was set from Git; see GitOps tools) doorman[] DoormanRoute Service ports routed to the doorman while paused: service, portName, doormanPort, and forwarded, set for a Service behind GKE NEGs routed through the forwarder doormanDraining[] DrainingPort Doorman ports that routed the workload until it woke: port, and until, before which no other workload is given it, so a client still sending the workload's traffic there never reaches another. Kept in status so an operator that restarts or takes over leadership honours it dryRun DryRunStatus What dry-run has measured; only while spec.dryRun is true dryRun.since time When dry-run started measuring dryRun.pauses int32 Times the workload would have been paused, one under way included dryRun.slept duration How long finished would-be pauses lasted in all dryRun.freedCPUHours, dryRun.freedMemoryHours quantity vCPU-hours and GiB-hours the replicas requested during slept dryRun.estimatedFreed string Those hours priced, for display, with the would-be pause under way counted up to the last status write: what pausing would have freed. Also the Would Free column of kubectl get managedworkloads dryRun.resources ResourceSnapshot What the workload ran when the current would-be pause began dryRun.queryActiveSincePause bool A Prometheus activity query has shown activity at every check since the would-be pause under way was asked for; until a check finds every query quiet, they don't end it, as they wouldn't wake a real pause prediction.dailyPhase, prediction.weeklyPhase string Each season's phase: Observing, Suggesting, or Active prediction.dailyConfidence, prediction.weeklyConfidence int Accuracy % over the last 24 and 168 observed hours prediction.timeZone string The IANA time zone the forecast counts hours and weekdays in, the operator's --timezone (Helm value timezone), such as Europe/London prediction.threshold int The confidence the forecast acts at: spec.prediction.confidence, or the mode's prediction.acting bool Whether the forecast drives decisions: holds off pauses and, with autoResume, wakes the workload ahead of demand prediction.startsActing time When the forecast is expected to start acting, if the coming days repeat the last week it saw; unset while it's acting or when it isn't expected to within four weeks prediction.reason, prediction.message string Why the forecast is or isn't acting: Acting, Observing, EarningConfidence, Relearning or NotLearning, and in a sentence. See When it acts prediction.history PredictionHistory What the forecast learned from Prometheus history when Hybernate began managing the workload: reason (Learned, NoPrometheusURL, NoHistory, NoCPURequests, QueryFailed), hours, from, to, message. See Learning from history prediction.state string The engine's learned state, gzipped and base64-encoded cost CostStatus Cost for the current calendar month, in UTC; see Cost Tracking cost.tracked duration How much of the month the totals cover cost.lastAccumulatedAt time When the totals were last brought up to date cost.awakeCPUHours, cost.awakeMemoryHours quantity vCPU-hours and GiB-hours requested while awake cost.storageHours quantity GiB-hours of the claims its pods mount, in every phase cost.pausedCPUHours, cost.pausedMemoryHours quantity vCPU-hours and GiB-hours the paused replicas had requested, while paused: what pausing freed cost.savedCPUHours, cost.savedMemoryHours quantity The workload's share of what its node pools' spare capacity couldn't hold of the paused replicas, measured every 5 minutes: what pausing saved, at least. See How saved is measured cost.costThisMonth string Awake and storage hours, priced cost.freedThisMonth string Paused hours, priced cost.savedThisMonth string Saved hours, priced; unknown while savingsUnknown is set cost.savingsUnknown string Why saved can't be measured, such as pods outside watchNamespaces not being visible; unset when it's measured cost.costWithoutHybernateThisMonth string costThisMonth plus freedThisMonth cost.projectedMonthlyCost, cost.projectedMonthlyFreed, cost.projectedMonthlySavings string The month so far carried to the whole month; pending until a day is tracked cost.running ResourceSnapshot What the workload ran when last brought up to date while awake cost.pricedAt, cost.pricedTemplateHash time, string When requests and list rates were last read, and the pod template then cost.listRates CostRates List rates of the nodes its pods last ran on, spot nodes at spot. Unset when its nodes have no list price cost.listPrice string Which list prices listRates are: OnDemand, Spot, or SpotAndOnDemand. Unset with listRates cost.resourceReduction ResourceReduction What the current pause freed: cpuMillis, memoryBytes, replicas. Only while paused

docs.title: WorkloadPhase Values
docs.text: Running, Idle, Pausing, Paused, Resuming. A ManagedWorkload has no phase until its first reconcile. Creating is accepted by the schema but never set.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
Hybernate supports Kubernetes 1.30 and later, and is tested in CI on 1.30 and 1.37.

Wake on request adds an EndpointSlice to each Service of a paused workload, one per IP family, pointing at the doorman. Anything that finds a Service's backends through its EndpointSlices sends traffic to the doorman without changes. Each project reads them a little differently, so this page records what's been checked.

Tested means an end-to-end test runs it on every change. Tried by hand means it was run once on a test cluster for the release listed. Checked against source means the project's endpoint code was read for the release listed, but nothing runs it yet.

docs.title: Service proxies
docs.text: Proxy Status Notes kube-proxy, kind's default mode Tested ClusterIP Services, called from pods in the cluster and through ingress-nginx kube-proxy, other modes (ipvs, nftables), and NodePort and LoadBalancer Services Not tested yet kube-proxy programs these from the same EndpointSlices as ClusterIP, but no test runs them. Their traffic usually reaches the doorman from a node's address, which doorman.networkPolicy.ingressFrom must admit as an ipBlock; see Restricting who can reach the doorman NodePort and LoadBalancer Services with externalTrafficPolicy: Local Partial Routed, but kube-proxy sends external traffic only to endpoints on the node it arrives at, so it reaches the doorman only through nodes that run a doorman pod; through any other node it's dropped, and the workload doesn't wake Cilium kube-proxy replacement (v1.20) Checked against source

docs.title: Ingress controllers and Gateway API
docs.text: Controller Status Notes ingress-nginx (v1.15) Tested nginx picks up endpoint changes on a timer, so for a second or two after a pause it can still send a request to the removed pod. It also closes upstream requests after 60 seconds by default; see How long a connection is held Traefik (v3.7): Ingress, IngressRoute, Gateway API Checked against source Envoy Gateway (v1.9) Checked against source Contour (v1.33) Checked against source Kong Ingress Controller (v3.5) Checked against source HAProxy Kubernetes Ingress (v3.2) Checked against source Cilium Ingress and Gateway API (v1.20) Checked against source

docs.title: Cloud load balancers
docs.text: Load balancer Status Notes AWS Load Balancer Controller, target type instance Checked against source Traffic reaches the doorman through the NodePort AWS Load Balancer Controller, target type ip Checked against source Registers the doorman pods as targets. The controller must watch the Hybernate namespace, which it does unless --watch-namespace is set GKE Ingress (GKE 1.36) on instance groups, its Service with cloud.google.com/neg: '{"ingress": false}' Tried by hand Traffic reaches the doorman through the NodePort. Google Cloud's load balancers send nothing to a backend that fails its health check, so the doorman answers Google's (GoogleHC/) with 200 while the workload is paused, without waking it, and holds the request that follows: the backend stayed healthy while paused, and a request through the Ingress woke the workload. See On GKE HTTPS health checks on the traffic port, any provider Partial The doorman can't read an encrypted health check, so it can't tell it from a request, and each check wakes the workload: it never stays paused longer than the check interval. AWS target groups that use HTTPS, and Google Cloud backend services that use HTTPS or HTTP/2, check over HTTPS by default. Check over HTTP, or on a port of its own listed in hybernate.io/doorman-ignore-ports; see Health checks the doorman can't recognise Services on GKE (1.36) that no GKE Ingress uses Tried by hand Routed like any other: GKE adds cloud.google.com/neg: '{"ingress": true}' to every Service of a VPC-native cluster, but no NEG exists until a GKE Ingress uses the Service, so the annotation alone doesn't keep it from the doorman. A request through ingress-nginx woke a paused workload. See On GKE GKE container-native load balancing (NEGs) Not supported by default A Service whose pods GKE puts in network endpoint groups isn't routed: the NEG controller rejects endpoints whose pods are in another namespace, and can stop syncing the load balancer altogether. That's a Service a GKE Ingress uses while it has cloud.google.com/neg: '{"ingress": true}', one with standalone NEGs (exposed_ports, which GKE Gateway sets), and one the NEG controller lists NEGs for in cloud.google.com/neg-status. A warning event names them, and the workload reports WakeOnRequest=False, reason UnsupportedLoadBalancer, when no other Service of its is routed. GKE adds cloud.google.com/neg: '{"ingress": true}' to every new Service of a VPC-native cluster, the default, but that asks for NEGs only should a GKE Ingress use the Service, so it doesn't keep a Service from being routed. The optional forwarder, below, routes such a Service; see On GKE GKE Ingress with NEGs (GKE 1.36), with doorman.negForwarder.enabled Tried by hand Optional, off by default. While a workload is paused, a forwarder Deployment beside it takes the doorman's place in the Service's endpoints, which the NEG controller accepts, and passes connections to the doorman. The NEG held the forwarder's pods, healthy, while the workload was paused; a request through the Ingress woke it, and a browser got the waking-up page; after the wake the forwarder was removed with no request failing. Right after a pause, GKE takes under a minute to swap the NEG's endpoints, and a request then can get a 502. GKE Gateway, whose Services always use NEGs, is checked against ingress-gce's source only. See GKE container-native load balancing

docs.title: Service meshes
docs.text:
Mesh Status Notes Linkerd (edge-26.9) Checked against source Connections to the doorman are plain TCP, without mTLS Istio sidecar mode, PERMISSIVE mTLS (v1.31) Tried by hand Istio's default. Callers in the mesh reach the doorman in plain text, and the doorman passes the connection to the woken pod, whose sidecar accepts it Istio sidecar mode, STRICT mTLS (v1.31) Partial The request wakes the workload, but the woken pod's sidecar refuses the doorman's plain-text connection, so the caller gets a 503. Requests once it's Running succeed Istio ambient mode (v1.31) Not supported ztunnel builds a Service's backends from its pods, not its EndpointSlices, so callers in the mesh never reach the doorman and the workload doesn't wake. Callers outside the mesh still do Istio AuthorizationPolicies that match on the caller's identity Not supported (not tried) Connections from the doorman carry no caller identity, so a policy that allows only certain callers denies them

If you run something that isn't listed, or hit a problem with something that is, please open an issue. To turn wake on request off for one workload, set wake.onRequest: false, or the annotation hybernate.io/wake-on-request: "false" on a workload opted in with the label; for the whole cluster, set the Helm value doorman.enabled: false.

docs.title: Operator Flags
docs.text:
These flags are passed to the binary (/manager), which runs as the operator, as the doorman with --doorman, or as a forwarder with --forwarder. The Helm chart sets them from its values; you only need them for your own manifests.

Flag Default Description --metrics-bind-address 0 (disabled) Address for the metrics endpoint. Use :8443 for HTTPS or :8080 for HTTP. The chart and the Kustomize manifests use :8443 --metrics-secure true Serve metrics over HTTPS, only to callers allowed to get /metrics, checked with a TokenReview and a SubjectAccessReview. false serves plain HTTP --metrics-cert-path Directory containing the metrics server's TLS certificate. Without it, a self-signed certificate is generated --metrics-cert-name tls.crt Metrics certificate file name --metrics-cert-key tls.key Metrics key file name --enable-http2 false Allow HTTP/2 for the metrics server --health-probe-bind-address :8081 Address for the health and readiness probes --leader-elect false Elect a leader, so only one replica reconciles. A leader that stops releases its lease, so the next replica, or the new one in a rollout, takes over at once. Ignored by the doorman --max-concurrent-reconciles 8 How many ManagedWorkloads are reconciled at once, so one slow metrics or Prometheus query doesn't hold up wakes, which are queued ahead of periodic checks. At least 1 --timezone UTC IANA time zone, such as Europe/London, whose hours and weekdays forecasts learn, so they follow daylight saving. The time zone database is built in --prometheus-url Base URL of the Prometheus API, such as http://prometheus.monitoring.svc:9090; http or https with a host. Required for workloads that set idlePolicy.activity.prometheus; with it, each new workload's forecast also starts from up to four weeks of its CPU history (see Learning from history) --prometheus-selector Label matchers added to the queries the operator builds itself, the history query, such as cluster="staging", written as inside PromQL's braces: =, !=, =~ or !~ and a double-quoted or backquoted value, comma-separated. For a Prometheus that holds more than one cluster's series, so same-named pods of another cluster aren't read as this one's. Activity queries are a workload's own and run as written. Needs --prometheus-url --watch-namespaces every namespace Comma-separated namespaces to work in, with a Role in each --protected-namespaces Comma-separated name patterns, such as prod-*, of namespaces Hybernate never manages, as if labelled hybernate.io/protected=true, unless labelled hybernate.io/allow-protected=true. The kube-* namespaces, $POD_NAMESPACE, and the doorman's namespace are always protected besides; see Protected namespaces --default-idle-after 1h Idle time before pausing, for workloads opted in with the label whose annotations and namespace don't set it. At least 1m --default-cpu-threshold 10 CPU percentage of requests that counts as active, for opted-in workloads that don't set it. 1 to 100 --default-dry-run false Measure opted-in workloads without pausing, unless they or their namespace set hybernate.io/dry-run --default-pause-early false Let a confident forecast that expects quiet hours pause opted-in workloads before their idleAfter runs out, unless they or their namespace set hybernate.io/pause-early. See Pausing Early --default-forecast balanced How soon the forecast acts, eager, balanced or cautious, for opted-in workloads that don't set hybernate.io/forecast --doorman false Run as the doorman instead of the operator. The doorman Deployment sets it --doorman-service hybernate-doorman Name of the doorman's Service, which the operator routes paused workloads to. Empty disables waking on request --doorman-ports-per-workload 32 The most doorman ports one workload may hold, one per routed Service port. A workload with more isn't routed (WakeOnRequest=False, reason TooManyPorts) --doorman-ports-per-namespace 256 The most doorman ports the workloads of one namespace may hold together --doorman-namespace $POD_NAMESPACE, else hybernate-system Namespace of the doorman's Service --doorman-health-check-user-agents Comma-separated User-Agent prefixes of health checkers and scrapers, besides the built-in ones, whose GET and HEAD requests don't wake a paused workload. Helm value doorman.healthCheckUserAgents --neg-forwarder false Route paused workloads' Services that sit behind GKE container-native load balancing (NEGs) through a forwarder Deployment the operator runs in each workload's namespace, instead of leaving them unrouted. Needs create and delete on Deployments. Helm value doorman.negForwarder.enabled; see GKE container-native load balancing --neg-forwarder-image The image forwarders run: the operator's own. Required with --neg-forwarder --neg-forwarder-replicas 2 Pods per forwarder. At least 1 --neg-forwarder-resources {"requests":{"cpu":"10m","memory":"32Mi"},"limits":{"memory":"64Mi"}} Each forwarder pod's resources, as JSON --neg-forwarder-doorman-service hybernate-doorman-pods Headless Service in --doorman-namespace selecting the doorman's pods, whose DNS name forwarders resolve to reach them --forwarder false Run as a forwarder instead of the operator. The operator's forwarder Deployments set it, with --forward, the routes as comma-separated listen=doorman port pairs, and --forwarder-doorman, the DNS name of the doorman's pods --guard Run as the chart's uninstall or upgrade hook instead of the operator. It waits up to two and a half minutes for ManagedWorkloads being deleted, then exits 1, listing those the operation would leave without an operator: for uninstall, every one in --watch-namespaces (every namespace when empty) or carrying the hybernate.io/cleanup finalizer; for upgrade, those carrying the finalizer outside the new --watch-namespaces. The chart's guard.uninstall and guard.upgrade hooks set it --kubeconfig in-cluster Path to a kubeconfig, only when running outside the cluster --zap-log-level info Log level: debug, info, error, panic, or a whole number above 0 for more verbose debug levels --zap-encoder json Log format: json or console --zap-devel false Development defaults: console encoding, debug level, stack traces from warnings --zap-stacktrace-level error Level from which stack traces are logged: info, error, or panic --zap-time-encoding RFC 3339 Time format of log entries: epoch, millis, nano, iso8601, rfc3339 or rfc3339nano

The operator checks its flags at startup and exits with an error naming the flag when one is invalid: a --protected-namespaces pattern that isn't a valid glob, a --prometheus-url that isn't http or https with a host, a --prometheus-selector that isn't label matchers or is set without --prometheus-url, a --default-idle-after under 1m, a --default-cpu-threshold outside 1 to 100, a --default-forecast that isn't eager, balanced or cautious, a --max-concurrent-reconciles, --doorman-ports-per-workload or --doorman-ports-per-namespace below 1, or a --timezone that isn't a known IANA zone.

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text: Endpoint Port Description /healthz 8081 Liveness probe. Returns 200 while the process is running /readyz 8081 Readiness probe. For the doorman, 200 once it has loaded its routes and reached the API server in the last 30 seconds; failing while it can't listen on a routed port for more than 30 seconds, and while it shuts down. For a forwarder, 200 while it reaches the doorman on every port it passes connections to, and failing from the moment it starts shutting down; its probes are on 8081, or the next port the workload doesn't serve /metrics 8443 in the chart Prometheus metrics, HTTPS by default; see Metrics

docs.title: Leader Election
docs.text:
For HA deployments with multiple replicas, enable leader election:

--leader-elect=true

The leader election ID is 479a98fc.hybernate.io, held as a Lease in the operator's namespace. Only the leader runs reconciliation loops; standby replicas take over if the leader fails.

The doorman doesn't use leader election: every replica serves traffic.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
By default, metrics are served over HTTPS, and a scraper needs a token allowed to get the /metrics URL; the chart's metrics.readerSubjects binds one, see Monitoring. To use HTTP (not recommended for production):

--metrics-secure=false --metrics-bind-address=:8080

docs.title: Custom Certificates
docs.text:
For your own TLS certificate, instead of a self-signed one:

--metrics-cert-path=/certs/metrics

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
The operator and the doorman log JSON by default, through logr (controller-runtime). Key fields in log entries:

Field Description name, namespace The object a reconcile is for, such as the ManagedWorkload, added by controller-runtime to every entry it logs, with controller and reconcileID workload The workload or ManagedWorkload an entry is about, on entries that name it themselves, with its namespace from, to The phases of a phase transition entry reason Why: what caused a phase transition phase The phase after a reconcile, on reconciled entries at debug level (--zap-log-level=debug) error What went wrong, on entries about a failure

For logs to read by eye, use --zap-encoder=console (the chart's logEncoder: console).

docs.title: Data and Access
docs.text: Everything the Hybernate operator and its doorman read, write, and send, for a security review. The RBAC the Helm chart grants matches this list.

docs.title: What it reads
docs.text:
Resource Why How Deployments, StatefulSets The workloads it manages: replicas, pod template, labels, and annotations Watched Pods What a workload's running pods request: the app containers', at most every 5 minutes, to judge CPU activity against, and all containers', sidecars included, to price it; and which pod sent a request that woke a workload. What every pod bound to a node requests, to measure the spare capacity on each node pool that saved is worked out from. The doorman reads the pod each of a woken workload's endpoints names, to check the endpoint's address is that pod's. With doorman.negForwarder.enabled, a forwarder's pods, for their addresses and readiness Watched, with only bound, unfinished pods cached, and of each only its name, node, phase and requests; read from the API server for the rest. Not watched by an operator limited by watchNamespaces. The doorman keeps a pod's addresses for 30 seconds Pod metrics (metrics.k8s.io) CPU use, the activity clock's main signal Read when needed, not cached Services Which Services to route a paused workload's requests through, and which workload an address in an environment names Watched Ingresses Their class and the Services they send traffic to, to tell which Services a GKE Ingress puts behind container-native load balancing, which can't be routed to the doorman Watched EndpointSlices Its own, routing paused workloads to the doorman, and the doorman Service's, to find the doorman's pods. The doorman reads every slice in the watched namespaces, to find a woken workload's Ready pods Watched ConfigMaps The ones a managed workload takes environment variables from, to learn its dependencies; and kube-system/cluster-autoscaler-status, whose existence shows Cluster Autoscaler runs Read one by one with get, not cached; never listed or written. Of cluster-autoscaler-status, only its metadata, every 10 minutes PersistentVolumeClaims Their size, to price the storage a paused workload keeps Watched HorizontalPodAutoscalers, KEDA ScaledObjects What scales a workload, and its range Watched Namespaces Their labels: opt-in, settings, and protection Watched Nodes Their labels (instance type, region, spot, node pool), to price workloads and group them into pools; and their allocatable CPU and memory, whether they're schedulable and Ready, to measure each pool's spare capacity Watched, keeping only those fields; their image lists and the rest are dropped. Their metadata is also listed every 10 minutes, to tell which node autoscaler runs Karpenter NodePools (karpenter.sh/v1) Their names and spec.disruption, to report which node autoscaler runs Listed every 10 minutes, not cached. Without Karpenter installed, nothing is read Deployments in kube-system Their names, to find a Cluster Autoscaler that hasn't written its status ConfigMap Metadata listed every 10 minutes, only while that ConfigMap is missing ManagedWorkloads Its own configuration Watched

Never read: Secrets, of any kind, anywhere. An address set in a Secret is learned only from the request it's used for.

docs.title: What it writes
docs.text:
Resource What Deployments, StatefulSets Their replica count, through the scale subresource, and, while one is paused, the hybernate.io/paused-from annotation: a copy of what the pause changed, removed when it's handed back. No other field, and never a delete Deployments of its own, with doorman.negForwarder.enabled A forwarder, hybernate-forwarder-<workload>, in the namespace of each paused workload whose Service is behind GKE container-native load balancing, owned by its ManagedWorkload and deleted a minute after the workload wakes. See GKE container-native load balancing KEDA ScaledObjects The autoscaling.keda.sh/paused-replicas annotation, while their workload is paused or resuming; afterwards the value it had before, or none EndpointSlices Its own, routing a paused workload's Services to the doorman; deleted when the workload wakes ManagedWorkloads Its own status, including each workload's forecast state; the ones it creates for labelled workloads; the hybernate.io/cleanup finalizer, added to each so that deleting it restores its workload first, and removed once it has, with hybernate.io/operator, the operator's namespace; hybernate.io/last-activity on a dependency it wakes; and, from the doorman, hybernate.io/last-request and hybernate.io/last-request-from (the caller's IP address) on one a request wakes Events On ManagedWorkloads and workloads, to say what it did and why Leases Leader election, in its own namespace

Never written: any other resource, any other field of a workload, and nothing is ever deleted but its own ManagedWorkloads, EndpointSlices and forwarder Deployments.

docs.title: What it sends
docs.text:
Nothing leaves the cluster, unless configured to:

Destination When The Kubernetes API server Always: everything above Prometheus, at prometheus.url Only with prometheus.url set: the Prometheus activity queries workloads configure, and, once for each new ManagedWorkload, one range query for up to four weeks of its own containers' CPU (container_cpu_usage_seconds_total), an hour a point, to start its forecast from, narrowed by prometheus.selector when it's set

No telemetry, no usage reporting, no update checks. The doorman answers requests to paused workloads and forwards them to the woken pod; it doesn't store or log their contents. Nor does a forwarder, which reads nothing from the API server and only passes connections on to the doorman.

docs.title: RBAC
docs.text:
What the Helm chart grants, for a release named hybernate; resource names start with the release's full name. Without watchNamespaces, the rules marked namespaced are in ClusterRoles; with it, they're in a Role in each watched namespace, and nothing marked namespaced is granted anywhere else.

Operator (ServiceAccount hybernate), ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding hybernate-manager:

API group Resources Verbs "" namespaces, nodes get, list, watch always cluster-wide karpenter.sh nodepools list always cluster-wide "" configmaps get namespaced "" events create, patch namespaced events.k8s.io events create, patch namespaced "" services get, list, watch namespaced networking.k8s.io ingresses get, list, watch namespaced "" pods get, list, watch namespaced "" persistentvolumeclaims get, list, watch namespaced discovery.k8s.io endpointslices get, list, watch, create, update, patch, delete namespaced apps deployments, statefulsets get, list, watch, patch namespaced apps deployments/scale, statefulsets/scale get, update namespaced autoscaling horizontalpodautoscalers get, list, watch namespaced keda.sh scaledobjects get, list, watch, patch namespaced hybernate.io managedworkloads get, list, watch, create, update, patch, delete namespaced hybernate.io managedworkloads/status get, update, patch namespaced hybernate.io managedworkloads/finalizers update namespaced metrics.k8s.io pods get, list namespaced

With watchNamespaces and the doorman enabled, a Role hybernate-doorman-endpoints in the release namespace lets the operator get, list and watch endpointslices there, to find the doorman's pods.

With leader election, a Role hybernate-leader-election in the release namespace grants coordination.k8s.io leases (get, create, update) and "" events (create, patch).

With doorman.negForwarder.enabled, a ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding hybernate-forwarder, or a Role and RoleBinding of that name in each watched namespace, grant apps deployments (create, delete), for the forwarders. A forwarder runs as its namespace's default ServiceAccount, without its token, and has no access to the API server.

Doorman (ServiceAccount hybernate-doorman), ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding hybernate-doorman, or a Role in each watched namespace:

API group Resources Verbs hybernate.io managedworkloads get, list, watch, patch discovery.k8s.io endpointslices get, list, watch "" pods get "", events.k8s.io events create, patch

Guards, with guard.uninstall and, with watchNamespaces, guard.upgrade (the defaults): a ServiceAccount hybernate-uninstall-guard, and a ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding of the same name, allowing list on hybernate.io managedworkloads, cluster-wide even with watchNamespaces; and the same named hybernate-upgrade-guard. They're Helm hooks, like the Jobs that use them: they exist only while helm uninstall runs its pre-delete hook, or helm upgrade or helm rollback its pre-upgrade or pre-rollback hook, which refuse to leave ManagedWorkloads without an operator.

People: ClusterRoles hybernate-view and hybernate-edit, which grant nothing to Hybernate itself. They're aggregated into Kubernetes' built-in roles: view, edit and admin gain get, list and watch on hybernate.io managedworkloads, and get on their status; edit and admin gain create, update, patch and delete.

Admission policy, with doorman.admissionPolicy.enabled (the default): a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy and binding hybernate-doorman, cluster-scoped, which refuse any change the doorman's ServiceAccount makes to a ManagedWorkload other than to its hybernate.io/last-request and last-request-from annotations; and a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy and binding hybernate-request-stamps, cluster-scoped, which refuse anyone else setting those two annotations, limited to watchNamespaces when set.

Metrics, with metrics.enabled and metrics.secure (the defaults): ClusterRoleBindings hybernate-auth-delegator and hybernate-doorman-auth-delegator to the built-in system:auth-delegator ClusterRole, so the operator and the doorman can check the tokens of whoever scrapes them; and a ClusterRole hybernate-metrics-reader allowing get on the /metrics URL, bound to metrics.readerSubjects by a ClusterRoleBinding of the same name.

docs.title: The plugin
docs.text: kubectl hybernate runs with your own kubeconfig and permissions, reads the same kinds of resources and their events, and changes nothing except for wake (activity annotations on a ManagedWorkload), pause (the hybernate.io/pause-requested annotation on a ManagedWorkload, with hybernate.io/pause-overrides-forecast when told to pause one the forecast expects demand for, and, with --clear-hold, removing its hybernate.io/active-until) and enable (the hybernate.io/dry-run annotation, on a workload or its namespace, or spec.dryRun on a ManagedWorkload you wrote). scan reads Prometheus through the API server's service proxy, or at --prometheus-url, and writes its report only to your machine, in a file only you can read, as status --html does its page. For a workload Argo CD applies, scan, status, pause and enable read Argo CD's Applications and its argocd-cm ConfigMap, to tell whether it leaves the workload's replicas to Hybernate.

docs.title: Helm Values Reference
docs.text:
Complete reference for the Hybernate Helm chart. Put the values you set in a file, starting with your users' time zone:

hybernate-values.yaml
timezone: Europe/London

and install with it:

helm install hybernate oci://ghcr.io/okedeji/charts/hybernate --version 0.2.0-rc.5 \
  --namespace hybernate-system --create-namespace \
  -f hybernate-values.yaml

Upgrade with the same file, so upgrades keep your settings; see Keeping your settings. The chart is published only as an OCI artifact; there's no helm repo to add. Its version has no v (0.2.0-rc.5); the image tags do (v0.2.0-rc.5). To see all defaults:

helm show values oci://ghcr.io/okedeji/charts/hybernate --version 0.2.0-rc.5

The chart validates values against its schema (values.schema.json), so a mistyped value, such as logLevel: warn or defaults.cpuThreshold: 0, fails the install or upgrade rather than the operator, and so does a value the chart doesn't have, such as watchNamespace for watchNamespaces, which Helm would otherwise ignore. Only what's passed through to Kubernetes as it is, such as resources, affinity, tolerations, nodeSelector and pod annotations and labels, is left for Kubernetes to check. timezone is the exception: the schema can't list every IANA zone, so an unknown one is caught when the operator starts, which then exits with invalid --timezone and unknown time zone in its log, and the rollout doesn't finish.

docs.title: Names
docs.text:
Value Default Description nameOverride "" Replaces the chart name in resource names fullnameOverride "" Replaces the full name the chart's resources are named after

The full name is the release name when it contains hybernate, and <release>-hybernate otherwise, cut to 40 characters, so that every name built from it, the longest being <fullname>-doorman-auth-delegator, fits in 63. For a release named hybernate, the operator Deployment and ServiceAccount are hybernate, and the doorman's are hybernate-doorman. The operator's pods are labelled app.kubernetes.io/name: hybernate, app.kubernetes.io/instance: <release> and control-plane: controller-manager; the doorman's the same, with control-plane: doorman.

docs.title: Image
docs.text: Value Default Description image.repository ghcr.io/okedeji/hybernate Container image repository image.tag "", the chart's appVersion, such as v0.2.0-rc.5 Image tag, for the operator and the doorman image.pullPolicy IfNotPresent Image pull policy imagePullSecrets [] Private registry credentials

docs.title: CRD
docs.text:
Value Default Description crds.install true Install the ManagedWorkload CRD, and upgrade it with each helm upgrade

The CRD is a chart template with helm.sh/resource-policy: keep, so helm uninstall leaves it, and every ManagedWorkload, in place: deleting the CRD would delete them all. Argo CD ignores that policy, so the CRD also carries argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options: Delete=false, and deleting or pruning the Application leaves it too. Set crds.install: false only if you manage the CRD yourself, for example from config/crd in the repository.

docs.title: Defaults version
docs.text:
Value Default Description defaultsVersion the chart's version, such as 0.2.0-rc.5 The chart version the defaults Helm renders with are from. Leave it as it is

helm upgrade --reuse-values to a newer version renders with the installed version's defaults rather than the new one's, and those lack every value added since. The chart tells from defaultsVersion that they're another version's, and fills in each missing value from its own defaults, kept in files/defaults.yaml, a copy of values.yaml, since templates can't read values.yaml itself. A value that's there is kept, false, 0 and "" included. With its own defaults, the chart fills in nothing, so a default you remove with null stays removed. See Keeping your settings.

docs.title: Operator
docs.text: Value Default Description replicaCount 1 Operator replicas. More than one needs leaderElection.enabled, so that only one acts at a time; the schema refuses more otherwise leaderElection.enabled true Elect a leader through a Lease, so only one replica reconciles. Without it, an upgrade stops the old operator before starting the new one (strategy: Recreate), so two never act at once maxConcurrentReconciles 8 How many ManagedWorkloads the operator reconciles at once, so one slow metrics or Prometheus query doesn't hold up waking another workload. Passed as --max-concurrent-reconciles timezone UTC IANA time zone, such as Europe/London, whose hours and weekdays the forecast learns. Use your users' zone, so forecasts follow daylight saving. Passed as --timezone logLevel info debug, info, error, panic, or a whole number above 0 for more verbose debug levels. For the operator and the doorman logEncoder json json, or console for reading by eye. For the operator and the doorman

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
Value Default Description resources.requests.cpu 10m CPU request resources.requests.memory 128Mi Memory request resources.limits.cpu 500m CPU limit resources.limits.memory 512Mi Memory limit

The operator caches the cluster's ManagedWorkloads, Deployments, StatefulSets, Services, Ingresses, PVCs, HPAs, Nodes and Namespaces, or only the watched namespaces' with watchNamespaces, and the EndpointSlices it writes and the doorman Service's, so its memory grows with the cluster. Nodes are cached without their image lists, and pods only as what spare node capacity needs: those bound to a node and not finished, as their node, phase and requests, about 2.6 KB a pod. Other EndpointSlices, ConfigMaps and KEDA ScaledObjects are read when needed, not cached. Raise the limit on clusters with many thousands of workloads. Go's garbage collector is given a soft limit of 90% of the memory limit, for the operator and the doorman alike, leaving the rest for memory outside its heap, so it works harder near the limit rather than letting either be OOM-killed. Setting GOMEMLIMIT in the pod overrides it.

docs.title: Namespaces
docs.text:
Value Default Description watchNamespaces [] Namespaces Hybernate works in. Empty means every namespace. Set, Hybernate gets a Role in each of them instead of a ClusterRole, so Kubernetes itself refuses it anything elsewhere; see RBAC. Passed as --watch-namespaces, to the doorman too. Each of several installs in one cluster needs its own; see More than one install protectedNamespaces [] Name patterns, such as prod-*, of namespaces Hybernate never manages, as if labelled hybernate.io/protected=true, unless one is labelled hybernate.io/allow-protected=true. kube-*, and the operator's and the doorman's namespace, are always protected, besides these, with the same exception. See Protected namespaces. Passed as --protected-namespaces values.yaml
watchNamespaces: [preview-1, preview-2, staging]
protectedNamespaces: ["prod-*", production]

Wake on request works with watchNamespaces: the operator always reads the doorman's own EndpointSlices in the release namespace, through a <fullname>-doorman-endpoints Role there. A dependsOn pointing into a namespace that isn't watched, and that allows the dependent's with hybernate.io/dependents-from, is reported on the dependent, as DependencyNotFound=True with reason DependencyNotVisible, and never blocks it.

An upgrade or rollback to a watchNamespaces that leaves out a namespace where the operator manages workloads, or that sets it where it was empty, is refused while they're there, since they'd stay paused with no operator: see Narrowing watchNamespaces.

docs.title: Opt-In Defaults
docs.text:
Settings for workloads opted in with the hybernate.io/managed label, used when neither the workload nor its namespace sets the annotation. See Opting In.

Value Default Description defaults.idleAfter 1h How long without activity before pausing; a Go duration of at least 1m, such as 90s or 1h30m. Passed as --default-idle-after defaults.cpuThreshold 10 CPU use, as a percentage of requests from 1 to 100, above which a workload counts as active. Passed as --default-cpu-threshold defaults.dryRun false Measure without pausing. Set true to roll Hybernate out across a cluster measuring first. Passed as --default-dry-run defaults.pauseEarly false Let a confident forecast that expects quiet hours pause a workload before idleAfter runs out. See Pausing Early. Passed as --default-pause-early defaults.forecast balanced How soon the forecast acts: eager, balanced or cautious. See Forecast setting. Passed as --default-forecast

docs.title: Prometheus Activity
docs.text: Value Default Description prometheus.url "" Base URL of the Prometheus API, such as http://prometheus.monitoring.svc:9090, for Prometheus activity queries and to start each new workload's forecast from up to four weeks of its CPU history (see Learning from history). Passed to the operator as --prometheus-url prometheus.selector "" Label matchers added to the history query the operator makes, such as cluster="staging", for a Prometheus that holds more than one cluster's series, as Thanos, Mimir or a shared Prometheus may; written as inside PromQL's braces, as kubectl hybernate scan --prometheus-selector takes them. Activity queries run as written. Needs prometheus.url. Passed to the operator as --prometheus-selector

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Value Default Description metrics.enabled true Expose Prometheus metrics, from the operator and the doorman metrics.port 8443 Metrics endpoint port, for the operator and the doorman. Not 8081, the health probes' port, nor 20000-29999, where the doorman listens for paused workloads' traffic metrics.secure true Serve metrics over HTTPS, only to callers allowed to get /metrics. false serves plain HTTP to anyone who can reach the port metrics.readerSubjects [] Subjects, such as your Prometheus's ServiceAccount, to bind to the <fullname>-metrics-reader ClusterRole, which may get /metrics

With metrics.secure, a scraper must authenticate with a token that's allowed to get /metrics. The chart creates the <fullname>-metrics-reader ClusterRole for that; bind your Prometheus to it with readerSubjects, or with a binding of your own:

values.yaml
metrics:
  readerSubjects:
    - kind: ServiceAccount
      name: prometheus-k8s
      namespace: monitoring

With metrics.enabled, it also creates ClusterRoleBindings to system:auth-delegator for the operator and the doorman (<fullname>-auth-delegator, <fullname>-doorman-auth-delegator), which they need to check those tokens.

docs.title: ServiceMonitor
docs.text:
Value Default Description metrics.serviceMonitor.enabled false Create Prometheus Operator ServiceMonitors for the operator and the doorman metrics.serviceMonitor.interval 30s Scrape interval metrics.serviceMonitor.additionalLabels {} Extra labels on the ServiceMonitors. Your Prometheus picks them up only if these match its serviceMonitorSelector: kube-prometheus-stack needs release: <its release name>

The ServiceMonitors set honorLabels: true, so the metrics keep the workload's namespace label. kube-prometheus-stack's Prometheus runs as the <its release name>-kube-prometheus-prometheus ServiceAccount, the subject for metrics.readerSubjects. See Monitoring.

docs.title: PrometheusRule
docs.text: Value Default Description metrics.prometheusRule.enabled false Create a PrometheusRule with the alerts in Monitoring. HybernateDown and HybernateDoormanDown, which match the ServiceMonitors' scrape jobs, only with metrics.serviceMonitor.enabled metrics.prometheusRule.additionalLabels {} Extra labels on the PrometheusRule. Your Prometheus loads it only if these match its ruleSelector: kube-prometheus-stack needs release: <its release name>

docs.title: Doorman
docs.text:
The doorman holds requests to paused workloads and wakes them. See Wake on Request.

Value Default Description doorman.enabled true Deploy the doorman. When false, requests to paused workloads fail doorman.replicaCount 2 Doorman replicas. Every replica serves traffic doorman.portsPerWorkload 32 The most doorman ports one workload may hold, one per routed Service port, so one tenant can't use up the 10,000 the cluster shares; 1 to 10000. A workload with more isn't routed: WakeOnRequest=False, reason TooManyPorts. Passed as --doorman-ports-per-workload doorman.portsPerNamespace 256 The most doorman ports the workloads of one namespace may hold together; 1 to 10000. Passed as --doorman-ports-per-namespace doorman.healthCheckUserAgents [] User-Agent prefixes, or names that follow (compatible; in a browser-style one, of health checkers and scrapers whose GET and HEAD requests don't wake a paused workload, besides the built-in ones (kube-probe, Prometheus, load balancers' checks, Blackbox Exporter/, Datadog/Synthetics, Amazon-Route53-Health-Check-Service, GoogleStackdriverMonitoring-UptimeChecks, UptimeRobot, Pingdom.com_bot, NewRelicPinger/, Uptime-Kuma/, Gatus/ and others), such as ["MyCorpMonitor/"]. See What wakes a workload doorman.admissionPolicy.enabled true Two ValidatingAdmissionPolicies: one that lets the doorman's ServiceAccount change only the hybernate.io/last-request and hybernate.io/last-request-from annotations on ManagedWorkloads, though its role may patch them, and one that lets no one else set those two, so a forged last-request-from can't have the operator learn a dependency. See Security doorman.podDisruptionBudget.enabled true A PodDisruptionBudget keeping one doorman serving through node drains, when replicaCount is above 1 doorman.nodeSelector {} Node selector; empty uses the operator's nodeSelector doorman.tolerations [] Tolerations; empty uses the operator's tolerations doorman.affinity {} Affinity; empty uses the operator's affinity doorman.topologySpreadConstraints [] Topology spread; empty spreads the replicas across nodes and zones where it can doorman.podAnnotations {} Pod annotations; empty uses the operator's podAnnotations doorman.podLabels {} Pod labels; empty uses the operator's podLabels doorman.priorityClassName "" PriorityClass; empty uses the operator's priorityClassName doorman.extraEnv [] Extra environment variables for the doorman. The operator's extraEnv doesn't apply to it doorman.resources.requests.cpu 10m CPU request doorman.resources.requests.memory 64Mi Memory request doorman.resources.limits.cpu 500m CPU limit doorman.resources.limits.memory 256Mi Memory limit doorman.negForwarder.enabled false Optional, for GKE: route paused workloads' Services that sit behind container-native load balancing (NEGs), as a GKE Ingress's or Gateway's do, through a forwarder Deployment the operator runs in each workload's namespace while it's paused, so requests through the load balancer wake them. Grants the operator create and delete on Deployments, in a ClusterRole <fullname>-forwarder or a Role in each watched namespace, and adds a headless Service <fullname>-doorman-pods. Needs doorman.enabled. See GKE container-native load balancing doorman.negForwarder.replicas 2 Pods per forwarder, spread across nodes, so one stays while a node drains doorman.negForwarder.resources.requests.cpu 10m Each forwarder pod's CPU request doorman.negForwarder.resources.requests.memory 32Mi Each forwarder pod's memory request doorman.negForwarder.resources.limits.memory 64Mi Each forwarder pod's memory limit

The doorman uses the operator image, the metrics.* settings, logLevel and logEncoder. It caches ManagedWorkloads and the EndpointSlices the EndpointSlice controller writes in the watched namespaces, cut down to what it reads: about 300 bytes per pod and 700 per Service. Held connections take up to 72Mi more under a flood. The default 256Mi limit covers a cluster of some 100,000 pods; raise it beyond that. On Kubernetes 1.30 and later it sleeps 5 seconds before shutting down, so kube-proxy and load balancers stop sending it new connections first. A rollout waits 5 seconds after a new doorman pod is Ready (minReadySeconds) before stopping an old one, so the operator has moved paused workloads' routes to it.

docs.title: Network Policy
docs.text:
Value Default Description networkPolicy.enabled false Create NetworkPolicies for the operator and the doorman doorman.networkPolicy.ingressFrom [] NetworkPolicy peers allowed to reach paused workloads through the doorman, such as your ingress controller's namespace. Empty leaves the doorman open to every caller. Needs networkPolicy.enabled doorman.networkPolicy.egress.enabled false Create an egress NetworkPolicy allowing the doorman to connect only to podCIDRs and the API server doorman.networkPolicy.egress.podCIDRs [] The cluster's pod CIDRs, in every IP family it uses. Required when enabled doorman.networkPolicy.egress.apiServer [] CIDRs of the API server's endpoints (kubectl get endpointslices -n default -l kubernetes.io/service-name=kubernetes), not the kubernetes Service's ClusterIP. Required when enabled doorman.networkPolicy.egress.apiServerPorts [443, 6443] The API server endpoints' ports

When enabled, the operator's and the doorman's metrics port admits only namespaces labelled metrics: enabled, and the doorman's routing ports (TCP 20000-29999) admit every source, since every client of a paused workload's Services is sent to them. With ingressFrom and doorman.negForwarder.enabled, they also admit the forwarders, from any namespace. To narrow who can reach the doorman, see Restricting who can reach the doorman.

The doorman's egress policy is separate from networkPolicy.enabled, and needs a CNI that enforces egress policies. The doorman needs no DNS: it reaches the API server by address, and pods by their endpoint addresses. If a routed workload uses hostNetwork, add your node CIDRs to podCIDRs.

On Cilium, a NetworkPolicy ipBlock may not match the API server, which Cilium identifies as the kube-apiserver entity rather than by address, so the egress policy can cut the doorman off from it: its pods then fail readiness and log API errors. Leave doorman.networkPolicy.egress.enabled off there, and write a CiliumNetworkPolicy instead that allows egress toEntities: [kube-apiserver] and toCIDR your pod CIDRs.

docs.title: Service Account
docs.text:
Value Default Description serviceAccount.create true Create the operator's ServiceAccount serviceAccount.name "" Name override (defaults to the full name)

The doorman always gets its own ServiceAccount, <fullname>-doorman.

docs.title: Guards
docs.text:
Value Default Description guard.uninstall true Refuse helm uninstall while ManagedWorkloads are left, through a pre-delete hook Job guard.upgrade true Refuse helm upgrade or helm rollback to a watchNamespaces that leaves out namespaces where the operator manages workloads, through a pre-upgrade and pre-rollback hook Job. Only with watchNamespaces set guard.nodeSelector {} The hooks' node selector; empty uses the operator's nodeSelector guard.tolerations [] Tolerations; empty uses the operator's tolerations guard.affinity {} Affinity; empty uses the operator's affinity guard.priorityClassName "" PriorityClass; empty uses the operator's priorityClassName guard.podAnnotations {} The hooks' pod annotations, over sidecar.istio.io/inject: "false" and linkerd.io/inject: disabled guard.podLabels {} The hooks' pod labels, over sidecar.istio.io/inject: "false". They can't replace the chart's own labels guard.resources 10m/64Mi requests, 100m/128Mi limits The hooks' resources

Without the operator, a ManagedWorkload's finalizer never runs: its workload stays paused at 0 replicas, and its Services keep routing to the doorman. The guards are hook Jobs that run the operator's image with --guard: each waits two and a half minutes for any ManagedWorkloads being deleted, then lists those it would leave without an operator, and fails, which stops Helm before it changes anything. Helm prints the list.

  • The <fullname>-uninstall-guard Job counts every ManagedWorkload in the watched namespaces, or in every namespace without watchNamespaces, and any elsewhere that the operator took on, with its hybernate.io/cleanup finalizer, but none another install took on, stamped with its namespace in hybernate.io/operator. See Uninstall. Argo CD 3.3 and later runs it as a PreDelete hook, so deleting the Application is blocked the same way; earlier versions skip it.
  • The <fullname>-upgrade-guard Job counts those the operator took on in namespaces the new watchNamespaces leaves out. See Narrowing watchNamespaces. Argo CD runs it as a PreSync hook, before every sync.

Each runs as a ServiceAccount of its own name, through a ClusterRole that may only list ManagedWorkloads, which read their metadata cluster-wide, even with watchNamespaces, since those they look for may be outside it. The ServiceAccounts and RBAC are hooks too, deleted once the hook has run; a failed Job is kept for an hour, for kubectl logs. The hooks use image, imagePullSecrets and logLevel. Meshes' sidecars are kept out of their pods, since a sidecar that keeps running would keep the Job from finishing. Their pods have their own control-plane: uninstall-guard and control-plane: upgrade-guard labels, so the operator's Service and NetworkPolicy don't select them. --no-hooks skips both.

docs.title: Pod Scheduling
docs.text: Value Default Description nodeSelector {} Node selector constraints, for the operator, and for the doorman unless doorman.nodeSelector is set tolerations [] Pod tolerations, likewise affinity {} Pod affinity/anti-affinity rules, likewise podAnnotations {} Pod annotations, likewise podLabels {} Pod labels, likewise. They can't replace the labels the chart selects pods by priorityClassName "" PriorityClass, likewise. A paused workload's requests wait on the doorman and the operator, so on a cluster that preempts, give them a class above the workloads they wake extraEnv [] Extra environment variables for the operator, as container env entries, such as GOMAXPROCS

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
The chart enforces a strict security posture by default:

Pod level:

  • runAsNonRoot: true
  • seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault

Container level:

  • readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
  • allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
  • capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]

These are not configurable via values. To override, use Helm post-rendering or Kustomize overlays.

docs.title: Health Probes
docs.text: Pod Probe Path Port Initial Delay Period Operator Liveness /healthz 8081 15s 20s Operator Readiness /readyz 8081 5s 10s Doorman Liveness /healthz 8081 15s 20s Doorman Readiness /readyz 8081 2s 5s

docs.title: RBAC
docs.text:
By default the chart creates a ClusterRole, <fullname>-manager, with permissions to:

  • Manage ManagedWorkload CRs, including creating them for labelled workloads
  • Read Namespaces, for the hybernate.io/managed label and settings annotations on them
  • Read Deployments and StatefulSets, scale them through the scale subresource, and patch them to set and remove the hybernate.io/paused-from annotation while they're paused. Hybernate can't delete them, and changes nothing else on them
  • Read PersistentVolumeClaims, to price the storage a paused workload keeps
  • Read HorizontalPodAutoscalers, and read and annotate KEDA ScaledObjects, to pause a KEDA workload through KEDA
  • Read pod metrics from metrics-server
  • Read pods, to price what pausing a workload frees, sidecars included, and watch them, to measure the spare node capacity that what pausing saved is worked out from. Only pods bound to a node and not finished are cached, as their node, phase and requests
  • Read Nodes, to price workloads at the list price of the instance types they run on, and to measure their spare capacity. They're cached without their image lists
  • List Karpenter's NodePools, and get Cluster Autoscaler's cluster-autoscaler-status ConfigMap and list Deployments in kube-system, to report which node autoscaler runs (hybernate_node_autoscaler). It reads NodePools' names and consolidation settings, and only the metadata of the rest
  • Get ConfigMaps, one at a time and uncached, to learn dependencies from the ones a workload's environment references. It can't list or change them
  • Create Events for user-facing status updates
  • Read Services, and manage the EndpointSlices that route paused workloads to the doorman

The doorman has its own ServiceAccount and ClusterRole, <fullname>-doorman: it reads ManagedWorkloads and EndpointSlices, gets the pods a woken workload's endpoints name, to check each endpoint's address is its pod's, patches ManagedWorkloads to wake them, and creates Events. With doorman.admissionPolicy.enabled, those patches may only set the two annotations that record a request.

With watchNamespaces set, both get a Role and RoleBinding in each of those namespaces instead. The operator keeps one ClusterRole, to read Namespaces and Nodes and list Karpenter's NodePools, which only a ClusterRole can grant, and gets a <fullname>-doorman-endpoints Role in the release namespace to read the doorman's EndpointSlices. Workloads in other namespaces can't be read, scaled, or opted in, and dependencies on them aren't held or woken. With metrics.enabled and metrics.secure, both ServiceAccounts also keep their cluster-wide system:auth-delegator bindings, which let them check scrapers' tokens and nothing else.

If leader election is enabled, a <fullname>-leader-election Role in the release namespace grants Leases (get, create, update) and Events.

With doorman.negForwarder.enabled, a ClusterRole <fullname>-forwarder, or with watchNamespaces a Role of that name in each watched namespace, lets the operator create and delete Deployments, for the forwarders it runs beside paused workloads behind GKE NEGs. It only ever deletes its own, owned by a ManagedWorkload. The forwarders run as their namespace's default ServiceAccount, without its token, and have no access to the API server.

For people, the chart adds ManagedWorkloads to Kubernetes' built-in roles, through two aggregated ClusterRoles: <fullname>-view, in view, edit and admin, lets whoever can view a namespace get, list and watch its ManagedWorkloads, as kubectl hybernate status and scan do; <fullname>-edit, in edit and admin, lets whoever can edit it create, update, patch and delete them, as pause, wake and enable do. The Kustomize manifests' managedworkload-viewer-role and managedworkload-editor-role are aggregated the same way.

What all of this reads, writes, and sends is listed in Data and Access.

docs.title: Example: Production Configuration
docs.text:
values-production.yaml
replicaCount: 2

leaderElection:
  enabled: true

timezone: Europe/London

resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 256Mi
  limits:
    cpu: "1"
    memory: 1Gi

metrics:
  enabled: true
  secure: true
  readerSubjects:
    - kind: ServiceAccount
      name: prometheus-k8s
      namespace: monitoring
  serviceMonitor:
    enabled: true
    interval: 15s
  prometheusRule:
    enabled: true

protectedNamespaces: ["prod-*"]

affinity:
  podAntiAffinity:
    preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
      - weight: 100
        podAffinityTerm:
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app.kubernetes.io/name: hybernate
              control-plane: controller-manager
          topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname

affinity applies to the doorman too unless doorman.affinity is set; the doorman's replicas are spread across nodes by default.

helm install hybernate oci://ghcr.io/okedeji/charts/hybernate \
  --version 0.2.0-rc.5 \
  -f values-production.yaml \
  -n hybernate-system --create-namespace

docs.title: Labels
docs.text: Label Value Applied To Description hybernate.io/managed "true" Deployments, StatefulSets, Namespaces Opts the workload, or every Deployment and StatefulSet in the namespace, in. Hybernate creates a ManagedWorkload for it from its annotations. "false" on a workload leaves it out of a managed namespace, like hybernate.io/ignore. Any other value doesn't opt in, and is pointed out in an event. See Opting In. hybernate.io/ignore "true" Deployments, StatefulSets Leaves the workload out, even in a managed namespace. A ManagedWorkload you wrote for it reports TargetAvailable=False, reason TargetIgnored, and does nothing; a workload Hybernate had paused is scaled back up first. hybernate.io/protected "true" Namespaces Hybernate never manages anything in the namespace, whatever its workloads' labels, and wakes what it had paused there. kube-* namespaces and Hybernate's own are protected without it. See Protected namespaces. hybernate.io/allow-protected "true" Namespaces Lets Hybernate manage a namespace that's labelled protected, matches protectedNamespaces, or is always protected, such as kube-system or Hybernate's own. The operator's and the doorman's own Deployments are never managed. Set on purpose; Hybernate never sets it. hybernate.io/from-label "true" ManagedWorkloads Set on ManagedWorkloads Hybernate created from the managed label. Hybernate updates and deletes only these; ManagedWorkloads without it are yours. hybernate.io/managed-workload ManagedWorkload name EndpointSlices Set on the EndpointSlices that route a paused workload's Services to the doorman, or to its forwarder, along with endpointslice.kubernetes.io/managed-by: doorman.hybernate.io. A name longer than 63 characters is shortened, with a hash. They're removed when the workload is Running. hybernate.io/operator namespace EndpointSlices, forwarder pods Set on the doorman EndpointSlices an operator writes, and on its forwarders' pods: the namespace of its install. Another install doesn't move them to its own doorman. See More than one install hybernate.io/forwarded "true" EndpointSlices Set on a doorman EndpointSlice that points a Service behind GKE NEGs at the workload's forwarder rather than the doorman app.kubernetes.io/name hybernate-forwarder Deployments, pods Set on each forwarder Deployment the operator runs beside a paused workload behind GKE NEGs, and on its pods. The Deployment also carries hybernate.io/ignore: "true", so a namespace opted in with its label doesn't have Hybernate manage it

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Opt a workload in, or a whole namespace:

kubectl label deployment my-api hybernate.io/managed=true
kubectl label namespace preview-42 hybernate.io/managed=true

Leave one workload in a managed namespace out:

kubectl label deployment my-critical-service hybernate.io/ignore=true

Find the ManagedWorkloads created from labels:

kubectl get managedworkloads -l hybernate.io/from-label=true --all-namespaces

docs.title: Settings Annotations
docs.text:
