Set on an opted-in Deployment or StatefulSet, or on its Namespace to apply to every workload in it. Each setting is the first value that can be read from: the workload's annotation, its namespace's, the Helm defaults (only idle-after, cpu-threshold, dry-run, pause-early and forecast have one), and the built-in default. See Opting In.

Annotation Accepted values Default Description hybernate.io/dry-run exactly "true" or "false" "false" Measure without pausing hybernate.io/idle-after a Go duration of at least 1m, such as "90m" or "2h" 1h How long without activity before pausing hybernate.io/cpu-threshold a whole number, "1" to "100" 10 CPU use, as a percentage of requests, above which the workload counts as active hybernate.io/auto-resume exactly "true" or "false" "false" Wake ahead of forecast demand hybernate.io/pause-early exactly "true" or "false" "false" Pause before idle-after runs out, once idle for 20 minutes, when a confident forecast expects the hours until then to be quiet and a request would wake the workload through the doorman. Sets spec.idlePolicy.pauseEarly. See Pausing Early hybernate.io/forecast exactly "eager", "balanced" or "cautious" "balanced" How soon the forecast acts: at a confidence of 60, 75 or 85. Eager acts sooner and wakes the workload for nothing more often; cautious acts later, for workloads costly to keep awake. Sets spec.prediction.mode; a spec.prediction.confidence set on the ManagedWorkload overrides it. See Forecast setting hybernate.io/depends-on comma-separated kind/name or namespace/kind/name, kind deployment or statefulset none Workloads this one needs. An empty value declares none, so a workload can drop its namespace's. On a namespace, it leaves out the workloads it names, and those they depend on by their own depends-on, which are dependencies rather than dependents. One in another namespace needs that namespace's hybernate.io/dependents-from hybernate.io/wake-on-request exactly "true" or "false" "true" Wake when a request reaches the workload's Service hybernate.io/wake-max-wait a Go duration above zero, at most 1h 2m How long a request is held while the workload wakes hybernate.io/wake-page exactly "true" or "false" "true" Show browsers a waking-up page

A value that can't be read, such as "True", "yes", "soon" or "0", is reported in an InvalidSetting warning event on the workload and skipped: the setting comes from the next place in the order above, never from the default in place of a namespace's value, and the other settings still apply. Two exceptions:

  • dry-run: a value that can't be read turns dry-run on, wherever it is, since a typo in the setting meant to stop pauses must never start them.
  • depends-on: an entry that can't be read is skipped and the rest apply; only a value with no readable entry at all falls through to the namespace's.

docs.title: Activity Annotations
docs.text:
Annotation Value Applied To Description hybernate.io/last-activity RFC 3339 time ManagedWorkloads, Deployments, StatefulSets Activity seen by another tool, such as a developer portal. A time in the future counts as now. A change while the workload is paused wakes it. See Activity annotations hybernate.io/active-until RFC 3339 time ManagedWorkloads, Deployments, StatefulSets Keeps the workload awake until that time, and wakes it if paused hybernate.io/last-request RFC 3339 time ManagedWorkloads Set by the doorman when it holds a request for a paused workload, and, with doorman.admissionPolicy.enabled, by no one else; set last-activity to wake a workload yourself. Wakes it like last-activity, and the clock records the wake as request. See Wake on Request hybernate.io/last-request-from IP address ManagedWorkloads Set by the doorman with last-request, and by no one else, like it: where the request that woke the workload came from, so the operator can learn which workload depends on it

A value that isn't an RFC 3339 time, such as epoch seconds, is ignored: it neither keeps the workload awake nor wakes it, and an InvalidActivityAnnotation warning event on the ManagedWorkload says so, once per value.

docs.title: Other Annotations
docs.text: Annotation Value Applied To Description hybernate.io/pause-requested any value that differs from the last request's, such as the time ManagedWorkloads Asks Hybernate to pause the workload now, as if its idle clock had run out; set by kubectl hybernate pause. Each value is acted on once and recorded in status.lastPauseRequest. An annotation, so a GitOps tool that owns the spec leaves it alone. See Pause Now hybernate.io/pause-overrides-forecast "true" ManagedWorkloads With a pause request, pauses the workload even when a confident forecast expects demand within the hour; without it, such a request is declined, saying when. It applies to the request it comes with, so set or remove it with every request; kubectl hybernate pause --yes sets it. See Pause Now hybernate.io/dependents-from comma-separated namespace names, or "*" for any Namespaces Lets workloads in those namespaces depend on this namespace's workloads. A dependency in another namespace, declared or learned, is only held awake, woken and waited for when its namespace lists the dependent's; otherwise the dependent reports DependencyNotAllowed=True. See Across namespaces hybernate.io/paused-from JSON, set by Hybernate Deployments, StatefulSets Written by Hybernate on a workload it pauses, before scaling it to zero, and removed when it's handed back: a copy of what the pause changed (the replicas, and the KEDA ScaledObject with its own paused-replicas value). If the ManagedWorkload's status is lost while the workload is paused, such as to a backup restored without status, Hybernate takes the pause up again from it, so the workload still wakes to the replicas it had. Don't set or edit it hybernate.io/ignore-dependencies comma-separated namespace/name, or a name in the workload's own namespace Deployments, StatefulSets, ManagedWorkloads Dependencies Hybernate shouldn't learn for this workload. See Learned dependencies hybernate.io/operator namespace, set by Hybernate ManagedWorkloads Written by the operator with its hybernate.io/cleanup finalizer: the namespace of the install that took the ManagedWorkload on. Another install leaves it alone, and doesn't count it in its uninstall and upgrade guards. See More than one install hybernate.io/doorman-ignore-ports comma-separated port names or numbers Services Ports the doorman never routes, such as a metrics port something else scrapes. They fail while the workload is paused. See Wake on Request

docs.title: Finalizers
docs.text:
Finalizer Applied To Description hybernate.io/cleanup ManagedWorkloads Added automatically by the operator. Ensures a paused workload is scaled back up, and its Services stop routing to the doorman, before the ManagedWorkload can be deleted. The operator removes it once that's done.

Note

Do not remove the hybernate.io/cleanup finalizer by hand. A ManagedWorkload deleted without it leaves a paused workload at zero replicas, and its KEDA ScaledObject held there, until a ManagedWorkload for the workload is created again and takes the pause up from its hybernate.io/paused-from annotation.

docs.title: Metrics Reference
docs.text: All metrics are prefixed with hybernate_ and registered with the controller-runtime metrics registry. They are served on the metrics endpoint, which the chart and the Kustomize manifests serve on :8443 over HTTPS; a scraper needs a token allowed to get /metrics (see Monitoring). The operator drops a workload's series when its ManagedWorkload is deleted; the doorman drops its hybernate_doorman_wakes_total series then too, on its next sync of routes, not when the workload merely stops being routed.

docs.title: Tier 1: Cluster Health
docs.text:
These metrics show whether the operator is healthy and what phase each workload is in.

Metric Type Labels Description hybernate_build_info Gauge version Always 1, labelled with the release the pod runs, such as v0.2.0. Served by the doorman too hybernate_workload_phase Gauge namespace, workload, phase 1 for each workload's current lifecycle phase hybernate_reconcile_errors_total Counter controller Reconciles that returned an error, by controller: managedworkload, or optin for the controller that creates ManagedWorkloads from the hybernate.io/managed label hybernate_lifecycle_transitions_total Counter from, to Phase transitions hybernate_lifecycle_action_duration_seconds Histogram action Duration of lifecycle actions (pause, resume)

docs.title: Tier 2: Operational Insight
docs.text:
These metrics help you understand what the operator is doing and why.

Metric Type Labels Description hybernate_prediction_confidence_percent Gauge season, namespace, workload Forecast confidence, 1 − WAPE, as a percentage, for season daily or weekly hybernate_prediction_phase Gauge namespace, workload Engine phase (0-4) hybernate_prediction_data_points Gauge namespace, workload Data points collected hybernate_prediction_anomalies_total Counter namespace, workload Anomalies detected hybernate_idle_detections_total Counter namespace, workload Times each workload's idle clock ran out hybernate_external_scale_ups_total Counter by Paused workloads scaled up outside Hybernate, by the GitOps tool that did it (argo-cd, flux, fleet, kapp, kluctl), or other

docs.title: Tier 3: Debugging
docs.text:
These metrics help troubleshoot specific workload behavior.

Metric Type Labels Description hybernate_idle_seconds Gauge namespace, workload Seconds since the workload's last activity. It keeps growing while the workload is paused, updated each time Hybernate checks it: every minute awake, every few minutes paused hybernate_prediction_regime_changes_total Counter namespace, workload Regime changes detected hybernate_dryrun_actions_total Counter action Actions that would have been taken in dry-run; action is idle_pause, early_pause for one the forecast brought forward (pauseEarly), or requested_pause for a pause asked for with kubectl hybernate pause hybernate_target_unavailable_total Counter namespace, workload Target workload not found

docs.title: Savings
docs.text:
Each node pool's figures from the operator's measure of what pausing saved, every 5 minutes, by the leader. pool is the first of a node's karpenter.sh/nodepool, cloud.google.com/gke-nodepool, eks.amazonaws.com/nodegroup and kubernetes.azure.com/agentpool labels, "" for nodes with none, and * for paused replicas whose pool wasn't recorded, which are set against what every pool has left over. There's a series for each pool with Ready nodes or paused replicas, so they number as the cluster's pools do. An operator limited by watchNamespaces can't measure them, and doesn't export them.

Metric Type Labels Description hybernate_capacity_paused_cpu_cores Gauge pool vCPUs the replicas Hybernate holds paused requested, by the pool they ran in hybernate_capacity_paused_memory_bytes Gauge pool Memory the replicas Hybernate holds paused requested hybernate_capacity_spare_cpu_cores Gauge pool Allocatable vCPUs on the pool's schedulable, Ready nodes that no bound, unfinished pod requests hybernate_capacity_spare_memory_bytes Gauge pool Allocatable memory on those nodes that no pod requests hybernate_savings_realised_dollars_per_hour Gauge pool What the paused requests the spare capacity can't hold would cost an hour at the pool's nodes' list rates, averaged over them (the defaults for nodes with no list price): what pausing takes off the bill each hour, at least hybernate_node_autoscaler Gauge kind 1 for each node autoscaler the operator found (Karpenter, Cluster Autoscaler, EKS Auto Mode, GKE Autopilot), or for none when it read everywhere it looks and found none, or unknown when it wasn't allowed to look, as in a watchNamespaces install. Looked at every 10 minutes. With none, what pausing frees doesn't come off the bill; see the Cluster Autoscaler Guide

docs.title: Doorman
docs.text:
Served by the doorman pods, on the same port and path as the operator's metrics.

Metric Type Labels Description hybernate_doorman_wakes_total Counter namespace, workload, result Connections the doorman accepted for a paused workload, by result (below) hybernate_doorman_wait_seconds Histogram result How long the doorman held a connection before passing it through or closing it hybernate_doorman_held_connections Gauge Connections held right now, waiting for their workload to wake hybernate_doorman_proxied_connections Gauge Connections passed to a woken workload and still being carried hybernate_doorman_port_conflicts Gauge Doorman ports claimed by more than one route, which the doorman refuses to serve. Should be 0 hybernate_doorman_listen_failures Gauge Routed doorman ports this pod can't listen on, which refuse every connection. Should be 0; a pod that can't listen on one for 30 seconds reports itself not Ready result Meaning success Passed to a Ready pod page A browser was shown the waking-up page timeout No pod was Ready within wake.maxWait error The woken pods couldn't be reached, or the wake couldn't be recorded, by wake.maxWait canceled The caller left, or the doorman shut down, while the connection was held ignored A health check or scraper, recognised by its User-Agent and answered 503, or Google's load balancer health check, answered 200 (see Health checks the doorman can't recognise); a request for a hidden file such as /.env, answered 404; or a connection that closed without sending anything, as each forwarder pod's check that it reaches the doorman does every 5 seconds limited Refused by a cap on held connections or a wake rate limit; see Limits refused The workload's route is draining and none of its pods is Ready

docs.title: Prediction Phase Values
docs.text:
The hybernate_prediction_phase gauge uses numeric values:

Value Phase 0 Observing 1 DailySuggesting 2 DailyActive 3 WeeklySuggesting 4 FullyActive

docs.title: Useful PromQL Queries
docs.text:
# Workloads with low prediction confidence
hybernate_prediction_confidence_percent{season="daily"} < 70

# Workloads that will pause within 10 minutes (with the default 1h idleAfter)
hybernate_idle_seconds > 3000 and on (namespace, workload) hybernate_workload_phase{phase="Running"} == 1

# How long a request to a paused workload waits for it to wake (p95)
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(hybernate_doorman_wait_seconds_bucket{result="success"}[1h])))

# What pausing takes off the bill an hour, across the cluster
sum(hybernate_savings_realised_dollars_per_hour)

# Pools where paused CPU still fits in spare capacity: freed, but not saved
(hybernate_capacity_paused_cpu_cores > 0) <= on (pool) hybernate_capacity_spare_cpu_cores

docs.title: Security
docs.text: What a security review of Hybernate needs: what it can do in a cluster, what it talks to, and how to check that what you install is what was released.

docs.title: What it can do
docs.text:
• It never deletes your resources. Its one action is to scale a Deployment or StatefulSet to zero, through the scale subresource, and back. The only other change it makes to a workload is its own hybernate.io/paused-from annotation while the workload is paused, though its role may patch workloads, and the only things it deletes are its own ManagedWorkloads and EndpointSlices, and with the optional forwarder below, its own forwarder Deployments.
  • It never reads Secrets.
  • It can write any EndpointSlice in the namespaces it works in. It only ever creates, changes and deletes its own, labelled endpointslice.kubernetes.io/managed-by: doorman.hybernate.io, and never overwrites one without that label, but RBAC can't limit a role by label, so its ServiceAccount is allowed the rest too. Whoever holds its token could redirect any Service there.
  • The optional GKE NEG forwarder needs more. With doorman.negForwarder.enabled (off by default), the operator may also create and delete Deployments in the namespaces it works in, to run a forwarder beside each paused workload behind GKE container-native load balancing. RBAC can't limit that to its own, so whoever holds its token could create Deployments there, as well as patch them, which it can already. It only ever deletes a Deployment of the forwarder's name that its ManagedWorkload owns. The forwarders run as their namespace's default ServiceAccount without its token, with no access to the API server, at the Pod Security Standards' restricted level.
  • It can be confined to namespaces. With watchNamespaces, the operator and doorman get a Role in each of those namespaces instead of a ClusterRole, so Kubernetes itself refuses them anything elsewhere. The operator keeps one ClusterRole, read-only, on Namespaces, Nodes and Karpenter NodePools, and a Role in its own namespace to read the doorman's EndpointSlices. With secure metrics (the default), both also keep a ClusterRoleBinding to system:auth-delegator, which only lets them check the tokens of whoever scrapes their metrics.
  • It can be kept out of namespaces. A namespace labelled hybernate.io/protected=true, or matching protectedNamespaces, is never managed; see Protected namespaces.
  • A namespace's workloads are only kept awake for another namespace that it allows. A dependency in another namespace, declared in dependsOn or learned, is held awake, woken and waited for only when its namespace's hybernate.io/dependents-from annotation lists the dependent's namespace. Otherwise it's ignored and reported as DependencyNotAllowed with the same message whether it exists or not, so a dependency can't probe another namespace. A dependency learned from a request that woke a workload is only learned from a hybernate.io/last-request-from the doorman wrote, which the chart's <fullname>-request-stamps admission policy lets no one else set, and which the operator also checks by the field manager the API server records, and only for a sender in a namespace the woken workload's namespace allows. See Across namespaces.
  • It doesn't fight people or tools. A paused workload scaled up by anything else wakes; a GitOps tool undoing a pause is reported, not fought; see GitOps tools.

Everything it reads, writes, and sends is listed in Data and Access, and the exact RBAC in Helm values.

docs.title: What it talks to
docs.text:
From To Why Operator, doorman The Kubernetes API server Everything it does Operator Prometheus, at prometheus.url Only with prometheus.url set: the Prometheus activity queries workloads configure, and, once for each new ManagedWorkload, one range query for up to four weeks of its containers' CPU, to start its forecast from Any client of a paused workload's Service: a pod, an ingress controller, or a load balancer through a NodePort Doorman The doorman holds the connection, wakes the workload, and forwards it Doorman The woken workload's pods, in any routed namespace, on their Service ports Passing the held connection through Google's load balancers, and any other client of a paused workload's Service behind GKE NEGs Forwarder, in the workload's namespace, with doorman.negForwarder.enabled The forwarder stands in for the workload's pods Forwarder Doorman, on its routing ports Passing connections on, untouched Prometheus Operator and doorman metrics Only with a token allowed to get /metrics, unless metrics.secure is off

Nothing leaves the cluster: no telemetry, no usage reporting, no update checks. The images run as a non-root user on a distroless base, with a read-only root filesystem. So do the chart's guards, hook Jobs that run only during helm uninstall, helm upgrade and helm rollback, from the operator's own image, each with a ServiceAccount that may only list ManagedWorkloads.

docs.title: The doorman is a way in to paused workloads
docs.text:
Any client that can reach a doorman pod can reach every routed, paused workload, in any namespace, on its Service ports, and a workload's own NetworkPolicy sees the doorman, not the client, as the source. The doorman listens on all of its pod's interfaces: binding to the pod IP would only shut out containers in its own pod, so a NetworkPolicy on the doorman is the control that matters. The chart's NetworkPolicy (networkPolicy.enabled, off by default) leaves the doorman's routing ports open to every source unless you restrict them. On any cluster where untrusted pods share the network, enable networkPolicy and set doorman.networkPolicy.ingressFrom. Where the default is too wide:

  • Admit only the callers your paused workloads really have, such as your ingress controller's namespace and the namespaces whose apps call paused services, with doorman.networkPolicy.ingressFrom. See Wake on Request.
  • Give them an egress NetworkPolicy allowing only your pod CIDRs and the API server: set doorman.networkPolicy.egress (off by default; see Helm values). The doorman only dials Pod-backed IP endpoints of EndpointSlices the EndpointSlice controller manages, and refuses loopback, link-local, and cloud metadata addresses (AWS's fd00:ec2::254 and Alibaba Cloud's 100.100.100.200 included). Anyone who can write EndpointSlices in a namespace can forge those labels, so the doorman also reads the pod each endpoint names and dials the address only if that pod is in the Service's namespace and has it: a forged slice can send it only to that namespace's own pods, never past a NetworkPolicy into another namespace. The operator checks the same way before it leaves a Service to pods it says are already serving it, so a forged slice can't keep a paused workload's Service from waking it either. The policy enforces the same bounds in the network.
  • With doorman.negForwarder.enabled, the chart's policy also admits the forwarders, from any namespace, by their labels: app.kubernetes.io/name: hybernate-forwarder, and hybernate.io/operator naming Hybernate's namespace. Anyone who can create pods can give them those labels, and so reach the doorman's routing ports as a caller in ingressFrom can. A forwarder passes on only its own workload's ports, but the doorman can't tell its connections from those of a pod that only claims to be one.
  • Its rate limits (see Limits) slow a port scan through the doorman; they don't stop one. One workload can hold at most 256 of a doorman pod's 2048 places, so a workload that never becomes Ready can't stop other workloads' requests from being held.

The doorman's ServiceAccount can patch ManagedWorkloads, to set hybernate.io/last-request and hybernate.io/last-request-from, the caller's IP address. The chart's <fullname>-doorman ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (doorman.admissionPolicy.enabled, on by default) holds it to those two annotations: the API server refuses a patch from it that changes a ManagedWorkload's spec, labels, finalizers, owners or any other annotation. The Kustomize manifests include it too, taking the doorman's ServiceAccount as its parameter, so it follows the namespace and namePrefix set in config/default or in an overlay on top of it.

The operator learns which workload depends on which from hybernate.io/last-request-from, so the doorman must be the only one who sets it. With the same doorman.admissionPolicy.enabled, the chart's <fullname>-request-stamps ValidatingAdmissionPolicy refuses anyone but the doorman's ServiceAccount, the operator and cluster admins included, a create or change that sets hybernate.io/last-request or hybernate.io/last-request-from on a ManagedWorkload; removing one is allowed. To wake a workload, set hybernate.io/last-activity, as kubectl hybernate wake does. With watchNamespaces, it applies in those namespaces only. Without it, the operator still ignores an address that wasn't written under Hybernate's field manager, but anyone who can patch a ManagedWorkload can write under that name with --field-manager=hybernate. The Kustomize manifests include it too, named hybernate-request-stamps, taking the doorman's ServiceAccount as its parameter like the doorman's policy, so it follows any namespace and namePrefix. If that ServiceAccount is deleted, both of the Kustomize manifests' policies let every write through, leaving stamps to the operator's field-manager check: the API server looks a policy's parameter up before anything else, so refusing without it would refuse every write to every ManagedWorkload, the operator's too.

docs.title: Verifying a release
docs.text:
Every release is built by the release workflow from a tag, and signed keylessly with Sigstore: the signature is bound to that workflow and tag, so there's no key to steal. Each command below fails unless the artifact came from that workflow. The signatures are made with cosign 3, so verify them with cosign 3 or later.

The image, its signature, an SBOM for each platform, and build provenance:

IMAGE=ghcr.io/okedeji/hybernate:v0.2.0-rc.5
cosign verify $IMAGE \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github.com/okedeji/hybernate/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/v' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
cosign verify-attestation $IMAGE --type spdxjson \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github.com/okedeji/hybernate/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/v' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
gh attestation verify oci://$IMAGE --repo okedeji/hybernate

The Helm chart:

cosign verify ghcr.io/okedeji/charts/hybernate:0.2.0-rc.5 \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github.com/okedeji/hybernate/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/v' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com

The plugin, install.yaml, and the other release files, through their signed checksums:

cosign verify-blob checksums.txt --bundle checksums.txt.sigstore.json \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github.com/okedeji/hybernate/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/v' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
sha256sum --check --ignore-missing checksums.txt
gh attestation verify kubectl-hybernate-linux-amd64.tar.gz --repo okedeji/hybernate

docs.title: Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
• Every pull request runs govulncheck on the Go code, which fails on any known vulnerability the code can reach, and Trivy on the built image, which fails on critical and high vulnerabilities that have a fix. A vulnerability with no fix yet is reported, not blocking.
  • Every release runs both again before anything is published, and attaches Trivy's full report for each platform to the GitHub release as vulnerabilities-linux-amd64.txt and vulnerabilities-linux-arm64.txt, alongside the SBOMs, sbom-linux-amd64.spdx.json and sbom-linux-arm64.spdx.json.
  • Every day, both run against main, and Trivy against the released image, ghcr.io/okedeji/hybernate:latest, for both platforms, so a vulnerability disclosed after a release is reported then rather than at the next pull request.
  • Dependencies (Go modules, GitHub Actions, base images) are kept current by Dependabot, weekly. Every Action is pinned to a commit, and the base images to a digest.

To report a vulnerability, see SECURITY.md: privately, through a GitHub security advisory.
